Iqunix Prepares EV63 EDG Edition Keyboard
Keyboard maker Iqunix has confirmed that the company is preparing a special EV63 EDG Edition to celebrate one of the most successful esports teams focused on Valorant. The EDG team features a signature black and gold aesthetic, which Iqunix claims underwent five rounds of joint fine-tuning for the EV63 EDG Edition color accents before the final release. This time, the company is introducing Timing Synchronization System (TSS) technology, which will align the keyboard's input processing with the PC's USB polling cycle for more consistent responses, lower latency, and more predictable input. To test this, Iqunix used its HyperCore v3.1 firmware to measure actuation latency and release latency.
According to internal testing, actuation latency is between 0.29-0.30 ms, while release latency hovers in an even tighter range of only 0.26-0.27 ms. In addition to low latency, the EV63 also offers traditional hardware enhancements like 8,000 Hz polling, 16,000 Hz scanning, and 0.01 mm Rapid Trigger Smart Switch Adaptation. Finally, the company leaves room for experimentation with different switches. Smart Switch Adaptation automatically recognizes 99% of mainstream Hall Effect switches, simplifying compatibility and making switch replacement more convenient. Combined with Magnetic X Ultra switches, designed for stronger magnetic flux and improved signal stability, the EV63 is built to deliver responsive input with dependable control.The Iqunix EV63 EDG Edition keyboard will join the existing lineup as the sixth option among the company's EV63 keyboards. We've already seen colorways like EV63 Violet, EV63 Silver Knight, EV63 Dark Knight, EV63 Ghost in the Shell Core, and EV63 Ghost in the Shell Cyber Blue. The MSRP of the EDG Edition keyboard is currently unknown, but we can expect the pricing to be anywhere from $169 to $249, similar to the prices of most EV63 keyboards.

articles.title: Europe could one day have a homegrown Starlink alternative — and four major carriers have teamed up to help develop it
articles.text:
Europe’s major mobile operators are teaming up to develop a Starlink competitor
Strengthening Europe’s sovereignty
- Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica, and Vodafone have signed a letter of intent to explore development of a European constellation
- This could work as an alternative to Starlink, and allow networks to plug coverage gaps with satellites
- However, they still need a satellite partner to deliver any such plan
Starlink has major mobile ambitions, seemingly seeing itself as a true rival to conventional carriers like Verizon and T-Mobile in the US. But over in Europe, mobile operators might look to offer a Starlink alternative.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica, and Vodafone have all signed a letter of intent to explore “a potential joint bid for the future allocation of spectrum for Mobile Satellite Services (MSS) in Europe.”
So, in other words, they might work together to allocate spectrum to a satellite-based connectivity service aimed at increasing their coverage in areas where masts and other ground-based infrastructure don’t currently reach.
Such a service would put them in direct competition with Starlink, which has partnered with the likes of T-Mobile in the US and O2 in the UK to plug coverage gaps in their networks, and which has ambitions to launch a standalone carrier.
A long way off
But it’s still very early days for this European initiative. The letter of intent is simply to explore a potential bid — wording which suggests nothing is very set in stone. And even if these carriers do jointly allocate this spectrum, they still need to “establish key ground network infrastructure” to go along with it.
And most importantly of all, they need access to a satellite constellation, and while part of the intent here is to “support the development of a European constellation,” they don’t actually plan to build a constellation themselves; rather, they’re looking for a satellite partner.
So don’t expect to see a European Starlink alternative anytime soon, but it’s sounding like there might be one at some point in the future — and this is a move that would make sense, given Europe’s ongoing attempt to lessen its reliance on US services.

articles.title: A Chinese hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites — Deere and SharkNinja among websites hit by open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform demo
articles.text:
A Chinese hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites — Deere and SharkNinja among websites hit by open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform demo
Why break into websites yourself when you can task AI bots to do it for you?
A Chinese-speaking hacker has been observed using artificial intelligence (AI) agents to probe and then gain unauthorized access to more than 100 websites belonging to some extremely well-known companies. From Deere, the farming equipment manufacturer, to SharkNinja, the company behind beloved kitchen appliances, the agents were able to leverage exposed instances of Carin, an open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform that has proven popular among hackers, a Reuters report explains.
This is just the latest example of hackers turning to AI agents in an attempt to level up their attacks on unsuspecting companies and services. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge, spotted the hacker's antics when observing Carin instances that had been inadvertently exposed.
Fagerland was able to watch multiple hackers go about their business, but the Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific, the report says. They targeted businesses based in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japanese e-commerce sites. Notably, the hacker didn't get into detail when commanding their legion of AI agents. Fewer than 100 Chinese characters were used, yet the agents had attempted ot break into more than 1,200 different websites as of the week ending October 18, 2026.
These agents weren't simply throwing everything at a wall and hoping it stuck, either. Security researcher Fagerland was "impressed" by some of the tactics that had been used. In one case, the AI agents scoured digital records to find infrastructure associated with their target, located a public-facing control panel, identified a weakness, and then leveraged it to force the execution of malicious commands, the Reuters report detailed. "It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland told Reuters. "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Vitally, the approach of using AI agents in this way means that they can be given instructions and then left to their own devices. With no supervision required, those commanding the agents are free to turn their attention elsewhere. While SharkNinja told Reuters that the attack only impacted a site used for product support information, the rest of the AI-aided hackers had more luck. One of the hackers monitored by Gargerland stole credit card data, while another tried to steal from a cryptocurrency exchange — although it isn't clear whether they were successful.

articles.title: Whatsapp testet einen In-App-Browser für iOS-Geräte: Was dank der neuen Funktion bald möglich ist
articles.text:
Warum Whatsapp einen eigenen In-App-Browser bekommen soll
Whatsapp testet derzeit einen In-App-Browser für Chats auf iOS-Geräten. Für bestimmte Unternehmenslinks war das schon seit Längerem möglich. Wie WABetainfo berichtet, soll diese Funktion jetzt aber auch auf andere Links ausgeweitet werden. Nutzer:innen des Messengers können diese dann direkt aus der Chat-Oberfläche heraus öffnen.
Whatsapp weitet In-App-Browser deutlich aus
Schon im vergangenen Jahr führte Whatsapp mit dem Beta-Update 25.14.10.72 eine Funktion ein, mit der Nutzer:innen Unternehmenslinks öffnen konnten, ohne zu Safari wechseln zu müssen. Der Messenger beschränkte die Funktion allerdings auf Links, die bestimmte technische Anforderungen erfüllten. Eine Voraussetzung war, dass die Website HTTPS verwendet, um eine sichere Verbindung zu gewährleisten. Nutzer:innen, die lieber ihren Standardbrowser nutzen wollen, können ganz einfach über das Drei-Punkte-Menü wechseln.
Whatsapp weitet die Funktion jetzt deutlich aus. Anstatt sie auf Unternehmenslinks zu beschränken, entwickelt der Messenger einen eigenen In-App-Browser, der mit jedem im Chat geteilten Link kompatibel ist. WABetainfo hat die Neuerung in der Beta-Version 26.41.10.72 für iOS entdeckt, die auf Testflight verfügbar ist. Demnach aktivieren Nutzer:innen den In-App-Browser über die App-Einstellungen, wo Whatsapp eine entsprechende Option hinzugefügt hat. Anschließend lässt sich jeder Link direkt im Chat-Bildschirm öffnen.
So soll der neue In-App-Browser funktionieren
Wenn Nutzer:innen die Option zum ersten Mal aktivieren, zeigt Whatsapp am unteren Bildschirmrand ein Popup-Fenster an, das die Funktionsweise erklärt. Dazu gehört auch, dass sie jeden Link direkt in Whatsapp statt im Standardbrowser öffnen können. Das bedeutet, dass sie nicht mehr zu Safari, Chrome oder einem anderen auf ihrem Gerät installierten Browser wechseln müssen. Die Browsersitzung ist vom Chat getrennt, sodass Nutzer:innen im Internet surfen können, ohne die Unterhaltung zu beeinträchtigen. Wer den In-App-Browser nicht verwenden möchte, kann jederzeit zum Standardbrowser zurückkehren.
Wie WABetainfo berichtet, umfasst der Bildschirm mit den Browsereinstellungen auch einen Abschnitt zur Datenverwaltung. Hier können Nutzer:innen Cookies und den Cache der Websites löschen, die sie in Whatsapp besucht haben. So behalten sie die Kontrolle über die Daten, die der In-App-Browser auf ihrem Gerät speichert. Genau wie Safari von Apple speichert der Messenger die Browsing-Daten lokal auf dem Gerät. So lässt sich von Dritten nicht einsehen, welche Links in der Unterhaltung geteilt und welche geöffnet werden.
Neue Funktion erhöht Nutzungsfreundlichkeit
Whatsapp ist in Deutschland sehr beliebt und für viele der Standard-Messenger, um mit Familie oder Freund:innen in Kontakt zu bleiben. Mehr als 85 Prozent der über 16-Jährigen nutzen die App mindestens einmal monatlich. Das hat eine Analyse von Meltwater und We Are Social ergeben. Der Funktionsumfang der App erweitert sich dabei ständig, um die Nutzung noch praktischer zu gestalten. So testet Whatsapp derzeit beispielsweise eine Funktion für die Nachrichtenplanung.
Auch der neue In-App-Browser könnte dazu beitragen, die Nutzungsfreundlichkeit des Messengers weiter zu verbessern. Für iOS-Geräte befindet sich die Funktion derzeit noch in der Entwicklung. Mit einem Update wird Whatsapp sie zunächst einigen Beta-Tester:innen zugänglich machen. Wann die Funktion für alle Nutzer:innen mit iOS‑Geräten verfügbar sein wird, steht aktuell noch nicht fest.

articles.title: Pour partir en vacances tranquille, ce duo de caméras connectées passe sous les 100€ sur Amazon
articles.text:
Amazon assure la sécurité de votre intérieur avec ce pack réunissant deux eufyCam C35 et le HomeBase Mini. En ce moment, ce jeu d'accessoires est vendu avec une réduction de 20 euros.
Qui dit vacances de la Toussaint dit Halloween. Pour partir l'esprit tranquille et éviter de vivre dans la crainte de laisser son appartement sans surveillance, Amazon retire 20 % au prix de ces deux caméras connectées de la marque eufy accompagnée d'un HomeBase Mini pour enregistrer les vidéos. L'occasion d'offrir une couverture complète de votre extérieur de jour comme de nuit.
Sur Amazon, le pack avec deux eufyCam C35 passe de 109 euros à 89,34 euros
Pourquoi choisir l'eufyCam C35 ?
- Facile à installer : Les caméras se fixent sur un support magnétique et ne demandent pas de tournevis ou de perceuse. Elles se rechargent à l'énergie solaire et ne demanderont pas de renouveler une pile.
- Une vision nocturne : Pour reconnaître les potentiels voleurs même la nuit, la caméra est dotée d'une vision nocturne ainsi que d'un système de dissuasion proactif.
- Pour sa formule sans abonnement : En plus de la réduction, eufy propose des caméras qui ne nécessitent pas d'abonnement supplémentaire. Seule une carte microSD sera nécessaire pour obtenir davantage d'espace de stockage
Une caméra dédiée à l'extérieur
S'il est possible d'installer une des deux eufyCam 35 en intérieur, elles exploiteront leur plein potentiel à l'extérieur. Avec deux caméras, vous pourrez en installer une à côté de votre porte d'entrée tandis que la seconde se chargera de surveiller votre jardin.
Côté installation, les caméras se fixent sur un support magnétique, ce qui ne demande pas de perceuse tandis qu'aucun raccordement électrique ne sera nécessaire puisqu'elle fonctionne sur une batterie. Il ne faudra que 2h30 d'ensoleillement pour recharger pleinement les appareils.
En ce qui concerne l'image, les caméras enregistrent en Full HD et disposent d'une vision nocturne pour assurer une surveillance même la nuit. Justement, si une personne malintentionnée surgit chez vous lorsqu'il fait nuit, un système de dissuasion proactif s'active avec un flash lumineux et un sirène pour essayer de le faire fuir. Également, l'IA pourra le tracer jusqu'au moment où il quitte le champ de vision de la caméra. L'intelligence artificielle est aussi capable de reconnaître les visages, les animaux et les objets comme votre voiture.
Pas d'abonnement requis
Ce pack ne se limite pas aux eufyCam C35 puisqu'il est complété par le HomeBase Mini. Ce boîtier permet de relier dix appareils simultanément ou d'enregistrer des vidéos en local. Le stockage interne est mesuré à 8 Go, mais il peut atteindre 1 To si vous glissez une carte microSD.
Enfin, l'appareil est compatible avec les assistants vocaux pour avoir un rapide coup d'œil sur ce qui se passe devant chez vous. Évidemment, une application existe pour suivre l'activité devant votre porte à tout moment.
✅ Les points forts
- Une installation magnétique qui ne demande pas de coups de perceuse
- La recharge solaire
- Un système de dissuasion proactive
❌ Les limites
- Une mémoire interne limitée, l'installation d'une carte microSD sera obligatoire
- La reconnaissance faciale de l'IA peut présenter quelques défauts
Le pack d'eufyCam C35 est affiché à 89,34 euros au lieu de 109 euros sur Amazon
Ce pack d'eufyCam C35 conviendra à ceux qui possèdent une grande maison puisque les deux caméras peuvent couvrir votre porte d'entrée et votre jardin. Si vous voulez obtenir davantage de caméras, Amazon en propose quatre à prix réduit affiché à 160,55 euros.
Néanmoins, avec cette offre, une caméra vous reviendra à 32 euros/pièce contre 30 euros/pièce pour le duo présenté dans cette offre.

articles.title: Disrupt Africa, Touch Inspiration launch accelerator to help non-technical founders build and launch apps - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Disrupt Africa has partnered with Kenya-based digital product and technology company Touch Inspiration to launch Disrupt Launchpad, an app development accelerator that helps non-technical founders turn their ideas into working applications and bring them to market.
Founded in 2014, Disrupt Africa is the leading news platform dedicated to the African tech startup ecosystem, and a producer of research publications and podcasts.
Touch Inspiration was founded in 2017 and helps entrepreneurs and businesses turn their ideas into working digital products. The company specialises in developing web and mobile applications, AI-powered solutions and business platforms, taking products from defined requirements through development and launch.
The two organisations have joined forces to launch Disrupt Launchpad, a programme designed for entrepreneurs who have a clear app idea but lack the technical skills, team or resources to bring it to life. Through Touch Inspiration, founders can get their apps professionally built and launched at startup-friendly rates, while Disrupt Africa helps put those products in front of a wider audience of potential users, customers and investors.
“We meet so many people who are inspired to create something, but don’t know how to bring it to life. What makes this partnership with Disrupt Africa so exciting is that we get to help those people build their apps and, just as importantly, get them in front of the people who will actually use them. It’s one thing to have a great idea, but seeing it come to life and reach the market is where the real value is realised,” said Robert M., founder of Touch Inspiration.
“The whole point of Disrupt Africa has always been to make entrepreneurship accessible to everyone, and with this partnership with Robert M. and the amazing team at Touch Inspiration we’re going right in at the start. Funding is important, networking is key, but being able to build your great idea in the first place is absolutely essential,” said Tom Jackson, co-founder of Disrupt Africa. “This programme will help you build, and launch, and put you in a strong position to turn it into a success.”
Aspiring entrepreneurs and existing startups with clear app ideas are invited to apply through Disrupt Launchpad. The programme offers startup-friendly development rates, while selected ventures may even qualify for an equity-based partnership, reducing the upfront cost of getting their applications built.

articles.title: How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
articles.text:
How Operation Sindoor reshaped India's private defence tech industry
From faster procurement to direct engagement with the armed forces, Operation Sindoor has opened new opportunities for private defence companies developing critical military technologies.
Following Operation Sindoor, India's private defence technology sector is seeing a shift in how the armed forces engage with domestic manufacturers. The transformation is marked by faster procurement, greater private-sector participation, and renewed emphasis on developing critical military technologies domestically, according to industry executives.
At TechSparks 2026, Ankit Kumar, Co-founder and Chief Business Officer of Tonbo Imaging; Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems; and Radhika P, Co-founder of Pinaka Aerospace; discussed how Indian private companies contributed to recent military operations and what the country must prioritise to prepare for the battlefield of 2035.
In a panel discussion titled 'War Room 2035: What technologies must India build for the battlefield' moderated by Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, the founders pointed to growing opportunities for indigenous companies in night-vision systems, electronic warfare, smart munitions, and autonomous defence platforms.
Operation Sindoor and the private sector's growing role
Priyanka Singhal, Founder and CEO of Ammunic Systems, a defence R&D firm specialising in electronic fuzes and munition technologies, described Operation Sindoor as a turning point for the industry. “The operation was an eye opener,” she said, adding that it had exposed the limitations of traditional defence procurement cycles.
Singhal said Ammunic supplied loitering munitions and gravity-drop bombs during Operation Sindoor, working with drone platform partners to integrate its weapons into systems used in the operation. According to her, the armed forces have begun moving away from an excessive focus on procedural compliance towards deploying equipment that meets immediate battlefield requirements. Initiatives such as iDEX and emergency procurement mechanisms have helped accelerate the process, she said.
Radhika P of Pinaka Aerospace echoed this assessment. Previously, private defence companies often worked through defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs), the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and other established channels. Following Operation Sindoor, she said, the armed forces had increasingly engaged directly with private companies, particularly in electronic warfare, avionics, and sensor technologies.
Radhika said Pinaka had contributed to the indigenisation of missile systems that were deployed during the operation. She argued that the effectiveness of military equipment increasingly depends on its payloads, including sensors and electronic warfare systems, rather than the platform alone.
“If there is an electronic countermeasure system, it can neutralise a platform which is probably 10 times more expensive,” she said, underscoring the strategic importance of developing indigenous payload technologies.
Kumar of Tonbo Imaging, which specialises in electro-optical and infrared technologies, said the shift towards indigenous defence procurement had begun even before Operation Sindoor, particularly following developments along India's eastern border. That had encouraged the armed forces to reduce their dependence on technologies sourced from countries sharing land borders with India.
Tonbo, which has spent nearly two decades developing indigenous imaging systems, was positioned to benefit from that shift, Kumar said. Its night-vision technologies have been deployed across several Indian military operations, including Operation Sindoor, when air-defence systems used the company's capabilities, he added.
Kumar said close engagement with the armed forces, including product trials and feedback from users, had helped Tonbo develop its technologies. “We've learned things the hard way. We've learned things on the ground. We've learned things with the customers,” he said.
What India must build by 2035
Looking towards 2035, Kumar said defence systems would increasingly move towards autonomy, reducing the need for direct human involvement in certain operations. He pointed to the potential use of autonomous systems in air combat and on the ground, including the possibility of humanoid robots supporting border operations.
As military platforms become more autonomous, sensors and intelligence will become critical to their ability to detect threats, interpret their surroundings and respond without constant human intervention.
“For autonomy, sensors, intelligence, both are very critical, very important,” Kumar said.
He argued that India had strengths in both areas, particularly in developing intelligence capabilities that can operate directly on military platforms. Such technologies, he said, could improve operational efficiency and reduce dependence on human operators, but they needed to be developed as sovereign capabilities rather than sourced from overseas suppliers.
“Intelligence, connectivity, sensing, these will be the mainstay of how the wars will be fought tomorrow,” he said.
For Radhika, a key battlefield priority is control over the electromagnetic spectrum, which underpins radar, communications, electronic warfare, and several other military capabilities. She argued that future military advantage would increasingly depend on how effectively forces detect, interpret and disrupt electromagnetic signals.
That also makes ownership of the underlying technology critical. Developing or assembling defence platforms in India is not sufficient if the software, electronics architecture and intellectual property remain controlled by foreign suppliers.
“It is very important to have good control on the source code, the board design, and things like that,” Radhika said.
She also emphasised that technology transfer should strengthen India's ability to develop and integrate systems independently, rather than create continued dependence on overseas suppliers. Control over intellectual property and systems integration would be especially important in reducing the risks associated with foreign supply chains, she added.
Closing the gaps in research and deployment
Singhal, meanwhile, called for greater integration across the three armed services.
She argued that the Army, Navy and Air Force needed better-connected platforms and weapons systems to coordinate effectively during emergencies. She also highlighted materials research as an area requiring greater attention.
Advanced materials would play an increasingly important role in developing next-generation weapon systems, including those requiring greater effectiveness and stealth capabilities. India, she said, needed to place more emphasis on materials R&D alongside investments in autonomous systems and other defence technologies.
The founders also identified persistent challenges in bringing together the armed forces, government research institutions and private industry. Singhal said startups and smaller defence companies could move faster than government research programmes, which often face bureaucratic delays.
Radhika said the challenge stemmed partly from differing expectations. The armed forces want sophisticated systems delivered quickly, research organisations operate through lengthy validation cycles and private manufacturers need commercially viable development timelines.
One way forward, she suggested, was to involve private industry from the prototype stage, with the armed forces funding development projects, research organisations working alongside manufacturers and clearer pathways to production orders.
She pointed to the Development-cum-Production Partner model as a mechanism that could help bridge the gap between research, development and large-scale manufacturing if implemented effectively.
For India's private defence technology industry, the next challenge is not simply to manufacture more equipment domestically. It is to develop and control the technologies that make military platforms effective, while building a procurement and research ecosystem capable of moving those technologies from the laboratory to the battlefield.

Points forts
- Format qui gagne (encore) en finesse.
- Affichage lumineux.
- De la puissance sans surchauffe.
- Charge (enfin) rapide.
Points faibles
- Téléobjectif un peu faiblard la nuit.
- Certification IP48 seulement.
- Pas de compatibilité S Pen.
Plus fin, plus puissant mais également plus cher, le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra profite de deux écrans très lumineux, d’une pliure discrète, d’un volet photo polyvalent, de performances remarquables et d’un multitâche maîtrisé. Son autonomie solide, sa charge améliorée et son suivi logiciel longue durée renforcent encore l’ensemble. Quelques limites subsistent, notamment l’absence de S Pen, une étanchéité perfectible et quelques logiciels préinstallés. Une évolution très aboutie, davantage fondée sur le perfectionnement que sur la révolution, réservée au nouveau format de son petit frère.

articles.title: Instagram se ha llenado de influencers creados con IA con el mismo corte de pelo estrafalario y millones de seguidores
articles.text:
Cada pocos meses alguien certifica la muerte de los influencers, y este verano le tocó a los españoles. Toda una cadena de polémicas desató el debate sobre el final de los influencers y se apuntaba a RoRo, acusada por otra creadora de copiarla, como la que más seguidores había perdido en TikTok en una semana. Mientras tanto, un extravagante francés generado por IA sumaba decenas de millones de visualizaciones y se ha convertido en uno de los negocios más imitados y, posiblemente, efímeros de las redes sociales actuales.
Movida influencer. Este francés que daba puñetazos al aire es Jean Phil. Su primer vídeo conocido en Instagram data del 17 de septiembre, y su aspecto es inconfundible: melena rubia a lo paje, bigote retorcido y traje de cuadros. Ocho días después, tenía más de 228.000 seguidores y una criptomoneda propia, JEANPHIL, con una capitalización estimada de 8,8 millones de dólares. Su réplica inglesa, Archibald Brown, iba por 110.000 seguidores y también tenía moneda.
Los dineros. Las cifras seguían elevándose para el 1 de octubre: más de 75 millones de visualizaciones solo en Instagram y un máximo por encima de los 12 millones de dólares para el token, aunque ese mismo día ya había caído a algo más de 3 millones. Se supo entonces que la cuenta se gestionaba desde Bélgica y que había cambiado seis veces de nombre de usuario. Este lunes, el perfil jean_philanthrope ha dejado de estar disponible y hay que buscarlo como jeanphilanthrope.co.
La fórmula. Desde entonces, decenas de influencers han imitado los pasos de Jean Phil, copiando no solo su curiosa apariencia externa (con trajes anticuados y peinados locos por encima de todo), sino también sus intenciones monetarias. Este hilo en X lo resumía como una receta: generar en ChatGPT a un tipo con traje gris y flequillo de tazón (y dotarlo de un nombre extravagante, añadimos nosotros: en este caso Harold Puddington) y usar Seedance 2.5 para ponerlo a pinchar en una sala a rebosar. Profit: 9,9 millones de visualizaciones y 19.433 dólares de beneficio (las cifras son estimación del tuitero). Y un detalle que parece estar claro con todos estos imitadores: funcionan como un gag visual de pocos segundos, no como un intento de influencer real.
Cuál es el negocio. El creador de Harold Puddington, por ejemplo, vende en la bio del personaje un curso para fabricar tu propio influencer por IA, aunque comienzan a abundar tutoriales en YouTube para montar uno con Higgsfield AI. Si todos estos productos son promocionados o no es una sospecha que siempre está ahí: en ese tutorial en vídeo, por ejemplo, hay enlace a Higgsfield en la descripción del vídeo, y se advierte que ganar dinero no está garantizado.
De hecho, la propia Higgsfield da bombo desde hace unas semanas a su programa Earn, que paga por publicar contenido hecho con su estudio de personajes. La empresa aseguró que ya supera los 1.000 millones de dólares de ingresos anuales. ¿Quién gana dinero en esta cadena? Posiblemente, más que nadie, quien vende la herramienta, como ya ocurría con las startups que ofrecían ejércitos de influencers sintéticos en la anterior oleada del fenómeno, más realista y reconocible.
La otra salida es la cripto. La estrategia es algo más sigilosa si hablamos de criptomonedas, aunque la táctica ya ha sido analizada: un personaje nuevo empieza a publicar, hace ruido, promociona un token, atrae compradores y, cuando la operación termina, la cuenta desaparece. Y vuelta a empezar. En ese vídeo lo llaman pump and dump, y ya hay expertos que advierten de que todos estos movimientos se mueven en una línea muy difusa: un catedrático de Derecho de Sociedades de Munich recordaba que para hablar de manipulación los promotores tendrían que haber planeado la caída de la cripto desde el principio, y a 1 de octubre el creador del token aún no había vendido su cartera.
Autores difusos. El negocio alrededor del personaje ni siquiera tiene por qué ser de su autor. Hay seis tokens distintos con el ticker $JEANPHIL, y el principal cotizaba este 19 de octubre con una capitalización de 5,9 millones de dólares. Lo que tienen las memecoins es que el personaje viral es un recurso que cualquiera puede explotar. Y además, todo queda inmerso en una peculiar neblina de autoría difícil de rastrear. Por ejemplo, el español y cayetano Borja Mari, una cuenta de Instagram con menos de 300 seguidores y cuatro reels que logró 16.000 me gusta con un vídeo del 7 de octubre. Ni siquiera está del todo claro si es una IA ni cuál es el negocio... pero posiblemente lo sabremos muy pronto.
¿Riesgo para los influencers? La duda de si estos personajes pueden sustituir a un influencer de carne y hueso nos obliga a volver a plantear el abismo que media entre alcance numérico e influencia real. Ya en 2019 andábamos contando el caso de una instagrammer con 2,6 millones de seguidores que vendió apenas 36 camisetas. Lo que sostiene a un creador es la relación construida durante años con su público, a base de enseñar su vida cotidiana. La visibilidad no es lo mismo que la reputación y Jean Phil no ha tenido tiempo de acumular reputación. Por eso, cuando los usuarios descubrieron que Phil era IA, muchos se mostraron decepcionados.
Otro rival. Visto desde ese enfoque, el rival dde estos personajes virtuales no son los influencers, sino el meme que esté de moda esa semana y al que hay que copiar sin piedad. Y contra eso la IA gana a base de volumen. Eso sí, tienen que ir con cuidado: desde el 2 de agosto, el artículo 50 del Reglamento europeo de IA obliga a quien genera personas con IA a hacer público que es artificial, aunque si el contenido forma parte de una obra "manifiestamente" satírica o de ficción basta con avisar de forma que no estorbe. Un boxeador con bigote de villano de opereta podría acogerse a esa excepción. Siempre hay excepciones.

articles.title: Acheter une voiturette électrique pourrait bientôt coûter moins cher grâce à cette aide
articles.text:
Bonne nouvelle si vous comptiez acheter une voiturette électrique. Le gouvernement a présenté l’acte 2 de son plan d’électrification, avec une aide pouvant aller jusqu’à 2 000 euros selon la catégorie du véhicule. On décrypte ensemble les contours de l’aide.
Jusqu’à 2 000 euros d’aides
Le plan d’électrification en arrive à son acte 2. En plus du coup de pouce pour l’achat d’une voiture électrique, les catégories inférieures, L7 et L6, vont profiter également d’une aide à l’achat. Concrètement, si vous souhaitez acheter une voiturette électrique, vous pouvez espérer une aide à l’achat allant jusqu’à 2 000 euros, ce qui est plutôt généreux quand on sait que le bonus écologique pour tous sur une voiture électrique à moins de 47 000 euros est de 3 500 euros.
Mais attention, cette aide de 2 000 euros est atteinte uniquement pour les voitures électriques de la catégorie L7, c’est-à-dire des véhicules pouvant rouler jusqu’à 90 km/h, avec au moins 150 km d’autonomie, la possibilité d’installer quatre personnes et une production en Europe. Autant dire que les modèles commercialisés en France et répondant à ces critères sont très peu nombreux, le Dacia Hipster pourrait bientôt arriver sur ce marché très spécifique.
Une aide plus généreuse pour les sans-permis ?
Les voiturettes sans permis (VSP) pourraient aussi voir arriver une aide généreuse. Si 2 000 euros sont accordés aux L7 limitées à 90 km/h, on peut espérer une nouvelle aide plus généreuse pour les VSP L6 électriques, limitées à 45 km/h, qui constituent le véritable cœur du marché actuellement.
Si un bonus allant jusqu’à 900 euros avait déjà été accordé, les VSP L6 électriques n’ont plus droit qu’à une prime CEE comprise entre 200 et 500 euros, selon le modèle choisi, ce qui est maigre pour des voitures vendues entre 10 000 et 15 000 euros.
Toutefois, les Citroën Ami et Fiat Topolino ne sont pas sûres d’y avoir droit. En effet, cette aide est réservée aux véhicules produits en Europe. Les VSP électriques du groupe Stellantis sont fabriquées au Maroc. Même si un accord commercial existe entre l’UE et le Maroc, rien n’assure formellement qu’elles seront éligibles à la nouvelle aide, qui doit être lancée le 1er janvier 2027.
Avec cette aide à l’achat des L7, le gouvernement français veut favoriser l’achat de petits véhicules électriques produits en Europe, favorisant ainsi les activités d’acteurs comme Ligier, Aixam, Microlino ou encore Silence. Mais si l’aide la plus généreuse est accordée uniquement à des véhicules quatre places capables de rouler jusqu’à 90 km/h et nécessitant le permis, pourquoi ne pas opter finalement pour une citadine électrique comme une Renault Twingo E-Tech ou une Citroën ë-C3, qui ne coûte pas beaucoup plus cher grâce à un bonus écologique plus généreux et qui offre surtout une meilleure polyvalence ?

articles.title: Nikkei discloses third data breach in a month, 1.8M records exposed
articles.text:
Nikkei Inc. disclosed a new data breach, the third in about a month, that exposed 1.83 million personal information records.
The Japanese giant says subsets of the data contained personally identifiable information and other sensitive details, but most records contained no identifying info.
The company said that 150,000 records contained at least one of the following data types: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in 120,000 records.
The remaining 1.68 million records contain no identifiers, the company said, and no credit card information was exposed.
Nikkei Inc. is a major Japanese business news and financial information group, owner of Financial Times, the country’s largest business-focused media company.
The company employs over 10,100 people and has an annual revenue of $2.5 billion (¥393.8 billion).
According to a notice Nikkei published late last week, hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within its network during the early morning hours of October 7.
The unauthorized access exposed personal information the company stored in the cloud.
Nikkei revoked the abused credentials and notified the Personal Information Protection Commission on October 11.
The company is currently examining the scope of the breach and noted that as of October 16, it had no evidence that the accessed information was misused or leaked online.
The company has also found no signs of system compromise or data tampering resulting from this incident, and has experienced no service outages.
The firm said those affected will receive individual notifications.
“We are working urgently to establish the extent of the damage and determine the cause, and will implement the necessary measures to strengthen security,” Nikkei stated.
This is the third cybersecurity incident that Nikkei disclosed recently. Earlier this month, the company disclosed a breach that occurred in late July, when hackers compromised an employee's Google Workspace account and accessed personal information belonging to employees and business partners.
In September, Nikkei announced that threat actors hijacked another employee’s Microsoft 365 account and used it to send spear-phishing emails to the firm’s staff.
BleepingComputer has contacted Nikkei for more information about the latest breach, and we will update this post once we receive a response.

articles.title: The Future of Web Apps: Will AI Agents Generate UIs on the Fly?
articles.text:
Rachel Lee Nabors, former React core team member, dives into the architecture and philosophy behind local-first applications, exploring how small language models (SLMs) running directly on-device can deliver privacy-focused, low-latency, and cost-effective alternatives to cloud-hosted LLM wrappers. Rachel shares key insights on evaluating models with golden datasets and leveraging client-side AI for moderation and social content aggregation.
The discussion also looks ahead to the future of web and application architectures in an AI-driven ecosystem. From the potential rise of OS-level personal agents and dynamic UI rendering standards like A2UI, to the evolving skill set required of software engineers.
Key Takeaways
- Building apps local-first delivers fast, offline capability for users while keeping cloud infrastructure costs low for developers.
- Utilizing SLMs locally (like Llama 3.2B) avoids high API costs, reduces latency, and protects PII compared to large cloud LLMs.
- Systematic evaluation using golden datasets is essential for right-sizing models and picking the best option for specific tasks like summarization or moderation.
- OS-level personal agents and standardized UI schemas (like A2UI) may replace traditional web apps and native interfaces for consumption.
- Software engineering is moving beyond basic code generation towards computer science fundamentals, system design, and AI collaboration.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Olimpiu Pop: Hello everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop and I have in front of me Rachel Lee Nabors. They are quite a creative person. They did a bunch of comics, I think, right? And also, they were involved with React and React Native frameworks. And because I don't know how to put it in a better light, Rachel Lee, can you please introduce yourself?
Rachel Lee Nabors: Thank you so much for the introduction. Yes, you may remember me from my pandemic babies, the react.dev and reactnative.dev portals. I worked on the React team for the pandemic. I've worked for FAANG on browsers for many years and with the W3C on web standards. But before all of that, I used to make comic books for teenage girls. I was one of the first web cartoonists that had their own personal website and mailing list, et cetera. So, I take my inspiration from Japanese comics and anime to this day. You can still find me illustrating my own slides and creating mascots for the different open source projects I work on.
Olimpiu Pop: Nice. Thank you for the idea for what you put so far. So, probably my kids will read some of the comics. Today we're going to talk about another endeavor that you have and that's local, I don't know, aggregator. It would be probably the best interface for the social literature that we use.
Rachel Lee Nabors: Oh, yes. I used to be really big on developer advocacy. When I moved to London, I was a developer experience consultant for lots of startups and AI in the Bay Area, but I've always wanted to get back into engineering. And finally, I found a project that inspired me to return to building again. And it's Mima, that's M-I-M-A. You can find it at mima.social. It is the client I've always wanted for managing all of my social and news connections. I don't know about you, but you can't do business in tech without being on X and LinkedIn and probably also Bluesky and Mastodon, depending on where your friends are. If you've got friends and data, you probably need to be on Bluesky.
If you got friends in open source, you got to be on Mastodon. I don't have time to check all of those different apps every day. And every one of them is like, "Oh my God, you got to spend all your time here on X. What are you doing posting links to other websites? How dare you?" They are very protective of their little circles, their bubbles. Problem is you stay in one of those bubbles, you only hear from people in that bubble. If you only listen to X, you'd think that everyone's using coding agents, but there are so many grads coming out these days that they've never touched Claude for coding. So, there's a whole world that you don't experience.
I built this to make it possible for me to exist and to see things coming in from any social network I wanted to connect to. So, I can repost something from X to Bluesky. It forms a local graph of all of my social connections, everything I've been saying, and it uses native web APIs under the hood. So, there's nothing particularly magical happening there. It's the browser I always wanted because for me, all of the big leaps I've made forward in my life in terms of career, understanding, et cetera, they all came through these social networks. But over the years, social networks have become harder and harder to access from outside the bubbles.
So, I started building Mima to solve my own problem, which was I just wanted to see what everyone was saying in one place and be able to reply from one place. And it's turned into its own little local app. It's got little local models on it to make the experience better. It's all privacy first and local first, which was kind of on purpose, kind of by accident. The truth is I just don't want to have servers with your personal information on it. The last thing I want is to have various countries come in and be in like, "Hey, we need all the DMs from user X, Y, Z." And me being like, "What? Oh, no."
So, I have no interest in owning other people's information. So, that's how it ended up starting. And yes, I'm actually going to be in San Francisco doing a little pop-up soft launch for Mima next week. It's really exciting.
Olimpiu Pop: Okay. Good luck with that. We are just curious about the technical details because you mentioned that you are part of the React crew and did a bunch of stuff. So, I'm curious about what were the choices you've made while building it, because you did mention also models and rather than having an L in front of the large language model, you have an S. So, guide us through the decisions, the technical decision you've made.
Local-First Architecture and Small Language Models [05:36]
Rachel Lee Nabors: I have been following along with the evolution of LLMs since GPT-3. One of the things I've noticed, especially in hackathon scenes, because developer experience consulting is like my bread and butter. So, I go to a lot of hackathons, I see what people are building, and I noticed a lot of what people started to build as soon as LLMs became API accessible was a wrapper. It's an app that takes everything the user gives it, sends it over to someone else's server somewhere where they do God knows what with that information, probably train your competitors model, and then they send you back a response.
First, this is incredibly wasteful. I did a series of articles on web.dev with Google about right sizing the model and a lot of research on the cost, the energy cost of running inference. On a multimodal model, it's four times higher than necessary to do most of the work that you could do with it. So, it's energy intensive. That means that cost gets passed to you in terms of the API costs. Now you've got linear costs going up with every time you call that. And also it brings in all these wonderful privacy concerns. Is that PII? We've had so many instances of private personal information showing up in public because somebody sent a prompt to a model and it got passed onto a search engine.
So, there are reasons why you don't want to just round trip with a big inference. Luckily for us, the technology has moved forward so fast, so well that small language models now do pretty much all the same things that people were trying to send off to big inference back in the day. Small models are perfectly fine for summarizing things. We've got Jev, which is great for picking the right tool or offering a simple yes or no. Jev just completely blows the lid off of everything. So, there's a lot we can do with a little model that we don't need to round trip to Gemini or to Claude to get done.
And I think it's the first thing we reach for. The idea is can we prove that it can be done with a big model? That's fine, but you probably don't need to be shipping to production the round trip or the high API costs that you are.
Olimpiu Pop: Kim, thank you. So, you have multiple models in Mima or you have one that has multiple hats?
Rachel Lee Nabors: Well, that is a great question. What's the right model for the job? Mima does have multiple different little models inside her. The one that I got started with was Llama 3. 2B. I was using Claude Sonnet to summarize, for instance, conversation threads when I first started building her, but very quickly I started feeling uncomfortable with sending my private messages to Claude. So, I actually set up some evals and with post-processing, I was able to get Llama 3. 2B to perform as well as Claude Sonnet at summarizing locally the conversations that I was having. Evals are really your best friend here. They let you actually rate and judge the inputs and outputs.
If I had just listened to my friends, I would've chosen Gemma four because Gemma four was really hot right then, but it turns out Gemma four would've actually substantially increased the latency on these summarizations and it wouldn't have provided as good summarizations as Llama 3. 2B did. So, I used Phoenix, which is a little evals library that you can set up there to run tests amongst real information and used a large model as a judge to pick the best model that could do the job. It turned out, of course, it was Llama 3. 2B, which is one of Facebook's models that they've trained on user data. So, it makes sense that it would be good at summarizing conversations between humans.
However, that model might not be the best at doing things like identifying when people are being toxic or if images, for instance, contain alarming things in them. I'm a big believer that our clients should be able to moderate for us rather than relying on the platform to do that because platform owners, Facebook, LinkedIn, et cetera, they always don't really invest in moderation. It's a cost center for them, so they cheap out on it. And that means that it's our Lord of the Flies, the kids are running the schoolroom in there. So, it's better if your client can do things like, "Oh, this is an incoming message from somebody this person doesn't follow. I'm going to check to see if it's abusive content."
You post a picture one night, you wake up, there's 40 comments on it. How many of them are, "That's a great picture," versus how many of them are like, "Oh, how dare you take this picture of a dog?" And you never know. But the idea is that you can use models that are specifically trained to check for different kinds of things to help you write better or to check to see if incoming content is abusive or unfriendly. And Mima is mostly geared around moderation right now, making sure your trigger warnings aren't being tripped up, et cetera. And for that, summarization's not necessarily the best option. There are smaller, lighter models that can do a better job of that, and all of them are opt-in.
If a person turns on a feature that needs another little model, they have the option to turn that on, download an additional model. It's never installed by default. I think this is something that companies who should know better, who have a lot of experience building products for humans have missed from back in the day when 15 years ago we were all reinventing the wheel and learning how to build apps and progressively enhance the user experience. There is this idea that the user should be able to opt in to enhance their experience. But if it's going to cost extra, extra storage space, et cetera, you need to ask their permission.
And of course you could always offer them a cloud solution as well, but for the reasons I already stated, I'm not really providing one of those at this time. It's not like, "Well, would you like me to process all of your incoming tweets on my servers or would you like to download this model?" You could do that, but for me, it's just going to be, "Would you like to download the model?"
Olimpiu Pop: That sounds closer to home. And also, I like the fact that the information doesn't leave your machine. So, that's quite useful from my perspective and probably others as well. And the moderation, it's highly important.
Rachel Lee Nabors: It is. I think one of the things we're going to see happening with AI assistance and personal agents in the near future is we've been building them thinking about HubSpot integrations and how to do business with them so far. But once they hit the consumer market, they're missing something important, which is your personal context. Yes, you can connect them to your email, but how are you going to connect them to your LinkedIn to help you find your next job? How are you going to connect them to your Facebook to keep up with the kids? How are you going to connect them to all of these walled gardens out there, each one of which wants to keep your data in their databases?
And remember that the power of that data is only really unlocked when it's cross-contaminated, which is a huge security risk I know. But there's also so much to be said for if we could just have access to the graph, our own social graph across multiple different networks, our own posts across multiple different databases, our personal agents would become much more powerful for having that context, not even necessarily to post, but they would just know more about us and be better able to help us as individuals.
Olimpiu Pop: Well, I like that you're looking only at the positive part and I'm all in supporting that. You did mention evals and that tweaking your model for that particular use case, it gives you the option of having the same output as a large language model. Well, outcome, I think it's more appropriate. Maybe a couple of hints on that, especially given that you discussed about something that doesn't have a terministic form. articles.title: How Five35 Ventures made 3.5 its investment from one deal
articles.text:
In April 2022, Five35 Ventures, a gender-focused venture capital firm, wrote one of its first cheques to Complete Farmer, a Ghanaian agritech company that connects smallholder farmers to buyers, inputs and financing.
In March 2026, it sold its entire stake. Five35 says the sale returned 3.5 times its money, an internal rate of return of 38% over four years, and that Complete Farmer’s valuation rose from $6 million to $49 million over the same period.
Five35 is a pan-African fund that writes pre-seed and seed cheques into tech-enabled companies, focusing on markets beyond the big four of Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt and South Africa.
“We invest in exceptional businesses first, and the gender lens helps us find overlooked ones,” said Hema Vallabh, Five35’s founding partner. “Turning that value into realised returns for our investors is the real test of our success. Over the next six to 18 months, we will write bigger cheques now that we have an anchor, invest more in secondary markets, and then move into our harvest period, where we will look harder at exits.”
Exits are rare in African venture capital and rarer in agritech, according to Briter, which calls exit routes the sector’s tightest constraint, as fragmented supply chains and heavy working capital needs make it hard for companies to scale.
Vallabh, an engineer who founded the women’s entrepreneurship platform WomHub, runs the fund with general partner Fatou Touré. Five35 was raising $30 million in 2022. When the capital winter hit, Vallabh cut the target and raised her first $1 million through cheques starting at $35,000, mostly from first-time investors. The Mastercard Foundation Africa Growth Fund came in as an anchor in late 2025, and she expects to close in the next three to six months.
The sale was partly a commercial call and partly a strategic one: a first-time manager still raising money needed to show investors it could return cash.
Vallabh explains below what Five35 means by a gender lens, why it sold its best performer early, how it raised money as a first-time manager, and what female founders face when they pitch that most investors never see.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
How do you invest on the continent?
We invest at pre-seed and seed in companies that are significantly tech-enabled, and we are sector agnostic. We are pan-African, with a bigger focus on sub-Saharan Africa and a small allocation for North Africa. We invest in the big four of South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt and Kenya, and we are also excited about secondary markets such as Ghana, Senegal and the DRC.
We invest with a gender lens, and for us that goes beyond female founders. Our definition is about intentionality. A company can be co-owned or co-led by women, with a woman in a real leadership role such as CEO or CTO.
It can have an intentionally female workforce, with women spread across the business and not only at the lower levels. Or it can have an intentionally female customer base. The test is how we get more women participating in economic activity, living better lives and making more money.
For the customer base, the example I use is a male founder who builds a maternal health app. He is deliberately serving women, and those women become healthier and more economically active. We are a fully gender-lens fund, and for every investment, it has to be clear why we consider it one.
Complete Farmer has a male founder. How does it fit your gender lens?
It is a good example of our thesis. Desmond is a male founder, but Complete Farmer is a B2B and B2C platform, and when we invested, about 55% to 60% of its customers were women. Women also made up about 80% of its post-harvest workforce.
Because of the platform, more female farmers were taking their produce to market more efficiently and more profitably. The model gave farmers a market before they planted, which made their income more predictable and reduced waste. The gender impact was built into what made it a commercially compelling business.
Why did you build Five35 around a gender lens?
I have worked in this space for 20 years. I am an engineer turned entrepreneur turned investor. My first organisation was a non-profit that helped get more women into engineering. I later turned it into a commercial business, WomHub, which today works across talent, incubation and acceleration, co-working spaces and capital.
Someone who starts a fintech fund usually comes from banking. Gender is my specialisation. It is the right thing to do, and it is also an overlooked market that repeatedly shows better returns. Our pipeline comes from the WomHub network and two decades of work, and our partners help us support founders in ways other funds cannot.
At pre-seed and seed, you are backing the founder more than the numbers, because the numbers are not there yet. Research shows female founders are disadvantaged at this stage because they do not fit the mould.
Pitch competitions, to put it a little facetiously, are designed for the very articulate white male American founder. A more introverted founder may not pitch as well and still be very good at building her business. That is why we need more fund managers and investment committee members who look like the founders we want to back.
You argue that gender-lens investing is commercial. On what basis?
Our name comes from data. Research shows that adding more female entrepreneurs to the African economy could lift GDP by up to 5%, and that diverse teams can deliver a 35% higher return than all-male teams when the playing field is level. Our job is to help level it.
Our investors expect competitive financial returns, as they would from any other venture fund. We compete for capital with gender-agnostic funds. We care about impact, including job creation, and we want it alongside strong financial returns.
You see this in our portfolio. We first made 16 small investments, which I call our track record builders, and Complete Farmer was one of them. After our anchor investment, we made two new investments and three follow-ons. We now have 18 investments and a zero per cent failure rate. A few are struggling, and none has folded, and we are in year four, going into year five. These are unrealised gains, and the fund overall sits at about 2x.
Agritech exits are rare. What did Complete Farmer do differently?
Part of it was deliberate, and part of it was timing. Agritech is hard to scale because supply chains are fragmented, working capital needs are different, and operations are complex.
Complete Farmer did more than build an app for farmers. It built a full commercial supply chain platform that solved real problems on both sides of the market. Connecting production to predictable demand was unusual.
It also had strong leadership and strong execution, and it showed commercial viability fairly early. I am yet to see a solution in the market as complete as theirs. They have competitors in individual verticals, and building the full platform is what sets them apart.
Why did you invest?
They met our core criteria: pan-African, tech-enabled, early-stage, and gender lens. They were solving a problem on both sides of the market, and they had a strong founder.
Desmond was not positioning itself as a gender-lens company. When we looked closely, the strong female customer base was almost incidental. We saw a way to add value by helping them make that intentional and by helping with teams and governance. We were a small investor working alongside others, so I do not claim his success is because of us. But we knew where we could help a company that was already growing strongly.
Why did you sell in March?
It was the right time, and it made commercial sense. When Complete Farmer was raising its next round, we considered doubling down, but the valuation was beyond our range. Anything we could add would have been too small to matter.
We did discuss staying in for a bigger exit later. We will never know how that would have turned out. There was also a strategic reason. Our target as a fund is at least three times the money on invested capital, and this exit exceeded it. As a first-time fund that is still fundraising and heading into its harvest period, we needed to show that we can deliver exits. Going through a real exit process was also a learning experience.
We did not sell because we lacked faith in the company. They were one of our strongest performers and still have potential. It was a commercial decision, a fundraising decision and a disciplined capital allocation decision.
Who bought your stake?
We cannot disclose the buyer because of confidentiality agreements. It was a secondary transaction, and we sold our entire position.
Which other portfolio companies are close to an exit?
We are still in our investment period, and our focus is on deploying capital and doubling down on our strongest performers. We will invest quite aggressively over the next 18 months. We keep assessing liquidity, and sometimes the market approaches us to ask whether we will sell a position, but we are not actively chasing exits. Give us two or three years, and then we will be thinking seriously about them.
What support do you give founders beyond capital?
We are entrepreneurs investing in entrepreneurs, and we have a structured value creation method. We run portfolio community sessions for peer learning. One of our companies has made two acquisitions and walked the others through how it did them. We also work with each company on what it needs at this stage, such as building teams, governance structures and systems.
Our anchor, the Mastercard Foundation Africa Growth Fund, adds a second layer of technical assistance for our portfolio, both cash and in-kind. Through us, companies such as Complete Farmer can reach support they would not otherwise get.
We also lead by example on the gender lens. One female founder told me she does not think twice about sending me a WhatsApp message at 10 pm, whereas she would worry about it being misread if she sent it to a male fund manager. The level of sexual harassment female founders face when pitching is a systemic problem that we have to talk about, and many do not feel safe in rooms where nobody looks like them.
I had a baby in the last two and a half years, and I was fundraising while pregnant. Many of our founders told me they did not know that was possible. A female founder raising while pregnant gets asked how committed she really is or whether her life will change after the baby. A male founder rarely faces those questions. We build support for these realities into how we work, before and after we invest.
What was fundraising like as a first-time manager?
Tough. Fund managers have to raise from LPs before we can invest, just as founders raise to grow. Fatou and I are both first-time fund managers.
When I conceived Five35 around 2021, the market was in its heyday, with a lot of liquidity on the continent. Then the capital winter hit. We started with ambitious targets, and we had to adapt and aim for a smaller fund.
I went to my own network first. I looked for strong women, often executives, who had made money and invested in property or stocks, or as angels, but had never considered venture capital as an asset class or invested as an LP.
Through what I call the 35 Club, we took cheques from $35,000 upwards, mostly from women, and raised our first $1 million. Small cheques from individuals would never get us to a fund of $15 million or $20 million, and they let us make our first investments and build a track record. When we approached institutions, we could answer the question every first-time manager gets: what is your track record?
That led to our anchor investment from the Mastercard Foundation Africa Growth Fund, and other investors came in around it. We are now in what we call the final circle, with a small allocation is left, and we hope to close in the next three to six months. Would I have liked to raise more? Yes. The market has not allowed it yet.
How do you structure your investments?
We are a pure equity fund and do not do debt. Our preferred early-stage instrument is a SAFE, and that is how we first invested in Complete Farmer and most of our other companies.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Spotify Famille : après le GPS et Google Maps, Spotify tente le QR code pour traquer le partage — Frandroid
articles.text:
Partager un abonnement Spotify Famille avec des amis qui vivent ailleurs va devenir nettement plus risqué. Depuis quelques jours, des abonnés racontent sur Reddit avoir reçu une demande de vérification d’un nouveau genre.
Vous allez devoir scanner un QR code affiché sur le smartphone du titulaire, ce qui l’oblige à se trouver physiquement à côté de vous. Celui qui échoue perd sa place à 3,54 euros par mois (le prix d’une offre Famille divisé par six) et se retrouve face à un abonnement individuel à 12,14 euros.
Spotify décrit lui-même la procédure sur sa page d’aide consacrée à l’abonnement Famille. Le titulaire affiche le QR code depuis l’application mobile, en touchant sa photo de profil, puis « Votre Premium » et « Gérer ». Le membre le scanne ensuite avec l’appareil photo de son propre téléphone. Le code change toutes les quelques secondes, ce qui rend inutile la capture d’écran envoyée par message.
Ce n’est pas systématique, puisque Spotify parle de « certains membres » de l’offre Premium Famille, sans dire comment il les choisit. A priori, selon les retours, la vérification tombe surtout quand le membre ne se trouve pas au même endroit que les autres comptes de l’abonnement.
Sept jours pour scanner, douze mois de pénitence
Le membre dispose de sept jours après la notification pour faire le scan. Passé ce délai, son compte repasse automatiquement à l’offre gratuite, avec publicités. Surtout, il ne peut plus rejoindre une autre offre Famille ou Duo pendant douze mois. Il garde en revanche le droit de payer son propre abonnement individuel.
Le « bannissement d’un an » qui circule depuis ce lundi est donc une interdiction d’offre partagée. Le compte, vous l’aurez compris, n’est pas fermé. La sanction n’a d’ailleurs rien d’inédit, puisque le même délai de douze mois s’appliquait déjà aux membres qui échouaient à la vérification d’adresse classique.
Quatre appareils pour tromper Spotify
Et… le contrôle se contourne déjà. Sur Reddit, des abonnés partagent leur écran en appel vidéo et scannent le code depuis un autre appareil.
Sur Reddit, on peut voir le témoignage d’un utilisateur qui a filmé le QR code avec la caméra d’une tablette, pour que l’autre membre le scanne sur un quatrième écran. Il s’en félicite, il ne lui a fallu « que » quatre appareils (on a connu plus simple pour économiser quelques euros).
Spotify en est à sa troisième tentative. En septembre 2018, la plateforme avait testé une vérification par GPS, avant de reculer face à la grogne des abonnés. Un an plus tard, Spotify modifiait les conditions de son offre Famille pour exiger que tous les membres vivent à la même adresse. Il fallait saisir cette adresse à l’activation, et Spotify se réservait le droit de demander une nouvelle vérification « de temps à autre », via la recherche d’adresses de Google Maps. Le QR code ajoute une étape de plus, la présence physique.
Spotify suit ainsi Netflix et les autres plateformes qui serrent la vis sur le partage. Le sujet remonte jusqu’au Parlement, où deux députés veulent interdire les restrictions sur le partage de compte. Les services de partage entre inconnus, comme Spliiit, sont en première ligne, et Numerama détaille les risques que l’on prend en y partageant ses comptes Netflix, Spotify ou Amazon Prime.
Si vous recevez la notification, prévoyez le scan avec le titulaire dans la semaine. Pour mémoire, l’offre Famille coûte 21,24 euros par mois pour six comptes, le Duo 17,20 euros pour deux, et l’abonnement individuel 12,14 euros.

articles.title: Sam Altman confirmó un robot humanoide: creado por OpenAI y con ChatGPT
articles.text:
El director ejecutivo de OpenAI, Sam Altman, confirmó que la empresa va a construir un robot humanoide y adelantó que habrá una demostración pública en 2027, aunque descartó que esos robots circulen por la calle en el corto plazo.
La confirmación llegó en dos entrevistas distintas. En el pódcast Sources, le preguntaron de manera directa si OpenAI fabricaría un robot humanoide. Su respuesta fue breve: “We will” (lo vamos a hacer), según citó Engadget.
A Fortune, Altman agregó el horizonte de tiempo: “Creo que vamos a tener una demostración genial en 2027... no creo que vaya a haber robots caminando por las calles por varios años más”, dijo, de acuerdo con el mismo reporte de Engadget, replicado también por el medio indio Mint.
OpenAI no precisó qué va a mostrar esa demostración, qué forma tendrá el robot ni cuándo alguien ajeno a la empresa podrá acercarse a uno. Ahora bien, se entiende que el ‘cerebro’ del autómata estaría impulsado por la tecnología de ChatGPT, la inteligencia artificial con la que la compañía se dio a conocer globalmente.
Por qué eligió la forma humana
Altman explicó que adoptar una anatomía de dos brazos y dos piernas responde a una lógica práctica y no estética. “El mundo está diseñado para personas”, sostuvo, según la misma nota.
Puertas, teclados y herramientas de uso cotidiano asumen un tipo de cuerpo determinado, por lo que un robot que deba moverse en esos mismos espacios conviene que replique ese formato. “Igualar ese tipo de forma parece una buena idea”, afirmó.
Sin embargo, el diseño físico no es, para Altman, el obstáculo central. Las preguntas sobre la apariencia del robot son “menos importantes que resolver de verdad... el cerebro que hace funcionar al robot”, señaló.
Esa distinción resume el desafío técnico de fondo: un cuerpo con brazos y piernas no sirve de mucho si el sistema que lo controla no sabe qué hacer con ellos. Levantar una taza, por ejemplo, exige identificar el objeto, ubicar el asa y calcular la fuerza justa para no derramar el contenido.
Una carrera que ya tiene competidores
OpenAI no llega a un terreno vacío. Tesla trabaja desde hace años en su robot Optimus, y la automotriz china XPENG mostró recientemente a su humanoide IRON saliendo de manera autónoma de la línea de ensamblaje tras ser armado.
La compañía ya tiene antecedentes propios en robótica. Su proyecto Dactyl entrenó hace años una mano robótica, íntegramente en simulación, para manipular objetos reales, y luego aplicó esa misma técnica para resolver un cubo Rubik.
Para avanzar en la nueva etapa, OpenAI mantiene abiertas 27 búsquedas laborales en robótica, que abarcan control de movimiento, estimación de posición, control de actuadores y comportamiento integral del robot, además de la infraestructura de aprendizaje automático necesaria para entrenar sistemas de inteligencia artificial física.
Otro grupo de esas búsquedas apunta a actuadores electromecánicos propios, con motores, transmisiones, sensores y sistemas térmicos diseñados a medida, mientras que un tercer grupo cubre manufactura y cadena de suministro para una eventual producción a mayor escala.
Un objetivo que empieza en la fábrica
Según una de esas publicaciones de empleo, el plan de corto plazo de OpenAI no apunta todavía a un robot doméstico. El primer objetivo son robots de uso general que ayuden a trabajadores calificados a construir infraestructura, mientras que la meta de largo plazo es un robot personal capaz de realizar una variedad mucho más amplia de tareas.
Por ahora, la empresa no difundió precio, fecha de lanzamiento comercial ni ninguna especificación técnica del humanoide. La próxima señal pública sobre el proyecto será, según lo que adelantó Altman, la demostración prevista para 2027.

articles.title: Chefe do Instagram admite que ainda não sabe como combater deep fakes • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Chefe do Instagram admite que ainda não sabe como combater deep fakes
Perfis usam avatares gerados por inteligência artificial para reproduzir conteúdo original.
O chefe do Instagram, Adam Mosseri, reconheceu que a rede social ainda não tem uma solução para perfis que reproduzem conteúdo usando deep fakes criados por IA. A prática tem sido relatada ao executivo por criadores no próprio Instagram, segundo o jornal britânico The Independent.
Um dos casos foi apontado pelo comediante norte-americano George Brett Olson, que encontrou uma conta que publicou uma de suas apresentações usando, no lugar dele, um avatar feminino gerado por IA. O vídeo mantinha o áudio e o texto da apresentação, mas a imagem foi substituída pelo deep fake.
O executivo da rede social afirmou estar “muito preocupado” com a prática, mas descartou uma proibição geral de conteúdos produzidos com a tecnologia e disse que discutiria medidas com a equipe da plataforma.
Segundo Olson, o mesmo tipo de conteúdo vem aparecendo em outros segmentos. Há perfis que usam vídeos de dançarinos como base para gerar gravações nas quais personagens criados por IA reproduzem as coreografias, por exemplo.
O perfil que reproduziu a apresentação do comediante tinha mais de 300 mil seguidores e direcionava usuários para uma página no OnlyFans. Outro perfil, citado pela também comediante Julia Jasunas, reunia cerca de 250 mil seguidores.
Mosseri respondeu diretamente à publicação de Olson no Instagram. Segundo o executivo, a Meta está preocupada com esses perfis, mas uma proibição ampla de conteúdo de IA não seria prática. “Vai ficar cada vez mais difícil de identificar, e nem todo conteúdo é ruim, embora haja muito lixo”, escreveu Mosseri.
Ele afirmou ainda que o Instagram pretende direcionar mais tráfego aos autores originais e reconheceu que a plataforma precisa avaliar como agir quando conteúdos são cópias integrais de produções desses autores. Há exemplos em redes vizinhas: o X, de Elon Musk, mudou recentemente seu algoritmo de recomendação para limitar o alcance de conteúdo copiado e promoveu mudanças no sistema de monetização para privilegiar criações originais.
Em outro comentário, Mosseri abordou as ferramentas disponíveis para solicitar a remoção de conteúdos. A plataforma permite denúncias por violação de direitos autorais, mas, segundo o executivo, o mecanismo nem sempre resolve as situações citadas pelos criadores.
Segundo ele, muitos criadores podem não ter tomado medidas formais relacionadas à proteção dos próprios trabalhos e que a rede precisa encontrar uma maneira “de ajudar esses criadores sem permitir que agentes mal-intencionados façam mais denúncias falsas”. Isso, de acordo com o executivo, “acontece o tempo todo”.
Mosseri abordou anteriormente essa encruzilhada no tratamento à IA na plataforma. Ele já disse que conteúdos gerados por inteligência artificial não deveriam aparecer para quem não demonstra interesse por eles, mas negou que os usuários devessem ter controle para bloqueá-los — isso continua a cargo do algoritmo.
