articles.title: Cómo proteger el número de teléfono y qué datos no compartir ante fraudes digitales en Centroamérica
articles.text:
Un número de teléfono puede parecer un dato menor, pero suele estar vinculado a cuentas bancarias, correos electrónicos, redes sociales y aplicaciones de mensajería. En Centroamérica, conocer los riesgos asociados a su exposición permite a los usuarios detectar maniobras de fraude antes de que los delincuentes obtengan información, dinero o acceso a servicios digitales.
La firma de ciberseguridad ESET Latinoamérica advirtió recientemente que un número telefónico puede convertirse en el punto de partida para fraudes, robos de cuentas y suplantaciones de identidad. El dato, por sí solo, no permite ingresar de forma directa a un celular, leer conversaciones de WhatsApp ni acceder a una cuenta bancaria. El riesgo aparece cuando los atacantes lo combinan con información disponible en internet o con engaños dirigidos a la víctima.
Para los usuarios de países centroamericanos, donde los teléfonos son una herramienta habitual para recibir transferencias, coordinar entregas, comunicarse con familiares en el exterior y validar operaciones digitales, la advertencia plantea medidas concretas de prevención.
El número puede ayudar a construir un engaño personalizado
Un ciberdelincuente puede vincular un teléfono con perfiles de redes sociales, publicaciones, nombres, direcciones de correo electrónico o datos que hayan quedado expuestos tras una filtración. Con esa información, tiene más elementos para hacerse pasar por un banco, una empresa de mensajería, un servicio de entrega o incluso un conocido de la víctima.
El propósito suele ser obtener contraseñas, códigos de verificación, datos personales o información financiera. También puede consistir en inducir a la persona a abrir un enlace malicioso que imita una página oficial.
La regla central es no entregar códigos de acceso ni datos personales ante llamadas o mensajes no solicitados. Si una entidad bancaria o una compañía pide información por WhatsApp, SMS o teléfono, el usuario debe cortar la comunicación y verificar el pedido mediante los canales oficiales de esa institución.
David González, investigador de seguridad informática de ESET, explicó que conocer un número no habilita por sí mismo el acceso al dispositivo. Sin embargo, puede servir para iniciar intentos de fraude que aprovechan la relación de ese dato con el resto de la vida digital de una persona.
Los códigos de WhatsApp no se comparten
Uno de los métodos más frecuentes apunta a tomar el control de cuentas de mensajería. La víctima puede recibir un código de WhatsApp que no solicitó y, poco después, un desconocido afirma que el mensaje llegó “por error” y le pide que se lo reenvíe.
Ese código puede ser la llave para registrar la cuenta en otro dispositivo. Si la persona lo comparte, el atacante podría apropiarse de su perfil y usarlo para pedir dinero a familiares, amigos o contactos laborales bajo una identidad conocida.
La recomendación también se aplica a códigos enviados por correo electrónico, plataformas de pago, redes sociales o aplicaciones bancarias. Son claves personales y temporales, por lo que ninguna empresa legítima debería solicitarlas por mensaje, llamada o chat.
El cambio fraudulento de SIM puede cortar el control del usuario
Otro riesgo es el SIM swapping, una modalidad en la que el delincuente intenta convencer a la empresa telefónica de que es el titular de la línea. Si logra transferir el número a otra tarjeta SIM, puede recibir llamadas y mensajes de texto que antes llegaban a la víctima.
Esto resulta relevante porque muchos servicios aún envían códigos de recuperación y validación por SMS. Una pérdida repentina de señal, llamadas que dejan de entrar o mensajes que no llegan pueden ser señales de alerta. Frente a esa situación, el usuario debe contactar de inmediato a su operador telefónico y revisar las cuentas asociadas a ese número.
Autenticación en dos factores y revisión de datos expuestos
Proteger las aplicaciones con autenticación de dos factores, revisar la información personal expuesta en redes y desconfiar de pedidos urgentes reduce la posibilidad de que un número telefónico habilite un fraude digital.

articles.text:

                        TECHNICAL PAPERS
		
								October 19th, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign published a technical paper titled “Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“The design space of modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures, including GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators; memory technologies, including HBM, GDDR, and SRAM; and interconnects such as NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet. No single architecture is optimal across LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC workloads, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present ArchAgent, a hierarchical multi- agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems, each handled by specialist agents.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026.

articles.title: Usuários recorrem à IA para remover anúncios e mudar interfaces de TVs • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Usuários recorrem à IA para remover anúncios e mudar interfaces de TVs
Projetos usam ferramentas como Claude Code para criar launchers personalizados.
Modificações em sistemas de smart TV ganharam as redes sociais nos últimos dias. Os consumidores estão adotando novos launchers porque os nativos podem conter poluição visual, em especial devido aos muitos espaços de publicidade. O tema está em alta principalmente no X/Twitter.
Os projetos são compartilhados nas redes sociais e mostram agentes como o Claude Code sendo usado para executar alterações no Android TV. Os usuários mostram telas iniciais próprias com integração a widgets de tempo e calendário, alguns até com controles de automação de dispositivos de casa inteligente.
O vibe coding, ou “programação intuitiva”, é um modelo de desenvolvimento com inteligência artificial em que a pessoa descreve a um chatbot o que deseja criar, e a tecnologia gera o código a partir dessas instruções. O termo se popularizou em 2025 e tem sido um grande foco da indústria de IA nos últimos meses.
Ao mesmo tempo, desenvolvedores profissionais se preocupam com aplicativos criados sem preocupações com barreiras de segurança.
Um dos relatos foi publicado pelo desenvolvedor Ryan Doyle, que utilizou o Claude Code para modificar a TV e desativar anúncios e serviços de rastreamento. Ele também criou um protetor de tela personalizado que reúne previsão do tempo, calendário, dados de faturamento do próprio negócio entre outras funções.
Outro projeto, chamado cleanyourtv, surgiu após o desenvolvedor encontrar um anúncio na tela inicial da Xiaomi Mi TV usada por seus pais antes da abertura da Netflix. O projeto foi publicado no GitHub.
Após receber informações sobre o modelo da TV, o Claude Code acessou o aparelho pela rede local e desativou 25 pacotes instalados pela Xiaomi. O projeto também substituiu a tela inicial por um laucher personalizado com uma interface mais simples. Outros usuários vêm explorando as ferramentas para criar funções adicionais, como representações 3D da própria casa com controles de sistema de iluminação.
As alterações aproveitam ferramentas já existentes no Android. Os projetos usam principalmente o Android Debug Bridge (ADB), recurso de desenvolvimento que permite enviar comandos a dispositivos Android. O usuário precisa habilitar as opções de desenvolvedor e a depuração da TV.
Após isso, ferramentas de IA podem executar comandos pelo terminal para alterar configurações e gerenciar os app instalados. Por depender do ADB, o método é usado principalmente em aparelhos com Android TV ou Google TV, utilizados por fabricantes como Sony, TCL, Xiaomi, Hisense e Philips. Vale lembrar que a Play Store já possui launchers para quem quer apenas mudar a interface sem passar por todo esse processo.
Sistemas proprietários, como Tizen da Samsung e webOS da LG, não oferecem o mesmo método de acesso. Mas alguns usuários já começaram a divulgar soluções próprias para esses sistemas.
A disseminação desses apps criados com ajuda da IA ocorre enquanto o Google também começa a facilitar a execução de programas desenvolvidos para uso pessoal. Uma nova função da Google Play permite executar apps criados pelo próprio usuário com o Google AI Studio em dispositivos Android sem publicá-los na loja.
Segundo o TechCrunch, esses apps ficam disponíveis em uma área chamada Sua biblioteca pessoal, associada à conta Google do desenvolvedor. Eles não aparecem nas buscas ou nas páginas públicas da loja.

articles.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
articles.text:
This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.
In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.
The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.
Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.
In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”
A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.
According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.
As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.
Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.
That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.
In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.
However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.
In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.
A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.
“There’s decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren’t built to guard against.”
Not its first rodeo
This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.
In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.
In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”
Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.
Google declined to comment for this story.
In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.
According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.
The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.
Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggling with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.
In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.
That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.
According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.
A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”
The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.
If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.
The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.
“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

articles.title: Norwegian undersea cable builder pitches 2,800-mile transatlantic data link between Canada and Europe to bypass the US — Canadian majority partner sought to help fund and build new $620 million fiber connection to reduce reliance on American routes
articles.text:
Norwegian undersea cable builder pitches 2,800-mile transatlantic data link between Canada and Europe to bypass the US — Canadian majority partner sought to help fund and build new $620 million fiber connection to reduce reliance on American routes
Further attempts to reduce reliance on US infrastructure
A Norwegian company building fiber networks and data centers across Europe is looking for a majority partner to help fund and build a transatlantic undersea cable that would connect Canada with Europe directly, bypassing the United States. The project follows worsening relations between Washington and Ottawa, with the Canadian government looking to reduce direct reliance on its immediate neighbor, Bloomberg reports.
Project Leif Erikson, if it goes ahead, would stretch more than 2,800 miles, starting at the southern tip of Norway and ending up at Happy Valley-Goose Bay in Canada's eastern province of Newfoundland and Labrador. From there, it would continue underground over Canadian territory, passing through Quebec before reaching Montreal.
According to Bulk's co-founder, Peder Nærbø, the link would be part of a "sovereign cable system" for Canada. The project was touted to investors at a global investors summit, arranged by the Canadian government, in September, where the project claimed to provide "direct, secure, high-capacity data transmission for AI, telecom and hyperscale markets."
Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joy, meanwhile, met with Nærbø earlier this year, and although the department declined to comment on Leif Erikson itself, it told Bloomberg that security and resilience for Canada's infrastructure are "key priorities" for PM Mark Carney's government. Only a few undersea cables currently connect Canada without passing through the United States first, and none by a company owned by Canada. The biggest, called Topez, is owned by Google owner Alphabet and connects Canada with Japan.
As for Bulk, it has, up until now, laid more than 6,200 miles of cabling locally and at sea. Bulk's goal is to "unlock the Nordics' potential for... renewable energy to be utilized for digital infrastructure." Nærbø believes that "Canada lacks resilience" but "the game-changer was when the current situation with the U.S. escalated."
Leif Erikson has backers, according to the report, but the EU and Canada still need to plan and sign off on the project and its route. Additional financing will be needed to get started, too, with it expected to cost more than $620 million to build. Bulk itself has significant Canadian investment, with 65% of the company owned by a real estate subsidiary of Canada's Sun Life Financial Inc., with several Canadian pension funds also invested.
Leif Erikson is a project that Nærbø has sought to kickstart for the last five years without success. With geopolitical pressures and old alliances fraying, however, new opportunities for its development have given it steam. To that end, Canada and Europe intend to endorse a statement in Montreal on October 29 that the two will look for "the best way to enhance digital links between Europe, Canada and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure."

It won't be without challenges, however, including a 1,180-mile underground route through Canada that'll require the backing of Indigenous communities. Meanwhile, other European efforts include an undersea cable project at the North Pole to link Europe with Asia to bypass Russia and the Middle East.

articles.title: Zoom can now tell you for sure that the person you're speaking to isn't a deepfake — Sam Altman’s World debuts ID verification for AI Agents
articles.text:
Zoom can now tell you for sure that the person you're speaking to isn't a deepfake — Sam Altman’s World debuts ID verification for AI Agents
Verifying human authenticity is a complex but important necessity
- World ID for Zoom will put a Human Badge on your video feed to prove you're... human
- Setting this up requires a physical iris scan and a verification selfie
- Verifying human authenticity is easier than identifying deepfakes
Sam Altman's biometric identity verification company, World, has launched a series of tools designed to help businesses distinguish real people from AI deepfakes as one of his other companies – OpenAI – becomes increasingly capable of mimicking humans.
One of the main announcements was the general availability of World ID for Zoom, which gives enterprise customers access to a verification process that can distinguish genuine video from AI content.
Under the newly-launched system, verified participants will receive a "Human Badge" displayed alongside their video feed so that other participants can be more confident that they're speaking with a human.
World ID for Zoom
While the problem World is aiming to solve seems rather dystopian and unlikely, recent Gartner research actually revealed that 36% of senior cybersecurity leaders reported at least one incident involving a deepfake during an video call over the past 12 months.
We also know that Microsoft has been launching numerous updates to address similar concerns in Teams, opening up its platform to enable third-party deepfake detection in the hope of stamping out AI-generated video and audio.
However, proving human authenticity isn't as simple as ticking a few boxes or scanning a passport. Workers will have to visit one of World's physical Orb devices, which scans their iris to create a cryptographically secure biometric reference.
To streamline the process, enterprises can choose to have an Orb installed onsite, though this could likely be a costly option.

A selfie through the mobile app then verifies the human participant against that biometric reference image during Zoom calls.
World says that detecting deepfakes can be especially challenging, "lead[ing] to an arms race between deepfake detection and creation," hence the decision to verify human authenticity instead.

articles.title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
articles.text:
Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
Millions of AI agents are descending on a web built for humans. Websites are trying to keep them out, but the arrival of these new visitors could transform the internet.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.
But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.
The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.
Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.
Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.
These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn.
If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans.
The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.
How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions.
That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.
Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.
These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

articles.title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.
Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.
Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round.
We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

articles.title: Mobilfunk aus dem All: Was europäische Anbieter planen – und warum Starlink wohl außen vor bleibt
articles.text:
Mobilfunk aus dem All: Was europäische Anbieter planen – und warum Starlink wohl außen vor bleibt
Europas große Telekommunikationskonzerne ziehen an einem Strang, um Handynutzer auch in entlegenen Gebieten mit Mobilfunk aus dem Weltall zu erreichen. Die Deutsche Telekom, der britische Anbieter Vodafone, Telefónica aus Spanien und Orange aus Frankreich teilten mit, dass sie gemeinsam für Frequenzen für mobile Satellitendienste bieten wollen. Eine entsprechende Absichtserklärung sei unterzeichnet worden. Es geht um Frequenzen, die aller Voraussicht nach 2029 frei werden und bislang etwa für Internetverbindungen im Flugzeug genutzt werden.
Man wolle eine flächendeckende Versorgung auch in unterversorgten Gebieten erreichen, die Resilienz mobiler Netze stärken, kritische Kommunikation schützen und die Entwicklung einer europäischen Satellitenkonstellation unterstützen, hieß es von den Unternehmen. Mit der Zusammenarbeit wolle man die eigenständige Position Europas im Bereich der Weltrauminfrastruktur sicherstellen. Man plane, zentrale Infrastrukturen am Boden sowie wichtige Koordinierungs- und Steuerungsfunktionen in Europa aufzubauen.
Weltraum-Funktion kommt erst noch in den Massenmarkt
Den Handykunden sollen Direct-to-Device-Dienste (D2D) angeboten werden – das Smartphone wird also da, wo bislang kein Handynetz ist, direkt mit Satelliten im Weltraum verbunden. Die meisten Smartphones haben diese D2D-Funktion bislang nicht integriert, in den kommenden Jahren dürfte das aber im Massenmarkt ankommen.
Es geht um weiße Flecken – also dort, wo Stand jetzt nicht mehr das veraltete 2G-Netz verfügbar ist. Bei der Deutschen Telekom waren das im Juni laut Bundesnetzagentur 1,2 Prozent der Fläche Deutschlands, bei Vodafone 1,7 Prozent und bei O2 Telefónica 1,6 Prozent. In solchen Gegenden sollen die Handynutzer künftig mit Satelliten im Weltraum verbunden werden. Wer der Satellitenbetreiber ist, ist noch unklar. Das Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX mit seinem Internetdienst Starlink von Elon Musk dürfte es nicht sein, da es bei dem Vorhaben der vier Firmen um europäische Souveränität geht.

articles.title: Jubilee, FSD Africa partner with 7 BimaLab insurtechs to pilot inclusive insurance in Kenya - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
East African financial services group Jubilee and development agency FSD Africa have partnered with seven insurtech startups from the BimaLab Africa accelerator network to develop and pilot affordable insurance products for underserved Kenyans.
BimaLab, an FSD Africa initiative, has supported 135 startups across 28 African countries over the past six years, helping develop more than 300 insurance solutions that now reach over 6.5 million customers.
The programme targets SMEs, informal sector workers, farmers and low-income households, segments that remain largely uninsured. East Africa is estimated to have more than 10 million SMEs, which account for over 70 per cent of jobs, yet insurance penetration among the segment averages about one per cent.
The seven firms – Dukatech Solutions, Aura Insure Technologies, Inclusivity Solutions, DPE, Fiinovate, Agrails and Ibisa Network – were selected through a competitive process from BimaLab’s alumni network. They will go through an eight-week product co-creation process with Jubilee before joint pilots kick off in Kenya next month.
The work will focus on three areas – low-cost bundled and embedded insurance distribution, insurance solutions for SME ecosystems, and wellness and engagement models that link customers to health and care services. Successful solutions could later be rolled out in other East African markets.
“There is a large group of Kenyans who work, earn and run businesses every day but still have little or no insurance coverage. We need to meet people where they are, with products that are affordable, relevant and simple to access,” said Juan Cazcarra, deputy group CEO of Jubilee Group.
“Working with these seven insurtechs gives us a practical way to test different products and distribution models with customers and learn what works.”
At Jubilee, the programme will be run through J-Hub, the group’s innovation and technology arm.

articles.title: Data is not a moat: What India’s CTOs say will define the next tech edge
articles.text:
Data is not a moat: What India’s CTOs say will define the next tech edge
At TechSparks 2026, technology leaders from ShareChat, Angel One, Amagi and Innovaccer said India’s next competitive edge will depend on deep industry expertise, customer insights, trust and the ability to turn AI into real-world solutions.
India’s technology industry has long relied on talent, cost efficiency and scale. But as artificial intelligence makes advanced tools more accessible, these advantages alone may no longer be enough to differentiate companies.
The next edge, according to technology leaders at TechSparks 2026, will come from how effectively companies use AI to solve specific problems, understand customers and build products that are difficult to replicate.
During a panel titled The New CTO Playbook: India’s Next Tech Advantage, Nitin Jain, CTO of ShareChat and Moj; Ajit Narayanan, CTO of Angel One; Srividhya Srinivasan, CTO of Amagi; and Ankit Maheshwari, founder and CTO of Innovaccer, discussed how Indian technology companies can remain competitive in an AI-driven market, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event, TechSparks.
India’s complexity is an advantage
For ShareChat and Moj, India’s linguistic and cultural diversity offers an opportunity to build products for varied audiences. Nitin Jain said companies must account for differences in languages, devices, network quality and user preferences.
ShareChat, which Jain said has around 200 million monthly active users, uses audience behaviour to improve content recommendations and identify emerging preferences.
He said the challenge is to deliver experiences comparable with global platforms while operating within India’s cost constraints. Building flexible technology that accommodates diverse users, he added, can help companies expand faster.
Data alone is not enough
In healthcare, Innovaccer’s Ankit Maheshwari said proprietary data is valuable but does not automatically create a competitive moat.
Healthcare information is often fragmented across medical records, billing systems and medication databases. Connecting these sources is only the first step; the real challenge is using the information to determine what action should follow.
“Data in itself, or having proprietary data, is not a moat,” Maheshwari said.
He argued that companies need a context and intelligence layer that understands industry workflows, exceptions and operational requirements. In healthcare, this means moving beyond general-purpose AI to solutions that can work reliably across hospitals, providers and complex processes.
Trust must be built into AI
For Angel One’s Ajit Narayanan, trust can be a differentiator in financial services, where technology failures can have direct financial consequences.
He cited the example of a trading order for which a customer receives no acknowledgement. Without knowing whether the order was processed, retrying could result in duplicate positions and potential losses.
Narayanan said trust must be embedded in system design through accurate information, safeguards and accountability, rather than treated merely as a brand promise.
He also outlined three considerations for AI automation: the cost of an incorrect decision, whether it can be reversed, and whether it can be audited. Human oversight, he argued, should focus on meaningful safeguards rather than simply assigning responsibility when systems fail.
Building in India, scaling globally
Amagi’s Srividhya Srinivasan said India’s complex media environment has helped the company develop products for global markets.
Multiple languages, subtitles, audience demographics and advertising formats expose technology providers to challenges that also arise in international media operations.
Srinivasan said Amagi developed solutions for India before taking some of them global. Emerging AI applications, including real-time dubbing, subtitling and short-form content creation, offer further opportunities.
However, she said expansion should depend on market readiness rather than a fixed India-first strategy. Companies must identify where customers are prepared to adopt a product and where it solves an immediate need.
The advantage lies in execution
Jain said AI is helping ShareChat accelerate content production and improve recommendations by analysing how users engage with videos and other formats.
The platform can use these signals to test content ideas, understand audience preferences and refine recommendations. The ability to feed user responses back into AI systems quickly creates a continuous improvement cycle.
The broader message from the panel was that access to AI alone will not guarantee a lasting advantage. Companies must combine technology with specialised knowledge, customer understanding, reliable systems and the ability to execute at scale.
For India’s technology industry, talent, cost and scale remain important foundations. But the next competitive edge will depend on how effectively companies turn those strengths into products that solve complex problems and deliver measurable value."

articles.title: Daredevil Born Again : le patron de Marvel parle de l'avenir du héros après la fin de la saison 3
articles.text:
Brad Winderbaum, à la tête de Marvel Television, a remis les pendules à l’heure en octobre 2026 dans l’émission américaine The Brandon Davis Show. Selon lui, Daredevil Born Again n’a pas été arrêtée par la direction de Marvel pour cause de mauvaises audiences.
Selon lui, le plan a toujours été de découper cette nouvelle ère en trois actes bien distincts, à la manière des trade paperbacks (ces recueils de bandes dessinées que l’on aligne fièrement dans sa bibliothèque).
Une structure en 3 parties pour Daredevil
L’argumentaire de Winderbaum se veut poétique, mais il dissimule à peine une volonté d’imposer un cadre strict : la série originale Netflix comptait trois saisons, Daredevil Born Again aura exactement le même traitement. Une manière propre de fermer le chapitre sériel avant d’envisager la suite des événements pour l’avocat aveugle.
« Le plan a toujours été de s’arrêter à la saison 3. C’est comme deux coffrets de trois volumes sur une étagère : on boucle la série, puis on prend une grande respiration pour décider de la suite pour le personnage », résume Brad Winderbaum.
Pour cette ultime salve d’épisodes, les scénaristes n’ont pas cherché bien loin leur inspiration, piochant directement dans The Devil in Cell-Block D, l’arc qui ouvre en 2006 la période d’Ed Brubaker au scénario de Daredevil. On y retrouvera un Matt Murdock piégé derrière les barreaux depuis des mois, contraint de cohabiter avec la faune de criminels qu’il a lui-même envoyée à l’ombre. Ce huis clos carcéral brutal, façon « C’est vous qui êtes enfermés avec moi », devrait laisser les rues de New York aux Defenders et marquer le retour de Bullseye.
Un avenir au cinéma aux côtés de Spider-Man ?
Marvel présente la fin de la série au bout de trois saisons comme une pause pour le personnage. Sans tournage de série chaque année, Charlie Cox aurait le champ libre pour revenir au cinéma.
Interrogé par GamesRadar+ au New York Comic Con, l’acteur est resté prudent : « Peut-être que ça ouvrira la porte. On verra. » Avec un nouveau Spider-Man en préparation, les fans imaginent déjà une vraie alliance entre le Tisseur et le Diable de Hell’s Kitchen. Pour l’instant, Marvel n’a annoncé aucun film avec Daredevil. Au cinéma, Charlie Cox s’est limité à des caméos, dans Spider-Man: No Way Home en 2021 puis dans Spider-Man: Brand New Day cette année.

articles.title: Meta dévoile Petal, un surpuissant câble sous-marin qui va relier les USA à la France pour booster l’IA
articles.text:
Meta vient de dévoiler Petal, un câble sous-marin qui reliera les États-Unis à la France dès 2029. Sa capacité doit doubler celle des meilleurs systèmes actuels, de quoi absorber le déluge de données que l’IA fait circuler.
On les oublie facilement, mais les câbles sous-marins sont la colonne vertébrale d’Internet. Meta rappelle qu’ils acheminent environ 99 % du trafic intercontinental, de vos messages WhatsApp à l’actualité consultée en ligne. Mais avec l’essor du cloud et de l’IA, les besoins explosent.
L’entreprise de Mark Zuckerberg, qui se décrit comme l’un des plus gros investisseurs mondiaux du secteur, entend bel et bien s’adapter à ces usages accélérés.
Meta 1 pétabit promet
Ainsi, Petal reliera les États-Unis à la côte atlantique française sur environ 7 000 kilomètres, pour une mise en service attendue en 2029. NEC, spécialiste des systèmes sous-marins, et Sumitomo Electric, l’un des grands fabricants de fibres, font partie du projet. En parallèle, Meta explique travailler avec Orange « sur des plans pour faire atterrir Petal sur la côte atlantique de la France ».
La société, qui revendique « des centaines de milliers de kilomètres » d’infrastructures déployées dans le monde, promet 1 pétabit par seconde de capacités. Les câbles actuels, eux, se mesurent en térabits. Il s’agit ainsi de « la plus forte hausse générationnelle de capacité » jamais enregistrée pour un câble transocéanique, assure-t-elle.
« C'est à peu près la capacité réseau nécessaire pour que 75 % de la population mondiale puisse écouter de la musique en streaming en même temps », illustre Meta. » En temps normal, transporter deux fois plus de données implique de poser deux fois plus de câbles, d’utiliser deux fois plus de fibre optique, de matériaux physiques et de ressources », poursuit-elle.
Une technologie de « fibre multicœur »
Ici, elle promet de transférer un volume double de données « sans augmentation proportionnelle de l’énergie ou de l’infrastructure physique ». Car dans les faits, une fibre optique classique n’a qu’un seul cœur, le minuscule canal où circule la lumière qui transporte les données. Mais Petal en utilise deux par fibre, soit le « premier système de câble doté de la technologie de fibre multicœur déployée à des distances transocéaniques », affirme l’entreprise.
Il ne faudra, malgré tout, pas s’attendre à une connectivité améliorée. L’enjeu pour Meta est surtout d’éviter la saturation à l’heure où l’intelligence artificielle requiert des capacités hors normes.

articles.title: Drupal Warns of Fast Exploitation Risk for Critical Core RCE Flaw
articles.text:
Drupal has rolled out patches for five vulnerabilities, including two critical-severity bugs that could be exploited for remote code execution (RCE).
The first resides in the Entity List module, which allows users to create lists of entities without Views, and is tracked as CVE-2026-108099. It is not exploitable with the module alone, but exploit paths exist with other contributed modules.
“At least one known exploit path does not require authentication. Custom code may also expose the vulnerable functionality,” Drupal notes.
The second impacts the Field UI module in Drupal core and is tracked as CVE-2026-108097.
It is not exploitable with Drupal core alone, but contributed modules provide serious exploit paths, including at least one that does not require authentication. As a mitigation, users can uninstall the core Field UI module.
To address them, users are advised to update to Entity List version 3.0.10 and to Drupal versions 11.4.10, 11.3.19, or 10.6.19. Previous Drupal releases have reached end-of-life and no longer receive security updates.
The fresh Drupal updates also resolve cross-site scripting (XSS) holes in the Drupal core Link module (collectively tracked as CVE-2026-108515) and an XSS flaw in the Navigation module (CVE-2026-108514).
Additionally, Drupal announced patches for a security defect in the administration theme Gin that could lead to XSS attacks. Gin versions 5.0.16 and 4.1.4 contain fixes for the bug.
Drupal makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild. On October 12, however, it urged users to reserve time for core updates, warning that “exploits might be developed within hours or days.”
Additional information can be found on Drupal’s security advisories page.

articles.title: Hackers hijack AOMEI update servers to secretly spread malware
articles.text:
Hackers reportedly compromised AOMEI's servers to distribute malware through a built-in promotional feature in its backup software, briefly tampering with configuration files before restoring them to their original state to hide the attacks.
The supply chain attacks took place between April and July 2026 and targeted the update and notification systems used by AOMEI Backupper, a Windows application for backing up data, cloning disks, and restoring systems.
Researchers at ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), working with Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign and investigated the attacks.
In reports published by Google and ManageEngine, the activity is attributed to a threat actor tracked as UNC7017, who used the compromised infrastructure to distribute a previously unknown malware downloader called CROSSROAD and a backdoor named SHINYROAD.
The researchers identified affected organizations in multiple countries, including the United States, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain, and Switzerland, across sectors such as IT services, telecommunications, and higher education.
However, Google warned that the attacks were opportunistic and could have affected additional organizations that checked for software updates during the brief periods when malicious files were being distributed.
Software
The attacks were first detected on May 28, when ManageEngine said its endpoint security software spotted AOMEI Backupper suddenly installing the legitimate remote administration tool Radmin on computers at two unrelated companies in different countries.
The Radmin installation was suspicious because AOMEI's built-in promotion processes launched it, which normally handle downloading and displaying promotional content and notifications.
However, when researchers attempted to reproduce the behavior on their own test systems, they found nothing malicious. Instead, the software contacted AOMEI's servers and downloaded the legitimate configuration file.
Further testing showed that instead of permanently replacing files on AOMEI's servers, the attackers briefly modified two configuration files used by the promotion and notification systems:
https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini
https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini
The first file, down_html.ini, tells AOMEI Backupper where to download update packages. The second, Notifycfg.ini, controls notifications and can trigger content to run on the computer.
By modifying these files, the attackers redirected the software to download a malicious ZIP archive and then used the notification mechanism to execute the malware without requiring user interaction.
Researchers at Google later confirmed this execution flow in their own tests.
After failing to reproduce the original attack, ManageEngine began continuously monitoring AOMEI's servers.
On July 16, that monitoring finally captured the malicious modifications as they happened, confirming that AOMEI's systems were serving the malicious content.
The researchers also found that the attackers had modified the expected checksum in the update configuration, allowing the malicious archive to pass the software's file verification checks.
Google and ManageEngine say they identified three windows where the malicious configuration file was being sent by Aomei's servers:
- May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC)
- July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC)
- July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC)
The attackers restored the configuration files back to its original form within minutes, making the compromise difficult to detect.
During these windows, the malicious configuration file was used to install the CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD malware.
When launched, the CROSSROAD downloader checked the performed reconnasaince on the infected computer, downloaded additional components, and established persistence through a scheduled task.
SHINYROAD is a backdoor that used legitimate Radmin components to load malicious code and establish an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled command-and-control server.
This allowed the attackers to potentially execute additional commands and payloads on compromised computers.
During the July 20 attack, Google also observed a second technique that attempted to steal Windows authentication hashes by forcing the software's notification system to access an attacker-controlled WebDAV resource through an invisible popup.
This technique could expose NTLM hashes that can be collected by the attacker-controlled server and later cracked using various tools.
The researchers also identified several IP addresses and hostnames used during the attacks, including 8.210.84[.]56, serv.oss-cn-hongkong[.]aliyuncs.com, hostnames under storage-data[.]com, and storage.googleapis.com, a legitimate Google Cloud Storage endpoint.
AOMEI says CTO is investigating
ManageEngine told BleepingComputer that it first notified AOMEI about the suspicious activity on June 7, more than a month before researchers directly captured the malicious configuration files being served from its servers.
At the time, AOMEI initially suggested that the content may have been intercepted and modified while in transit, an explanation the researchers disagreed with.
"The evidence did not support AOMEI’s explanation of interception in transit," reads ManageEngine's report.
"Both endpoints had retrieved the content over HTTPS from AOMEI-owned hostnames, across different countries and unrelated network paths, and the executable had arrived through the application’s own extraction sequence rather than being written directly to disk by an external process. The content had been altered before it reached either endpoint, within the vendor-hosted delivery path."
When ManageEngine captured another attack on July 16, it immediately provided AOMEI with the original and modified file hashes, file differences, and altered files.
"AOMEI engaged, conducted its own review, and told us its initial examination had not found evidence of a breach," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer.
The researchers said AOMEI indicated that it planned to move the affected configuration files to new infrastructure with more detailed logging.
ManageEngine told BleepingComputer it advised AOMEI to preserve existing evidence before making those changes and to bring in incident-response specialists, connecting the company with Mandiant to assist with the investigation.
AOMEI later informed the researchers that its technical team had upgraded its servers, patched potential vulnerabilities, and verified that the files hosted on its infrastructure were correct.
Google also confirmed in its report that Mandiant notified AOMEI about the configuration file tampering on July 17 and that the company responded on July 29th, stating it took corrective action.
When contacted by BleepingComputer about the findings, AOMEI said it was treating the matter as a high priority and that its chief technology officer was leading an internal investigation.
"We have also internally detected this report and have classified it as a high-priority matter. Our CTO is currently leading a dedicated investigation to ensure accurate issue identification," AOMEI told BleepingComputer.
The company said its CTO would provide a more detailed response about the incident and the investigation's progress, and BleepingComputer will update this article if we receive new information.
AOMEI did not immediately confirm how attackers gained access to its update infrastructure or whether the reported compromise had been fully resolved.
While AOMEI says it has secured its servers, ManageEngine warns that these changes would not remove malware previously installed on customers' computers.
"A server-side fix stops new infections; it does not remove the backdoor from machines that received it during an earlier window," ManageEngine told BleepingComputer.
Organizations using AOMEI Backupper are advised to review the indicators of compromise published by Google and ManageEngine, including suspicious scheduled tasks, unexpected executable files in AOMEI installation directories, and connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

articles.title: Buildkite Adds Scoped Secrets and New Agentic CI Tools
articles.text:
Continuous integration provider Buildkite has introduced pipeline-scoped secrets and new Model Context Protocol tools for validating pipelines, diagnosing failed builds and repairing webhooks. The company has also added Linux arm64 support to its GitHub Actions compatibility layer and expanded OpenTelemetry data in Buildkite Agent v4.1.0.
The new secrets view is available under Pipeline settings. It lets engineers create cluster secrets whose access is restricted to the current pipeline, rather than managing every secret from the wider cluster interface. Teams can add conditions for a branch, queue, build source or build creator. Secret values remain hidden after creation.
Matt Mejia, writing in Buildkite's announcement, says the change "keeps pipeline-specific secrets together" while showing how many other secrets the cluster manages. Users need permission both to edit the pipeline and manage its cluster. GitHub Actions pipelines also display a prompt linking to secret configuration before their first workflow runs.
"Pipeline secrets are cluster secrets restricted to the current pipeline, and branch, queue, build source, or creator conditions narrow access further."
Matt Mejia
The Buildkite CLI now includes a command for migrating GitHub Actions secrets. Version 3.59.1 fixes handling of relative workflow paths during that migration. Agent v4.0.9 also redacts Buildkite tokens by prefix in job logs, while v4.0.8 redacts captured job errors using secrets registered for the job.
The work addresses several places where credentials can be exposed or configured incorrectly, although scoped storage does not remove the need to control their use inside steps. InfoQ reported in 2025 that HashiCorp was advocating prevention-first secret management throughout developer tools and CI/CD systems. Buildkite's own documentation advises teams to expose a secret only to the steps that require it.
The most extensive feature changes are in Buildkite's open-source MCP server. The new validate_pipeline tool checks pipeline YAML syntax and structure against Buildkite's official schema without uploading it or starting a build. It returns paths and error messages that an AI coding agent can use to correct invalid steps. The check does not cover environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dependency references or dynamically generated steps.
A second tool, compare_builds, compares a failed build with the most recent earlier successful build on the same branch, or with another selected build. It reports steps that have newly failed, recovered or remained broken, together with changes in runtime and retries. For up to three newly failing steps, it includes the end of the job log so an agent has some immediate diagnostic context.
"Log access alone does not debug a build."
Matt Mejia
The MCP release also adds Test Engine execution traces and slowest-execution queries. Another tool, create_pipeline_webhook, can add a missing GitHub webhook to an existing pipeline, avoiding the need to recreate it. Version 1.23.0 changed create_pipeline so that callers must specify create_webhook, which is a breaking change.
Buildkite reversed one earlier default after running evaluations, with failure summaries now again including jobs that never ran because making that behaviour optional led agents to issue extra tool calls. Remote MCP connections can now be pinned to one Buildkite organisation by adding it to the server URL. The option works with both toolset and read-only URLs.
Giving agents discrete validation, comparison and repair tools should reduce their reliance on parsing full logs and composing lower-level API calls. Permissions remain important because webhook repair and pipeline creation can modify CI configuration. InfoQ's coverage of GitHub agentic workflows describes a related security model based on isolated execution, restricted permissions and auditable actions.
Buildkite's GitHub Actions compatibility layer can now run its importer and generated jobs on Linux arm64 agents. Labels such as ubuntu-24.04-arm require an explicit queue mapping and do not fall back to x86-64 or emulation. The feature allows organisations with arm64 CI fleets to retain that architecture when bringing compatible Actions workflows to Buildkite.
Other compatibility fixes resolve environment values, named secrets, runtime variables and matrix values in service-container configuration. Buildkite has also exposed more strategy.* values to job and step expressions. The changed-file limit used by path filters has risen from 300 to 3,000, alongside a fix for push workflows where a branch moved after the original push.
Agent v4.1.0 adds cache save and restore durations and sizes to Buildkite telemetry. OpenTelemetry job spans now include the commit, pull request and build author. These fields add context for teams investigating slow jobs or retry patterns. Pinterest previously described using Honeycomb with Buildkite to separate agent waiting time from script execution and identify jobs behind build-time spikes.
The associated Elastic CI Stack v7 release brings Agent v4 to Linux and Windows instances on AWS. It removes Agent v3 support and retires or replaces some tracing and cancellation parameters. Buildkite advises users to review custom parameter files, deployment automation and values supplied through AgentEnvFileUrl before upgrading. Support for all Agent v3 releases ends on 3 September 2027.

articles.title: The Next Wave: Are layoffs good for AI’s business?
articles.text:
First published on October 18, 2026
Microsoft ADC offices at Dunhill Towers in Nairobi, Kenya. Image: TechCabal
Microsoft has shut its Africa Development Centre (ADC) in Nairobi, Kenya, leaving more than 400 engineers without jobs, following the closure of its Lagos engineering operation in May 2024. It has also closed sales offices in Windhoek, Abidjan, Dakar, Accra and Port-Louis. Microsoft says it “remains committed to Kenya”, but its retreat from the places where it once promised to build African engineering talent tells a different story. As the company and its peers pour billions into artificial intelligence (AI), these closures also reinforce a message that benefits the industry selling it. AI is coming for your job, and the companies building it are worth investing in.
The Nairobi decision is difficult to explain through performance alone. Employees familiar with the centre say it had no quality or performance problems, and some received strong appraisal ratings before learning their jobs were at risk. Microsoft has not publicly said poor performance prompted the decision. People close to the matter say about five employees across customer and partner solutions, recruitment, and sales will remain in the affected operation.
Announced in 2019, the centre was part of Microsoft’s $100 million commitment to build engineering capacity in Africa. The company planned to hire 500 engineers across Nairobi and Lagos, Nigeria, giving it access to local talent while offering African engineers the chance to work on products used worldwide. The Lagos hub closed in 2024, and Nairobi is now following suit, exiting Microsoft’s engineering business on the continent.
Microsoft may continue to serve African customers through its sales teams, cloud services, and other operations. But the closure of both engineering centres raises questions about the company’s long-term commitment to developing local technical talent. The people losing their jobs are not the only ones affected. Governments and universities that treated Microsoft’s investment as evidence of Africa’s place in the global technology industry must now reckon with its withdrawal.
The cuts also feed a narrative that AI will soon become central to how businesses operate. AI companies have raised enormous sums on the promise that their technology will change work, and layoffs attributed to AI give investors another reason to believe that promise.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Layoffs are becoming part of the AI sales pitch
Microsoft is not alone in using AI to explain workforce reductions. Amazon eliminated 14,000 corporate jobs in October 2025 and another 16,000 in January 2026, while Salesforce has linked its AI agents to a reduced need for customer support staff after cutting about 4,000 roles. In February 2026, Salesforce also laid off fewer than 1,000 employees across several functions. Across software, customer service, and other knowledge-based industries, AI has prompted companies to reconsider how many people they employ.
Some of these changes are real, given that AI tools can write code, summarise documents, answer customer queries, and handle repetitive administrative tasks. Companies have good reason to test whether these tools can reduce their costs, and some jobs will disappear as businesses automate work. It would be wrong to dismiss every AI-related redundancy as a publicity exercise.
The problem is that companies rarely separate the work AI can already perform from the work they expect it to perform in the future. A business might cut jobs because demand has weakened, teams overlap, or management wants to improve margins. AI may contribute to the decision, but it can also provide a convenient explanation for restructuring that would have happened anyway.
Cutting staff can improve a company’s financial results immediately, while the productivity gains promised by AI may take years to materialise. A company can reduce its payroll and report better margins before proving that its AI investments will generate enough money to cover its costs. The promise of future productivity can therefore help justify decisions whose immediate financial benefits come from employing fewer people.
There is also a commercial benefit to making AI appear unavoidable. When Microsoft, Amazon, or Salesforce announces cuts linked to AI, other executives face pressure to show they are preparing for the same future. Businesses fear falling behind, workers worry about their jobs, and investors look for companies positioned to profit. The announcements help sell AI as a necessity rather than a technology whose value must be judged against its cost.
There is no evidence that companies are coordinating layoffs to drive up demand for AI stocks. But the language surrounding the cuts can still benefit an industry whose valuations depend on investors believing that AI will become indispensable. That is worth examining, especially as two of its biggest players prepare to approach public markets.
The IPO is where the story gets expensive
OpenAI announced a funding round involving $122 billion in committed capital in March 2026, valuing the company at $852 billion after the investment. Microsoft has committed $13 billion to OpenAI through their partnership since 2019, of which $11.9 billion had been funded by June 2026, according to Microsoft’s annual filing. These figures cover different parts of OpenAI’s financing and should not be treated as separate investments.
Anthropic has attracted similarly large sums, raising $65 billion in May 2026 at a post-money valuation of $965 billion. That same month, the company reported an annualised revenue run rate above $47 billion.
A public listing would give the companies access to a broader pool of investors and allow some existing shareholders to sell their stakes. Investors who backed them privately could realise substantial returns if the market values them at levels above their previous funding rounds. The story they sell to public investors will need to justify those valuations.
OpenAI has reported rapid revenue growth, but it has yet to establish sustained profitability. Its spending on computing infrastructure and model development remains high, and projections suggest it may not generate positive cash flow until 2030. Revenue growth alone does not indicate whether the company can earn enough to cover the costs of developing and operating its systems.
Anthropic reported $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue in October 2026 and adjusted profitability for a second consecutive quarter, although its growth has slowed from earlier in the year. Adjusted profitability does not tell investors everything about the company’s long-term costs or whether it can sustain its margins.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have found strong demand for their products, and AI already has practical uses in software development, research, and customer support. They still need to prove they can turn that demand into profits and justify what investors are paying for them.
The blockchain boom of the 2010s offers a useful comparison, as investors were told the technology would change finance, agriculture, and supply chains, yet many promised applications never reached mainstream use. Blockchain had practical uses, but that did not make every company built around it a sound investment. AI could have a far greater commercial impact, but its potential does not guarantee that every company selling it will succeed.
Microsoft’s African closures do not prove a plan to inflate AI valuations, but they show how the company can abandon a long-term investment in local engineering while the industry it belongs to asks investors to believe AI will define the future of business. More than 400 engineers are losing their jobs, while investors are being offered a chance to profit from the technology being presented as the future of work.
The market should judge AI companies by the money they make, not just the money they raise or the jobs their customers cut. By the time OpenAI and Anthropic reach public markets, investors will have heard plenty about AI’s ability to replace workers. They will need to ask a harder question about whether the businesses promising that future can make enough money to justify their valuations.
Kenn Abuya
Senior Reporter, TechCabal

articles.title: Préparer deux croque-monsieur à la fois : l’appareil Tristar SA-3052 est à 11,99 €
articles.text:
L’appareil à croque-monsieur Tristar SA-3052 est à 11,99 € (-40 %)
L’appareil à croque-monsieur Tristar SA-3052 possède des plaques antiadhésives, une puissance de 750 W et un format permettant le rangement vertical.
Amazon propose l’appareil à croque-monsieur Tristar SA-3052 à 11,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 19,99 €, soit une réduction de 40 %. Le prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours est indiqué à 17,11 € : l’économie atteint donc également 5,12 €, soit environ 30 %, par rapport à ce repère. L’offre est expédiée par Amazon, avec des conditions de livraison à vérifier selon votre commande.
Deux croque-monsieur par fournée et une puissance de 750 W
L’appareil à croque-monsieur Tristar SA-3052 prépare deux sandwichs à la fois, avec des plaques dessinant des portions triangulaires. La surface de cuisson mesure 21,6 × 12 cm. Ce modèle est consacré aux croque-monsieur : il ne dispose pas des plaques interchangeables des appareils combinant également gril et gaufrier.
Sa puissance est de 750 W, avec une régulation automatique de la température. Des témoins lumineux renseignent sur le fonctionnement et la chauffe. Il n’y a ni thermostat réglable ni minuterie : la préparation repose sur un fonctionnement simple, en surveillant la cuisson selon le résultat souhaité.
Des plaques antiadhésives et un rangement vertical
Les plaques fixes possèdent un revêtement antiadhésif pour limiter l’accrochage des aliments et faciliter l’entretien. Elles ne se retirent pas et ne passent pas au lave-vaisselle. Le nettoyage s’effectue donc directement sur l’appareil, une fois celui-ci débranché et refroidi.
Le couvercle est équipé d’un loquet de fermeture et d’une poignée isolante. Les pieds antidérapants contribuent à la stabilité sur le plan de travail. Après utilisation, l’appareil peut se ranger horizontalement ou verticalement, avec un emplacement prévu pour son cordon : un équipement utile lorsque la place dans les placards est limitée.

articles.title: Apple dit tout sur la batterie de l'iPhone Duo : l'autonomie sera-t-elle à la hauteur ?
articles.text:
Pas le choix pour Apple : la marque a été forcée de publier sur son site l’étiquette énergétique européenne de son iPhone Duo. Historiquement, on pouvait connaître la capacité de batterie des produits Apple seulement en démontant ces derniers. Pour l’iPhone Duo, c’est plus simple et ça donne une idée de l’autonomie à attendre du premier smartphone pliant d’Apple.
Rien d’alarmant pour la batterie de l’iPhone Duo
L’iPhone Duo est équipé d’une batterie d’une capacité de 4 883 mAh, divisée en deux cellules. Un chiffre évidemment à comparer ave les batteries d’autres smartphones. Par exemple, l’iPhone 18 Pro dispose d’une batterie de 4 288 mAh (en version eSIM : la version SIM notamment vendue en France a une batterie de 4 056 mAh). Quant à l’iPhone 18 Pro Max, il affiche une grosse batterie de 5 567 mAh (5 391 mAh pour la version avec carte SIM). On le voit, l’iPhone Duo n’a pas à rougir sur les étagères des Apple Store.
Qu’en est-il comparé aux autres smartphones pliants similaires ? Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, sorti récemment, affiche une capacité de 4 800 mAh. Autre smartphone pliant au format passeport, le Xiaomi 18 Fold est vendu avec 6 000 mAh. En bref, c’est assez similaire avec l’iPhone Duo, bien que le modèle de Xiaomi surpasse la concurrence sur ce point.
Pas d’inquiétude non plus sur l’autonomie
Il faudra évidemment attendre les tests de l’iPhone Duo dans la presse pour se faire une idée, mais son endurance devrait être suffisante. En effet, Apple déclare que son iPhone Duo tient 31 heures en lecture vidéo (déplié, contre 44 heures plié). C’est moins bon que l’iPhone 18 Pro (34 heures) ainsi que la version Pro Max (43 heures).
En Europe, Apple doit donner un autre nombre sur l’étiquette énergétique européenne, l’« endurance de la batterie par cycle ». Il s’agit d’un test d’autonomie normalisé avec un scénario d’usage européen. Sur l’iPhone Duo, c’est 51 heures et 30 minutes, contre 52 heures sur l’iPhone 18 Pro et 62 heures sur l’iPhone 18 Pro Max. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 tient 49 heures et 10 minutes sur ce même test. Si l’on en croit ces chiffres, alors l’iPhone Duo serait un peu plus endurant que son concurrent de chez Samsung. Un comparatif qui sera vérifié par notre test de l’iPhone Duo grâce à notre protocole du 01Lab.
Tout ceci fait penser que l’iPhone Duo devrait permettre de l’utiliser une journée à une journée et demie par cycle de charge. Une autonomie suffisante pour la plupart des usages (écran plié ou déplié) : lecture vidéo, réseaux sociaux, messages, appels, etc. Pour rappel, l’iPhone Duo sortira ce 23 octobre, mais les précommandes sur le site d’Apple ne permettent qu’une livraison à partir du 25 janvier 2027. Il semblerait qu’Apple n’ait pas suffisamment anticipé les stocks de son nouveau smartphone.
