articles.title: Bloquear robots que hacen domicilios puede llevarte a la cárcel: el caso de Uber Eats
articles.text:
La policía de Filadelfia arrestó a Carolyn Marvin, una profesora jubilada de 78 años, por impedir durante varios minutos que un robot de reparto de Uber Eats completara su recorrido por una calle céntrica de la ciudad.
Marvin, profesora emerita de la Universidad de Pensilvania, fue acusada de conducta desordenada después de negarse a moverse pese a las órdenes reiteradas de los oficiales que respondieron al llamado.
La policía informó que recibió un reporte de “travesura criminal con un robot” en la cuadra 1200 de la calle Filbert, cerca del mercado Reading Terminal, alrededor de la 1:16 de la tarde.
Según el parte policial, Marvin bloqueó reiteradas veces el paso del robot e ignoró varias órdenes de los agentes para despejar el camino, lo que terminó en su arresto.
Una protesta que venía de antes
Los robots de reparto operados por la empresa Avride para Uber Eats comenzaron a circular por las calles de Filadelfia en marzo. Marvin dijo que desde entonces los enfrenta cada vez que se cruza con uno.
“Sé que le están quitando el trabajo a los repartidores humanos, así que los vengo protestando cada vez que los veo, parándome frente a ellos para impedir que avancen”, declaró Marvin al canal local WPVI.
La exprofesora, que dictó una materia sobre libertad de expresión en Pensilvania, dijo que sus protestas previas ya habían circulado en redes sociales, pero que esta fue la primera vez que intervino la policía.
Una vecina del barrio, Ashley Baldwin, contó que presenció uno de esos episodios anteriores. “Pensé que el robot la había chocado”, relató Baldwin, y agregó que Marvin le explicó que tenía que “detener esto” porque, según la propia Marvin, los robots “se están apoderando del mundo”.
El derecho a protestar, en disputa
Marvin sostuvo que actuó amparada por la primera enmienda de la Constitución de Estados Unidos. “Creo que es mi derecho constitucional manifestarme públicamente en una vereda para protestar contra los robots de reparto”, afirmó.
La exprofesora aclaró que nunca bloquea el paso de peatones y que, pese al arresto, piensa seguir parándose frente a los robots. “Me permite hablar con la gente sobre lo que está pasando”, explicó sobre las conversaciones que surgen durante sus protestas.
Un vocero de Uber a cargo de reparto autónomo celebró, en un comunicado citado por The Washington Times, el lanzamiento del servicio en la ciudad junto a Avride y dijo que la empresa espera “seguir llevando esta tecnología a más clientes de Uber Eats en colaboración con la comunidad de Filadelfia”.
Bajo las normas estatales de Pensilvania para dispositivos de reparto personal, los robots están obligados a ceder el paso a los peatones, según el Departamento de Transporte del estado. Las infracciones de los operadores pueden implicar multas de entre 25 y 1.000 dólares, de acuerdo con el diario The Philadelphia Inquirer.
Otros residentes ya los enfrentaron antes
El caso de Marvin no es aislado. Otros vecinos de Filadelfia patearon, voltearon o bloquearon unidades del mismo tipo de robot desde su llegada a la ciudad, según reportó el Inquirer.
La policía advirtió que quienes dañen los dispositivos podrían enfrentar cargos por daño criminal o infracciones al código municipal, dependiendo de las circunstancias de cada caso. Uber Eats permite a sus clientes optar por no recibir pedidos a través de los robots cuando el servicio está disponible en su zona.
Marvin dijo esperar que la atención generada por su arresto abra una discusión más amplia sobre los robots de reparto, la inteligencia artificial y su creciente presencia en la vida cotidiana.

articles.title: Valencia-based Linkener raises €7.5 million to digitise and optimise energy management for businesses | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Linkener, a Valencia-based EnergyTech startup that digitises and optimises energy management for businesses through a platform combining consumption metering, data analytics and AI, has closed a €7.5 million funding round.
The round was led by Klima Energy Transition Fund, Alantra’s energy transition fund, with GoHub Ventures remaining a shareholder. 
José Ignacio Ruiz, CEO of Linkener, said, “This funding round will allow us to accelerate the transformation of a highly fragmented sector, where energy management remains rooted in practices from 40 years ago. We want businesses to have reliable data and technology to understand how much they spend on energy, anticipate their costs and make better decisions.”
Founded in 2011, Linkener has developed an Intelligent Energy Management System (SIGE) with proprietary remote metering technology. It enables businesses and organisations to measure consumption using their own data, digitise and validate bills, analyse energy supply arrangements, and receive alerts, recommendations and savings proposals to help them reduce and control energy costs.
The company also has an engineering team that turns identified savings opportunities into practical projects and has delivered more than 400 solar PV and battery storage projects across Spain.
The Spanish startup reports that it serves more than 2,000 customers, ranging from self-employed professionals to large companies, and manages 10,000 energy supply points and 1.7 TWh annually. 
According to Linkener, there is significant scope to digitise and optimise energy management in the services sector, where monitoring and controlling consumption can deliver 20% savings and more efficient cost management.
Iñigo Echaniz, Partner at Klima, Alantra’s energy transition fund, said, “Energy management for businesses and organisations remains a highly fragmented market with enormous potential for digitisation. Linkener combines proprietary technology, independent energy data and direct relationships with thousands of customers, creating a distinctive foundation on which to add further capabilities and solutions. Our investment aims to support the team in this next stage of growth, both organically and through acquisitions, with the goal of building a leading technology platform for energy management.”
With this investment, the company aims to accelerate the development of its technology and proprietary artificial intelligence models for energy management. The company aims to use AI and advanced data analytics to automate the processing of energy information and bills, detect anomalies, and identify opportunities for optimisation and savings for its customers.
It also revealed that through M&A, Linkener intends to add new products and companies that complement its existing business and broaden the solutions available to customers, strengthening its product, technology and commercial capabilities.
Through this transaction, Linkener aims to grow both organically and through acquisitions. According to Ruiz, the company seeks to bring, in his words, “transparency and results to the thousands of businesses and organisations that do not want to manage their energy solely through a monthly bill that is biased, incomplete and fails to provide the full picture.”

articles.title: VSDC Free Video Editor
articles.text:
The program offers rich functionality and yet has a simple and intuitive interface, allowing you to create videos with a bare minimum of efforts.
Features
Non-linear video editor
Our editor is a non-linear tool. This means that unlike in most other editors, where scenes come one after another in a linear sequence and certain order, our software allows objects to be placed in any position on the timeline and have any size. Besides, various parameters, shape and position of objects can change arbitrarily over time.
Visual and audio effects
You can apply various visual and audio effects to your videos to achieve the necessary result. Since the number of available visual effect is very high, they are split into five categories for ease of navigation: color correction, object transformation, object filters, transition effects and special fx.
Blending modes and Instagram-like filters
One more way of changing the look of your video image according to your preferences is color blending. Using a wide array of adjustable parameters, you can attach a unique professional style to your video. Newbies or those, who would like to save time, can benefit from stylish Instagram-like filters applied in one click.
Masking
VSDC Free Video Editor allows for creating different shaped masks for hiding, blurring or highlighting certain elements in your video. You can use it to apply special effects inside or outside the masked area. One of the most common reasons for masking are to blur a face to protect the identity or remove unwanted marks.
Motion tracking
The Motion tracking tool allows for registering and tracking movements of any objects in a video and then assigns the resulted trajectory to other elements – titles, captions, icons, images, masks, and more. With its help, placing a censorship mask on a moving object or making captions follow a selected element in a video becomes easy.
Easy export to social networks
To prepare a video for Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Twitter and Vimeo without any problems, VSDC Free Video Editor offers you special export profiles which significantly reduce the stress of selecting a suitable format and meeting all the requirements.
Subpixel accuracy
Objects in a scene are positioned with subpixel accuracy, which makes for smooth animation, rotation, transformation and precise relative positioning.
Support of popular formats
Our software supports virtually all video, image and audio formats and codecs. That is why you won't need any additional conversion tools to edit your files, as is often the case with other programs.
4K and HD export
VSDC is currently the only free video editor that allows you to export in a new H265/HEVC codec to maintain the highest quality at a minimum file size which is essential for those often processing 4K and HD files.
Creation of videos for specific multimedia devices
Thanks to a large set of preconfigured profiles, you can easily create videos for most popular multimedia devices, such as DVD players, iPod/iPhone/iPad, PSP, Galaxy, any smartphones and regular phones, Sony PlayStation, Xbox, Zune, Archos, iRiver, Creative Zen, Blackberry, MP4 players and many others.
Working with charts
You can create diagrams of different kinds, including 3D diagrams: Bar, Stacked Bar, Point, Bubble, Line, Scatter Line, Fast Line, Step Line, Spline, Area, Spline Area, Stacked Area, Stacked Spline Area, Range Bar, Gantt, Pie, Pie 3D, Torus 3D, Radar Point, Radar Line, Radar Area, Radar Spline, Radar Spline Area, Funnel, Pyramid, Pyramid 3D, High Low, Candle Stick. These objects can be based on dynamically changing data of different types. Besides, the appearance of diagrams is fully customizable (appearance of charts, coordinate axes, user-defined axes, legends, names of charts and axes, lines, labels and other elements), which will help you tailor them to your specific needs. Integrated color themes make it possible to quickly change the way your charts look.
Video library (to be included in the next program release)
The editor software lets you create your own library of multimedia files with brief or detailed descriptions. This will help you organize your video collection and simplify access to the necessary files.
Video stabilization tool
Footage taken from drones, action cameras or other devices on the go often needs improvement. VSDC Stabilization tool, as your virtual tripod, helps remove jitter or any other shaking effects, caused by camera movement and turn it into a much smoother video image.
YouTube uploader
VSDC Free Video Editor not only provides ready-made profiles for exporting to social networks, but also offers you to upload your video directly to YouTube right from the app without switching windows or tabs.
Built-in DVD burning tool
The editor comes with a DVD burning tool, allowing you to easily burn the results of your work to optical discs.
Video File Converter
The application is designed to quickly convert video files from one format to another. It has some basic features for editing videos: removing unneeded segments, splitting your video into parts, and merging several files into one.
Desktop video capture
The video editor features a desktop video capture utility that saves captured footage to a video file for subsequent processing in the editor.
Video capturing
Another feature of the our editor is the ability to capture video from various video tuners, webcams, IP Ñameras and save the captured footage on your computer in an arbitrary format for subsequent editing.
What's New
VSDC 11.3 expands the editor with AI video and image generation, AI-powered image editing, new Garmin and DJI telemetry data, and major improvements to the Key Editor and scene editing workflow. The update also enhances project recovery, multi-object editing, interface customization, Lens Distortion accuracy and overall stability.
- Added AI-powered content creation tools:
 
  - AI image generation;
  - AI video generation;
  - AI-powered image editing.
- Expanded Garmin and DJI telemetry support:
 
  - Garmin telemetry now supports cadence, heart rate and compass data;
  - DJI telemetry now supports coordinates, speed and altitude.
- Improved the Key Editor for faster keyframe editing:
 
  - added Y-axis auto-scaling;
  - improved zooming and scrolling while changing the scale;
  - added multi-selection and simultaneous editing of multiple keyframes and points.
- Enhanced scene editing and object transformation:
 
  - added orthogonal movement while holding Shift for objects, custom points, FreeShape/Polyline points, service/tracking points and control points;
  - added proportional resizing for transformed objects while holding Shift;
  - added resizing relative to the object center while holding Alt or Alt+Shift.
- Project files now preserve the state of Timeline and Key Editor tabs, making it easier to continue editing after reopening a project.
- Added the ability to copy Basic Effects property values to selected objects by pressing Enter in the input field, improving multi-object editing.
- Improved Windows shutdown handling: VSDC can now create a recovery project when necessary if the computer is turned off while the editor is running.
- Added a dedicated menu command for removing offline media files from projects.
- Added Ribbon customization for a more flexible editing workspace.
- When multiple objects are selected, Basic parameters with different values are now highlighted in green for easier comparison.
- Added the ability to assign custom hotkeys to the compositing and waveform menus.
- Improved the precision of the Lens Distortion effect for more accurate image correction and creative distortion workflows.
- Added object type filtering through the Properties window to simplify navigation in complex projects.
- Minor improvements and bug fixes:
 
  - Fixed an issue where Quick Access Toolbar customization did not work correctly.
  - Fixed an issue where the Quick Access panel in the Telemetry templates window could disappear after restarting the application.
  - Fixed an issue where columns in the Link media window could be deleted without an option to restore them.
  - Improved rendering of curves and shapes on sharp bends.
  - When combining objects into a sprite, applied effects are now transferred to the sprite as well.
  - Improved keyboard shortcut handling.
  - Fixed an issue where block movement could become locked when snapping to the grid at 200% zoom and with negative coordinates.
  - Fixed an issue where a pane could not be dragged between monitors in certain multi-monitor configurations.
  - Fixed Unicode handling in XMP metadata.
  - Other stability improvements and minor fixes.

articles.title: Rivian's CEO says autonomy will enable 'dramatically different' vehicle designs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rivian is going full steam ahead on developing autonomous vehicle software for its EVs, to the point that it is willing to delay profitability. Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said last week at TechCrunch Disrupt that he thinks autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the outdoorsy SUVs and trucks it currently makes.
“Where it gets really interesting is when you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
This is not a new idea, to be sure. A decade ago, autonomous vehicle companies, legacy automakers, and many others promised that autonomy, combined with the proliferation of battery-electric drivetrains (which are simpler and take up less space than their gas-powered predecessors), would produce a Cambrian explosion of new mobility form factors.
This led to all kinds of crazy concepts getting bandied about at the time. Mercedes-Benz touted a bubbly pod-like design, as well as a long sedan packed with tech. Toyota and others dreamed up “rooms on wheels.” Hyundai once even showed off its idea for a car with legs.
This promised design revolution never escaped the concept and prototyping phase. Autonomy took longer than those companies anticipated to develop, and automakers (new and old) struggled with the harsh realities of manufacturing and selling an entirely new category of vehicle.
The difference now is that Scaringe’s comments come at a time when there are real robotaxis roaming the streets of multiple cities around the world. The software that powers them has seemingly developed to a level that is capable enough to operate them safely on public roads at scale, even if there are still some issues to work out when it comes to integrating them into the urban fabric of cars, bikes, pedestrians, and emergency vehicles. The components that make up electric vehicle motors and batteries have gotten cheaper, and companies like Tesla and Rivian (and many more in China) have gotten better at building them at scale.
Rivian has a lot of work ahead before it gets to driverless vehicles. The company is at the beginning of its effort to scale production of the R2 SUV, which it needs to get right in order to reverse years of losses that it incurred to become a major EV player.
On the autonomy side, Rivian is just a few years removed from completely reworking its approach to self-driving software, and it still has a ways to go.
The company has shipped a driver-assistance system that allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel, while still watching the road. It has promised that, by the end of this year, that software will be capable of driving from start to finish — which the company calls “point-to-point navigation” — without intervention, though still under driver supervision. And it is working toward full autonomy, which it plans to deploy in robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on Uber’s ride-hail app.
But if Rivian achieves full autonomy, most of that driving will be done in personally owned vehicles, Scaringe said in the interview, echoing previous comments he’s made.
“You know, 95% of the miles driven in the United States — so this is trillions of miles — 95% of these miles are in things that we personally own, so like you own it, or your household owns it. And so our view is it’s unlikely, even with Level 4 capabilities, that we’re going to see a dramatic societal shift away from that,” he said, referencing the Society of Automotive Engineers’ classification for autonomous vehicles that operate in a specific area.
That figure “may go from 95% to 90%, it may go from 95% to 80%, but still the vast majority of the miles driven for a lot of societal and psychological reasons are likely to stay the same,” he said.
It’s this belief that has Scaringe dreaming about the design of a fully autonomous, personally owned Rivian, he said.
As for what that looks like, though, Scaringe was mum.
“So we did R1, then we did R2, then we did R3. The thing after R3 is going to be called R4 — we just haven’t shown what it looks like,” he said. “It’s going to be cool. It’s going to be great.”

articles.title: Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
Pulsar Gaming Gears (AplusX Inc.), a leading developer of high-performance esports peripherals, and VAXEE Corporation, a respected innovator in gaming hardware, today announced the official launch schedule of the new Pulsar eS Xlite. This highly-anticipated product line is the result of the strategic exclusive partnership and joint development work between the two companies, aimed at delivering unparalleled innovation and performance to the esports community.
The Pulsar eS series is a unified vision for the future of competitive gear. Crafted from the absolute finest materials with flawless finishing and extreme precision, the eS Xlite is in running production and is not a limited edition, confirming Pulsar's commitment to making this reference-standard equipment widely available.Evolved Ergonomics for the Biggest Stages 
Retaining the beloved ergonomic advantages of the original Xlite, the eS Xlite introduces refined geometry to maximize grip stability and comfort. The mouse features a slimmer width that allows for an agile, secure grip, while the raised rear and rearward-shifted center of gravity provide full, stable support for the palm. This advanced shape allows the wrist to rest in a more natural, lower position, significantly reducing strain during extended tournament sessions. Additionally, the sensor position has been moved forward to perfectly align with the user's index and middle fingers, delivering highly consistent and precise horizontal tracking. 
Uncompromising Hardware & Next-Generation Performance 
Under the hood, the eS Xlite is powered by the next-generation XS2 Sensor, boasting up to 42,000 DPI, 800 IPS, and 70G acceleration. This significant upgrade ensures flawless tracking without spinouts, even during the most aggressive flick shots. The mouse fully supports an 8000 Hz (8K) polling rate in both wired and wireless modes. To drive this extreme performance, Pulsar integrated a dual-core-class MCU alongside a high-capacity 500mAh battery—delivering 2.5 times the capacity of its predecessor (200mAh) and offering up to 119 hours of continuous use at 1KHz. 
Weighing a perfectly balanced 51 g, the eS Xlite is presented in the signature Pulsar eS blue color. To guarantee hardware longevity and prevent double-clicking issues at the source, it is fully equipped with Pulsar Optical Switches. 
The Link 8K Dongle Integration
The eS Xlite signals a major milestone in competitive peripheral design with its seamless integration of the Link 8K Dongle. Functioning as an active controller rather than a passive wireless receiver, the Link 8K allows players to instantly adjust critical settings—such as DPI, polling rate, and profiles—using its built-in buttons, eliminating the need to interrupt intense gameplay by flipping the mouse or accessing software. 
Pricing & Availability 
The Pulsar eS Xlite carries a suggested retail price of $179.95 USD. The Pulsar eS Xlite is available as of today.

articles.title: "Grampo" na OpenAI: juiz vê risco de fuga e nega liberdade a ex-engenheiro da empresa
articles.text:
Um juiz federal dos Estados Unidos determinou que Abdulrahman Alfozan, ex-engenheiro da OpenAI, permaneça preso sem direito a fiança enquanto aguarda o andamento do processo criminal em que é acusado de instalar um dispositivo de gravação clandestino em um escritório da empresa em São Francisco, na Califórnia (EUA).
A decisão foi tomada nesta segunda-feira (19), após o magistrado Alex Tse considerar que há risco significativo de o acusado não comparecer à Justiça. Durante a audiência, o juiz também questionou a proposta do consulado saudita de assumir integralmente o pagamento de uma eventual fiança, classificando a oferta como problemática.
Alfozan, de 35 anos, foi preso em 9 de outubro. Ele é acusado de interceptar comunicações orais por meio de dispositivo eletrônico e pode enfrentar até cinco anos de prisão se for condenado.
Promotores apontam contatos com a família real saudita
- Em documentos judiciais, os promotores afirmaram que Alfozan mantinha contato frequente com um integrante não identificado da família real da Arábia Saudita. Segundo a acusação, essa pessoa teria tentado recrutá-lo em diversas ocasiões para participar de uma iniciativa de inteligência artificial (IA) no país;
- Uma das mensagens trocadas pelo WhatsApp, reproduzida no processo, trazia a frase: “A Arábia Saudita precisa mais de você do que os Estados Unidos”. De acordo com os promotores, Alfozan respondeu com “100”, expressão usada para indicar concordância;
- Os procuradores também apontaram que o engenheiro havia comprado uma passagem aérea só de ida para Riade, capital saudita, com embarque previsto para 12 de outubro. Para a acusação, a compra reforça o risco de fuga;
- O advogado de defesa, William Pernik, contestou essa interpretação. Ele afirmou que Alfozan tinha uma entrevista para obter a cidadania estadunidense marcada para 6 de novembro;
- A esposa do engenheiro e o bebê do casal deixaram os Estados Unidos em 10 de outubro, um dia após a prisão. Segundo os promotores, as passagens foram pagas por um oficial militar saudita.
Leia mais:
- 8 estados dos EUA processam OpenAI e acusam ChatGPT de colocar jovens em risco
- OpenAI alerta Polícia Federal sobre ameaças contra Lula feitas no ChatGPT
- Deepfakes podem dificultar análise de provas, alertam OpenAI e Meta
Dispositivo foi encontrado em sala de reuniões
Alfozan trabalhava na OpenAI desde 2025. A empresa descobriu um dispositivo de gravação escondido atrás de uma televisão em uma sala de reuniões executiva, em setembro. O equipamento estava envolto em papel higiênico e conectado a uma porta USB.
De acordo com a acusação, as reuniões realizadas no local frequentemente envolviam informações confidenciais sobre pesquisas, produtos, estratégias comerciais e decisões da companhia.
Embora o caso tenha levantado preocupações sobre segurança nacional entre autoridades estadunidenses, Alfozan não foi formalmente acusado de espionagem. Os promotores afirmam que a investigação continua e que ela pode resultar em acusações adicionais.
A próxima audiência está prevista para 6 de novembro.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
articles.text:
About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest.
The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.
The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before.
Once around the Earth
The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered something unusual while combining his cornfield for the fall harvest. A circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks in Scott Township, a community in west-central Minnesota.
The Stevens County Sheriff’s Office said it received a phone call reporting the discovery Wednesday.
“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” the Sheriff’s Office wrote on Facebook. “The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field.”
Law enforcement officials said the debris posed no danger to the public. That might not have been true had the object reentered over a more populated area. Space junk routinely falls out of orbit, and fragments of old rockets or satellites sometimes survive the heat of reentry to reach the ground. No one has ever been seriously injured by falling space junk, but there are a few examples of property damage.

articles.title: Anthropic quer barrar IAs apenas diante de riscos extremos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Anthropic quer barrar IAs apenas diante de riscos extremos
Projeto prevê bloqueio de modelos que ameacem causar mais de 50 mortes ou ferimentos graves, ou prejuízos acima de US$ 1 bilhão.
A Anthropic, dona do Claude, propôs que o governo federal dos EUA só possa bloquear modelos avançados de IA diante de riscos catastróficos, incluindo ameaças de morte, ferimentos graves em mais de 50 pessoas ou prejuízos acima de US$ 1 billhão (R$ 5,08 bilhões).
O site Politico obteve o rascunho do projeto de lei. A iniciativa da Anthropic seria uma forma de estabelecer regras mais claras sobre o desenvolvimento e o uso de modelos avançados de inteligência artificial.
O texto prevê análises regulares dos laboratórios e de seus modelos por avaliadores independentes. Se identificassem um risco iminente previsto no documento, eles deveriam comunicar suas conclusões em até 72 horas ao Departamento de Comércio. Caberia ao órgão apresentar as evidências a um juiz federal, que decidiria sobre a suspensão.
Outros departamentos, agências ou autoridades federais também ficariam impedidos de suspender o desenvolvimento, a implantação ou o uso de um modelo. O texto transferiria esse poder apenas ao Departamento de Comércio e Justiça federal.
A discussão ocorre após episódios de segurança relatados pela própria Anthropic. Em uma revisão de mais de 141 mil execuções de testes, a companhia identificou incidentes envolvendo acesso não autorizado a sistemas de organizações reais. Segundo a empresa, uma falha de configuração permitiu que modelos alcançassem a internet durante avaliações que deveriam ocorrer em ambientes isolados.
Em setembro, a Anthropic também afirmou ter bloqueado consultas ao Claude que poderiam contribuir para a criação de armas biológicas. Em paralelo, o desenvolvedor Jacob Coxon deixou a companhia e criticou a corrida pela superinteligência, alertando sobre possíveis riscos à vida humana.

articles.title: Warum in Windows 11 ein Relikt aus Windows 95 steckt - und was SimCity damit zu tun hat.
articles.text:
Windows 11: Dieser Teil von Windows 95 ist im System noch immer aktiv
Der offizielle Support von Windows 95 endete am 31. Dezember 2001. Doch auch 25 Jahre später ist ein Teil des Betriebssystems von Microsoft im Nachfolger Windows 11 aktiv. Selbst in dessen aktuellem Funktionsupdate 26H2, das Microsoft am 26. September 2026 veröffentlichte.
EmulateHeap als Relikt von Windows 95
Bei dem Relikt handelt es sich laut Windows Latest um EmulateHeap. Dieser Kompatibilitäts-Patch ermöglicht es den Nutzer:innen von modernen Microsoft-Betriebssystemen, alte Software oder Spiele aus der Ära von Windows 95 zum Laufen zu bringen.
EmulateHeap kopiert die Eigenschaften des Speichermanagers von Windows 95 für neuere Systeme. Denn der hält gerade für Games Vorteile bereit, die spätere Inkarnationen von Windows nicht haben.
Microsoft änderte für SimCity Code von Windows 95
Wenn Windows Programme ausführt, greifen die temporär auf Speicherkapazitäten zurück. Sobald man die Applikation beendet, wird der Speicherplatz wieder freigegeben.
Doch manchmal kann es zu einem Bug namens Use-after-free kommen. Dabei greift ein Programm auf einen Speicherbereich zu, nachdem der bereits freigegeben wurde. Dies kann zu einem Absturz führen.
Einen dieser Softwarefehler enthielt SimCity, das 1989 auf den Markt kam. Doch auf Rechnern, die mit Betriebssystemen aus der 1990 gestarteten Windows 3.x-Familie liefen, fiel dies nicht auf. Windows 3.0 und Co. funktionierten mit einer anderen Speicherarchitektur.
Doch als SimCity auf der Beta von Windows 95 getestet wurde, stürzte die Städtebausimulation ab. Anstatt auf einen Patch vonseiten der Macher von SimCity zu warten, änderten die Verantwortlichen bei Microsoft kurzerhand den Code von Windows 95 und ermöglichten dem Spiel den Zugriff auf eigentlich wieder freigegebenen Speicher.
Darum erschuf Microsoft EmulateHeap
Der Fix von Windows 95 war als Ausnahme für SimCity gedacht. Doch später zeigte sich, dass auch andere Spiele und Programme auf die Eigenheit des Speichersystems vertrauten. Bei späteren Versionen von Windows stürzten diese Apps ab. Als Lösung für dieses Problem schuf Microsoft EmulateHeap. Der Patch leitet Befehle wie HeapCreate oder LocalLock auf die simulierte Speicherverwaltung von Windows 95 weiter.
Bei Windows 11 findet man EmulateHeap in den Systemdateien. Um es zu finden, muss man laut der Lernplattform Microsoft Ignite bei alten Spielen oder Programmen einen Rechtsklick auf die .exe-Datei machen. Danach „Eigenschaften“ den Reiter „Kompatibilität“ auswählen. Dort dann einen Haken bei „Programm im Kompatibilitätsmodus ausführen für: Windows 95“ setzen.

articles.title: Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
articles.text:
Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.
Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
The Baseus U2 Pro can deter intruders instead of just capturing them on camera.
The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.
Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.
Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

articles.title: Creality Pika 3D scanner review: Good things come in small packages
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Creality Pika is a truly portable scanner with excellent software. We were impressed with its ability to work cordlessly when paired with an iPhone 15 or Android 10 (or newer).
Reasons to buy
- + Inexpensive
- + Small and lightweight
- + Doesn’t need marking dots with NIR mode
- + No problem with small, shiny, or black colored objects
- + Improved calibration routine
Reasons to avoid
- - Tracking using Near-Infrared (NIR) mode is challenging
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
A 3D scanner is an amazing tool to add to your 3D printing workflow, allowing you to scan real-life objects to import into sculpting or CAD software, then print out your own modified copies on a 3D printer. In the past, a good scanner cost thousands of dollars, but Creality has finally given us a device within reach of hobby-level consumers. The Creality Pika is easy to use, with the look, feel, and size of a point-and-shoot digital camera. It can wirelessly tether to a mobile phone running a Creality scanning app, which makes scanning on the go easier than ever before.
It can also be tethered to a laptop wirelessly or with a cable for more stable scanning, but marker-free laser scanning can only be performed while physically tethered to a computer. The scanner runs on AA-sized rechargeable batteries, which are provided.
It weighs just 260 grams (just slightly over a half-pound) with the batteries installed, reducing arm fatigue when operating without a tripod. A tabletop tripod and manual turntable are included for scanning small items. While not as precise as Creality’s Sermoon series, the Creality Pika, currently on pre-order for $699, is a fraction of the price. The best part is that both use the same software, Creality Scan, which is excellent.
The Creality Pika’s portability and price make this one of the best scanners we’ve reviewed in 2026.
Specifications: Creality Pika
| Scanning Mode | Blue laser | NIR structured light | 
| Light Type | 7 parallel lines | NIR (Near-Infrared) | 
| Single Frame Accuracy | .03mm | Up to .08mm/m | 
| 3D Resolution | 0.05-2mm | 0.1mm | 
| Working Distance | 160-400mm | 140-1000mm | 
| Min Scan Volume | 10 x 10 x 10 mm | 50 x 50 x 50 mm | 
| Scan Speed | Up to 90fps | Up to 90fps | 
| Alignment | Markers/global marker/marker free | Geometry/Texture | 
| Connectivity | Wired USB, Optional WiFi | Row 8 - Cell 2 | 
| Color Texture | Supported | Row 9 - Cell 2 | 
| Output Format | OBJ, STL, PLY | Row 10 - Cell 2 | 
| Operating System | Windows or Mac | Row 11 - Cell 2 | 
| MSRP | $699 | Row 12 - Cell 2 | 
| Release Date | July 22, 2026 | Row 13 - Cell 2 | 
Included in the Box: Creality Pika
The Creality Pika comes with a very nice tripod. Also included are the glass calibration board, a manual turntable, marking blocks, batteries (including a spare), a generous pack of marking dots, and a mostly useless quick start guide. The Quick Start guide is just a packing list in eleven different languages and QR codes to Creality’s website and Facebook community.
Design of the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika is a small handheld scanner that weighs only 260 g with its battery. It has a 3-inch touch screen on the back that shows the scan in progress while paired to a phone or PC on Wi-Fi, or allows exposure and zoom adjustments when scanning via cord. There are two buttons on the top of the scanner for power and start/stop, and a selector switch for USB or Wi-Fi.
The scanner has a play button to start and stop scans, as well as a button to adjust the lights and a toggle for zoom. The front of the scanner has an RGB camera, two 3D scanning cameras, a DOE projector, a parallel-line laser, four blue and white fill lights, and four infrared fill lights. There is an always-on cooling fan with grills on the top and bottom of the scanner. Two batteries are included, which can be charged in the camera or via a USB-C port located near the top of the battery.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The batteries, curiously, have both positive and negative terminals on top of the battery. Care should be taken when carrying these to avoid shorting them together with anything metal in a purse or pocket.
Getting Started and Calibrating the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika uses a glass calibration board to do an initial calibration of the scanner. The calibration process involves holding the scanner above the board at various heights and at various angles. The process takes about ten minutes.
Installing the Software for Creality Pika
Creality Scan app can be downloaded from Creality's website, with versions for PC, Mac, Android, and iPhone. A really good user guide with links to tutorials and troubleshooting help is located on the Creality Scan homepage. The discovery tab has links to items scanned by other Creality users.
The Pika must be tethered by cable or Wi-Fi. Though the Pika does have an onboard 8-core 2.0 GHz CPU, it passes along a big chunk of computer processing to whatever it’s connected to. My iPhone 15 has just enough oomph to power the scanner, so you may have an even better experience with a newer device. Either way, using a wireless connection is slower, and using it with hardware near the minimum requirements can be frustrating.
My old laptop, with only 8GB of RAM, did not work, despite being enough to run previous scanners. Thankfully, my admittedly low-end gaming laptop, with 16GB of RAM, was good enough to run the scanner quite well. The software installed on the computer is used for both scanning and processing.
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Minimum Requirements | Creality Recommends | 
|---|---|---|
| For Windows | · i7-Gen7 CPU · Nvidia GPU (8GB VRAM) · 16GB RAM · Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit) | · i7-Gen13 CPU or above · Nvidia GPU RTX 3060 or above · 32GB RAM · Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit) | 
| For Mac | · macOS 14 or above · M2 Apple CPU · 16GB RAM | · macOS 14 or above · M3/M4/M5 Apple CPU · 32GB RAM | 
| For iPhone | · iOS15+ with an A15 chip or above · 6GB RAM | · iOS15+ with an A17 chip or above · 8GB RAM | 
| For Android | · Android OS 10+ · Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen2 chip or better · 8GB RAM | · Android OS 10+ · Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen4 chip or better · 12GB RAM | 
Creality Scan can export scans as STL, PLY, OBJ, or ASC files. These files can be tidied up in other modeling software or uploaded directly to your 3D printer’s slicer.
Blue Laser Line 3D Scanning with the Creality Pika
The Creality Pika uses blue laser line scanning for detailed geometry capture, with seven parallel laser lines. The provided manual turntable works well when plastered with a bunch of the included marker dots. Unfortunately, it has a few millimeters of play in the center bearing, which can lead to a rough surface texture if not careful.
The photo above shows the raw scan of a copy of Michelangelo’s David. I did get much better scans later, but even this one is easily made usable in the software. The first step is fusing the model, which allows you to remove the marker dots and noise from the scan.
After fusing, the model is much smoother. There are still some unattached pieces and holes, and the bottom of the model is not flat. The lasso tool can select and remove the unattached pieces, and a clipping plane can be generated by choosing markers surrounding the scan. The plane can then be raised or lowered to give you the best base of the model.
The next step is mesh processing of the model. In this step, you can further smooth the model, simplify it, and fill small holes shown in yellow. Don’t select “make watertight” if you have a large hole (like the bottom of a model), as it will cover the holes by ballooning out a good bit. After running the mesh processing, you will have another opportunity to simplify, smooth, and fill holes.
Use Plane type hole filling for large flat surfaces.
The final model: filled, smoothed, simplified, and ready to export for printing.
This bust of David came with an early Creality scanner, so I’ve been using it as a test model for some time now. This may be the best scan I’ve gotten of it. The main reason is that the Creality Pika is small and lightweight, and tracks well enough to scan the underside of David’s hair and chin for the most part. The software’s hole filling and smoothing did the rest, with phenomenal results.
The above image on the right was printed on the Prusa Core One L with Inland Bone White PLA. The model looks nearly perfect.
Since the Pika did so well with David, I decided to try a smaller model. This little guy (below) came with my kid’s Fisher-Price castle. He’s only 62 mm tall and was just too small to paint for 3D printing. He was also printed in Inland bone white on the Prusa Core One L.
Both the print and scan are nicely detailed.
I swiped my husband’s vintage Saint Louis University Billiken bobblehead for more tests. I had to put some sticky tack on his head to keep it steady on the turntable. Creality Scan did a terrific job smoothing out the wrinkles, and the model is perfect. I used the clipping plane to remove the logo of an old wireless company that provided the game day freebie. I gave it a quick coloring job in PrusaSlicer, but skipped doing the face.
The model was printed on the Prusa XL using Anycubic turquoise and orange PLA, with Creality white and black PLA.
NIR 3D Scanning with the Creality Pika
I spent a ton of time putting random dots on the included turntable, which made Blue light scanning a breeze. NIR 3D scanning doesn’t use them. Scanning a person seems to work well until you get hair involved. Then it gets dodgy.
I ran two good scans using NIR. This time I borrowed my husband to operate the scanner, since scanning yourself is a bit more difficult than taking a selfie. I stitched together two scans of my foot, which I’ll use later to size some TPU shoes. I was able to further clean up the scan in Nomad Sculpt, since the scan wasn’t very flattering. It works quite well for sizing, however. The shoes will turn up in a future printer review.
After the less-than-stellar scan he took of my head for the Creality Sermoon S1, my husband graciously volunteered to have me scan his head for this review. Using any of the modes available, hair just seems to flummox the scanner. Fortunately, my husband has less hair than I do, so the scan did complete, and no, I’m not going to 3D print it. 3D scans are quite brutal, but if he ever wants a custom driver for his Death Racer, we’re covered.
Bottom Line
The Creality Pika is a small and light, yet totally capable scanner. It needs a good mobile phone or fairly decent laptop to drive it. The software backing up the hardware is easy to use and really does an excellent job cleaning up the rough areas of your scans. Currently, it is available at a comparatively bargain-basement pre-order price of $699.
If you want a scanner with a little more horsepower, check out the Creality Sermoon S1, which retails for $2,069. Creality also makes the Sermoon P1, which can run completely untethered and retails for $3,299.
Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

articles.title: 'What AI mostly brings is persistence': AIs from Anthropic and OpenAI are cracking ciphers and encryption protocols in record time
articles.text:
'Is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years?': AI keeps breaking old encryption mysteries, and quietly dunking on humans in the process
Code cracking made to look easy
- GPT-6 Astra has cracked the code on a 19th-century military cipher
- Claude AI has also been busy testing elliptical curve encryption
- Both breakthroughs highlight the increasing capabilities of AI models
AI continues to push the boundaries in almost every task it gets given, and two new reports highlight the tech's growing capabilities when it comes to code-breaking and testing widely used encryption security protocols.
First up, Japan Today reveals that AI engineer Carter Church has used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to crack a written code used by one of Napoleon Bonaparte's generals more than 200 years ago. The message dates from 1809, and mentions the positions of troops belonging to France and its allies.
The letter was sitting ignored in an online archive when Church decided to give it a go. Manually decoding the symbols, numbers, and letters could have taken weeks, but the AI was done in just six hours.
"What AI mostly brings is persistence," Church told AFP, adding that he felt "an unbelievable sense of satisfaction and excitement" when the result appeared. It was verified by patent engineer Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains an online list of unsolved ciphers for amateur cryptographers to tackle.
Curves and keys
Our second bit of AI code-breaking concerns cryptographic key generation — the methods software and hardware use to encrypt and secure data. Elliptic curves are one way to produce the keys required, and 'seeds' are starting points for these curves.
As reported by Cyber Security News, an internal Claude AI model used by Anthropic has now traced the origins of five elliptic curve seeds generated by the US National Security Agency (NSA) in less than 30 minutes. For more than 25 years, since the seeds were published, there have been claims that they contained weaknesses the NSA could use as backdoors.
Not so, Claude has now determined — there are no weaknesses, and no inside jokes. As Anthropic points out, most researchers trusted the curves already and no action is necessary, but it's a "fun closing chapter" that again demonstrates the AI's prowess.

Claude also had time for a quiet dig at human cryptographers. "Is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn't discovered in 25 years?" the AI asked on its way to finding the correct solution, according to the internal thinking logs. Not only are these models outperforming us at the core math, they're dunking on us along the way.

articles.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
articles.text:
“We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.
After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.
That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”
Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”
“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”
Knotted networks
It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.
Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025.)
Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.
The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.
Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot. But despite a few breakthroughs, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail.
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.
Nothing but neurons
At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don't know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.
What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don't want to give up too quickly.”
Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”
But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”
Back to cars and cats
Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.
It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”
It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.
Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.
The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”
Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. He is saying that he no longer thinks full understanding is impossible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.
“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”
He adds: “And if that's true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”
Boundless optimism
Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.
In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.
In a series of posts on X, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”
Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he wrote on X.
Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.
Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”
Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge risks—needs a lifeline right now. They think that things are looking bad and that even if things do turn out okay, it will be because we got lucky, not because we fixed anything, he says: “I don’t really hear a lot of optimism.”
That’s why Cammarata thinks what he has to say matters. The job of figuring out how this technology works, and thus how to control it, has barely begun. But at least it’s not a nonstarter. “I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network,” he says. “My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read.”

articles.title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
Interesting research:
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns.
Clive Robinson • October 19, 2026 9:49 AM
@ ALL,
Training a Current LLM AI to solve a CAPTCHA should be well within it’s capabilities…
But what price the LLM usage cost compared to some 1$/Day person or a bowl of rice and beans captive in a slave compound just the right side of a totalitarian national boarder?
Also the humans tend to learn from each and every CAPTCHA that they solve. So there is a degree of equality in the arms race.

articles.title: El Galaxy A56 recibe One UI 9: todo lo nuevo que llega con la actualización de Android 17
articles.text:
Samsung ha comenzado el despliegue global de One UI 9 para el Galaxy A56. Uno de los móviles más populares de la gama media recibirá por fin la actualización a Android 17, que viene cargada de novedades y un diseño más refinado. Tras lanzarse en Corea del Sur, la actualización ya comenzó a llegar a más países, por lo que pronto podrás instalarla en tu móvil.
De acuerdo con SamMobile, la actualización a One UI 9 para el Galaxy A56 se identifica con el firmware A566BXXUEDZJ1 y pesa unos 2,3 GB. Samsung la ha catalogado como una de las actualizaciones más importantes para este móvil, ya que incorpora Android 17 y una larga lista de mejoras en productividad, personalización y seguridad.
Entre los cambios más importantes de One UI 9 se encuentran las opciones de personalización para el panel rápido, cambios en DeX y actualizaciones a casi todas las apps de Samsung. Esta versión cuenta con un rediseño en el que se mejoró la organización de algunos elementos del sistema y se añadieron más posibilidades de configuración para que cada usuario adapte el móvil a sus preferencias.
El Galaxy A56 recibe estas funciones con One UI 9
En el apartado de la IA, Samsung añadió tarjetas generativas y editables a Now Brief, que permiten personalizar la información que aparece en el resumen diario. En el caso de Now Nudge, el sistema ofrecerá sugerencias contextuales en tiempo real para mejorar la productividad. One UI 9 también incluye Creative Studio, que propone ideas visuales para cumpleaños o festividades, así como My FanCam, una función de la cámara que sigue automáticamente a una persona y ajusta la toma según su movimiento.
Pasando a la seguridad, One UI 9 añade alertas de privacidad más avanzadas, las cuales te avisarán sobre posibles comportamientos sospechosos. Si bajas una app y el sistema detecta permisos inusuales, tu Samsung lanzará una notificación para que no caigas en la trampa. La compañía también ha reforzado los mecanismos de protección para identificar software potencialmente peligroso, de modo que tu dispositivo se mantenga protegido siempre.
Otros ajustes incluyen una actualización a Samsung Notes, que recibe nuevas herramientas creativas y mejoras orientadas a la productividad. Las funciones de accesibilidad añaden opciones que facilitan la lectura y mejoran la interacción con personas con distintas necesidades. Por último, el panel rápido ofrece un mayor nivel de control, mientras que varias aplicaciones del ecosistema reciben pequeños retoques destinados a agilizar las tareas diarias.
¿Qué móviles de Samsung recibirán One UI 9?
El Galaxy A56 no es el único que ha recibido la actualización de One UI 9. Hace unos días, Samsung anunció el despliegue para el Galaxy S23 y otros modelos que tuvieron que esperar algunos meses para tener la versión estable. articles.title: Shopify CTO Mikhail Parakhin to depart after two years
articles.text:
Former Microsoft executive Mikhail Parakhin is departing as CTO of Ottawa-based retail technology giant Shopify after just over two years in the role, BetaKit has confirmed.
The news: An anonymous X post from Saturday was the first to indicate Parakhin’s departure. BetaKit has since confirmed with Shopify that Parakhin is leaving that position and transitioning to an advisor.
Shopify did not disclose when or why Parakhin is departing, or share any other details regarding this move. BetaKit has also reached out to Parakhin for comment, but he had not responded by publication time.
From the source: “Mikhail has left an indelible mark on the company and has helped us level up in engineering and machine learning [ML],” a Shopify spokesperson told BetaKit over email. “As he leaves, we’re grateful for his contributions and glad that he’ll continue as an advisor.”
The context: Parakhin previously served as CTO of Moscow-based tech firm Yandex, and held senior executive roles at American tech giant Microsoft, including CEO of advertising and web services. Shopify brought on the Russian-trained physicist-turned-ML engineer as CTO in late 2024 for his deep expertise in AI. In that role, he took over for Allan Leinwand, who stepped down in early 2023 for “personal reasons.”
Final thought: Under Parakhin’s leadership, Shopify has invested heavily in building AI for merchants and deploying the tech internally to improve its efficiency and expedite product development. Parakhin’s LinkedIn profile, which is not yet updated, lists his focus as “bringing AI into the shopping space.” Parakhin appeared in an ad for OpenAI’s Codex just last week, highlighting how he was using the agentic tool at Shopify. Time Magazine recently named him one of its tech executives of the year for his work rebuilding the commerce platform for the age of AI. It is not yet clear what Parakhin plans to do next or who, if anyone, will replace him in Shopify’s CTO chair.
Disclosure: BetaKit majority owner Good Future is the family office of two former Shopify leaders, Arati Sharma and Satish Kanwar.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’
articles.text:
President Donald Trump announced this afternoon that Elon Musk’s SpaceX shares for children will be given through Trump Accounts. Musk said earlier today that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” sometime next year. Musk had thanked Trump Account booster Brad Gerstner for “helping enable this,” and Trump appeared to confirm the plan in a post on Truth Social.
Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’
The White House said 60 million of the tax-advantaged accounts for kids were created automatically in October.
Given the value of SpaceX’s stock on Friday, 72 million shares would be worth approximately $10.5 billion, according to CNBC. “This will be the first of many,” Musk said.
Michael and Susan Dell, Ray and Barbara Dalio, Gerstner, and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell have all also promised contributions to Trump Accounts. In October, the White House said that after automatically enrolling some 60 million children, over 70 million accounts had been created.

Opimizing embedded memory IP for RibbonFET and PowerVia.
								October 19th, 2026 - 
								By: Synopsys
								
							
Embedded memory, not compute, has become the limiting factor in AI and HPC SoCs, consuming more than half of total die area while constraining bandwidth, latency, and energy efficiency. As the industry transitions to gate-all-around (GAA) devices and backside power delivery network (BSPDN) technology, embedded memory architectures must evolve to keep pace.
This white paper examines how these shifts redefine embedded memory requirements and how Synopsys Embedded Memory IP addresses them through device-aware architectures, power-optimized designs, and highly configurable compilers. It also presents silicon results from SRAM and Register File test chips on the Intel 18A process node, including density improvements in the 5–10% range and ISO-power performance gains of up to approximately 4%.
Read the paper to discover how RibbonFET and PowerVia enable PPA improvements and reduce advanced-node integration risk.

- Why embedded memory, not compute, is limiting AI and HPC SoC performance
