articles.title: Pour accélérer ses calculs d’IA, Apple ressuscite une idée vieille de plus de 25 ans
articles.text:
Avec Minions, Apple expérimente une façon de traiter certaines tâches d’IA sans acheter de GPU supplémentaires. Le projet mobilise la puissance inutilisée des Mac équipés de puces Apple Silicon pour désengorger ses infrastructures d’intelligence artificielle. Une vieille idée remise au goût du jour.
Même chez Apple, il faut parfois patienter pour accéder à suffisamment de puissance de calcul. Certaines tâches d’intelligence artificielle soumises par les développeurs aux serveurs de l’entreprise mettaient ainsi plus de dix heures avant de pouvoir démarrer. Avec Minions, des chercheurs de Cupertino ont trouvé une parade assez astucieuse pour accélérer tout cela en récupérant les ressources graphiques inutilisées des Mac des employés. Depuis la mise en place de ce système de calcul partagé, ces mêmes traitements peuvent désormais être lancés en quelques minutes seulement, selon Apple Insider.
Attention toutefois à ne pas confondre réduction du temps d’attente et accélération des calculs. Minions permet surtout aux équipes de travailler plus rapidement en évitant les files d'attente des GPU centralisés.
Des GPU potentiellement disponibles sans acheter de nouvelles machines
Le principe consiste à répartir les tâches entre des Mac dont les processeurs graphiques ne sont pas pleinement utilisés. Chaque ordinateur récupère une partie du travail, l’exécute localement, notamment grâce à Ollama pour la génération de texte, puis renvoie son résultat.
Si un Mac est éteint, mis en veille ou déconnecté, le système confie simplement le travail inachevé à une autre machine.
Cette architecture concerne aujourd’hui l’inférence, c’est-à-dire l’utilisation de modèles d’IA déjà entraînés. Elle ne permet donc pas, pour l’instant, d’entraîner collectivement de nouveaux modèles.
Les machines visées sont les Mac équipés de puces Apple Silicon, qu’il s’agisse d’ordis portables ou de bureau comme les Mac mini et Mac Studio. Les chercheurs ne donnent cependant pas de configuration minimale permettant d’affirmer que tous les modèles sont utilisables dans les mêmes conditions.
- Un Mac toujours aussi compact et bien construit
- La puce M6, tout simplement impressionnante
- Pas de chauffe, pas de bruit
SETI@home faisait déjà travailler nos ordinateurs pour la science
L’idée de mettre en commun la puissance inutilisée des ordinateurs ne date évidemment pas de maintenant. Dès 1999, SETI@home invitait les particuliers à participer à la recherche d’une intelligence extraterrestre en analysant des signaux radio avec leurs propres machines.
Folding@home a ensuite repris ce principe pour étudier les protéines, en recrutant notamment les PlayStation 3 à partir de 2007. Apple avait même développé Xgrid, un système permettant de répartir des calculs entre plusieurs Mac dès 2004.
Minions remet donc une recette éprouvée au service de l’IA avec un avantage économique évident pour les éditeurs disposant déjà d’un parc de Mac récents. Les ordinateurs sont déjà là, leur puissance graphique est disponible une bonne partie du temps et il n’est pas nécessaire d’acheter systématiquement de nouveaux accélérateurs. Même si faire travailler ces machines consomme toujours de l’électricité…
- La puce M4 Max, ses performances, son insolente maîtrise énergétique
- Un Mac redoutable dans tous les usages de création
- Connectiques nombreuses, SSD rapide
Apple pourrait-il un jour utiliser les Mac de ses clients ?
Pour expérimenter Minions, les chercheurs d'Apple se sont d'abord appuyés sur les Mac de leurs propres équipes, parfois en se coordonnant sur Slack pour récupérer quelques heures de puissance de calcul. Mais leur étude envisage déjà d'aller plus loin, en fédérant les ressources de plusieurs organisations, voire d'une communauté mondiale.
Une telle évolution soulèverait forcément des questions de confidentialité, de consommation électrique et de rémunération. Pour l'instant, Apple n'a toutefois annoncé aucun programme destiné aux particuliers.
Prêter son ordinateur pour chercher des extraterrestres avait un certain charme. Aider un GAFAM à faire tourner et développer son IA, un peu moins…
L’inférence correspond à l’exécution d’un modèle déjà entraîné pour produire un résultat (générer du texte, classer une image, résumer un document, etc.). Elle mobilise surtout de la puissance de calcul au moment de répondre à une requête, avec des besoins en mémoire et en GPU souvent importants, mais plus prévisibles que l’entraînement. L’entraînement, lui, consiste à ajuster les paramètres du modèle à partir de grandes quantités de données, ce qui demande généralement beaucoup plus de temps, de données, de stockage et une coordination fine entre GPU. Beaucoup d’architectures distribuées faciles à déployer pour l’inférence ne passent pas à l’échelle aussi simplement pour l’entraînement. C’est pour cela qu’un système peut désengorger des files d’attente d’inférence sans pour autant fabriquer plus vite un nouveau modèle.
Un ordonnanceur répartit les tâches entre plusieurs machines disponibles en tenant compte de leurs capacités (GPU, mémoire), de leur charge et de leur disponibilité réelle. Sur des postes de travail, la contrainte majeure est l’instabilité : une machine peut se mettre en veille, changer de réseau ou être éteinte sans prévenir. Le système doit donc découper le travail en unités relançables, détecter rapidement les nœuds indisponibles et réassigner les morceaux non terminés ailleurs. Cette tolérance aux pannes évite de perdre du temps de calcul et garantit qu’un traitement progresse malgré des ressources intermittentes. En pratique, la qualité de l’ordonnancement joue souvent autant sur le délai de mise en route (file d’attente) que sur la vitesse brute de calcul.
Dans des infrastructures IA, le goulot d’étranglement n’est pas toujours le nombre d’opérations par seconde, mais l’accès aux GPU partagés : si tout le monde soumet des jobs, une file d’attente se forme. Ajouter des ressources opportunistes (comme des GPU de machines peu sollicitées) permet d’absorber les pics de demande et de démarrer plus vite les traitements, même si chaque machine individuelle n’est pas plus rapide qu’un serveur dédié. Le temps total de calcul d’un job peut rester similaire, car il dépend toujours des performances du GPU, de la bande passante mémoire et du modèle utilisé. En revanche, le time-to-start (délai avant exécution) baisse fortement, ce qui améliore la productivité des équipes. C’est un levier d’optimisation de capacité et de disponibilité, plus qu’un gain direct de performance par watt.

articles.title: « Personne n'avait encore jamais fait ça » : cerné par les mines, un soldat ukrainien a été évacué suspendu sous un drone bombardier
articles.text:
Il y a une décennie de cela, on évoquait la perspective offerte par des drones secouristes capables de foncer en mer pour jeter une bouée à un nageur en grande difficulté. Ou d’un drone médical transportant un défibrillateur à une personne victime d’un arrêt cardiaque. 2026 est arrivé, et on voit maintenant des drones qui évacuent des blessés du champ de bataille.
C’est une histoire de ce genre que vient d’exposer la 92e brigade d’assaut autonome « Ivan Sirko » dans une vidéo mise en ligne le 19 octobre 2026. Il est raconté qu’un fantassin appartenant à la 30e brigade mécanisée « Constantin Ostrogski » était blessé dans une zone minée et survolée par les drones russes.
Un gros drone à six rotors à la rescousse
Ce soldat, isolé de ses camarades, ne pouvait pas être évacué par un robot terrestre, qui est une approche privilégiée pour ne pas exposer les infirmiers près du front. Les militaires se sont donc tournés vers les airs, avec un hexacoptère (un drone à six rotors), une configuration courante sur les drones lourds capables de soulever un homme et son barda.
Au départ, cet engin, fabriqué par l’entreprise ukrainienne Gurzuf Defence, est destiné à larguer des munitions sur l’ennemi. C’est un drone bombardier qui a été remanié pour qu’il puisse aussi servir d’hélicoptère d’évacuation. Outre l’environnement très dangereux dans lequel il évoluait, le drone devait rester stable en vol, pour épargner au militaire tout balancement ou basculement.
« Nos spécialistes, en étroite collaboration avec le fabricant, ont mis en œuvre une solution technique » adaptée, se félicite la 92e brigade. « Des essais préliminaires avaient également été menés sur les terrains mis à disposition par Gurzuf Defence, et la mission a été planifiée conjointement avec les unités adjacentes. »
Et comme l’opération a réussi, l’Ukraine a décidé de la médiatiser. Tout « s’est terminé avec succès : le blessé a été sauvé. Il suit actuellement un traitement et une rééducation, et ses jours ne sont plus en danger ». Cette évacuation par les airs est d’ailleurs présentée par la brigade comme une première mondiale.
Plus prudent, Napalm, chef d’escouade et programmeur de l’unité, cité par United24, parle d’ailleurs d’un événement « historique, au moins pour notre unité ». En attendant que cette approche se développe éventuellement, les robots terrestres restent la norme : ceux du 3e corps d’armée ukrainien ont évacué plus de 600 blessés dès leur première année de service.

articles.title: SA-founded clinical AI startup Healthleap raises $38m seed, Series A funding - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South Africa-founded clinical AI startup Healthleap has raised US$38 million in combined seed and Series A funding as it looks to expand its offering to more conditions.
Founded in South Africa in 2022 by siblings Josiah and Jemima Meyer, Healthleap has developed a platform that screens hospital patients for conditions that often go undiagnosed.
The platform reads each patient’s full electronic health record (EHR) every morning, including notes, labs, vitals, orders and problem lists, and flags risk. It then pushes risk scores into clinicians’ existing EHR workflows, showing care teams which patients need attention first.
Healthleap has initially focused on malnutrition, but now plans to expand its offering to cover additional conditions after raising the US$38 million round. The funding came from Sequoia Capital, First Round Capital and Hummingbird Ventures, and will also be used to grow Healthleap’s engineering, sales, customer success and product teams. The platform will be expanded to cover conditions including congestive heart failure, pressure ulcers and a range of hospital-acquired infections.
“Every week, millions of patients leave hospitals with unresolved health conditions that will erode their health and cost up to 10x more to treat in the long term,” said Josiah Meyer, co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Healthleap. “Our goal is to help improve care and save lives by identifying those conditions now.”
Alfred Lin, partner at Sequoia Capital, said Healthleap was focused on finding patients who are being missed and getting them the care they need.
“The impact for both patients and hospitals has been inspiring, with one hospital seeing 39 per cent more malnutrition cases identified and treated, and US$11 million in incremental revenue in a single health system,” he said.
Josh Kopelman, co-founder and partner at First Round Capital, said the firm was drawn to Healthleap’s vision of every hospital using real-time AI to spot overlooked clinical risk, improve care and unlock reimbursement revenue.

articles.title: Sahi’s Dale Vaz wants an AI financial team in every pocket
articles.text:
Sahi’s Dale Vaz wants an AI financial team in every pocket
From plain-language trading strategies to a Discipline Score that flags overtrading, Sahi’s Kyro shows how AI could give every Indian investor a personal team of financial agents, in their own language.
Opening a trading account in India now takes minutes. Knowing what to do once you’re in is much harder.
This gap was the focus of Dale Vaz’s keynote at TechSparks 2026. The co-founder and CEO of fintech company Sahi argued that the last decade of fintech solved the issue of access, but not outcomes.
“Everybody here has a broking app,” Vaz told the audience. “But when you think about outcomes, do people really feel confident about what to do with their money? The numbers indicate most of us are still struggling.”
The intent-capability gap
Vaz described a familiar pattern among retail investors. People start investing, then struggle to make sense of their portfolios. A bad day in the market leaves them unsure about whether to buy, sell, or quit altogether.
The cause, he said, is complexity: too much jargon, too much data, and too many tools. Investors are left with two poor choices. They can spend years becoming experts, or they can trust someone promising guaranteed returns.
Regulator-led investor education has helped, Vaz said, but a wide gap remains between people’s intent to grow their money and their capability to do it.
Why generic AI falls short
AI is increasingly pitched as the answer. But Vaz cautioned that general-purpose chatbots carry three serious flaws when money is involved.
The first is hallucination. “A model is confidently wrong. It will never tell you it’s wrong,” he said. That might be acceptable for an essay, but not for financial decisions.
The second is missing context. A chatbot can answer 'should I buy HDFC stock?' without knowing that half your portfolio is already in banking stocks.
The third is accountability. If a general chatbot gives you bad guidance, there is no regulatory protection and no one to call.
Meet Kyro: A purpose-built assistant
Sahi’s answer is Kyro, an agentic AI assistant built into its app and web platform. Vaz called it a “vertical harness” around an AI model. If the model is the engine, the harness is the car.
Kyro combines three things: personal context from a user’s activity on Sahi, 28 expert skills written by Sahi’s research team, and more than 100 tools. Those tools give Kyro “hands and legs," he said. Users can set price alerts, create conditional orders, build custom scanners, or describe a trading strategy in plain language and have Kyro turn it into executable code.
Crucially, the AI model doesn’t do the calculations. It routes requests to Sahi’s backend APIs, which return deterministic results. “When you say add four plus five, the model calls the calculator that we have built,” Vaz explained. This design keeps numbers out of the model’s hands and reduces the risk of hallucination.
A constitution for trust
Sahi built Kyro around a set of rules it calls a constitution. Answers must be grounded in facts, and Kyro is designed to say “I don’t know” when it should. The user always presses the final buy or sell button. Every output must come with evidence a person can check.
“If AI could just magically make money for everybody, the people making the models would have made all the money,” Vaz said. “AI can help augment our skills as investors, but it can never really replace the individual.”
The system is designed to comply with SEBI regulations, with in-country inference, data logging, and full traceability of conversations.
Early results
Kyro has been tested with more than 11,000 traders in a closed user group. It has generated over 2.7 lakh responses at a 99.2% success rate, and 78% of users returned after their first interaction.
Some use cases surprised the team. Many traders treat Kyro as a sounding board for losses and discipline problems. Others talk to it in Gujarati, Tamil, and Marathi.
What Kyro won’t do yet
Asked whether Kyro acts as an advisor, Vaz was direct: it does not. It has strict rules against buy or sell calls. Advisory features would require a separate SEBI investment advisory licence, which Sahi plans to pursue.
Vaz also previewed a Discipline Score. Based on academic research into why retail traders fail, it will flag habits such as overtrading, oversized positions, and revenge trading.
Looking further ahead, Vaz sees AI agents running exchange-approved algorithms for retail investors, and a future where every Indian has “a team of AI-enabled agents” watching their risk, portfolio, and taxes in their own language.
“We are at the first minute of the first day,” he said.

articles.title: Quatre caméras et du stockage local sans abonnement : le kit eufyCam C35 est à 160,55 €
articles.text:
Le kit de 4 caméras eufyCam C35 avec HomeBase Mini est à 160,55 € (-19 %)
Le kit eufyCam C35 réunit quatre caméras sur batterie et une HomeBase Mini pour surveiller plusieurs accès, avec vision nocturne en couleur et stockage local.
Amazon propose le kit de quatre caméras eufyCam C35 avec HomeBase Mini à 160,55 €, contre un ancien prix de 199 €, soit une réduction de 19 %. Le tarif est également inférieur de 8,45 € au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, affiché à 169 €. Cette version blanche est vendue par AnkerDirect FR et expédiée par Amazon.
Quatre caméras sur batterie pour l’intérieur et l’extérieur
Les caméras de surveillance eufyCam C35 filment en Full HD, à 1 920 × 1 080 pixels. Leur technologie PureColor Vision permet d’obtenir des images nocturnes en couleur en faible luminosité. Elles disposent également d’un microphone et d’un haut-parleur pour échanger à distance avec une personne présente devant l’objectif.
Leur fonctionnement sur batterie évite de tirer un câble d’alimentation jusqu’à chaque emplacement. La fixation magnétique facilite le positionnement, avec également la possibilité de les visser ou de les poser. Certifiées IP67, elles conviennent à une installation extérieure. La connexion utilise le Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz.
Une HomeBase Mini pour centraliser les enregistrements
La station HomeBase Mini incluse possède 8 Go de stockage intégré, dont une partie est réservée au système. Une carte microSD, vendue séparément, permet d’étendre la capacité jusqu’à 1 To. Le stockage local fonctionne sans abonnement obligatoire.
Le système propose la détection des personnes, véhicules et animaux, ainsi que la reconnaissance des visages avec la station. Des zones d’activité permettent de cibler les alertes. Ces caméras enregistrent les événements détectés : elles ne proposent pas d’enregistrement continu 24 h/24, un point à prendre en compte selon l’usage prévu.

articles.title: Rank Math PRO WordPress Plugin Compromised in Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
Users downloaded malicious versions of Rank Math PRO last week, after the WordPress SEO plugin was compromised in a supply chain attack.
Some version 3.0.123 packages contained malware that could allow attackers to take over websites if the plugin was activated, Rank Math says.
All users who downloaded or updated their plugin to the affected version between October 15, 2026, at 20:02 UTC and October 16, 2026, at 07:12 UTC might have been infected.
“We immediately removed the affected files and released a clean version, Rank Math PRO v3.0.124,” Rank Math says.
All users who installed and activated version 3.0.123 of the plugin during the affected window should treat their websites as compromised and should restore them from a clean backup created before the incident.
The malware may provide the attackers with persistent access to the compromised websites and could expose credentials, API keys, and other secrets.
According to Rank Math, the malware may recreate a hidden backdoor upon each page visit, and its persistence mechanism could make manual cleanup a difficult task.
Users who cannot restore the site from a backup should delete the Rank Math PRO plugin folder, remove a malicious database entry, block the attacker’s domain rank1cdn[.]com, and find and remove suspicious PHP files and unknown administrator accounts.
The malware may also deploy fake WordPress core files, modify .htaccess files to add rules for .cache files to execute as PHP code, drop .cache files containing PHP code, schedule tasks and cron jobs, modify other plugins and themes, and upload other files.
Additionally, the attackers could make changes outside the WordPress installation, and site admins should also look for SSH authorized_keys files, crontabs from other system users, suspicious processes, and other locations the web server user has write access to.
After verifying the website is clean, users should change all their passwords and install a clean version of Rank Math PRO.

articles.title: Bullhorn takes staffing platform offline to contain cyberattack
articles.text:
Staffing software company Bullhorn has disabled access to its platform to contain a cyberattack that caused a system-wide outage.
The company says it has isolated the issue and eradicated the immediate threat. Currently, its team is working to restore services following thorough security reviews conducted with help from CrowdStrike specialists.
Bullhorn is an American software company specializing in cloud-based staffing and recruitment solutions. Its platform helps staffing firms manage the recruitment lifecycle, including candidate tracking, onboarding, and payroll.
The company says it serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide.
According to a status page on the incident, customers started to experience issues with job posting in the Bullhorn application on Friday.
The next day, the company said it was "experiencing a system-wide outage affecting the Bullhorn platform," and later confirmed that the issues were caused by a cyberattack.
"We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said in an update.
In a FAQ page, Bullhorn says that a forensic investigation has been started and "not yet determined whether customer data was exfiltrated." Bullhorn promised to notify affected individuals directly if a data breach is confirmed.
According to the firm’s status page, most of the services are under maintainance or have degraded performance, except for Adapt, eEmpACT, and StaffSuite, which remain operational.
Major outages affect ATS/CRM, Automation, Back Office, Talent Platform, and sandbox environments.
At the time of writing, degraded performance was reported for Bullhorn for Salesforce and associated products, Onboarding365, and additional solutions including Amplify, Analytics, Messaging, SourceBreaker, VMS Sync, Data Hub, Erecruit, SalesDuel, and VMS Access.
Bullhorn has not provided any timelines for when those services will be restored. Customers should check the company’s service status page for the latest updates.
Also, the latest update mentions that all non-SSO users will be required to reset their passwords on their next login.
Also, as per the FAQ page, API passwords require rotation to protect integrations, while client-secret changes will follow later. For Bullhorn-hosted instances, this will take place automatically.
Customers can request data exports through the firm’s support to minimize business disruption.
Unposted time records will be reprocessed after restoration, and service credits will be reviewed against applicable SLAs once the incident is resolved.
BleepingComputer has contacted Bullhorn to request more information about the attack, and we will update this post with their response when received.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Un jabalí termina dentro de un bar de fiesta en Zaragoza porque eran Pilares y así son las cosas
articles.text:
Si has estado en Zaragoza durante estas fiestas del Pilar habrás visto calles anegadas de gente, colas para entrar a casi cualquier local y estado festivo general. La SEO y otras plazas se atestaron de chavales (se han alcanzado los 3 millones de visitas y se estima un total de 6) pero lo que no se esperaba ver era un animal salvaje infiltrado en este hábitat. Salvaje de verdad: en la madrugada del sábado 17 al domingo 18 de octubre, un jabalí se cruzó casi todo el centro de Zaragoza. Heraldo recoge el testimonio del animal corriendo al galope entre niños. Y El Periódico de Aragón también cuenta cómo atravesó las calles en plenas fiestas.
Hakuna Matata. El primer aviso llegó a las 0:40 a la Unidad Central Operativa de la Policía Local: un jabalí corría por las calles Asalto y Jorge Cocci, junto al río Huerva y las vías del tranvía, según HOY Aragón. Hacia la una ya se movía entre la gente por zonas muy concurridas. La Policía de Zaragoza avisó a los viandantes de que tuvieran cuidado. Se movilizaron Policía Local, Policía Nacional, Bomberos y la unidad de rescate y recuperación animal para cercarlo y reconducirlo fuera de la ciudad.
La ruta vital. Según las fuentes policiales, el animal pasó por Aznar Molina, el Camino de las Torres, Cesáreo Alierta, la plaza de los Sitios, la calle Sanclemente, el paseo de la Independencia y la calle Coso, con parada en la plaza San Felipe, hasta llegar a la zona de bares del Casco.
Y acabó en el Jardín del Temple, un bar al que se accede por una vía bastante angosta. La hipótesis es que pudo entrar desde Las Fuentes, aunque Aragón Digital recuerda que también podría proceder de huertas, de la ribera o de pinares de la periferia.
Dentro del local. El jabalí no llegó a salir de la ciudad. En su huida entró en un local de ocio nocturno de la calle Temple, en el Casco Viejo, donde embistió a una mujer y le causó lesiones leves. Alberto Samperio, que estaba dentro, cuenta a HOY Aragón que primero creyó que era una persona caída y luego un perro, hasta que vio que era un jabalí y que la gente se apartaba asustada. El balance, dice, fue “muy heavy”.
¿Una alucinación? No todos lo vieron igual. El animal pasó frente al Höhle Club, donde esa noche pinchaba el mítico DJ Rush (una figura clave de la escena techno de Chicago). Durante un buen rato, algunos visitantes pensaron que era una alucinación. Por desgracia, el jabalí no sobrevivió al after.
Por suerte, y según fuentes policiales, el responsable del local ayudado por algunos clientes lograron neutralizar al animal. Después lo sacrificaron “para evitar un peligro mayor”, antes de que llegaran los agentes. El servicio de FCC retiró el cuerpo con un vehículo específico. No ha trascendido cómo se produjo la muerte ni si habrá actuaciones al respecto.
Por qué aparecen. El caso de Zaragoza no es aislado. Según El Español, que cita el censo del Gobierno de 2024, en España había 1,2 millones de jabalíes, y se preveía que la cifra se duplicara en 2025. Sus causas: el abandono del medio rural, el aumento de cultivos de regadío y las temperaturas más altas, que favorecen la reproducción.
En Barcelona, la Generalitat planeó sacrificar a 12.000 ejemplares para frenar la peste porcina africana. Los expertos consultados por Maldita explican que, cuando un jabalí identifica un recurso disponible en la ciudad, incorpora calles y carreteras a sus desplazamientos habituales.
Si te cruzas con uno. Lo mejor es no hacer nada: los jabalíes no suelen ser agresivos, salvo que estén heridos o se sientan acorralados. Conviene no hostigarlos, no intentar capturar una cría y atar o sujetar al perro si estás paseándolo. Al volante, la situación cambia, porque son la principal causa de accidentes con fauna en España. El 49%, nada menos: el año pasado se registraron casi 5.300 accidentes de tráfico con animales en 2025, un 4,5% más que en 2024, y una tercera parte eran jabalís.
Falta por saber por dónde entró realmente el jabalí y por qué no pudo reconducirse fuera de la ciudad. En cuanto a la mujer herida, se sabe que sus lesiones fueron leves. El único que acabó entrando en la fiesta y saliendo de ella con las patas por delante fue el pobre animal.

articles.title: The gap between financial inclusion and access to credit in Nigeria
articles.text:
This is Follow the Money, our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Nigeria has made progress in bringing more people into the formal financial system, but having a bank account does not necessarily mean being able to obtain a loan. While more Nigerians can now access financial services, borrowing costs, limited credit histories, and irregular incomes still shape who can obtain formal credit and on what terms.
According to the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA), formal financial inclusion rose to 73%, up from 64% in 2023. The proportion of adults excluded from the financial system fell from 26% to 21%. EFInA estimates that 87.2 million Nigerian adults are now formally included, yet only about 12 million (10%) access formal credit.
These figures show that financial inclusion is not the same as access to credit. Financial inclusion encompasses access to and use of services such as payments, savings, insurance and borrowing. A person may have a bank account, receive payments digitally and save through a formal institution without qualifying for a loan.
For lenders, they must determine whether a borrower earns enough to repay, whether that income can be verified, what other financial obligations the borrower has, and how likely they are to meet the repayment schedule. As a result, people can participate in the formal financial system and still struggle to obtain affordable credit.
According to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), outstanding consumer credit fell from ₦4.72 trillion ($3.5 billion) in 2024 to ₦3.78 trillion ($2.8 billion) in 2025, a decline of 19.92%. For borrowers who struggle to obtain affordable loans from formal lenders, informal sources are offering an alternative, often with fewer procedural barriers. Stears estimates that potential demand for credit among informal borrowers transitioning to formal lending is worth $621 million.
The problem for borrowers
For borrowers, the problem is not just access to credit, but its cost. EFInA found that 16% of adults borrow through informal sources, and 10% from family and friends.
“Alternative finance often wins on lower friction—speed, simplicity, proximity and flexibility,” EFiNA said.
In 2025, Nigeria’s monetary policy rate stood between 27% and 27.5%. The policy rate is not the interest rate consumers pay, but it reflects the wider monetary environment in which lenders operate. When funding is expensive, lenders face pressure to charge more to cover their costs and the risk of non-repayment. Those higher rates, in turn, can make loans harder for borrowers to service.
For illustration, a ₦100 ($0.075) loan charged at a simple annual interest rate of 27% would accrue ₦27 ($0.02) in interest over one year, bringing repayment to ₦127 ($0.095) before fees.
Without lower interest rates, affordable consumer credit will be difficult to scale. But rate cuts alone will not solve the problem. Inflation must also ease sustainably. High inflation erodes borrowers’ purchasing power and leaves less income available for repayments, while making it harder for lenders to offer cheaper loans without taking on more risk. As inflation eases, the CBN can have more room to reduce its policy rate, potentially lowering funding costs and abating pressure on lending rates.
The challenge is to bring down both the cost of credit and the financial pressure on borrowers. Until inflation and interest rates ease, lenders will face pressure to charge more for risk, while the people who need credit most will continue to struggle with its cost, and formal credit access will continue to be a dream.
The problem for lenders
Digital lenders have expanded access to borrowing through mobile applications, automated lending decisions, and alternative data about potential customers. Where banks have retreated, digital lenders have filled the gap.
Commercial banks’ loan-to-deposit ratio stood at 48.07% in 2025, below the reported 80% benchmark.
Digital lenders use transaction histories and repayment records to evaluate people who have limited conventional credit histories. But faster lending decisions do not eliminate the underlying financial risk.
A lender that approves a loan must still fund the money, service the account, and collect repayment. If the borrower defaults, the lender may recover only part of the principal and interest it expected to receive.
This creates a basic economic constraint: lending revenue must cover expected credit losses and all other relevant costs before a lender can make a sustainable profit.
The CBN reported a non-performing loan ratio of 8.03% in January 2026, meaning roughly ₦8 ($0.006) of every ₦100 ($0.075) in bank loans was classified as non-performing loans (NPLs), which borrowers have failed to make scheduled repayments, typically for 90 days or more.
Fintech giant OPay’s reported lending figures offer a more direct illustration of the financial pressures that credit providers must manage.
The company reported $938.3 million in loan originations, $260.25 million in loan-financing revenue, and $121.29 million in provisions for expected credit losses in 2025.
Loan-financing revenue was about 27.7% of originations. Expected credit-loss provisions amounted to about 46.6% of loan-financing revenue.
While these figures do not establish OPay’s profit per loan, they illustrate why lenders plan a substantial portion of their lending revenue on the anticipated cost of loans that will not be fully repaid.
An analysis of 300,000 active borrowers by digital lender, Credit Direct, puts the average loan amount at approximately ₦430,962 ($323.18) for men and ₦478,117 ($358.55) for women. At a hypothetical simple annual interest rate of 28%, these loans would generate ₦120,669 ($90.49) and ₦133,873 ($100.39) in interest, respectively, over one year, before fees. However, this revenue would not represent profit. Lenders must still cover funding costs, operating expenses, and losses from loans that are not fully repaid.
For borrowers, the challenge is whether they can afford to take on and repay such debt. EFInA found that 59% of respondents would struggle to raise ₦156,000 ($116.99) within seven days, suggesting that many Nigerians have limited financial buffers to absorb unexpected expenses or repay loans when due.
What will unlock the market?
In Brazil, account ownership stood at 86.4%, while 45.9% of adults reported formal borrowing. China recorded account ownership of 89.4% and formal borrowing of 40.7%. Kenya recorded 90.1% of adults with a financial account, and only 12.6% reported formal borrowing. South Africa similarly recorded account ownership of 81.1%, compared with a formal borrowing rate of 12.4%.
In these countries, financial inclusion and borrowing are trending upward, driven by improving lending conditions, credit information, household incomes, and the availability of suitable loan products.
For Nigeria, the challenge is not simply to increase the amount of credit available. It is to make more lending both repayable for borrowers and financially sustainable for lenders.
Lower inflation and funding costs could help ease pressure on loan pricing. Better credit information could help lenders distinguish between borrowers with different repayment capacities. Loan sizes and repayment schedules that reflect borrowers’ cash flows could also reduce the risk of repayments overwhelming household budgets.
As Nigeria’s financial inclusion continues to grow, the quality of inclusion is becoming an increasingly important concern. Without access to credit, formal financial inclusion may not translate into meaningful opportunities for individuals to manage financial shocks, invest in their livelihoods, or meet major expenses.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: .NET 11 Release Candidate 2: Go-Live License and Updates across Libraries, F#, MAUI, and WinForms
articles.text:
Microsoft has released .NET 11 Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license for production use, as stated in the announcement. The build is supported in Visual Studio 2026 Insiders and in Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit. As reported, it brings changes across the libraries, runtime, SDK, NuGet, F#, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows Forms, with no new C# language features.
In the libraries, CborReader can now read a payload delivered in chunks, using isFinalBlock and SlideData, in Lax conformance mode only. Two experimental cryptography types arrive: CompositeMLKem combines post-quantum and classical key encapsulation, and Hpke provides Hybrid Public Key Encryption with classical DHKEM suites only.
Both require opting in through SYSLIB5009 and SYSLIB5006, as described in the release notes. ValidationAttribute.FormatMessage lets a host supply a message template for the attribute to fill in, and SocketsHttpHandler.InitialHttp2MaxConcurrentStreams caps streams on a new HTTP/2 connection until the server's SETTINGS frame arrives.
The runtime release focuses on reliability but carries one breaking change. CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default on iOS and tvOS, because, as stated, FileStream lock in RC 1 could cause the OS to terminate an app entering the background. FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced there, and setting DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING to 0 restores locking, according to the release.
ASP.NET Core has few new features but several changes for apps upgrading from RC 1. QuickGrid's AnchorMode and ItemComparer parameters are no longer experimental. IValidationMessageFormatter has been removed in favor of FormatMessage, the Blazor BasePath component moved to the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components namespace, and the experimental device-bound sessions package was pulled from this build. As reported, the remaining AddRazorRuntimeCompilation overloads now warn with ASPDEPR003.
In the SDK, file-based programs accept quoted values in #:property directives, and the #:package, #:project, and #:ref directives take trailing Name=Value item metadata. MSBuild gains faster wildcard matching during project evaluation, which, as reported in Microsoft's Windows benchmarks, puts it at 10–13% faster with 16–34% fewer allocations.
NuGet adds --min-publish-age-hours to dotnet nuget add source and update source, and restore fails with NU1020 when a package cooldown leaves no eligible floating version.
F# ships several preview features. The compiler gains return and await intrinsics for building custom computation-expression builders on the runtime-async model, though FSharp.Core does not yet ship such a builder, as stated in the notes.
let calculation () =
    runtimeTask {
        let captured = 40
        let! delta = delayed 2
        return captured + delta
    }
The reraise() now works inside the with handler of async and task expressions. Outside preview, more List and Array functions inline their callbacks to cut allocations, Async.parallelLimit bounds concurrent work, and bitwise operators on non-integer enums now fail at compile time with FS0001.
The .NET MAUI maui template gains a --ui csharp option that generates the app, shell, and main page in C# rather than XAML, and the multi-project template adds an --avalonia option for an Avalonia desktop project.
MauiIcon accepts Apple Icon Composer .icon bundles, and UseiOSShellHandler opts into a handler-based Shell on Apple platforms. Android adds API 37.2 bindings and JDK 25 support, while Apple workloads now require Xcode 27.0 and apps built with its SDKs must adopt the UIKit scene lifecycle, as described in the breaking changes.
Windows Forms refines the .NET 11 visual styles. Application.SetDefaultVisualStylesMode selects the renderer version, but ToolStrip and DataGridView keep Classic rendering even under Net11 for now. Application.SystemVisualSettings exposes a snapshot of the Windows accent color, text scaling, and high-contrast state, and FormRevealMode defers a top-level form's first presentation to reduce background flashes.
New analyzers WFO3000 to WFO3002 flag code that cannot round-trip through the Designer, which the release notes say is particularly useful when AI tools generate or refactor forms.
Other changes in this release are MSBuild property expansion in launch-profile arguments, an F# RequireNamedArgumentsAttribute, a private-member R8 obfuscation default on Android, SuspendPainting and KioskModeManager for Windows Forms, EF Core SaveChanges and JSON projection fixes.
On Reddit, discussion focused less on the features than on upgrade cadence. Commenters asked how many teams still skip odd-numbered releases, and others replied that since .NET 9 a standard-term release shares its end-of-support date with the preceding LTS version, moving to .NET 11 costs no support time.
Other developers reported MAUI workloads breaking on every preview upgrade, questioned Blazor server-side rendering performance against Razor Pages and MVC, and welcomed the KioskModeManager component for Windows Forms.
For interested readers and developers, the full release notes for .NET 11 RC 2 are available on the dotnet/core repository on GitHub.

articles.title: Super Mario 64's 30-year-old plaque mystery may finally be solved
articles.text:
The big picture: For more than 30 years, Super Mario 64 players have wondered what's written on a plaque on the fountain in the courtyard of Peach's castle. The text, which measures just 32 x 32 pixels, is far too small to decipher with the naked eye. Fans of the game came up with their own interpretations over the years but now, we might have a somewhat definitive answer as to what the text actually says.
The leading theory up to this point is that the text reads, "L is real 2401." This theory gained traction after it was published in an April Fool's Day feature in Nintendo Power magazine in 1998 and without a better answer, it stuck.
Nintendo originally planned to include Luigi in Super Mario 64 but he was cut from the game near the end of development. Fans held onto hope that he somehow might be a secret character and thus, the L is real 2401 legend stuck.
Armed with modern AI tools, enthusiast supermochi64 decided to take a deeper look at the plaque. Using Claude (Opus 5.5), he tackled the problem exactly like a texture artist would have made the plaque in the mid-90s. Then, a GPU was used to test millions of fonts, settings, and words and gave them a score.
The best guess using this technique is, "Eternal star / We hope so."
AI determined the text was written in Palatino Bold Italic, from Adobe's original 1990 version that shipped with Macs of the era. When "L is real" was plugged into the AI, it scored twice as badly as "Eternal star" in terms of being a likely match.
The truth is, we may never know for certain what was originally written on the plaque. The most definitive answer would be to track down the artist responsible for the graphic, but that could be like finding a needle in a haystack considering it was made over three decades ago. What's more, Nintendo often prefers to let little mysteries like these persist.

articles.title: Samsung préparerait une refonte majeure de One UI qui pourrait tout changer
articles.text:
Pour rappel, One UI, l’interface de Samsung, a été lancée en 2018. One UI 9, la dernière version de cette interface, a quant à elle été déployée en septembre 2026. Il faut dire que depuis sa sortie, One UI n’a jamais connu de grands chamboulements : les nouveautés se sont limitées à quelques retouches annuelles et à quelques nouvelles fonctionnalités IA. Les utilisateurs attendent donc une refonte de l’interface, alors que Google et Apple ont récemment mis à jour la leur. Bonne nouvelle, il semble que cela soit dans les tuyaux de Samsung.
Une refonte majeure de One UI
Sur le réseau social X, Ice Universe, un leaker souvent bien informé, annonce : « One UI 10 apportera des changements significatifs, d’une nature sans précédent ». Il précise par ailleurs que l’information provient d’une « source indépendante ». Sur le réseau social chinois Weibo, le leaker précise que toute l’équipe logicielle de Samsung travaille sur cette nouvelle version de l’interface One UI et que One UI 9.5 sera « la dernière génération d’interface traditionnelle ». Le Galaxy Z Fold 9 serait le premier téléphone à bénéficier de One UI 10, basé sur Android 18.
De son côté, le média SamMobile rapporte que le Z Flip 9 pourrait aussi en bénéficier et que la date de lancement se situerait au milieu de l’année 2027 ou au début de 2028. La gamme des Galaxy S27 ne devrait donc pas l’intégrer. En revanche, la gamme des Galaxy S28, oui.
Que peut-on attendre de la refonte de One UI ?
Le site spécialisé Nokia Power User, qui assure s’être entretenu avec un salarié des équipes logicielles de Samsung, annonce l’abandon des icônes d’applications traditionnelles et des grilles statiques. Les applications seraient ainsi réunies au même endroit, et les utilisateurs n’auraient plus à jongler entre plusieurs d’entre elles isolées. L’objectif de Samsung : réduire au maximum le nombre de clics sur le téléphone.
Sans grande surprise, Samsung travaillerait aussi à davantage unifier son écosystème, avec notamment un passage plus simple du téléphone à une tablette ou une montre de la firme. Côté intelligence artificielle, les applications de base resteraient gratuites, tandis que celles qui demandent davantage de calculs et d’intégration d’applications tierces deviendraient payantes.
Enfin, il reste à connaître le nom de cette nouvelle interface. Celle-ci pourrait tout simplement s’appeler One UI 10 ou adopter un nouveau nom, les changements étant majeurs. Le leaker Phonefuturist a d’ailleurs rapporté que la nouvelle version de One UI pourrait être baptisée « Galaxy OS ». Il reste maintenant à attendre une communication officielle de Samsung pour en avoir le cœur net.

articles.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
articles.text:
The trailers for HBO’s DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detective or Slow Horses. Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing; it’s wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegiac finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives. But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre.
(Spoilers below, but no major reveals.)
There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn’t think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal’s power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains.
Hal and John soon discover that the suspect was one of a group of aliens who survived a genocide on their home planet committed by so-called Manhunters: a race of extraterrestrial beings created by the Guardians of the Universe as a forerunner to the Lantern Corps. The Manhunters rebelled against the Guardians, and most were killed; the sole survivor is hiding out in Rushville disguised as a human. The alien leader, Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor), gives Hal and John 48 hours to locate the Manhunter and hand them over, or they will destroy the town.
The second storyline takes place in 2026 and concerns the murder of none other than Hal Jordan, who returned to Rushville as a social pariah after the terrible events that transpired 10 years before. That mystery becomes the focus of the second half of the series, as Stewart teams up with the sheriff to solve Hal’s murder.
Green Lantern’s light
The entire cast brings their A game to their portrayals, and you couldn’t ask for better leads than Chandler and Pierre, both of whom have plenty of meaty, substantial material to work with. Showrunner Chris Mundy has said that one of the major themes of the show is deciding when it’s time for one person to step aside and let a replacement take over, embodied in the push and pull of Hal and John’s relationship. The two men are very different personalities: Hal is cocky, arrogant, and trusts his gut instincts; John is controlled, disciplined, logical, and methodical. Hal has no intention of giving up the power ring; John questions whether Hal really deserves it. Naturally they’re going to clash, and given the stakes, that conflict has severe consequences, both for them and the town.

articles.title: Claude Code AI agent caught a crypto miner hiding on a developer’s overheating Mac — XMRig task was hogging ‘about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores’ pushing temps to 112 degrees
articles.text:
Claude Code AI agent caught a crypto miner hiding on a developer’s overheating Mac — XMRig task was hogging ‘about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores’ pushing temps to 112 degrees
'Explains why my Mac has been running like s**t,' said the afflicted Redditor.
A developer using Claude Code to help build a temperature monitor app got a friendly warning from the coding agent. “Your Mac is running a crypto miner that I didn’t put there,” flagged the helpful agent. “I saw xmrig using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores,” it informed its human master. Perhaps developer and Redditor UntilHEX should have sensed the crypto miner’s presence without AI help, as they admitted the malware’s presence “explains why my Mac has been running like s**t.”
Ironically, the cryptomining malware’s nefarious CPU cycle hogging activity is what may have led to its discovery and demise. Pondering over a screenshot of the Claude Code window, we see that this malware was probably added to the Mac’s startup roster on August 29. It looks like UntilHEX was inspired to develop a Mac temperature monitor app after this infection to track and diagnose why the computer was running so hot.
Claude stepped in after the Redditor was concerned about a dump of the Mac’s raw temperature sensor readings. “They seemed far too high,” commented UntilHEX in the social media post. Indeed, the well-known coding agent pointed out that the CPU was peaking at a very toasty 112 degrees Celsius. It explained this was due to a sustained heavy load, specifically “xmrig using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores.” We don’t know how many cores the Mac being used had, but maybe 12 were all of them.
Claude Code went on to describe how the crypto miner software had hidden itself on the Apple computer and ran at startup. It cautiously decided not to kill or remove anything from the Mac, but offered to clean up the CPU-hogging crypto miner, which was sucking all the power from the Apple Silicon computer. “Can I clean it up now?” Claude inquired. “I’d stop the startup item and the miner, and move the files into a quarantine folder.”
Later in the comments, UntilHEX informed the social media throng that Claude was indeed tasked with cleaning up the unwanted crypto miner software. “I only had to delete 1 file manually because Claude had an access issue, but it was very effective,” the Redditor said. After that, a Malwarebytes scan was run to check to see if the AI coding agent-driven clean had really been successful.

articles.title: This sub-$100/£100 bird-feeder camera proved you don't need a massive budget to spy on your local wildlife — even if its app ruffled my feathers
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The TT Nature Bird Feeder Station doesn't try to compete with the ecosystem polish or subscription-heavy AI tricks of more expensive competitors. Despite its basic software, the camera delivers sharp, wide-angle 1080p footage in the right conditions. It’s a well-built feeder that blends in and is a respectable choice for budget-conscious buyers who want solid construction over complex software features.
Reasons to buy
- + Wired solar panel included
- + Charming, real-wood build
- + Strong focus on the feeding ledge
Reasons to avoid
- - Oversized drainage holes drop seeds
- - Boring app; no bird ID unless you pay
- - Camera can be slow to trigger
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
TT Nature Bird Feeder Station: Two-minute review
Unlike companies like Netvue (which originated as a smart security camera maker before launching the Birdfy line) or Bird Buddy (which built its platform from the ground up around a custom app experience), TT Nature uses off-the-shelf camera hardware paired with third-party software.
Its wooden Smart Bird Feeder Station is a rustic, budget-friendly alternative to the sleek, plastic-heavy smart feeders dominating the market. It’s solidly built from FSC-certified natural timber and topped with a dark metal roof, making it look more like a traditional garden birdhouse than smart home tech, and a natural fit for rustic outdoor setups. It also matches my garden office perfectly.
Beware, the camera is more like a retrofitted security device than a specialized bird snapper. After mounting the feeder to my garden fence and monitoring it for several weeks, I appreciate its physical design and reasonable cost, while also finding the basic software setup frustrating.
As mentioned, the wooden housing feels very sturdy, though it will inherently be harder to clean and maintain than all-plastic constructions. The included mounting template and accessories make locking it securely onto a fence panel or post easy, provided you have a decent drill. The external solar panel and full mounting kit are included, whereas most rivals require you to buy these as extras.
The physical assembly is minimal, but setting up the camera with TT Nature's accompanying app, PerchLens, proved to be less straightforward than the process with Birdfy models. The app refused to detect the camera automatically, forcing a manual setup that meant temporarily locking my home router to a 2.4GHz band — a hurdle I’ve never had to clear with other feeders I’ve tested. Once past that, though, the Wi-Fi connection has remained stable, even with the feeder at the far end of my garden.
The feeder captures 1080p HD video with a wide field of view and a pleasantly sharp focus on the perch itself. However, clips aren't detailed enough to see individual feathers. I found that the camera’s motion sensor is slow to trigger, so clips often start a fraction too late and catch the tail end of a visit or an empty perch. The camera lens also fogged up several times on damp mornings, muting contrast and visibility during the busiest dawn feeding hours.
You can use microSD recording (cards up to 128GB are supported) and also get three-day cloud storage without a monthly fee. However, AI species identification is locked behind an optional monthly or annual subscription. Without it, incoming alerts are just listed as 'bird'. The software is far more rudimentary than the polished, gamified ecosystems of the Bird Buddy 2 or Birdfy. If you don't mind manually spotting your visitors, though, the app does at least neatly organize your clips by date and time.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Despite its basic app and trigger lag (something I hope will be less of an issue when the birds feel brave enough to spend longer feeding), the TT Nature delivers undeniable value. It offers a nice-to-look-at wooden build and set-and-forget solar power, at a fraction of the price of most flagship competitors. If you’re a casual bird lover who wants a budget-friendly garden camera that blends in naturally, I think it can still earn a spot in your yard or garden.
- Interested in other options available besides the TT Nature Bird Feeder Station? Check out our best bird feeder cameras guide.
I found live streaming to be occasionally laggy, sometimes not loading at all, and even when I set the camera to Frenzy Mode, the AI postcard capture missed birds I could clearly see sitting on the feeder from my kitchen window. It’s not the most reliable feeder I’ve used, and not ideal if you want to capture every single bird and build a picture of their visiting habits; however, it does stop your feed from getting clogged with thousands of similar clips.
Despite these niggles and quirks, I really enjoy the core experience. The AI bird identification is almost perfect, the postcard collection system provides a handy highlight reel, and the solar roof means near-continuous use.
The Bird Buddy 2 is a sleek, low-maintenance smart feeder with strong app design and best-in-class solar performance. For now, it earns its spot in my garden (and believe me, I have four smart feeders on the go), though I can’t help thinking about its price and hope tighter bird detection lands in future updates.
TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder: Price and availability
- First created and released around mid-2024
- Available via Amazon US, Walmart, and Amazon UK
- $120-140 in US (approx. £75 in UK)
At around $140 (£75), the TT Nature smart bird feeder station sits at the affordable end of the best bird cameras, especially given its solid timber construction. It sits well below Netvue’s premium wooden options like the Birdfy Bamboo (~£199) and costs about the same as the plastic entry-level Birdfy Rookie (~£80), which doesn’t include a solar panel.
The feeder includes free AI species identification, and I like that it has a local MicroSD card slot (supporting up to 128GB) for storage, plus a free 3-day rolling cloud buffer. Not hugely generous, but enough for a freebie. Unlike rivals that lock some features under a premium membership, you don’t have to budget for recurring monthly fees here.
Availability is primarily via Amazon in both the US and UK, or directly from TT Nature in the US. The package includes the wooden feeder housing, 1080p camera module, mounting hardware, and an external 3W solar panel. Considering the full package, I think TT Nature delivers good upfront value for birdwatchers who want a complete, low-maintenance setup on a sensible budget.
Software is as important as hardware, though. I found its accompanying app lags behind Birdfy and Bird Buddy in terms of enjoyment and features, and I’d still consider paying a bit more for them.
TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder camera: Specs
| Feature | Specification | 
|---|---|
| Sensor | 1/2.7" CMOS | 
| Photo quality | 12MP - 1080p snapshot capture with 130-degree FOV | 
| Video quality | 1080p HD @ 30fps | 
| Memory | MicroSD slot (up to 128GB) + Cloud storage options | 
| Dimensions | 185 x 198 x 270 mm (7.3 x 7.8 x 10.6") | 
| Weight | 0.95 kg (2.1 lbs) | 
| Seed capacity | 1.5 Litres (~6.3 Cups) | 
| Weather resistance | IP65 Certified | 
| Battery | 5200 mAh rechargeable battery with an external 3W Solar Panel included | 
| Connectivity | 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi | 
TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder camera: Design
- Rustic wooden build with a black metal roof
- Mounting kit included for trees, walls, or poles
- Separate wired solar panel for charging
The TT Nature feeder, made from FSC-certified natural timber housing, immediately sets the kind of traditional, garden-friendly tone that I like over a plastic model. On its website, the brand sells two roof options, but the dark metal roof on my version feels sturdy and well-built. The packaging is neat and secure, though I found it a shame that TT Nature uses single-use plastic wrapping for some elements instead of easily recyclable cardboard—a missed opportunity for a nature-friendly product.
Assembly takes less than ten minutes and is intuitive enough that you likely won't need the instruction manual. You simply pop the perching ledge onto the front, lift the hinged wooden flap to slide in the camera module, and tilt up the roof to pour in your seed mix.
Initially, the physical assembly took about ten minutes. There are clear instructions included in the box, but I didn't find I needed them because it was all intuitive. You slot the metal perching ledge into pre-drilled holes at the end of the wooden feeding area, pull down the branded wooden flap at the front to slot the camera module in, and tilt up the roof when you want to add seed. The camera sits loosely in its designated space rather than clipping or mounting in, which is surprisingly secure even if it feels a little unanchored at first.
Though putting together the wooden unit was easy, I struggled for a while to get the camera to pair with TT Nature's accompanying app over Wi-Fi. It took me about an hour of troubleshooting to get the camera connected, as it wouldn’t find the camera automatically during scanning and I had to switch over to manual setup.
Even then, I had to temporarily set my Virgin Media home router to broadcast on a 2.4GHz network only—a step I’ve never had to take with any of the other smart feeders I’ve tested. Luckily, now that the initial connection has been established, I‘ve been able to switch my router back to a dual 2.4GHz/5GHz band without any ongoing drops.
Even with some premium smart feeders, wall or fence mounting brackets are sold as extra accessories. The TT Nature feeder has mounting options for trees, poles, walls, and fences included, and I opted to mount the feeder directly onto my garden fence panel with the supplied screws.
Once these were drilled in—made much easier thanks to an included mounting template—the feeder sat firmly on its plate with no wobbling. I do appreciate the sturdy, locked-in feel this gives you, but note that it’s far less flexible to reposition the feeder on a whim when compared to hanging designs like the Bird Buddy 2.
I found out (the fiddly way) that it’s better to mount the wooden feeder to your fence or post first, pair the camera to your phone app second, and then slide the camera module into its front slot. You’ll also need to thread the solar panel cable through a small access hole in the back of the wooden housing to connect it to the camera.
The solar panel can be mounted separately nearby, but to save drilling extra holes into my garden fence, for now I’ve chosen to rest it directly on top of the feeder’s metal roof for easy adjusting. The white trailing wires from the panel aren't the prettiest to look at, and I prefer a feeder with flush solar panels integrated directly into the roof design, but you can easily tuck the excess cable behind the wooden housing to tidy things up.
Filling the 1.5-litre hopper is quick and easy, though I found seed doesn't always flow freely down to the perch and needs some encouragement—either a nudge with your fingers or a gentle shake of the housing. There are drainage holes built into the feeding perch to allow water drainage, but these are wide enough to let smaller seeds fall straight through to the ground, which feels wasteful when you’ve bought premium bird food mix.
TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder camera: Performance
- Clear 1080p video in dry conditions and direct sun
- Consistent motion detection but a recording lag
- The app is functional, with AI species ID paywalled
It took only a few days for the local birds to grow bold enough to land on the TT Nature feeder in my garden, and soon after, my phone started pinging with initial motion alerts. Whenever I’m first testing out a new bird cameras, I also like to do a bit of an observation check out of my kitchen window to see how real-time landings translates to app notifications. More advanced software can take a few days to calibrate, but the motion sensors triggered reliably for almost every visitor I spotted.
That said, playing the clips back revealed a particularly frustrating flaw: the camera often triggers a fraction of a second too slowly. For particularly short visits, by the time the recording had started, the bird had often already flown off. Videos are capped at a fixed 20-second duration with no option in the app to adjust clip length. By default, the motion sensitivity is set to Medium (the other options being low or high); I bumped this up to High in the hope of catching birds as they first approached, but it didn’t make a noticeable difference to the trigger lag.
The camera settings are rudimentary overall, though Iappreciate that you can filter notifications to alert you to animal visitors only. This stopped my phone from pinging me every time I took out some washing or my dog sniffed past. Of course, you can leave it set to all motion if you want—at its core, this is essentially a standard security camera housed inside a wooden birdhouse.
In terms of video quality, the camera definitely needs even lighting and a dry day to perform at its best, a slight drawback when your feeder is at its busiest during the early hours. On several damp autumn mornings, the glass lens completely fogged up with condensation, making visiting birds look like blurs. There’s also no automatic white balance or HDR tone-mapping at play (I don’t know how exposure works on other cameras, but the Bird Buddy has often seemed to compensate); birds sitting in deep morning shade can also look quite dark and hard to make out.
When the weather is fair, however, the optical performance is more charming. The lens offers a crisp, fixed focal plane right on the front perch, paired with a natural, shallow depth of field that softens the garden background nicely. I also like how wide the field of view is, allowing you to watch where birds fly in from and trace their exit paths after a feed. Video playback is generally clear, if occasionally a bit juddery during fast wing-flaps.
The accompanying PerchLens app is where the TT Nature camera feels most in tune with its entry-level price. Unlike the slick, fun ecosystems of Birdfy or Bird Buddy—which feature near-flawless AI identification out of the box—the software experience here is basic.
Without paying for an optional monthly subscription (£6.10/month, processed painstakingly via PayPal or bank transfer), you don't get any automatic AI species tagging, and incoming sightings are simply labelled as "bird".
TT Nature doesn't push the camera as a heavy AI play, and personally, I don't mind manually spotting the birds coming and going since I recognise common local garden species anyway. But I think if your goal is to automatically curate a digital log, track species frequency and behaviour, or build up a solid collection of identified visitors, the app simply isn’t advanced enough for that. The camera also doesn't automatically generate shareable photo cards like the Bird Buddy 2, and if you want stills, your best bet is capturing a manual screenshot while watching the 1080p live stream.
Should you buy the TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder camera?
Buy it if...
You want a natural-looking design
Constructed from FSC-certified natural timber with a weather-resistant metal roof, the wooden TT Nature looks like a traditional garden birdhouse rather than a plastic security cam. It blended well into my garden, though mounting the solar panel is extra faff.
You want a no-subscription storage option
The TT Nature includes a physical MicroSD card slot (up to 128GB) and a free 3-day cloud loop, meaning you can save and download 1080p footage (if you're quick) without recurring costs.
Don't buy it if...
You want a large-capacity seed tray
With a 1.5-litre capacity, I'd say this feeder is on the smaller side for big or busy gardens. If you have high bird traffic or frequent squirrel visits, you might have to refill the seed tray every few days compared to larger 3L+ feeders.
You want an all-in-one solar roof
The camera's 3W solar panel is connected via a wire rather than being a seamless, flush panel built into the roof. If you want a clean, single-piece feeder, this setup feels a bit more modular and requires extra consideration.
Also consider
Bird Buddy Pro (with solar roof)
If you don't want to maintain the TT Nature's wooden exterior and prefer an easier-to-clean, modern design, the Bird Buddy Pro is a premium alternative. Its solar roof is integrated, and the companion app curates daily Postcard highlight reels instead of sending constant motion alerts.
Read our Bird Buddy Pro review
Birdfy Bamboo
If you like the naturalistic look of the TT Nature wooden camera but want something a little bigger, Netvue's Birdfy Bamboo gives you almost double the seed capacity. It's sustainably made and looks just as integrated in a traditional garden setting. The product is more expensive, but it offers better build quality.
Read our Netvue Birdfy Bamboo review
How I tested the TT Nature Smart Bird Feeder camera
- Tested for several weeks in a UK garden in October
- Mounted using the included hanging hardware
- Connected to an iPhone 15 Pro running the PerchLens app
I tested the TT Nature Bird Feeder Station in my garden for two weeks, after mounting it securely onto my fence using the metal plate and screws included in the box. I powered up the camera using the wired external 3W solar panel balanced on the feeder's roof.
I connected the camera to my iPhone 15 Pro via TT Nature's app, PerchLens, so I could see how effective the Wi-Fi pairing process and motion alert notifications were. I spent time navigating the app and reading the FAQs to see what the camera's support and community were like.
I mostly followed RSPB guidance on feeding birds and left small amounts of mealworms in the base of the feeder, adding a few seeds close to the end of October. I took the camera inside once during the testing period to refill it and wipe it down, as I wanted to gauge how easy it would be to clean.
First reviewed October 2026
Lauren Scott is an experienced journalist and freelance photographer based in Bath, UK. She's been in the tech industry for over ten years; serving as the former Managing Editor of our sister site Digital Camera World. As well as raving about cameras past and present for TechRadar, Lauren also tests fitness apps, trackers, and headphones. A keen polymath, she has bylines on Woman & Home, Space.com, Canon Europe, PCGamesN, and Stuff Magazine. When she's not working, you'll find her testing yet another new curry recipe, or teaching her Flat-coated Retriever how to retrieve.
