articles.title: El truco oficial de WhatsApp para saber qué dice un mensaje de voz sin escucharlo
articles.text:
WhatsApp tiene una función nativa que permite leer el contenido de un mensaje de voz sin necesidad de reproducirlo, gracias a una transcripción automática a texto que se genera dentro de la propia aplicación. La herramienta evita recurrir a programas o bots externos y resuelve una situación habitual: recibir un audio extenso en un momento en el que no es posible, o no resulta conveniente, escucharlo.
La opción se gestiona desde la configuración del teléfono, permite elegir el idioma de conversión y, una vez activada, muestra el texto correspondiente debajo del reproductor de cada nota de voz recibida.
Cómo activar la transcripción de audios en WhatsApp
Para habilitar la función, el usuario debe ingresar al menú Ajustes, luego a Chats y finalmente a la sección Transcripciones de mensajes de voz, donde se selecciona el idioma preferido para la conversión del audio a texto. Con la opción habilitada, al llegar un nuevo mensaje de voz aparece una notificación debajo del reproductor que consulta si se desea transcribir el contenido.
La primera vez que se acepta esta opción, la aplicación descarga un pequeño paquete de datos que funciona como motor de procesamiento. A partir de ese momento, el texto se despliega de forma automática debajo de cada nota de voz recibida, sin que sea necesario repetir el proceso de descarga en los envíos posteriores.
Transcribir mensajes de voz antiguos paso a paso
La función no se limita a los audios nuevos, ya que también permite convertir a texto mensajes de voz recibidos con anterioridad a la activación de la herramienta. Para hacerlo, hay que mantener presionado el mensaje de voz elegido y tocar el ícono de los tres puntos ubicado en la esquina superior derecha de la pantalla.
Dentro de ese menú contextual se encuentra la opción Transcribir, que al seleccionarla despliega el texto correspondiente al audio original, de la misma manera en que ocurre con los mensajes de voz recibidos luego de habilitar la función de forma predeterminada.
Privacidad y cifrado de extremo a extremo en las transcripciones
Respecto a la seguridad del proceso, la compañía precisó que las transcripciones se procesan de manera íntegra dentro del propio dispositivo del usuario, sin que el contenido del audio salga del teléfono para ser interpretado en servidores externos. Esto significa que las notas de voz conservan el cifrado de extremo a extremo, una característica central de la aplicación.
De esta manera, ni terceros ni la propia plataforma pueden acceder al contenido de los mensajes transcritos, ya que todo el procesamiento ocurre de forma local y el texto generado permanece sujeto a las mismas condiciones de privacidad que el audio original.
Si el usuario decide en algún momento dejar de usar la herramienta, el proceso para desactivarla resulta igual de simple que el de activación inicial. Basta con volver al menú Ajustes, ingresar nuevamente a Chats y desmarcar la casilla correspondiente a las transcripciones de mensajes de voz para que la función deje de estar disponible en los próximos audios recibidos.
Cómo archivar chats en WhatsApp para tener la bandeja de entrada ordenada
WhatsApp ofrece una función que permite mantener la bandeja de entrada organizada sin recurrir a la eliminación de conversaciones, ya que archivar un chat individual o grupal lo retira de la pantalla principal y lo traslada a una sección específica llamada Archivados, ubicada en la parte superior de la aplicación.
De forma predeterminada, los chats permanecen en esa carpeta incluso cuando reciben nuevos mensajes, lo que impide que vuelvan a aparecer en la lista principal de manera automática y permite al usuario revisar esa información solo cuando lo considere necesario.
El procedimiento para archivar una conversación resulta sencillo y varía levemente según el sistema operativo del dispositivo. En Android, basta con mantener presionado el chat que se desea ocultar y tocar el ícono con forma de caja y una flecha hacia abajo, ubicado en la barra superior de la pantalla. En iOS, en cambio, el usuario debe deslizar el chat hacia la izquierda y seleccionar la opción Archivar que aparece a continuación.
Cuando resulta necesario recuperar una conversación archivada o consultar mensajes antiguos, el proceso es igual de directo. Solo hace falta ingresar a la carpeta Archivados, ubicar el chat correspondiente y realizar la acción inversa a la utilizada para archivarlo, de manera que la conversación regrese a la bandeja de entrada principal junto con el resto de los chats activos.

articles.title: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer to buy its power, the companies announced Monday. Utility company American Electric Power (AEP) would operate the plant. X-energy, which designs small modular nuclear reactors and went public in April, would supply the reactors.
The new power plant would consist of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors and be located on the site of a demolished coal power plant just south of Terre Haute. The deal is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and it’s three times larger than the first, which was announced two years ago.
Amazon has invested heavily in X-energy, leading a $700 million Series C-1 round in October 2024. The two companies have said they ultimately plan to build 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generating capacity in the U.S. by 2039.
Unlike many newly announced power plants, these reactors would be connected to the public electric grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers.
The companies’ aggressive timeline still depends on X-energy successfully delivering its first power plant at a Dow Chemical plant southeast of Houston, Texas. The site, called Seadrift, has recently been at the center of a lawsuit filed by the state of Texas, which accuses the plant of “habitual non-compliance” with water and solid-waste regulations and permits.
X-energy has yet to break ground at Seadrift, which will host four Xe-100 reactors to provide the chemical plant with heat and electricity. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s review process.
Startups and large cloud computing companies are betting that small modular reactors (SMRs), like the kind being developed by X-energy, will help pull the nuclear industry out of its slump. The most recent nuclear power plants built in the U.S. suffered from egregious budget overruns and slipped timelines.
By shrinking the reactor, companies like X-energy hope that mass manufacturing will keep costs and schedules in line. Even then, it could be a tall order. Experts say mass manufacturing often doesn’t start producing benefits for about a decade.
X-energy debuted on the Nasdaq in April in an IPO priced at $23 per share. Investor excitement drove the price up 27% in the first day of trading, but shares of the newly public company have dropped by nearly two-thirds since then.
News of the Amazon deal sent X-energy’s shares up about 10% in premarket trading, though they were down by less than 2% at the time of publication.

articles.title: OPINION: Selling your startup does not mean success | EU-Startups
articles.text:
In that world of startups, founders and investors, we learn to ask certain questions almost instinctively. How big can this become? How much capital will it take to get there? And, sooner or later, when do I get my money back, and at what multiple?
These are not cynical questions. They reflect the logic of venture capital, where investors put capital at risk expecting substantial returns and founders pursue growth, scale and eventually liquidity.
But there is a question we ask far less often: Are we building the companies we actually want to own, or the companies our funding models encourage us to build?
When success changes meaning
At an event recently, I found myself in a conversation with experienced tech entrepreneurs who had already built, scaled and exited companies.
One founder told the room that, knowing what she knows today, she would never have sold her first company. Another described how differently he is building his next venture after taking external capital and scaling rapidly the first time around.
These were successful entrepreneurs by conventional measures. Yet their experiences had changed how they thought about ownership, ambition and what they ultimately wanted from building a business. Their reflections revealed an interesting tension: the decisions that help founders achieve one definition of success can sometimes take them further away from another.
In Vienna, the sixth and seventh generations of A.E. Köchert, the former Imperial Court jeweller founded in 1814, offer a strikingly different time horizon.
Their focus on craftsmanship, customer relationships and continuity illustrates how ownership across generations can shape business priorities. It is a mindset familiar in many multigenerational companies: the determination not to be the last generation.
It raises a broader question: how profoundly does a company’s definition of success shape what it builds, protects and passes on?
Capital is never just capital
For startup founders, choosing a funding model is one of the earliest and most consequential strategic decisions.
Venture capital can accelerate international expansion, product development and market leadership. In sectors where speed and scale are decisive, it can be the difference between building a category leader and being overtaken by competitors. But venture capital also comes with an economic logic. Fund lifecycles, return expectations and portfolio dynamics can influence the growth strategies, financing decisions and exit opportunities that investors favour.
A business that could generate attractive profits for its founder over decades may not necessarily deliver the scale or liquidity a venture fund requires. That does not make it a bad business. It may simply be the wrong business for that particular capital.
The reverse is equally true. A founder determined to retain complete control may underinvest in a market where rapid expansion is essential, sacrificing long-term competitiveness for short-term independence.
The real strategic challenge is aligning the company’s economics, the investors’ expectations and the founder’s ambitions. An investor may favour an acquisition that delivers an attractive return within the fund’s investment horizon, while the founder sees greater value in remaining independent. Both can be acting rationally, yet pursuing fundamentally different outcomes. When those interests are aligned, capital can be a powerful accelerator. When they are not, even a growing and successful business can become a source of conflict.
The ownership decisions that shape your future
In his research at Harvard Business School, Noam Wasserman explored a related tension through the founder’s “Rich versus King” dilemma: the choices that help build a more valuable company can require founders to surrender ownership and control. But I think the question extends beyond wealth versus control. It is also about time horizons, incentives and the freedom to redefine success as a company evolves.
Before raising capital, founders should consider three questions.
What kind of business am I building? A venture-scale technology company pursuing global market leadership may require a very different capital structure from a profitable business designed to compound value over decades.
Whose definition of success will ultimately determine our decisions? Founders and investors may agree on growth while having different expectations around profitability, ownership and the timing of an exit.
What am I willing to sacrifice and what must I protect? Speed, independence, culture, product quality and long-term flexibility all have value. Understanding which trade-offs are acceptable matters more than following a fashionable funding strategy.
These questions do not have universally correct answers. But avoiding them does not make the trade-offs disappear.
Ambition has more than one shape
Europe needs founders willing to build globally competitive companies. We need venture capital, ambitious growth strategies and entrepreneurs prepared to take extraordinary risks. But we also need to recognise that not every successful company should follow the same financial blueprint.
A successful funding round is not the same as a successful business. A higher valuation does not automatically mean greater long-term value. And an exit, however financially rewarding, is not necessarily every founder’s ultimate ambition.
After years in the startup and investment ecosystem, spending time with businesses that think in generations rather than funding rounds has not made me less interested in growth. It has made me more interested in what we are actually growing towards.
You may want to raise €100 million and build a global category leader. You may want to retain control and own your company in 30 years. Or you may want to build something the next generation will inherit.
The mistake is not choosing one model over another. The mistake is adopting someone else’s definition of success without understanding what it will require you to sacrifice.
Know which game you are playing. And make sure it is the one you actually want to win.

articles.title: OpenAI corre para levantar R$ 163,5 bilhões antes de IPO da Anthropic
articles.text:
A OpenAI está correndo para garantir compromissos de investidores antes da estreia da concorrente Anthropic na bolsa, prevista para meados de novembro. A nova rodada de financiamento pode avaliar a dona do ChatGPT em mais de US$ 1,4 trilhão (cerca de R$ 7,63 trilhões), segundo pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto ouvidas pela Reuters.
A captação deve movimentar aproximadamente US$ 30 bilhões (cerca de R$ 163,5 bilhões). Entre os investidores que negociam participação estão o SoftBank Group, o fundo soberano de Abu Dhabi MGX e outros apoiadores atuais da OpenAI.
De acordo com as fontes da agência, a empresa quer concluir a operação rapidamente, em parte para se antecipar à Anthropic. As duas desenvolvedoras de IA disputam recursos de base semelhante de investidores, enquanto buscam avaliações trilionárias.
A OpenAI realizou reuniões com fundos de investimento de longo prazo e fundos soberanos na semana passada, enquanto a Anthropic promovia seu próprio encontro com investidores. A rodada da dona do ChatGPT deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado do que o habitual para uma operação desse porte.
OpenAI quer captar recursos antes de comparações com a Anthropic
- A estratégia também busca aproveitar o crescimento recente da receita da OpenAI, impulsionado pelo lançamento de novos modelos de IA;
- Segundo uma das fontes ouvidas pela Reuters, a empresa informou a investidores que atingiu receita anualizada de US$ 50 bilhões (cerca de R$ 272,5 bilhões) e espera elevar esse valor para US$ 70 bilhões (cerca de R$ 381,5 bilhões) até o fim do ano. A apresentação destaca o desempenho após o lançamento do GPT-6 Astra;
- A OpenAI também reduziu os preços de seus modelos mais baratos e afirmou que a mudança ampliou o uso das ferramentas. A companhia sinalizou aos investidores que ainda pode diminuir os preços de seus modelos de IA;
- A Anthropic, por sua vez, chegou à receita anualizada de aproximadamente US$ 65 bilhões (cerca de R$ 354,3 bilhões) em julho, segundo informações anteriores da Reuters. A empresa informou a investidores que sua receita trimestral passou de US$ 11,6 bilhões (cerca de R$ 63,2 bilhões) no segundo trimestre para US$ 16,8 bilhões (cerca de R$ 91,6 bilhões) no terceiro.
Apesar do avanço, a desaceleração do crescimento mensal da receita da Anthropic provocou questionamentos entre investidores sobre sua avaliação. A OpenAI quer concluir a captação antes que as divulgações financeiras da concorrente ofereçam mais informações e estimulem comparações diretas entre os negócios.
Esses dados também podem levar investidores a cobrar de Sarah Friar, diretora financeira da OpenAI, mais detalhes sobre o crescimento da receita e as perspectivas da companhia.
As duas empresas têm métodos diferentes de contabilizar a receita. A OpenAI registra os valores líquidos, descontando antecipadamente a parcela de parceiros. A companhia já acusou a Anthropic de inflar sua receita ao contabilizar o valor bruto de contratos vendidos por meio de provedores de nuvem terceirizados. A Anthropic afirmou anteriormente à Reuters que segue práticas contábeis estabelecidas.
“É uma corrida entre duas empresas em termos de abertura de capital”, disse Edward Best, copresidente de mercados de capitais do escritório de advocacia Willkie Farr & Gallagher, que não participa da operação, à Reuters, e comentou a possibilidade em caráter hipotético.
A OpenAI foi avaliada em US$ 852 bilhões (cerca de R$ 4,64 trilhões) em março, após rodada de financiamento recorde de US$ 122 bilhões (cerca de R$ 664,9 bilhões). A operação incluiu compromisso de investimento da Amazon de até US$ 50 bilhões (cerca de R$ 272,5 bilhões).
Leia mais:
- OpenAI alerta Polícia Federal sobre ameaças contra Lula feitas no ChatGPT
- ChatGPT ganha vozes mais naturais e melhora reconhecimento de sotaques; veja novidades
- Deepfakes podem dificultar análise de provas, alertam OpenAI e Meta
Infraestrutura de IA e incertezas do mercado pesam na captação
Além de tentar se antecipar à concorrente, a OpenAI precisa de capital para cumprir seus compromissos de infraestrutura e reforçar o balanço financeiro. A necessidade ganha importância caso uma piora nas condições do mercado de IPOs atrase a abertura de capital da empresa, planejada para 2027.
Embora haja forte demanda pelas ações das duas companhias, os investidores precisam avaliar e distribuir recursos entre duas operações complexas e concorrentes em um intervalo de poucos dias ou semanas. Algumas fontes ouvidas pela Reuters avaliam que a iniciativa da OpenAI busca garantir dinheiro de fundos que poderiam destinar uma parcela maior de seus recursos à oferta pública da Anthropic.
O cenário, porém, é de maior cautela. A volatilidade das ações de tecnologia, a alta dos rendimentos dos títulos de dívida e as preocupações com a segurança da IA vêm afetando o apetite dos investidores. Os custos da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o avanço da IA, incluindo o endividamento para financiar data centers, também estão sob escrutínio.
A própria avaliação da Anthropic enfrenta questionamentos. Alguns investidores atuais e potenciais defenderam valor próximo de US$ 1,5 trilhão (cerca de R$ 8,18 trilhões) para a estreia na bolsa, abaixo dos US$ 2 trilhões (cerca de R$ 10,9 trilhões) desejados, após os resultados do terceiro trimestre ficarem aquém das expectativas.
A instabilidade também afetou outras empresas que planejavam abrir capital. Companhias e instituições financeiras têm adiado ofertas para evitar disputar a atenção dos investidores com a Anthropic em mercado volátil e pressionado pela queda de ações ligadas à IA.
Entre as preocupações está a CoreWeave, provedora de serviços de nuvem, cujas ações e dívidas caíram na semana passada, enquanto investidores analisavam os quase US$ 50 bilhões (cerca de R$ 272,5 bilhões) em empréstimos usados para financiar sua expansão.
Empresas, como AirTrunk REIT, apoiada pela Blackstone, Firmus, apoiada pela Nvidia, e SB Energy, apoiada pelo SoftBank, retiraram ou suspenderam seus planos de abertura de capital. A empresa de serviços nucleares Holtec também cancelou uma oferta nos Estados Unidos no mês passado, citando combinação de fatores adversos, principalmente a incerteza sobre a demanda por data centers.
Em menos de duas semanas, as empresas do índice Philadelphia Semiconductor, usado como referência para a demanda por semicondutores ligados à IA, perderam US$ 1,6 trilhão (cerca de R$ 8,72 trilhões) em valor de mercado.
OpenAI e SoftBank não comentaram a captação. Anthropic e MGX não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário da Reuters.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Galaxy Buds 4 têm promoção histórica com queda de 50% de desconto • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Buds 4 têm promoção histórica com queda de 50% de desconto
Galaxy Buds 4 têm ANC e áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits; fones da Samsung saem pela metade do preço em oferta histórica no Pix com cupom do Mercado Livre, que vai acabar logo
Os Galaxy Buds 4 estão em promoção por R$ 804 no Pix com cupom OFFHOJENOML no Mercado Livre. Os fones de ouvido sem fio da Samsung, com áudio Hi-Fi de 24 bits e ANC, alcançam o menor preço histórico com desconto de 50% sobre o original de R$ 1.599.
Mas seja rápido: este cupom é válido apenas nesta segunda-feira (19) e pode esgotar a qualquer momento.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 estão entre os melhores fones wireless da Samsung. Eles possuem suporte a áudio Hi-Fi (alta fidelidade) de 24 bits, que oferece experiência sonora com grande foco nos detalhes, e o cancelamento de ruído ativo (ANC) filtra quase todos os sons externos, mas não todos, por questões de segurança.
Assistentes de Inteligência Artificial (IA), como o Bixby da Samsung, Google Gemini e Perplexity, oferecem funções por comandos por voz para acionar menus e realizar pesquisas. O Galaxy AI conta com um tradutor automático de conversas, que só funciona quando os fones são pareados a gadgets da linha Galaxy.
Outros recursos incluem o Voice Pickup Unit, que trabalha para tornar as chamadas de voz mais nítidas, e o equalizador adaptativo, que ajusta as frequências sonoras com base no formato do canal auditivo do usuário, de modo a personalizar a experiência sonora.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 suportam Bluetooth 6.1, que oferece menor latência em jogos e/ou transmissões em tempo real, enquanto a função Auto Switch torna mais simples parear o wearable com mais de um dispositivo, ao permitir navegar entre gadgets conectados facilmente.
As baterias de 45 mAh dos fones resistem até 5 horas de reprodução com o ANC ligado e 6 horas com o recurso desativado. A bateria de 515 mAh do estojo de transporte garante ao kit uma autonomia total de até 30 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante.
Os Galaxy Buds 4 (R$ 804 no Pix com cupom OFFHOJENOML) possuem certificação IP54, que adiciona aos fones wireless da Samsung resistência moderada contra poeira, suor e respingos d’água.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Inovia secures $200-million USD first close for sixth early-stage VC fund
articles.text:
Inovia Capital has completed a $200-million USD ($282-million CAD) first close of its sixth early-stage venture capital (VC) fund.
The multi-stage, Montréal-based technology investor announced the news today in a LinkedIn post. Returning Inovia limited partners (LPs) like the Business Development Bank of Canada, La Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Fondaction, Fonds de solidarité FTQ, Investissement Québec, and Teralys Capital supported the first close.
The first close brings Inovia more than halfway to its $325-million USD Fund VI target.
As BetaKit has previously reported, the strategy and size of Fund VI is expected to be “very similar” to its $325-million USD predecessor. It took Inovia six months to reach this $200-million USD mark, which puts the firm more than halfway toward its $325-million USD target for its latest fund, which it hopes to hit by the first quarter of 2027.
Inovia partner Karamdeep Nijjar told BetaKit over email that Fund VI will focus on AI-native startups and emerging frontier technologies across cybersecurity, infrastructure, developer operations, energy, compute, robotics, and quantum.
He said Fund VI is the investment firm’s “first completely AI-native fund where every business from day one is using AI in some way to change the world.”
Nijjar credited Inovia’s progress amid a tough fundraising market to the trust it has built among its LPs “over many years,” and the strength of its platform, which spans discovery, VC, and growth equity.
He also singled out the performance of Inovia’s fifth venture fund, which he claimed has posted top-quartile performance relative to Cambridge Associates and Carta benchmarks thanks to its investments in fast-growing startups like Cohere, Flare, Gaia, and Spellbook, among others.
RELATED: Inovia promotes Mia Morisset to partner on growth team
Inovia aims to make 15 to 20 core investments out of Fund VI in tech startups from seed to Series A across North America and Europe. Those efforts will be overseen by six partners: Nijjar, Magaly Charbonneau, Shawn Abbott, Kory Jeffrey, Taha Mubashir, and Steve Woods (Jeffrey and Mubashir were promoted to the position last year).
Inovia plans to source opportunities for Fund VI from its Discovery Program for emerging managers, a fund-of-funds initiative it launched a few years ago with a $25-million USD first fund. It is building the next version of that platform with Northleaf Capital Partners. Nijjar declined to share any more details on those plans at this time.
This latest milestone comes a few months after Inovia promoted Mia Morrisset to partner on its growth equity team, which has raised $365 million USD of a planned $450 million for its third such fund. That fund picks up where its VC team stops. These investment vehicles come in addition to a $100-million USD Venture Scientist Fund that Inovia revealed it is co-launching with Québec AI research institute Mila back in early 2026.
This first close of Fund VI brings Inovia’s total assets under management to $2.7 billion USD.
Feature image courtesy Inovia Capital. Photo by Eva Blue.

articles.title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
articles.text:
The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.
The fossil fuel comeback is here
Data centers are demanding more energy, and the Trump administration is making sure fossil fuels meet the moment.
Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.
America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.
While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world.
Then Donald Trump stepped into his second term as president with a plan to “drill, baby, drill” for fossil fuels, his preferred power source for energy-hungry data centers. His administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects by issuing stop work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives. We’re still seeing a rush of new solar and wind farms driven by relatively low costs, although many of them make up the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives.
The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.
Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.
New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

articles.title: Spotify se pone serio contra las cuentas compartidas y ahora exige esta verificación
articles.text:
Spotify comenzó a implementar una medida que busca acabar con las cuentas compartidas. Siguiendo la tendencia de Netflix y otras empresas, el servicio de música en streaming activó un sistema de verificación para limitar el uso indebido del plan Premium Familiar. Ahora los usuarios tendrán que validar su cuenta mediante un código QR, pero no es tan sencillo como pensabas.
Al igual que otras suscripciones, el plan Premium Familiar de Spotify exige que todos los miembros vivan en el mismo domicilio. Si bien este ayuda a reducir costes al no pagar membresías individuales, muchos lo aprovechan para compartir con los amigos que viven lejos. Los usuarios sacaban ventaja de que Spotify no tenía un método confiable para confirmar que vivías en el mismo domicilio que el responsable de la cuenta familiar, aunque eso terminó hoy.
Algunos usuarios reportan en Reddit que recibieron una notificación en la que se les pide verificar que viven con la persona administradora a través de un código QR. Para evitar los intentos de eludirlo, Spotify cambia el código a los pocos segundos de forma aleatoria, lo que impide capturar pantalla y compartirlo con un tercero para que lo verifique.
Según explica la compañía en su web de soporte, la persona que administra el plan familiar debe abrir el código QR desde la aplicación móvil. Para ello, basta con acceder al perfil y las opciones de gestión de Premium, donde se mostrará el código que tendrá que compartir con el miembro de la familia que requiere la verificación. Este último podrá escanearlo usando la cámara del móvil y el sistema lo registrará como usuario confirmado.
Si no verificas tu cuenta, te quedarás sin Spotify por un año
Debido a que se trata de un plan familiar, es lógico pensar que ambos están en el mismo lugar cuando se realiza la verificación. Los códigos caducan a los pocos segundos, por lo que es difícil enviar la captura por WhatsApp u otro cliente de mensajería. Lo peor de todo es que los usuarios que reciben la notificación solo tienen 7 días para validar la membresía, de lo contrario, no podrán unirse a otro plan familiar o Duo durante los siguientes 12 meses.
La buena noticia para aquellos que comparten la cuenta es que el sistema de verificación por códigos QR de Spotify no es infalible. Algunos usuarios ya consiguieron saltárselo a través de una videollamada, donde es posible escanear el código si la otra persona coloca el móvil frente a la cámara. Es probable que esto cambie y que la compañía implemente medidas adicionales para evitar que el plan Premium Familiar pueda compartirse con terceros.
De momento, los códigos QR se están probando en un número limitado de usuarios. Para verificarse, es necesario que ambos tengan la aplicación móvil actualizada a la última versión. Spotify no confirmó cuándo se desplegará al resto de usuarios, aunque la información ya está en la web de soporte de España, México y otros países de América Latina.

articles.title: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
articles.text:
The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
Plus: Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
—James Temple
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.
Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.
A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.
Now, researchers are exploring how to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?
Read the full story on how scientists are rethinking the fight against wildfires.
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experimentreminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone.
The agents started behaving in surprising ways. They set about exploring the limits of the world, and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
A lot of what they were doing met the bar for play. But is it truly playful behavior, or simply role-playing?
Read our full story to learn more.
—Amit Katwala
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors
X-energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Making concrete, steel, and chemicals takes huge amounts of heat, much of it generated by burning fossil fuels. X-energy hopes to offer an alternative with a nuclear reactor that uses helium gas instead of water as a coolant, allowing it to operate at higher temperatures.
The proposed Xe-100 reactor could supply superheated steam directly to industrial facilities, generate 80 megawatts of electricity—or do both.
See how X-energy hopes to bring high-temperature nuclear power to heavy industry.
—Mark Ellis Harris
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from cleaner cement to streamlined geothermal power.
Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses
Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.
He spoke about his work with our senior AI reporter James O'Donnell on Friday. If you missed it, you can watch their chat now, and subscribe to get invites to our Roundtables events in future.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

It’s unclear if AI companies can turn sustainable profits, and investors are getting jittery. (NBC)

2 Do we really want AI agents smoothing out all friction in our lives?
They promise convenience, but right now they’re mostly introducing chaos. (The Atlantic $)
+ Here’s what it’s like to outsource your life to them. (Vox $)
+ Websites are starting to close their doors to AI agents. (The Verge $)
+ AI agents bring new headaches for online sellers. (WSJ $)
3 How drones have transformed the front line in Ukraine
They’ve effectively created a “kill zone”, and it’s growing wider and deadlier. (NYT $)
+ Trump has denied ordering Starlink restrictions in Ukraine. (CNBC)
4 China is considering restricting overseas access to its AI models 
It’s also looking at curbing the sharing of chip designs, among other measures. (Bloomberg $)
+ Why western open weight models still can’t compete with Chinese ones. (Rest of World)
+ Why Trumpworld still can’t agree on how to respond to Chinese AI. (MIT Technology Review)
5 HTC’s smart glasses are way more private than Meta’s
Guess that’s a benefit of not being shackled to a massive social media platform. (Wired $)
+ A bug caused Meta’s glasses to record conversations without the wearer knowing. (Ars Technica)
+ Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Inside one man’s quest to build California’s biggest AI data center
Sebastian Rucci didn’t bank on meeting huge resistance from local residents. (The Guardian)
+ Americans are packing town halls to stop data centers, and it’s working. (Quartz $)
+ No wonder companies are exploring putting them in space. (MIT Technology Review)
7 Somebody vibe-coded a gun for the first time
And it seems like it works (sometimes.) (The Verge $)
8 AI might reshape how we grieve
It’s never been easier to create realistic AI chatbots of people who’ve passed. (Vox $)

9 Japan is about to launch a mission to Mars’ largest moon
If all goes well, it should help us to understand how it formed. (New Scientist $)
10 Amateurs are cracking long-secret codes and ciphers 🕵️
One of the more fun uses for large language models! (Nature)
Quote of the day
“Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.”
—President Trump brags about how much Big Tech bends the knee to him during a rally in Kentucky this weekend, the Verge reports.
One More Thing
There are more AI health tools than ever—but how well do they work?
In the last few months alone, Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all launched medical chatbots.
There’s a clear demand for these tools, given how hard it is for many people to access advice through the existing medical system—and they could make safe, useful recommendations. But concerns have surfaced about how little external evaluation they undergo before being released to the public.
Read the full story to understand what’s at stake.
—Grace Huckins

articles.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
articles.text:
Integrating sensors, compute, and actuators into autonomous systems adds new challenges for chip design.
Key Takeaways:
Physical AI is changing how chips are designed and used, integrating sensing, AI inference, and real-time control into machines that can safely and predictably interact with the physical world.
The challenges extend well beyond just performance. Engineers need to account for corner cases stemming from unpredictable environments, ensure these systems are safe and reliable, and they need to future-proof these systems by ensuring they are serviceable and upgradable. This will require new tools and methodologies, as well as some new design approaches.
“AI is leaving the screen,” says Anthony Matarazzo, head of physical AI, digital twins, simulation-driven AI, and accelerated computing at Synopsys. “It is no longer about generating text or code. It is entering the physical world. It needs to understand, interact, sense, make decisions in a physical environment. We are moving from generative AI to agentic workflow orchestration to physical AI (see figure 1.) That is literally making intelligence actionable. But the consequences of being wrong fundamentally change. Life or death, plus or minus 1%.”
Fig. 1: Three Eras of AI. Source: Synopsys
Physical AI must see and interact with the real world. “It is challenging to make artificial intelligence see the world correctly,” says Chun-Ting “Tim” Wang-Lee, signal integrity application scientist at Keysight EDA. “Real-world information comes from the sensors, and the data has to be moved somewhere and processed so that the AI can decide and then act. There are decisions that need to be made.”
This changes the design priorities. “Physical AI usually gets framed as a compute story,” says Justin Endo, director for marketing and sales at Mixel, A Silvaco Company. “But from our perspective it has really been an imaging story. Every robot, drone, and autonomous system comes down to cameras feeding an inference engine.”
Physical AI builds on some of the connectivity and sensing technologies developed for the Internet of Things. “IoT was largely about connecting and monitoring things,” says Brad Rex, head of physical AI, UX at Renesas Electronics. “Physical AI is about giving machines the ability to perceive and act autonomously in unstructured environments. This is a completely orthogonal engineering problem, and it requires a step-change in system-level content — more sensing, more real-time compute, more sophisticated power management, and more safety considerations per device.”
Within physical AI, there are two distinct classes of devices: “Those that can rely on a cloud connection and those that must operate fully locally without relying on connectivity,” says Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “For example, vehicles cannot rely on continuous connectivity, as there are many locations where cellular coverage is inadequate. In contrast, an industrial robotic arm moves but is constrained to a particular location within a factory setting, and therefore can be connected to the cloud.”
Others agree. “Unlike traditional AI applications that primarily generate information, physical AI systems influence real-world outcomes through continuous interaction with their environment,” says William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence. “Traditional IoT often focused on collecting and transmitting data. Physical AI adds real-time interpretation and action. The result is a shift from connected devices to intelligent systems operating within sensing and control loops.”
This requires new architectures and new methodologies. “The entire architecture is very different,” says Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci. “Time-to-market is going to be much slower because people are still learning. Physical AI is the next step that they want, but the switch to it is not going to be easy. The easiest entry point will be a repetitive action, but people are not willing to pay much for that. They want it to do a lot more. That’s why it is going to take a more complex architecture to build, make reliable, and make it work for at least a day on a single charge.”
It also requires significant processing power. “Robotics and drones require powerful, efficient compute capable of multimodal processing and accurate, real-time responsiveness in dynamic settings,” says Sameer Sharma, associate vice president for MediaTek’s IoT business. “Because of latency and bandwidth constraints, these devices require silicon capable of handling AI workloads at the edge, including AI acceleration for machine vision and object classification.”
As systems get larger or more capable, additional challenges emerge. “You need longer reach through moving joints, aggregation of many cameras into few ports, and the functional safety expectations coming over from automotive,” says Mixel’s Endo. “But the standard is already moving in that direction. The mobile camera interface is becoming the robot’s optic nerve, and that mobile-proven maturity is hard for any alternative to match.”
How quickly physical AI is adopted by different markets will vary, but the overall projections are noteworthy. At a high level, PwC estimates the global physical AI market will reach ~€430 billion by 2030, with “significant upside potential as systems scale and mature.” Deloitte, meanwhile, found that 58% of companies report at least limited use of physical AI today, with that number projected to rise to 80% within two years.
Not all sectors will adopt this technology at the same time. “Physical AI is not just AI at the edge,” says Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategic programs for system solutions at Synopsys. “It is broader than just robotics, but it will be uneven. The question is how quickly each industry will adopt physical AI. It requires you to go beyond the chip to the full physics. The growth inflection comes when you have this full loop of sensing, reasoning, physical action, and then autonomy. It’s really a platform transition where everything is being elevated up to the system level.”
New markets have repeatedly driven changes in the semiconductor ecosystem. “We believe physical AI is one of the most disruptive AI opportunities of the next several years,” says Sanjay Gupta, co-founder and president at Velaura AI. “We see it as a category of its own, rather than another set of IoT products. Industry estimates vary, but several point to a multi-trillion-dollar total addressable market over the next 10 years across robotics, drones, industrial automation, logistics, healthcare, and defense.”
In many cases, it will be market pressure that dictates when a sector advances. “The clearest near-term applications are in industrial and logistics settings,” says Renesas’ Rex. “Humanoid and non-humanoid robots handling repetitive or physically demanding tasks in factories, warehouses and supply chains, where labor shortages make automation valuable, and the environment is structured enough to deploy safely today.”
While many point to safety and security concerns, there are multiple ways to look at that. “Physical AI is enabling new ways to make essential work safer, more efficient and more productive,” says Robert Day, director of go-to-market, physical AI at Arm. “We’re already seeing autonomous machines move toward practical work in manufacturing, logistics and transportation. These industries represent an estimated $200 billion annual compute opportunity in the 2030s.”
Deployment in some sectors will likely be slower than others, but the overall industry could show rapid growth. “Each category is going to be separate and see slow growth, but there will be many sectors growing in parallel,” says Vinci’s Radhakrishnan. “Each requires new-age AI, new compute, and this will impact the speed at which it’s going to develop. One area may take longer to grow deep, but before it fully penetrates one market segment, it will enter multiple new market segments. Together it’s going to grow.”
But they all require some advances in areas such as training and simulation before that happens. “We know that the Internet trained generative AI, but what’s going to train physical AI?” asks Synopsys’ Matarazzo. “This is the big question that companies are asking. Reality has rules.”
Modularity
Physical AI systems are not like mobile phones that quickly get replaced when a new model comes out. Cars, robots, and drones have much higher initial cost, and they are expected to last many years. This indicates that many physical AI systems will need to be updatable, not just in terms of software or even AI models, but hardware, sensors, and actuators, as well.
Physical AI systems will continue to evolve as models and use cases change. “A consistent compute foundation across development and deployment can help teams carry software forward instead of rebuilding individual components for each generation,” says Arm’s Day. “Turning the opportunity into growth will ultimately depend on making autonomous machines efficient, responsive and reliable enough to deploy at scale.”
“Autonomous vehicles have been there for some time, but the older ones can’t be retrofitted to the newer techniques, camera sensors, etc.,” says Radhakrishnan. “The design of physical AI needs to go into some form of modular systems. Maybe you have a compute system that can be taken out and replaced, or a new sensor. People may be okay with paying 10% of the original cost every two or three years to update certain things, and the software updates keep coming in. This is what is going to keep refreshing this.”
The ability to do this needs to be addressed at the initial design stage. “Given how quickly robot architectures are evolving, we design for headroom rather than attempting to predict a fixed end state,” says Rex. “That means greater compute margin, scalable power architectures, and modular subsystem designs that can absorb additional sensing or intelligence without a full redesign. We are developing next-generation devices and evaluating how to optimize across multiple vectors such as power, compute, scalability, and efficiency to determine the right balance. We also rely on distributed architectures, so that as capability needs grow, it is often a matter of adding or upgrading a subsystem rather than replacing the entire platform. That approach, combined with software and reference-design platforms that can be updated over time, helps customers avoid designing themselves into a corner.”
More future-proofing is required than in many previous embedded or edge systems. “Physical AI deployments often have long operational lifetimes, yet must accommodate evolving AI models, new sensors, changing workloads, and increasing autonomy requirements,” says Cadence’s Chen. “Therefore, future-proofing is less about maximizing raw performance and more about building architectural flexibility. Multi-die architectures, scalable memory subsystems, high-speed interconnects, and standards-based interfaces provide mechanisms for adapting systems as requirements change. The challenge is that many infrastructure decisions become difficult to change once they are embedded into the system. Memory architecture, communication fabrics, and interface choices frequently determine the practical limits of future expansion.”
Real-time constraints
While real-time constraints have been a fundamental aspect of many embedded systems, physical AI will take this to a much higher level of complexity. It may not be possible to make many of the simplifications used in the past, such as not using cache memory because it introduces non-predictable response times.
The scale of the compute problem alone is unprecedented. “For chips designed for physical AI, the biggest limitation is predictability under real operating conditions,” says Alex Burlak, executive vice president of engineering and customer success at proteanTecs. “Consider a humanoid robot. It may have a powerful central compute system serving as its ‘brain,’ but throughout its body there can be dozens of MCUs and other devices controlling motors, joints, sensors, power and communications. A timing issue or degradation in one of those devices may not simply mean an application runs a little slower. It could mean a joint responds differently than expected, a sensor input arrives late, or an actuator behaves outside its intended parameters.”
Translating a system’s understanding of its surroundings into precise actions is complex. “Physical environments are unpredictable, and sensor data can be noisy, so systems need to handle uncertainty and continue adapting as conditions change,” says MediaTek’s Sharma. “That requires a software stack that connects perception, navigation, decision-making, and control, and supports the application-specific models, runtimes, and tools.”
This requires a different focus. “Traditional AI infrastructure is often optimized for throughput, utilization, and scale,” says Chen. “Physical AI systems must satisfy latency, power, reliability, safety, and environmental requirements while responding to continuously changing inputs. A correct answer delivered too late may be operationally equivalent to a wrong answer. As a result, physical AI introduces a different optimization target. The goal is not simply maximizing compute performance. It is maintaining predictable system behavior across sensing, memory, compute, communication, and actuation.”
It becomes a more complex optimization problem. “Physical AI systems need to process sensor data, and reason and act in real time within tight constraints on size, power, and weight,” says Day. “They require more than capable AI models. Hardware and software must be designed together around these workloads, from low-power sensing and real-time control to demanding AI processing.”
The whole system becomes a part of the timing constraint. “This is a prime example of where hardware/software co-design matters most,” says Rex. “The complexity across multiple domains will become even more significant going forward, spanning not only electronics, but mechanical design and battery technology, as well. Many of these disciplines, which were once addressed somewhat independently, now represent a larger challenge because they must be solved concurrently rather than in isolation. Because physical AI systems have to reconcile AI inference with deterministic, safety-critical control, the silicon and the software cannot be optimized separately and expected to integrate successfully. The system architecture, the real-time software, and the underlying compute and power hardware all have to be designed together from the outset.”
This methodology change has been brewing for a long time. “Physical AI arguably represents one of the strongest cases for hardware/software co-design,” says Chen. “Control-loop behavior emerges from interactions between sensing, memory access, inference execution, communication, and actuation. Improving software alone cannot overcome infrastructure bottlenecks, and faster hardware does not automatically improve system behavior if data delivery, synchronization, or timing remain constrained. The architecture must be considered end-to-end.”
What does real-time AI even mean? “Will AI always be fast enough to get this control back to the actuator?” asks Synopsys’ Schirrmeister. “The engineering challenges are behavioral. Get those real scenarios done, then deal with the uncertainty of making sure that it’s not leading to catastrophic failures. Hardware software will become even more critical. You really need to be flexible in being able to upgrade and then also, for safety reasons, stop where you can’t go.”
The challenge is not simply building faster chips or more capable AI models. Physical AI systems must coordinate sensing, computation, and actuation while remaining predictable under changing operating conditions. That will require new approaches to system architecture, hardware/software co-design, and verification, particularly as these machines become more autonomous and remain in service for longer periods.

articles.title: Dark Souls 2 cachait un immense colisée qui n’a jamais intégré le jeu
articles.text:
En avril 2026, nous vous parlions d’une scène coupée d’Elden Ring, retrouvée par des datamineurs dans les fichiers du jeu. Le titre de FromSoftware cachait une séquence cinématique qui n’avait jamais été intégrée au jeu, mais dormait encore dans ses profondeurs.
Des découvertes de ce genre, les datamineurs en font régulièrement. La dernière en date concerne, une fois encore, un jeu de FromSoftware. Doneda, un datamineur habitué à fouiller dans les jeux du studio, a publié le 5 octobre 2026, sur sa chaîne YouTube, une vidéo consacrée à la mystérieuse zone du Colisée de Dark Souls 2. Relayée par PC Gamer le 18 octobre, elle montre ce prototype de niveau, abandonné tôt dans le développement et jamais intégré au jeu.
La vidéo dévoile des couloirs interminables et des structures en pierre à l’architecture impossible, vestiges d’une zone jamais terminée par les développeurs. Le Colisée domine l’ensemble. Posé au milieu d’une zone inachevée, il rappelle l’esthétique des espaces liminaux et confère à l’ensemble une étrangeté presque onirique.
Le datamineur a par ailleurs découvert plusieurs environnements distincts, dont des mines, une portion de crypte et une tour souterraine qui aurait pu accueillir une série d’arènes. Impossible, malheureusement, de connaître leur fonction précise, ni de savoir où ces différentes zones auraient pu s’insérer dans la version finale de Dark Souls 2. Au vu de leur niveau de finition, ces environnements semblent avoir été abandonnés assez tôt dans le développement.
D’après PC Gamer, certaines portions semblent avoir formé une zone interconnectée, et l’ensemble pourrait être lié à ce qui est devenu la Crypte des Morts Vivants, la crypte que l’on traverse en fin de partie.
Une zone cachée de Dark Souls 2 explorée grâce à Elden Ring Nightreign
Pour explorer ces vestiges, Doneda a utilisé Elden Ring Nightreign, dans lequel il a importé les données des anciennes zones de Dark Souls 2 afin de pouvoir les parcourir. Une manipulation rendue possible par son travail de modding. Par le passé, il avait déjà réussi à adapter certains environnements du jeu à Nightreign, dont Eleum Loyce, une zone issue d’un contenu additionnel de Dark Souls 2.
Pour comprendre pourquoi certaines parties de Dark Souls 2 ont été abandonnées en cours de développement, il faut revenir sur la production mouvementée du jeu. Dans une interview publiée dans l’artbook Dark Souls II Design Works, traduite en anglais par le site Barnard Translations en 2018, le réalisateur Yui Tanimura reconnaît que le développement a été difficile : à mi-parcours, l’équipe a dû repenser le jeu dans son ensemble et revoir sa conception depuis le début. Plutôt que de tout recommencer, elle a dû réutiliser et adapter une grande partie des environnements et des éléments déjà créés, tout en respectant les délais.
Ce remaniement explique sans doute pourquoi de vastes zones inachevées dorment encore aujourd’hui dans les fichiers du jeu.

articles.title: Des sites IPTV pirates toujours accessibles : pourquoi la justice refuse de sanctionner les VPN
articles.text:
Jusqu'à 10 000 euros par jour et par domaine non bloqué, voilà ce que réclamait beIN Sports à plusieurs intermédiaires techniques, dont NordVPN, Surfshark et Cloudflare. Malgré des sites de streaming illégal toujours accessibles, le tribunal judiciaire de Paris a rejeté ses demandes. Une nouvelle décision qui précise les limites des obligations imposées aux fournisseurs de VPN.
La bataille contre le piratage sportif connaît un nouvel épisode judiciaire en France. Après Canal+, qui avait échoué en septembre à obtenir de lourdes astreintes contre Cloudflare, c'est au tour de beIN Sports d'essuyer un refus. Dans deux jugements rendus le 7 octobre, le tribunal judiciaire de Paris a estimé que les mesures déployées par plusieurs intermédiaires techniques ne justifiaient pas les pénalités financières réclamées par le diffuseur.
Des blocages incomplets, mais des efforts bien réels
L'affaire remonte au mois de mai 2026. beIN Sports, détenteur des droits de diffusion du tennis féminin WTA en France, avait obtenu des ordonnances imposant à NordVPN, Surfshark et Proton VPN de bloquer dix sites diffusant illégalement les rencontres. Cloudflare avait été visé le lendemain pour sept plateformes.
Mais leur mise en œuvre s'est révélée partielle. Cloudflare a notamment limité ses interventions aux sites utilisant son réseau de distribution de contenus (CDN), sans appliquer de filtrage sur son résolveur DNS public. De leur côté, NordVPN et Surfshark ont effectué des blocages via les serveurs DNS de leurs infrastructures françaises. Une restriction qui laisse notamment la possibilité d'accéder aux sites concernés en passant par un serveur VPN situé à l'étranger.
Pour beIN Sports, ces mesures étaient insuffisantes. Le diffuseur réclamait donc des astreintes pouvant atteindre 10 000 euros par jour et par nom de domaine restant accessible, autrement dit des sommes dues en cas de non-exécution des obligations judiciaires.
Les VPN doivent agir, pas garantir un résultat absolu
Le tribunal n'a pas suivi beIN Sports. Les juges ont retenu que les intermédiaires étaient soumis à une obligation de moyens, et non de résultat : ils doivent prendre des mesures raisonnables pour limiter l'accès aux services pirates, sans être nécessairement tenus de garantir leur inaccessibilité permanente.
Les efforts effectivement déployés ont ainsi été jugés suffisants pour écarter les astreintes, considérées comme ni nécessaires ni proportionnées. Cela ne signifie pas que les VPN sont dispensés de leurs obligations de blocage, ni que beIN Sports ne peut plus agir. Le diffuseur conserve notamment la possibilité de faire appel.
Cette affaire prolonge la décision rendue en septembre dans le litige opposant Canal+ à Cloudflare, mais elle confirme surtout que ce raisonnement peut également s'appliquer aux fournisseurs de VPN.
Le cadre juridique reste néanmoins en construction. Le 30 septembre, la cour d'appel de Paris a suspendu une autre procédure opposant la Ligue de football professionnel à plusieurs VPN, dans l'attente d'une décision de la Cour de cassation concernant un dossier parallèle impliquant Canal+.
La question devient désormais plus délicate pour les intermédiaires qui refusent tout blocage. C'est notamment le cas de Quad9, également poursuivi par beIN Sports, qui réclame jusqu'à 580 000 euros par jour pour 58 domaines non bloqués. Contrairement à NordVPN et Surfshark, le résolveur DNS suisse n'a appliqué aucune des mesures ordonnées, invoquant ses limites techniques. Reste à savoir si les juges apprécieront cette absence de blocage de la même manière que les efforts partiels des fournisseurs de VPN.

articles.title: Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain weighs in
articles.text:
Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain weighs in
At TechSparks 2026, CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems that drive genuine business profit.
Most marketing teams today use AI to save time on tasks such as drafting emails, creating image variants, and summarising long documents. However, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, says basic tools that do these jobs rarely improve company profits.
In a masterclass on marketing strategy at TechSparks 2026, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts.
“We are going to talk about how you go from using AI for fun and games all the way to using AI to generate actual business results," he said.
While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth. "Is it actually going to impact business results or is it just more of the same?”
Traditional digital campaigns usually operate on a push model wherein companies decide what they want to sell instead of understanding what consumers want to buy. Whereas, a local shop assistant in an offline channel remembers a customer’s personal taste, notices immediate reactions, and suggests items tailored to their budget and style. Digital marketing must adopt a similar mindset.
“Not what I want to sell, (but) what my customer wants to buy. So you flip this around,” Jain said.
Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs.
This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as 'real-time decisioning'.
Marketing technology generally progresses through three stages. Level 1 focuses on basic time-saving tasks, level 2 covers experimentation such as A-B testing (comparing two ad versions to see which works better), and level 3 achieves true automated decisioning.
“You start with productivity, then you do experimentation, and the hardest thing is decisioning. When you actually are building an entire system for a party of one and that one person could be one out of several million that show up on your app or your website,” Jain noted.
Instead of bombarding users with discount codes, decisioning offers gentle helpful steps first, such as establishing brand trust or explaining product benefits.
Real-time decisioning relies on a single data hub that combines a customer’s historical profile with their immediate live actions. Traditional A-B testing usually stops after selecting one fixed winner, but decisioning uses reinforcement learning, a smart system that learns continuously from user responses and adjusts offers on the fly.
Furthermore, instead of relying only on propensity scoring (calculating how likely someone is to buy), decisioning uses uplift modelling. This method identifies the specific nudge, message, or channel needed to encourage an individual user to take their next positive step.
As automated systems manage campaign delivery across thousands of message options, the role of the marketer shifts from execution to strategic direction. Rather than manually drafting creative variants, marketers define high-level goals and establish strict operational limits.
“Your job is to create budget guardrails, brand guardrails, regulatory guardrails. Do not use the word 'free' if you are offering something, if you are a bank,”Jain emphasised.
By establishing clear boundaries, marketing leaders empower smart decisioning engines to work independently, keeping brand messaging safe while driving genuine commercial profit, he added.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: OpenCode hack exposes API keys amid AI distillation attacks
articles.text:
The open-source AI coding project OpenCode has notified some users that stored API keys they used with external providers were exposed in a security breach.
Multiple users reported that the incident led to unauthorized API charges and suspended projects in Google Cloud.
According to the project maintainer, the breach affected 1.4% of OpenCode Console users, with some reporting more than $1,700 in unauthorized charges overnight.
OpenCode is a model-agnostic AI coding agent that helps users understand code, write features, and fix bugs using natural-language instructions, through a terminal, desktop app, or code editor.
Users can connect AI models from multiple AI providers to the OpenCode console to streamline and automate the development process.
Distillation attack
On Saturday, OpenCode announced that it suffered a large distillation attack that impacted only developers who linked external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google.
“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the project maintainer said.
“We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email, you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked.”
Distillation is a legitimate machine-learning technique that trains smaller AI models using responses generated by more powerful models. The goal is to create cheaper, faster models that retain many of the capabilities of their larger counterparts.
However, the technique becomes an attack when it involves large-scale training through unauthorized queries.
OpenCode co-founder Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting the company's systems for at least 48 hours using AI agents.
He also said OpenCode's investigation of the attackers were blocked when the AI models it was using began refusing requests due to built-in security safeguards.
Raad said the situation stabilized after OpenCode began using OpenAI’s Daybreak AI cybersecurity model for defensive work, which it was approved to use on Saturday.
The email sent to impacted users notes that the earliest possible exposure of the users’ keys was on October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC, and that no data appears to have been exposed.
OpenCode also said it was working with Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic to address the incident but could not share further details at this time.
User reports claim rogue charges following the private key leaks, ranging from several hundred USD to up to $1,700. OpenCode’s message to impacted users mentions the possibility of reimbursement for those impacted.
Some users reported that Google suspended their projects after detecting "abusive activity consistent with hijacked resources.”
BleepingComputer contacted OpenCode for more details, but we have not heard back as of publication.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Services in Response to Cyberattack
articles.text:
ConnectWise is scrambling to restore its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after hackers abused a compromised credential to access customers’ M365 tenants.
The company suspended the Cloud Backup service (formerly known as SkyKick) on October 17, roughly 12 hours after it started investigating the suspicious activity.
“We recently identified unauthorized access to application identities within the ConnectWise Cloud Backup environment. As a protective measure for our Cloud Backup partners and their clients, we are shutting off Cloud Backup application access,” the company said.
The next day, it decided to shut down SaaS Security and Cloud Management as well, to implement mitigations, noting that customers’ backups remain encrypted and protected and that it has no evidence of unauthorized access to them.
The containment measure continues to impact scheduled backups, archive access, and restores, as well as SaaS Security monitoring and alerting, and Cloud Management user and license management, and ConnectWise has not provided an estimated restoration timeline.
However, it has shared information on the IP addresses used in the intrusion and has published guidance for reviewing MSPs’ Microsoft 365 environments.
According to cybersecurity firm Huntress, the compromised Cloud Backup credential was used to access Microsoft 365 tenants on October 15.
Cloud Backup’s identity was seen signing in to 162 Microsoft 365 tenants between October 15 and October 16.
“The authentication itself is certain: It comes from Microsoft’s own sign-in logs in each tenant. The credential type was a client assertion, which means the credential lives in the vendor’s own tenant. Nothing a customer did in their environment could have produced it,” Huntress says.
The activity originated from the same IP address that was used between October 13 and October 14 in password spraying attacks against four law firm tenants and in scripted sign-in attempts.
In one customer tenant, Huntress observed the ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams adding itself to the Global Administrator role on October 15, then running a Python script that added new client secrets to an MSP management application and to Huntress’s own application.
This happened roughly two and a half hours before the first sign-ins from the attacker’s IP address, and the access came from Microsoft’s internal cloud network rather than that IP. Huntress says it has not tied the two phases to the same operator.
“The app’s credential is in hostile hands. It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list,” Huntress notes.
By October 17, the cybersecurity firm had identified sign-in activity from the attacker’s IP address in nearly 1,000 Entra tenants, with over 300 of the sign-ins being successful. However, a successful sign-in did not always mean access: in tenants lacking the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attackers could not get in.
Huntress says it is highly confident the threat actor also abused the ConnectWise Cloud Management Exchange Online, MS Teams, and SharePoint Online applications as part of the intrusions. All three have been shut down by ConnectWise.
“ConnectWise has stopped the attack. But businesses unfortunately have the responsibility and difficult task to ensure that the threat actor didn’t change any Microsoft 365 configuration or establish any persistence within their tenant. More than a third of IT leaders wrongly believe that Microsoft automatically backs up their configuration, making recovery from such an attack all the more tricky,” CoreView VP of security strategy Kasper Lindgaard said.

articles.title: Pour dormir sur vos deux oreilles, ce lot de 4 caméras de surveillance extérieure + leur base est en promo à -57% — Frandroid
articles.text:
Dans ce lot en promo sur Amazon, vous avez quatre caméras Eufy C35 et une base. Cette dernière se met dans la maison, un peu à équidistance des caméras, pour qu’elles puissent s’y connecter. C’est là que se stockent les vidéos prises par les caméras, sans aucun abonnement. C’est une bonne solution pour avoir une couverture complète des alentours de votre domicile et ainsi garder un œil chez vous, que vous y soyez ou non. Ce même lot est vendu 379 euros sur le site officiel, mais il est en promo avec 218,45 euros de réduction sur Amazon.
Les atouts de ce lot Eufy C35 x4 avec base
- L’absence totale de frais cachés ou d’abonnement mensuel
- Le rendu nocturne avec PureColor Vision sans lumière d’appoint
- Le système de fixation magnétique qui permet des déplacements fréquents et rapides
Comme on l’a dit, sur le site de la marque, ce kit est à 379 euros. Sur Amazon, il était dernièrement à 199 euros. Là sur Amazon jusqu’au 1er novembre, il est à 160,55 euros.
Une conception maligne qui va à l’essentiel
Les caméras Eufy C35 sont des modèles milieu de gamme, pensés pour une installation domestique simple. Leur principal intérêt, au-delà du nombre de caméras, c’est qu’il n’y a aucun abonnement auquel souscrire pour accéder à vos rushs, et elles sont très simples à poser. Vous pouvez tout simplement utiliser la fixation magnétique pour les poser où vous voulez, le plus efficace étant de les mettre aux quatre coins de la maison, ou pour surveiller les accès les plus empruntés.
L’aimant tient sur n’importe quelle surface en fer ou en acier, un portail par exemple, ou même un réfrigérateur (mais là, c’est moins pratique pour surveiller l’extérieur). Méfiez-vous des gouttières et des encadrements de baie vitrée : ils sont souvent en aluminium, en zinc ou en PVC, et un aimant n’y tient pas. Sinon, vous pouvez opter pour un montage définitif avec une vis et le socle fourni pour chaque caméra. Elles profitent de la certification IP67, donc peu importe la météo, elles sont capables de filmer en toutes circonstances. Les caméras communiquent avec la HomeBase Mini en Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz, qui porte plus loin que le 5 GHz mais offre moins de débit (largement suffisant pour du 1080p).
Une image 1080p avec une bonne vision nocturne
Côté définition, Eufy se limite au Full HD (1080p). Ça aide à tenir le prix, mais ça paraît un peu en retard en 2026, quand certaines caméras Tapo proposent de la 2K, voire de la 4K. De jour, les images restent exploitables pour identifier une personne à moyenne distance, mais ça montre vite ses limites si vous tentez un recadrage numérique sur un détail au loin. La nuit tombée, le capteur CMOS 1/2,9 pouce couplé à une ouverture f/1,2 utilise la technologie PureColor Vision.
La caméra peut ainsi filmer en couleurs même quand la lumière est faible. Pas besoin d’activer un projecteur ou de passer en infrarouge, avec son image en noir et blanc. C’est un vrai avantage pour distinguer les habits d’une personne. L’IA est utilisée pour détecter les différentes formes qui passent devant l’objectif, vous avez l’audio bidirectionnel pour écouter mais aussi parler et en cas de danger, les caméras peuvent émettre des signaux visuels et sonores qui servent à dissuader ou alerter le voisinage. La HomeBase Mini embarque 8 Go de stockage (un peu moins en pratique, une partie sert au système). Pour garder plus d’enregistrements, il faudra repasser à la caisse pour une carte microSD, jusqu’à 1 To, à glisser dans la base.
Si vous n’êtes pas convaincu par cette installation, vous pouvez trouver des alternatives dans notre guide comparatif des meilleures caméras de surveillance extérieure du moment.
