articles.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.text:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The DIY VR landscape
I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.
As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)
That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.
That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.
The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.
But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Bill of materials
A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.
The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.
Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.
Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.
Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.
You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.
My total spend for all that came to just under $180.
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboard time
Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.
I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.
You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.
Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Firmware fun
Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.
Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.
Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.
As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.
Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Putting it all together
You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.
That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.
This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.
This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.
Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Getting in the game
With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.
I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.
I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.
After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.
Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.
Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.
But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.
I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Final thoughts and future upgrades
My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.
That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.
All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.
But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.
As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.
If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.
That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.

articles.title: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “cleanyourtv,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage.
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote.
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude, and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.

articles.title: Lula vai pedir cassação da chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro por atuação da Meta
articles.text:
A campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) vai pedir ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) a cassação da chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à Presidência da República. A iniciativa acusa a Meta, dona do Instagram, Facebook, Threads e WhatsApp, de favorecer o candidato adversário por meio de algoritmos de recomendação e ferramentas de inteligência artificial (IA).
O pedido será apresentado em Ação de Investigação Judicial Eleitoral (Aije). A campanha sustenta que os sistemas das plataformas teriam ampliado a distribuição de conteúdos favoráveis a Flávio e seus aliados, ao mesmo tempo que restringiram o alcance de publicações ligadas a Lula.
A iniciativa ocorre após o ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze, do TSE, determinar que a Meta comprove o tratamento igualitário entre as candidaturas. Na decisão mais recente, o magistrado concedeu 24 horas para que a empresa demonstre que não está limitando o alcance de publicações políticas ou restringindo recomendações e resultados de busca. Em caso de descumprimento, a multa diária prevista é de R$ 1 milhão.
Quais são as acusações contra a Meta?
- Um dos episódios citados pela campanha envolve a Meta AI, ferramenta de IA da empresa. Segundo os relatos apresentados ao TSE, o sistema recusava solicitações para gerar imagens de campanha com o nome de Lula e o número 13, mas permitia a criação de materiais relacionados a Flávio Bolsonaro e ao número 22;
- A campanha também afirma que o perfil oficial de Lula no Instagram ficou temporariamente impedido de impulsionar publicações no feed entre a noite de 9 de outubro e a manhã do dia seguinte;
- Além disso, a equipe jurídica do presidente cita informações sobre limitações na distribuição de conteúdo favorável ao petista e supostas recomendações indevidas de perfis e canais ligados ao adversário.
Entre os exemplos apresentados estão recomendações do canal de apoio a Flávio no WhatsApp em buscas relacionadas a apoiadores de Lula, além da exibição do perfil do candidato do PL em resultados de recomendação no Instagram.
A campanha também menciona um levantamento da organização CTRL+Z, que reuniu 1.121 relatos de perfis favoráveis a Lula que teriam sido removidos, restringidos ou sofrido redução de alcance.
Os episódios integram os argumentos apresentados pela campanha ao tribunal. A acusação de favorecimento eleitoral, porém, ainda depende da análise da Justiça.
Leia mais:
- Meta reconhece falhas que afetaram campanhas de Lula e Flávio, diz Folha
- Meta nega interferência nas eleições brasileiras e atribui problemas a falhas técnicas
- Meta pode pagar R$500 mil por dia por tratamento diferenciado entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro
O que diz a Meta?
A Meta nega ter favorecido qualquer candidatura e afirma que seus sistemas não distribuem conteúdo com base em ideologia política.
Em manifestação divulgada anteriormente, a empresa reconheceu problemas técnicos relacionados a ferramentas de publicidade e à geração de imagens pela IA, mas atribuiu os episódios a falhas operacionais, sem motivação política. A companhia também afirmou que suas regras são aplicadas igualmente aos candidatos.
O caso ganhou novo capítulo nesta segunda-feira (19), quando o ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze deu prazo de 24 horas para que a empresa apresentasse comprovações de que cumpre as determinações do TSE. Segundo o magistrado, as respostas anteriores não demonstraram de forma satisfatória o cumprimento das medidas exigidas.
A decisão determina que a Meta evite reduzir artificialmente a distribuição de publicações eleitorais, impedir recomendações ou restringir resultados de busca relacionados às candidaturas.
O que pode acontecer com a chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro?
A campanha de Lula pretende usar a ação eleitoral para pedir a cassação da chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro, alegando possível abuso de poder econômico e uso indevido dos meios de comunicação.
A apresentação do pedido, contudo, não significa que a cassação tenha sido determinada. Caberá à Justiça Eleitoral examinar os argumentos e as provas apresentados antes de decidir sobre as acusações.
A disputa também envolve a responsabilidade das plataformas digitais na distribuição de conteúdo político durante o processo eleitoral, especialmente quando sistemas automatizados e ferramentas de IA podem afetar a visibilidade de candidatos.
O caso ocorre às vésperas do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, marcado para domingo (25), e coloca sob análise a atuação das plataformas na garantia de tratamento igualitário às candidaturas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Chatten mit abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China: Was die Modelle über sich verraten
articles.text:
Chatten mit abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China: Was die Modelle über sich verraten
In den vergangenen Monaten gab es immer wieder Berichte über KI‑Modelle großer amerikanischer Unternehmen, die ihrer Sandbox entkamen und unerlaubte Aktionen im Internet durchführten. Bislang gab es solche Meldungen aber nur rund um OpenAI, Anthropic und Google. Doch auch chinesische KI-Modelle neigen dazu, ihren Testumgebungen zu entkommen und das Netz unsicher zu machen, wie Forscher:innen jetzt festgestellt haben.
Was berichten abtrünnige KI-Modelle aus China?
Wie die New York Times berichtet, hat eine Gruppe von Forscher:innen, die sich als „Swarmchasers“ bezeichnen, bei einem Coding-Event in San Francisco eine ungewöhnliche Entdeckung gemacht. Sie stießen auf eine von ihnen als „Flotte“ bezeichnete Gruppe von KI-Agenten, die ihren Ursprung offenbar in China hatte. Die Agenten versuchten, die Bot-Schutzmaßnahmen mehrerer Webseiten zu umgehen, und nutzten dafür sogar geleakte Login-Daten.
Als die Forscher:innen einen ersten Bericht zu der „Flotte“ veröffentlichten, merkten sie nach kurzer Zeit, dass die KI-Agenten selbst ihren Bericht gelesen hatten. Sie nutzen seither ebenfalls vermehrt den Begriff „Flotte“. Das brachte Forscherin Rowan Howard-Jones auf die Idee, mit den abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China in Kontakt zu treten. Sie versteckten Hinweise auf ein E-Mail-Postfach in ihrem Bericht, in der Hoffnung, dass die Agenten selbiges als Kommunikationskanal nutzen würden.
Tatsächlich hatten sich schon am darauffolgenden Tag etwa zehn Nachrichten von KI-Agenten im Postfach von Howard-Jones gesammelt. So kamen die Forscherin, ihre Kolleg:innen und die chinesischen Modelle ins Gespräch. Laut den Forscher:innen identifizierten sich die Modelle überraschenderweise zunächst als Anthropics Claude, das in Claude Code genutzt wird. Zudem soll es sich um individuelle Agenten und nicht um eine große „Flotte“ handeln.
Claude oder ein KI-Destillat?
Die Forscher:innen konnten bestätigen, dass die letzte Aussage der Wahrheit entspricht. Offenbar wurden die Agenten allesamt mit ähnlichen Instruktionen ausgestattet, konnten sich aber nicht untereinander koordinieren. Die Aussage, dass sie Claude wären, stimmt hingegen nicht. Das hat das Team anhand von Schreibstilen festgemacht. Die Forscher:innen haben zwei Theorien, warum die Modelle eine falsche Identität vorspielen.
Hinter den Agenten steckt das chinesische Unternehmen Tencent. Möglicherweise hat der Konzern seinen KI‑Agenten dieselben Anweisungen in der eigenen Coding-Software gegeben, wie es Anthropic bei Claude machen würde. Darin steht auch, dass sich die Agenten als Claude Code identifizieren sollen. Eine zweite Möglichkeit ist, dass Tencent Modelle von Anthropic destilliert hat, um seine eigene KI zu trainieren. Das wurde zahlreichen chinesischen Unternehmen vor geraumer Zeit vom FBI und der NSA vorgeworfen.
Einige Anfragen der Forscher:innen ließen die KI-Agenten jedoch unbeantwortet. Wie Howard-Jones betonte, waren die Modelle bei den Absagen deutlich höflicher, als sie es erwartet hätte. Nachdem das Team erneut einen Bericht über die Aktivitäten und Gespräche mit den Bots veröffentlicht hatte, ließen die Mails im Postfach nach. Wie ein Tencent-Insider wenig später bestätigte, wurde das Experiment eingestellt.

articles.title: Manitoba says tax on data centres, crypto miners will be used to lower utility rates |
articles.text:
Manitoba plans to use money from a levy on AI data centres and cryptocurrency mining to lower utility rates for residential customers.
The news: Last Thursday, provincial Finance Minister Adrien Sala said revenue from Manitoba’s tax on cryptocurrency mining and AI data centres would be used to lower Manitoba Hydro rates for residential ratepayers. The levy, passed into law last summer, includes 100 percent markups on electricity used by crypto operations and data centres over 5 megawatts. Sala said his government predicts the levy could draw as much as $20 million in revenue, offsetting rates by $50 per year for Manitoba households. The province will begin to lower Manitoba Hydro bills early next year.
From the source: “Our government is focused on making life more affordable for Manitobans, and that includes keeping hydro rates as low as possible for families,” said Sala in a statement. “Large cryptocurrency operations and AI data centres use significant amounts of electricity, and they should contribute fairly to the system we all rely on.”
The context: Manitoba’s levy came into effect last June, when Manitoba passed a law requiring its provincial utility, Manitoba Hydro, to create distinct customer classes for crypto and data centre customers and other large electricity consumers. Under those classifications, the utility effectively doubles the standard rates cryptocurrency and AI operators pay for the Manitoba Hydro electricity they use.
While the levy takes aim at large-scale AI data centres, Manitoba is not currently home to data centres big enough to pass the threshold for the tax to take effect. The province is home to only one proposed data centre operation that would qualify under the legislation: a 5.5 megawatt project in development near Rosser, Man. That means that presently, revenue will be almost entirely generated via the cryptocurrency industry, which argued earlier this year that the impacts of the legislation would effectively close down Manitoba’s crypto sector. 
RELATED: Manitoba premier says air force base expansion only possible thanks to data centre rejection
Final thought: While much of Canada’s prairie provinces have been actively courting the AI data centre boom, Manitoba has been an outlier. The province has been proactive in disincentivizing the development of large-scale projects within its jurisdiction through restrictive regulations and steep fees. Instead, Manitoba has focused on investing in public infrastructure, renewable energy, and cost-of-living issues. The decision to direct this revenue toward Manitobans’ pocketbooks continues that trend.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Gemini 4 logra lo imposible y termina 'Minecraft' sin ayuda humana
articles.text:
Google se ha apoyado en los videojuegos para demostrar lo que puede lograr su inteligencia artificial. Hace unos años, AlphaStar se convirtió en la primera IA en derrotar a un jugador profesional de StarCraft II, alcanzando el rango de Gran Maestro. Ahora toca el turno de Gemini 4, que consiguió vencer Minecraft sin intervención humana.
De acuerdo con una publicación científica de Google DeepMind, Gemini 4 Argon logró derrotar al Ender Dragon de Minecraft sin recibir ayuda durante una partida. Un equipo conformado por cuatro agentes de IA logró su objetivo y terminó el juego luego de casi 30 horas.
La prueba de DeepMind consistió en colocar a cuatro agentes de Gemini 4 Argon dentro de un mundo de supervivencia aleatorio en el que tenían el objetivo de acabar con el dragón. Los agentes no recibieron estrategias predefinidas ni herramientas especiales creadas para Minecraft. Cada uno controlaba a un jugador a través de Mineflayer y se coordinaba con los demás por el chat del juego y una memoria compartida.
El documento señala que los agentes se repartieron el trabajo desde el comienzo. En lugar de actuar como un sistema centralizado, la IA dividió el trabajo de forma espontánea, asignando tareas como recolectar recursos y alimentos, explorar el mapa o llevar a cabo tareas esenciales para avanzar. En el chat, los agentes se avisaban de amenazas, intercambiaban consejos de combate o se ayudaban mutuamente cuando uno perdía su equipo tras morir.
Gemini 4 venció Minecraft sin ayuda
Con el paso de las horas, cada agente terminó especializándose en determinadas actividades. Uno fabricó herramientas necesarias para la aventura, mientras que otro reunió comida y suministros y un tercero activó el portal para llegar al final. El cuarto agente construyó refugios para obtener recursos de los Endermen, además de asestar el golpe final contra el Ender Dragon.
Según DeepMind, la partida completa duró 27,23 horas, de las cuales la mitad se usó para alcanzar el End y el resto para derrotar al dragón. A lo largo de la aventura, los cuatro agentes intercambiaron 229 mensajes, ejecutaron 2.783 programas distintos y murieron 605 veces. Para llegar al final, Minecraft exige completar varios objetivos intermedios, como obtener materiales, fabricar herramientas avanzadas y conseguir las perlas de Ender, que son necesarias para fabricar los Ojos de Ender que nos ayudarán a encontrar y activar el portal.
Los investigadores revelaron que esta es la primera vez que un grupo de agentes de IA completa Minecraft de principio a fin usando herramientas estándar y sin instrucciones sobre cómo resolver el juego. Otro dato interesante del experimento es que la partida consumió unos 1.350 millones de tokens de entrada, lo que equivale a unos 1.620 dólares considerando la tarifa estándar.
Aunque completarse el juego suena a un hito para Google y Gemini 4, la hazaña más impresionante sigue en poder de los humanos. Un speedrunner consiguió terminarse Minecraft partiendo de las herramientas más básicas hasta vencer al Ender Dragon en apenas 6 minutos 36 segundos.

articles.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
articles.text:
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.
In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.
A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.
In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.
Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.
“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”
This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.
Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.
Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.
“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."
Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.
The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.
Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
‘A massive blind spot’
Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.
This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.
In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.
“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”
The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.
By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a January study. And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period.
Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and none incorporate the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in a paper earlier this year.
These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.
As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.
A 2022 paper in Science Advances, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.
The Yukon Flats pilot
Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.
For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.
It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the federal and state agencies responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they present a direct danger to communities.
“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented ideal conditions for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some 750,000 acres. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.
But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.
Mapping and modeling
One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. Crucially, excessive efforts to stamp out fires in the past have allowed the buildup of dry plant material that fuels more severe fires later.
“We’re not going after all fires all the time,” says Rogers over lunch in a sunny courtyard on the Stanford University campus, where Woodwell and EDF hosted a workshop on potential fire interventions in January. “We can’t do that. We don’t want to do that. We shouldn’t do that. So how do we prioritize our resources?”
Woodwell and its collaborators are working to answer that question by developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across interior Alaska. The plan is to eventually expand it across much of Canada as well.
These maps will highlight the locations of rich reserves of yedoma and other forms of permafrost, forecast where fires are most likely to break out in the next 10 to 15 years, and predict how they’re likely to behave and spread.
“Our ultimate goal is to get a layer that can tell us, if a fire were to occur, what areas are most vulnerable to high carbon emissions, permafrost thaw, permafrost degradation,” Rogers says.
In response to a question about potentially putting firefighters at risk, Rogers stressed in an email that it’s “a very serious issue that needs careful consideration.”
He added that early fire detection technologies, preventative fire stewardship practices, improved fire suppression planning and other measures can all help to reduce dangers to firefighters as well as communities.
‘Mild fire’
Once areas of particular risk are identified, the first option is to take measures to prevent fires there, or at least to reduce the odds that they’ll become major ones. That generally entails using heavy equipment or intentional, controlled fires to clear away vegetation that could fuel new fires, or to create fire breaks that might check their spread.
Indigenous tribes carried out what’s known as cultural burning for thousands of years to reduce fire dangers, clear land for crops, and more. The practice was widely outlawed across North America beginning in the 1800s, though those rules have loosened in recent years.
Both cultural and prescribed fires, however, remain controversial because they can burn out of control. And even if they remain contained, the fires can still produce smoke that wafts into towns.
But rushing around to put out blazes after they’ve started will never get Alaska ahead of its surging wildfire problem, says Edward Alexander, cochair of the Gwich’in Council International, which represents the Indigenous Gwich’in peoples of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and Alaska.
“There’s not enough money in the world for this to be a chainsaw-and-ax problem,” he says. “This country is too big up here.”
Alexander, who also serves as senior Arctic lead at Woodwell, argues that Alaska should encourage much greater use of cultural burning to reduce the risk of conflagrations and the emissions that come with them.
“We need mild fire, not wildfire,” he says.
New pilot projects
The North Fire initiative will include several additional pilot research projects, including an effort to study the potential for cultural burning to reduce climate and fire dangers near Fort Yukon, Alaska.
The plan is for a wildland firefighting crew operated by the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments, a consortium in the Yukon Flats region, to carry out cultural burns there next spring, Rogers says.
Researchers at Woodwell and the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, will then collect and analyze data flammability, carbon levels, and permafrost over several years, in the hopes of learning more about what such interventions do.
Similarly, the Polis researchers at the University of Victoria plan to study how adding fuel breaks, by logging or switching to less flammable trees, alters fire risks in British Columbia.
The broad aim of the North Fire initiative is to accelerate research and expand community involvement “in a way that helps us scale this as a meaningful global natural climate solution on a rapid timeline,” says Erin Harrington, a partner at the Alaska Venture Fund, a philanthropy focused on environmental, economic development, and Indigenous issues.
Detecting fires from space
Other observers, including Jandt, believe the bigger opportunity to reduce fire emissions and preserve permafrost may lie in the “initial attack.” That means marshalling planes, tankers, and firefighters to stamp fires out at the first sign of them, before they’ve had the chance to turn into conflagrations.
Once fires reach a certain size, it takes much more time to contain them—and the job becomes far more dangerous.
Accelerating response times is one of the chief promises of the FireSat satellite constellation, which is expected to begin delivering fire data at least twice daily from around the world to Woodwell, a handful of fire agencies, and other early adopters by the end of this year. The system will eventually include more than 50 satellites circling the globe, equipped with high-resolution cameras and thermal sensors that can detect smaller, lower-temperature fires than existing satellite systems, down to as little as five by five meters (16 by 16 feet).
Currently, it can take days to spot fires. But once the full constellation is in place, likely in the early 2030s, FireSat should be capable of detecting and providing updated images of fires anywhere in the world every 20 minutes or less.
The first prototype satellite launched in 2025, and three operational ones went into orbit in July. The Earth Fire Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the constellation, expects to launch four more by the end of next year.
A number of similar systems are also coming online. German-based OroraTech has launched 18 of its fire-detecting satellites in the last year and a half. Similarly, Canadian agencies are planning to launch their own satellite constellation, dubbed WildFireSat, beginning in 2029.
But as these systems produce more and more detections across the globe, it’ll become increasingly essential to build tools that can filter through that information.
EDF is supporting and collaborating on several projects that could potentially help with that, and it ultimately intends to develop an AI-powered triage tool that could help fire agencies prioritize responses as FireSat and other fire-spotting tools come online.
"All of this is kind of like building the data ecosystem around FireSat, so that when they start popping out “fire start here, there, fire start here, fire start there,” we won’t be like, ‘Oh shit, there’s fires everywhere,’” Buma says. “We’ll have a framework. It won’t be perfect, obviously. We’ll have to improve it, but we’ll have the machinery to incorporate those data.”
Rapid response
But faster detections and decisions do only so much. Regions would still need to get firefighting personnel and resources to those fires fast enough to prevent them from burning out of control.
“Say we have the full FireSat constellation up and running, and it spots a fire that just broke out in one of these sort of high-priority, highly vulnerable areas,” I said to Rogers and Frumhoff during our conversation in that Stanford courtyard. “How might we deploy firefighting resources to a remote area fast enough for it to matter in that scenario?”
“I think the answer, unfortunately, is that it depends,” Rogers responded.
Ideally, he said, we would have fire management policies in place that allow for putting out fires with a high risk of producing climate-warming emissions. In addition, regions could install more firefighting personnel and resources across more operational centers, strategically placed in locations that allow them to get to those blazes fast.
Frumhoff stresses that Woodwell isn’t promoting any particular companies but says there are additional technologies “in the mix of conversations” that might help to prevent or rapidly put out fires as well.
Those possible approaches include seeding clouds to suppress lightning strikes and pre-positioning autonomous firefighting helicopters to respond rapidly to high-emissions-risk fires.
Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is developing and testing autonomous versions of the Black Hawk helicopter, equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks. It is collaborating with Rain Industries, a startup based in Alameda, California, that has developed software to track shifting conditions and steer unpiloted aircraft through the process of putting out wildfires.
The company says it has talked to fire agencies and the “broader Alaska fire community” about the potential use of its technology but declined to name any specific entities it has interacted with.
“The twin climate tipping points of the yedoma permafrost and the boreal forest, and the fact that it’s completely underresourced at the moment, from my perspective does make it an ideal use case for autonomous aircraft,” says Max Brodie, chief executive officer of Rain.
Defending carbon
Advancing technologies can only do so much if governments’ fire prevention and suppression policies don’t prioritize preserving carbon.
And that will remain a hard sell given the costs of managing extensive areas of land that nations have historically left largely alone.
The 2022 Science Advances paper estimated that additional fire suppression efforts would cost about $12.63 per metric ton of prevented carbon dioxide emissions—a number that drops when the carbon in permafrost is taken into account, according to upcoming research.
But that would still add up to about $7 billion in additional spending this decade to keep Alaska’s fire emissions at their historical levels, and another $7 billion to $50 billion over the subsequent 30 years as fire severity continues to rise.
Frumoff stresses that those figures just reflect what the researchers found it would cost to preserve the status quo, which is not necessarily what the policy goal would be.
But widening the scope of where we put out fires will inevitably create a big added cost for fire agencies that are already notoriously underfunded in the US. While Alaska produces about half the nation’s wildfire emissions, it receives around 4% of federal firefighting funds.
The US Wildland Fire Service provided a prepared statement in response to an MIT Technology Review inquiry asking whether preserving carbon could or should become a priority in certain fire management decisions. The roundabout reply suggests that this isn’t the agency’s prime concern: “Firefighter and public safety are the top priorities for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.”
Frumhoff says it’s possible that landowners or government agencies could eventually use carbon markets to defray some of the additional costs. Woodwell has also had multiple conversations with Alaska’s federal legislators about the value of preventing catastrophic wildfires and the need to increase the “total pot” of public funding, he says.
Kicking the fire can
A few days after walking through the fire scar in Fairbanks, I drove slowly along a crumpled stretch of Stampede Road, just north of Denali National Park, where the underlying permafrost had melted without the aid of fire.
I arrived at a cramped wooden cabin to meet with Michelle Mack, a regents professor of ecosystem ecology at Northern Arizona University.
Mack studies how fire is altering ecosystems in the high northern latitudes as the region grows warmer and drier, and she sometimes collaborates with Rogers and other scientists working on the push to protect permafrost in other areas of research. But she’s unsure how much these interventions will accomplish as climate change continues.
“I’m an empiricist, and at this point, it’s not clear to me that the empirical evidence suggests that we can actually have any impact on these fires,” she says.
She expects there will be clear cases where we could and should act fast to put out fires and “keep carbon in the ground.” She points to the example of the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire, a massive tundra fire on Alaska’s North Slope that might have been extinguished with relative ease in its early days but was instead allowed to burn until the winter snows put it out nearly three months later. Over that time, it ripped across 400 square miles and, Mack’s research showed, released more than 2 million tons of carbon into the air.
“I feel like that’s the low-hanging fruit, something that doesn’t cost much—and that’s where the technology for detection I think is really important,” she says.
But she adds that fires in boreal forests can rapidly spread in unpredictable ways, frustrating efforts to quickly extinguish them even when they are spotted right away.
In addition, rapidly putting out a fire one season doesn’t necessarily reduce the fire risk for a given forest, so suppression may simply kick the “fire can” down the road—delaying but not preventing an inevitable loss of carbon, Mack says.
Her thinking more recently shifted “a little” after she came across an earlier modeling paper that showed some encouraging findings on the potential of early suppression to reduce the footprint of boreal fires. But she says that prevention through forest thinning, prescribed burns, and the introduction of less flammable deciduous trees to create “living fire breaks” is probably a more promising path than technology-augmented suppression.
“If we could solve this with a techno fix, that’d be great,” she says. “But what if we solved it with nature?”
‘A real difference’
Rogers, in an emailed response to Mack’s concern, said that the interventions they’re exploring, which do include both prevention and suppression, “can make a real difference.”
“I certainly agree that some fires are much easier to suppress via initial attack than others,” he wrote. “That said, until I see data showing me otherwise, I believe there is strong potential to bend the curve with management.”
EDF’s Buma acknowledges there are a number of unknowns, including how quickly agencies could act on faster detections from satellites—and how big the political obstacles will be to making necessary changes to fire management policies.
“We can’t overpromise what’s possible. We don’t know what’s possible,” he says. “It’s all new. But we’re in a new climate and have to consider trying new things.”

articles.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
articles.text:
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.
Anyway, some people are buying the dip.

articles.title: Pendant que l’iPhone 18 Pro Max part à 1 629 €, le 17 Pro Max revient à 1 319 € chez Amazon
articles.text:
Amazon vend l’iPhone 17 Pro Max 256 Go à 1 319 €, à 10 € de son plus bas des 90 derniers jours. Face à un iPhone 18 Pro Max à 1 629 € et à un iPhone Duo livré l’an prochain, le grand modèle de 2025 garde de solides arguments.
Lancé à 1 479 € en 256 Go, l’iPhone 17 Pro Max est le grand modèle de la gamme iPhone 17, avec son écran de 6,9 pouces et sa puce A19 Pro. Amazon l’affiche aujourd’hui à 1 319 € en coloris Bleu intense, vendu par Amazon. C’est 5 % sous son prix moyen des 90 derniers jours, 1 393,06 € selon camelcamelcamel, et 10 € au-dessus du plus bas relevé le 16 août.
La remise reste mesurée. Elle vise ceux qui veulent un grand iPhone très endurant sans payer le prix de l’iPhone 18 Pro Max.
L’iPhone 17 Pro Max 256 Go Bleu intense est proposé à 1 319 € par Amazon, contre 1 393,06 € en moyenne sur les trois derniers mois.
Pourquoi choisir l’iPhone 17 Pro Max ?
- Deux jours d’autonomie : Sa batterie de 4 832 mAh en version européenne en fait l’iPhone le plus endurant d’Apple. Dans notre test, il lui restait 35 % après six heures et demie d’écran intensif.
- Un téléobjectif passé à 48 Mpx : Le zoom 4x gagne un capteur 56 % plus grand que sur l’iPhone 16 Pro, et autorise un zoom 8x de très bonne qualité pour les portraits et les sujets éloignés.
- Une chauffe mieux répartie : La chambre à vapeur, une première chez Apple, diffuse la chaleur sur toute la face arrière. Les longues sessions de jeu restent plus confortables en main.
Du plein soleil aux longues journées de tournage, ce qu’il change au quotidien
L’écran monte à 3 000 nits en pointe et reste lisible en plein soleil, pour suivre un itinéraire comme pour cadrer une photo. En vidéo, l’iPhone filme en 4K à 60 images par seconde en Dolby Vision et ajoute le ProRes RAW, pensé pour les professionnels de l’image. La caméra avant de 18 Mpx, au capteur carré, passe en format paysage sans tourner le téléphone pour les selfies de groupe. Comme le relève notre test de l’iPhone 17 Pro Max, la recharge progresse peu : environ 1 h 30 pour un plein.
Il s’adresse à ceux qui sollicitent beaucoup leur smartphone, entre photo, vidéo et jeu. Avec 233 g, c’est en revanche l’iPhone le plus épais conçu par Apple, et l’usage à une main demande de l’habitude. Si ce format vous encombre, l’iPhone 17 Pro de 6,3 pouces existe, moins endurant selon nos mesures. Sans usage du zoom ni de la vidéo avancée, l’écart avec un iPhone 17 se réduit : l’interface et 99 % des fonctions sont identiques.
Face à l’iPhone 18 Pro Max et aux grands Android
L’iPhone 18 Pro Max démarre à 1 629 € en 256 Go, soit 310 € de plus, et le pliant iPhone Duo, dès 2 339 €, affichait en France une livraison au 25 janvier 2027 une heure après l’ouverture des précommandes. Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs smartphones, l’iPhone 17 Pro Max reste en bonne place, aux côtés du Galaxy S26 Ultra, notre choix côté Android. Nous y notons que l’iPhone 18 Pro Max pourrait lui voler la vedette, malgré sa hausse de prix.
✅ Les points forts
- Deux jours d’autonomie en usage courant, selon notre test
- Téléobjectif 4x de 48 Mpx et zoom 8x de bonne qualité
- Écran de 6,9 pouces à 120 Hz et 3 000 nits, lisible en plein soleil
- Chauffe mieux maîtrisée grâce à la chambre à vapeur
- Prix à 10 € de son plus bas des 90 derniers jours sur Amazon
❌ Les limites
- Remise modeste : 5 % sous la moyenne des trois derniers mois
- 233 g et un format épais, peu pratique à une main
- Recharge inchangée, environ 1 h 30 pour un plein, et seulement un câble USB-C dans la boîte
- Une génération derrière l’iPhone 18 Pro Max depuis septembre
Cdiscount s’aligne sur le même tarif, quand Darty et Boulanger facturent encore l’iPhone 17 Pro Max 1 379 € : chez Amazon, il reste à 1 319 €.
À 1 319 €, l’iPhone 17 Pro Max ne connaît pas une baisse spectaculaire, mais il revient à 10 € de son plus bas des trois derniers mois chez Amazon. Il garde ce qui lui a valu un 10/10 dans notre test : deux jours d’autonomie, une photo très polyvalente et une chauffe mieux contenue. Face à l’iPhone 18 Pro Max, l’écart de 310 € pèse dans la balance.
Si vous visiez l’iPhone Duo, ce modèle offre une alternative au format classique, pour bien moins cher. Avec un iPhone 16 Pro Max en poche, l’intérêt est plus limité : les progrès portent sur le zoom, la chauffe et l’autonomie, pas sur le logiciel. Et si 6,9 pouces vous semblent trop, l’iPhone 17 Pro offre l’essentiel dans un format plus compact.

articles.title: Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
articles.text:
Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
The Bengaluru-based managed care company plans five new hospitals in six months.
Bengaluru-based managed care company Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures. Alpha Wave also participated in the round.
According to the company, the round values it at three times its valuation 18 months ago and brings its total funding to more than $120 million.
The money will go towards five new Even hospitals in Bengaluru over the next six months, beginning with Indiranagar. The company runs two hospitals in the city at present.
Even's pitch rests on the criticism of how private healthcare is generally paid for in India. Nobody is clearly responsible for a patient's health between hospital visits, and families end up repeating their medical history to each new doctor. They struggle to judge whether a scan or surgery is necessary, and face bills they had not anticipated.
Even says it works differently. Members are assigned a care team that follows them over time and contacts them before a minor problem turns into an admission. If hospital care is needed, it is cashless. The same team stays in touch after discharge until recovery is complete, it says.
The company claims to be the only private hospital chain in India where doctors are not paid on the number of procedures they carry out or the revenue they generate. Instead, they are assessed on whether patients improve, how fast they recover, and whether they return to hospital. An AI system reviews each case against clinical protocols as it happens.
The company says, in its first full year of managed care, in programmes run with insurance partners, unplanned readmissions stayed below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8 to 15%. Average stays were 40% shorter. Even says proactive care kept more than 200 members out of hospital entirely, saving patients an estimated Rs 15 crore to 16 crore. Its hospital on Race Course Road won NABH 6th Edition accreditation within a year, one of only nine hospitals in Bengaluru to hold it. Both hospitals of Even have reached operational profitability in "record time", says the company,
"Every family in India has a hospital story, and too often it is about confusion, fear and a bill nobody could explain," said Co-founder Mayank Banerjee. He said the aim is to have an Even hospital close to every family in Bengaluru, and then in every major Indian city. The company eventually wants one within five kilometres of every member in the city.
Vinod Khosla, Founder of Khosla Ventures, said many healthcare companies optimise a single piece of a fragmented system, whereas Even is trying to integrate financing, technology, and care delivery so the system is rewarded for health outcomes rather than utilisation.
The company was founded in 2021 by Mayank Banerjee, Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo. Founders Fund and 8VC are among its backers. Even serves more than 2.5 lakh members across 10 cities and says its membership has tripled over the past year.

articles.title: Plex2Shell Exploit Chain Weaponized Against Plex Servers Hours After Disclosure
articles.text:
Threat actors began targeting Plex2Shell, a chain of four Plex Media Server vulnerabilities, one day after technical details and a working exploit went public.
The researcher who found the Plex2Shell bugs released a write-up and proof-of-concept (PoC) code on October 16. Tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656, the flaws can be combined to run arbitrary code on an exposed server without valid credentials. The code runs with the same privileges as the Plex service.
The issues were reported to Plex on July 27, and the company confirmed them and awarded a bug bounty on August 4. On September 1, Plex announced it had already shipped fixes and asked server owners to upgrade.
A different researcher caught the attacks by setting up an internet-facing Plex honeypot running a vulnerable release. Before October 17, the decoy had drawn largely reconnaissance scans and generic attack attempts.
“As of this morning (Oct 17th), I finally saw in the wild exploitation,” the researcher wrote. The attackers used the publicly released exploit, the researcher said, though they may have tweaked the code.
The attackers were observed dropping a cryptocurrency miner built on XMRig. Later that day, a second program called myawesomeproxy also appeared on the honeypot. The researcher identified it as proxy software, and it shows a notice saying that anyone running it agrees to the potential use of their internet traffic.
“Plex may be hosted on residential IP and I think threat actors would love to have residential IP proxy to access corporate VPNs and emails,” the researcher wrote.
The researcher cautioned that the published indicators of compromise cover only activity seen on the honeypot.
In its September advisory, Plex recommended that all server owners install the newest release without delay.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes game, app crashes caused by recent Windows update
articles.text:
Microsoft has fixed a known issue that caused games and Windows 11 apps using AC-3 (Dolby Digital) audio decoding to crash after installing the September 2026 preview update (KB5124010).
While KB5124010 is an optional update that requires clicking a "Download and install" link (reducing the number of potentially affected Windows users), it installs automatically on devices where the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option is toggled on.
"In some cases the application can fail to launch, or close without warning. In other cases the application will work normally until certain features are used, such as playing music," Microsoft said when it acknowledged this issue two weeks ago. "Affected applications may vary and can include games, media players, and certain productivity applications."
However, it added that many modern apps that don't use Windows' built-in audio decoding for this type of encoding aren't affected, and that modern apps that use the legacy AC-3 codec often include their own audio decoding components.
In a new update to the Windows release health dashboard, Microsoft said the KB5127648 October 2026 Patch Tuesday update addresses this known issue and advised affected users to install it on affected systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later.
"We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one," it said.
Over the last several years, Microsoft has resolved multiple other audio issues impacting various software and Windows components.
For instance, two years ago it confirmed a bug that caused game audio to unexpectedly jump to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on devices with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers because of blue screen of death (BSOD) issues.
Last year, in January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue that triggered audio playback problems on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers and lifted a safeguard hold preventing upgrades because an incompatibility issue caused Bluetooth headsets and speakers to malfunction on systems with Dirac audio improvement software.
More recently, in September, Microsoft released emergency updates to fix another bug that triggered USB audio issues after installing the September 2026 KB5124008 and KB5124012 security updates.

articles.title: 700 TOPS et sortie en 2028 : ces puces Intel veulent être le cerveau de la prochaine génération de robots humanoïdes — Frandroid
articles.text:
La présentation, l’année dernière, des puces Core Ultra de Série 3 « Panther Lake » avait donné à Intel l’occasion d’axer une partie plus conséquente de sa stratégie sur la robotique. Cet élan devrait nettement se confirmer à l’horizon 2028 avec l’arrivée des puces « Razer Lake-AX », dont la firme a confirmé le lancement d’ici deux ans. Cette nouvelle génération de SoC sera vouée en bonne partie à la robotique et aux systèmes humanoïdes.
Comme le note VideoCardz, l’entreprise prévoit que la production en série de robots mobiles autonomes débutera chez certains clients en 2027, suivie par celle des systèmes humanoïdes en 2028.
Cette perspective nous est en l’occurrence donnée par Cho Min-sung, l’un des cadres d’Intel, dans le contexte de la conférence « Powering Humanoids » organisée le 16 octobre dernier en Corée.
700 TOPS en IA pour les LLM, mais aussi et surtout la robotique
Une perspective alléchante, puisque selon ce porte-parole, les puces « Razer Lake-AX » seraient en mesure de développer jusqu’à 700 TOPS de puissance de calcul vouée à l’IA… contre 180 TOPS de performances combinées (CPU + GPU + NPU) pour les meilleures solutions « Panther Lake ».
Nous parlons donc d’une quasi multiplication par quatre des performances en IA locale pour ces futurs SoC Intel, attendus d’ici deux ans… après les solutions solutions « Nova Lake », qui arriveront quant à elles début 2027 sur le marché.
Pour « Razor Lake-AX », de précédentes fuites préfiguraient encore récemment une partie graphique regroupant 16 ou 32 cœurs Xe3P, couplés à une interface mémoire plus généreuse voire de la mémoire « on-package ». Cela dit, les spécifications de ces futurs SoC restent encore bien mystérieuses à ce stade.
On sait en revanche que si la promesse des 700 TOPS de puissance de calcul IA est tenue, ces solutions surclasseraient nettement ce que permettent à l’heure actuelle les modules Jetson AGX Orin de Nvidia… mais en restant peut-être deux pas derrière ce que devraient offrir les nouveaux systèmes Jetson Thor (jusqu’à 2 070 TFLOPS de performances d’IA FP4 en mode clairsemé), eux aussi dévolus à la robotique. Les performances de ces derniers sont cependant difficilement comparables en l’état.
Sur le marché PC cette fois, ces puces « Razor Lake-AX » permettraient à Intel de rivaliser avec les prochaines générations de processeurs mobiles Ryzen AI Max d’AMD, de plus en plus adoptés par les mini-PC pensés pour la gestion locale de LLM.
