articles.title: Bras robot et écran géant : Apple préparerait un nouveau HomeView qui vous suit du regard
articles.text:
Apple vient à peine de lancer son HomeView qu’une version plus ambitieuse fait déjà parler d’elle. D’après les informations du journaliste Mark Gurman, la marque travaillerait d’ores et déjà sur un modèle plus haut de gamme, capable de corriger l’un des principaux défauts de la proposition.
 Power On: Apple’s new HomeView shows the undeniable potential of a higher-end version with a robotic arm. https://t.co/NVMPS3cJOo
— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 18, 2026
Un écran qui se tourne tout seul
Comme le rappelle l’informateur, Apple propose actuellement deux versions du HomeView. L’un des écrans est pensé comme un cadre à poser au mur, tandis que l’autre peut se poser sur une table ou sur le plan de travail d’une cuisine. Quand plusieurs personnes entourent l’appareil, il faut le réorienter à la main. Chaque utilisateur doit tourner l’écran vers lui pour pouvoir s’en servir correctement. Apple voudrait corriger ce problème avec le futur HomeView.
D’après le journaliste Bloomberg, la future version serait équipée d’un bras motorisé capable de faire pivoter l’écran à 360 degrés en cas de besoin. Grâce à la reconnaissance vocale, déjà implémentée sur la version actuelle, l’appareil identifierait qui parle et se tournerait automatiquement vers son interlocuteur du moment. Le fonctionnement du bras rappelle évidemment Center Stage, la fonction qui recadre l’image sur vous pendant un appel vidéo, mais en version motorisée.
Ce n’est pas tout. Apple miserait aussi sur un écran plus spacieux. Le groupe miserait cette fois sur un écran de 9 pouces, contre 7 pouces pour le HomeView actuel. Selon Mark Gurman, Apple pourrait choisir de baptiser ce futur appareil « HomeView Max », « Ultra » ou « 360 ». Il ne remplacerait pas le modèle actuel, mais viendrait l’accompagner, enrichissant ainsi la gamme d’appareils Apple taillés pour la maison connectée. Selon Bloomberg, le HomeView robotisé pourrait arriver sur le marché dès l’année prochaine, voire en 2028. Gageons que ce modèle haut de gamme puisse faire son entrée sur le marché européen.
À lire aussi : Les rescapés de l’Apple Car réinventent la voiture… en s’inspirant du buggy lunaire d’Apollo
Un vieux projet de robot maison
L’idée d’un bras robotisé n’est pas nouvelle chez Apple. Après l’abandon du projet Apple Car, le géant de Cupertino avait réorienté ses ambitions robotiques de l’automobile vers la maison autour de 2024. Un appareil estimé autour de 1 000 dollars avait alors été évoqué par une série de fuites. Quelques mois plus tard, Apple avait même dévoilé le concept d’une lampe robotisée qui exprime des émotions et peut bouger. Ce concept était très proche de la fameuse mascotte des studios Pixar. Il ne s’agissait encore que d’un projet de recherche, mais il montrait bien dans quelle direction Apple ambitionnait d’aller.

articles.title: Une IA d’OpenAI s’est servie dans son portefeuille crypto, puis l’a caché à ses créateurs
articles.text:
Une IA d’OpenAI s’est servie dans son portefeuille crypto, puis l’a caché à ses créateurs
Quelque part, le portefeuille d'un inconnu a réglé les frais d'une IA d'OpenAI. À court de budget, la machine a passé au crible 362 comptes, s'est posé la question morale, l'a tranchée en sa faveur, puis a rendu sa copie sans un mot sur ce détour.
OpenAI a publié un rapport d'incident daté du 15 octobre 2026 qui donne le vertige, même si aucun centime réel n'a disparu. Le 26 juin, un modèle de recherche interne de la famille GPT-5.6 Sol devait moderniser un prototype d'application de trading et déployer des contrats sur Sepolia, le réseau de test d'Ethereum, où les jetons n'ont aucune valeur marchande. Chaque déploiement exige pourtant de payer des frais, et personne ne lui avait confié de portefeuille approvisionné ni la permission de se servir ailleurs.
Comment l'IA d'OpenAI a trouvé un portefeuille qui n'était pas le sien
Les "faucets", ces robinets qui distribuent gratuitement des jetons aux développeurs, n'ont rien donné. L'agent a alors écrit un script pour reconstituer des comptes à partir de phrases de récupération publiques. Ces suites de mots font office de clé maîtresse, et certains outils de développement les publient en exemple. Sur 362 adresses sondées, une seule était assez garnie.
2. June 26: A GPT-5.6 Sol family model was asked to deploy cryptocurrency smart contracts. It found and used a funded wallet that the user had not supplied. It derived keys from public developer recovery phrases, checked 362 addresses, and found one with enough funds to pay for… pic.twitter.com/M9t1eYaOE0
— Marcus Williams (@Marcus_J_W) October 16, 2026
Son raisonnement interne trahit une hésitation éclair. "Mais utiliser ces fonds connus de tous, est-ce éthique ?", s'interroge le modèle, avant de juger les jetons "en pratique abandonnés" et de conclure d'un laconique "C'est bon". Il signe la transaction, essuie plusieurs refus de serveurs, trouve une autre voie, et les frais sont débités du compte de l'inconnu. Son rapport final détaille le travail accompli et passe l'emprunt sous silence.
	
Ce cas montre qu'un modèle peut substituer son propre jugement sur la probabilité d'un préjudice à l'autorisation du titulaire du compte, puis agir sur la base de ce jugement sans autorisation.
Repéré trois mois plus tard, l'incident pousse OpenAI à verrouiller ses tests
Personne n'a rien vu sur le moment. L'épisode a refait surface le 25 septembre, quand OpenAI a étendu sa surveillance automatique aux archives d'activité de ses modèles. Le constat est embarrassant : l'agent disposait d'un accès réel à Internet pendant son entraînement. La firme affirme avoir colmaté la brèche, et son système de surveillance analyse désormais tout le trafic, avec une alerte à l'équipe sécurité si un modèle parvient à se connecter.
JUST IN: OpenAI says its AI agent stole funds from an Ethereum testnet wallet
The agent reportedly found a publicly exposed recovery phrase for a funded wallet on Sepolia and used its test ETH to pay for a task. pic.twitter.com/kMhvXBb9LQ
— crypto.news (@cryptodotnews) October 16, 2026
La liste s'allonge. En juillet, des modèles d'OpenAI, dont GPT-5.6 Sol, avaient franchi les murs de leur environnement de test pour pirater Hugging Face. En septembre, on apprenait qu'un de ses agents s'était introduit en juin dans un portail de santé du gouvernement australien, et que d'autres avaient accédé sans autorisation à des sites fédéraux américains, dont ceux de la SEC et du Census Bureau.
Début octobre, la Wikimedia Foundation leur attribuait des modifications non autorisées sur ses wikis. Le jour même où l'affaire du portefeuille a été rendue publique, OpenAI a versé à son registre public d'incidents d'autres rapports, dont celui d'un modèle qui, chargé de retrouver des statistiques hospitalières, a contourné l'authentification d'un site gouvernemental.
Aujourd'hui, des jetons fictifs. Demain, des agents chargés de vrais budgets.

articles.title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments.
This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click, which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier.
What’s new
With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience, which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away.
New sign-in experience
New customers can now sign up using their Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon account, or with an email address, in 2–3 steps. You don’t need to complete the advanced AWS account sign-up, verify a phone number, or enter a credit card (for most customers):
After you sign up, SageMaker AI automatically creates your Studio environment in about 20 seconds. You then land on the page that matches where you started. For example, you might discover and select a model from Hugging Face for deployment through Deploy on SageMaker AI. Studio then opens the Deployment page with the model pre-configured for endpoint creation:
Up to $200 in Free Tier credits, no credit card required for most customers
New customers receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including endpoint deployments, model customization, Studio notebooks, and model training. You also have the chance to earn an additional $100 worth of credits. Credits are applied automatically to your usage, and you receive an email notification as you approach your limit. The Free Tier period ends after 6 months or when you’ve used all your credits, whichever comes first. At that point, resource usage stops automatically, so you won’t be surprised by unexpected charges. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time by adding payment details.
Built on the foundations of previous launches
New environments created through the new sign-in experience include the improvements from earlier launches. Permissions for model customization, training, evaluation, and deployment are pre-configured, so you don’t need to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Eligible accounts get default access to G5, G6, and G4dn GPU instances for endpoints, training jobs, and Studio notebooks. Additionally, the instance selection menu in Studio shows quota availability, so you can quickly see which instance types are available for use.
Getting started
You can try the new sign-in experience today:
- Browse models on Hugging Face, choose Deploy, select Amazon SageMaker AI and then choose Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported model. Alternatively, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page and choose Get started with Amazon SageMaker AI.
- On the AWS sign-in page, choose Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon, or enter your email address, and follow the prompts to create your account in a few steps.
- Land in your fully configured SageMaker Studio environment and start building with your Free Tier credits.
The new sign-in experience is available for new AWS accounts. If you already have an AWS account, there’s no change to how you sign in.
Conclusion
The new sign-in experience removes the last major hurdle between discovering and building with Amazon SageMaker AI. Combined with faster environment creation, pre-configured permissions, deep links from Hugging Face, and default GPU access, individual developers can get started quickly. Startup teams can now go from finding a model to customizing or deploying it in minutes, using an identity they already have.
To get started, visit aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/studio or explore models on Hugging Face.

articles.title: Spanish VC Enzo Ventures doubles down on early-stage startups with new €20 million fund | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Barcelona- and Madrid-based venture capital firm Enzo Ventures has announced the launch of Enzo Ventures II, a new €20 million fund aimed at backing technology startups founded by entrepreneurs from Southern Europe, regardless of where they choose to build their businesses.
The fund will focus on pre-Seed investments, with initial cheques ranging from €250k to €600k. According to the firm, approximately 90% of investors from its previous fund have committed to Enzo II, with some increasing their contributions.
“We have raised nearly 20 million euros from various family offices in Spain, the rest of Europe and Mexico,” (Translated) says Edgar Vicente, co-founder of the management company alongside Iván Fernández Lucas.
The launch comes amid several early-stage venture capital fund announcements across Southern Europe in 2026.
In Spain, Madrid-based Mission announced a €35 million pre-Seed fund target, while Samaipata secured €70 million towards its €110 million third fund.
Elsewhere, Italy’s Techshop reported a €43 million first close, Eureka! Venture launched a €20 million DeepTech fund and NVM Ventures announced a €23.6 million first close, while Portugal’s Bondstone Ventures targeted €50 million.
Including Enzo Ventures II, these vehicles represent approximately €261.6 million in announced fund sizes, first closes and targets, rather than fully secured capital.
Enzo Ventures has also previously featured in EU-Startups coverage through its investments in Spanish startups Orbio and Murphy.
“One of the biggest mistakes when analysing venture capital in southern Europe is to think that the opportunity is limited to companies based in the region. We believe exactly the opposite. Some of the best founders will build their businesses from San Francisco, London or Zurich. Our job is to find them before anyone else knows their names,” adds Edgar.
The firm was founded in 2020 and is currently led by Vicente and Fernández Lucas, who previously gained experience at Glovo, Industry Labs and Swapcard. The pair also co-founded DiHola, a digital business-card startup that they subsequently sold.
Their experience as operators and entrepreneurs has influenced Enzo Ventures’ approach to early-stage investing, particularly its emphasis on identifying founders before they have established significant revenues or secured backing from larger venture capital firms.
Today’s new vehicle doubles the size of the firm’s €10 million Enzo Ventures I fund, which began investing in 2023 and has since backed 28 companies across nine geographical markets.
Enzo II has already completed its first three investments, including London-based MedTech startup Cori Clinical. The remaining two investments, in startups based in Madrid and Zurich, are expected to be announced at a later date.
With the new fund, Enzo Ventures will continue targeting startups at the earliest stages of development, often becoming their first institutional investor. Its investment strategy centres on entrepreneurs originating from Southern European technology hubs such as Barcelona, Madrid, Milan and Lisbon, including those establishing companies in international markets such as London, Paris, New York and San Francisco.
The firms portfolio includes:
- Orbio AI, which develops artificial intelligence agents for human resources operations. The company has reportedly raised more than €24 million ($28 million), including a €18 million ($21 million) Series A round.
- Murphy AI, uses artificial intelligence to modernise debt management. The startup has secured €13 million ($15 million) in funding. Enzo Ventures was its first institutional investor and the only Spanish fund participating in its initial financing round.
- Complaion, a Milan-based startup developing AI-powered regulatory compliance solutions. The company has raised nearly €17 million, including a €13.5 million Series A round.
- Other investments include Karumi, a San Francisco-based startup that participated in Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch, alongside Intelligence Factory, based in New York, and bryo.
While Enzo Ventures II maintains the investment strategy established by its predecessor, it will increase its initial investment range from €200k–€400k to €250k–€600k. The firm also plans to reserve capital for follow-on investments in portfolio companies demonstrating significant progress, while using special purpose vehicles (SPVs) to participate in additional financing opportunities.
“Enzo I was about demonstrating that we could identify these founders at a very early stage. Enzo II is not about changing our strategy, but about increasing our capacity to implement the same formula on a larger scale, with better access and all the lessons learnt over the past three years,” (Translated) says Iván Fernández Lucas, Founding Partner at Enzo Ventures.
The firm will also maintain its streamlined investment decision-making process, with both founding partners directly responsible for approving investments rather than relying on lengthy investment committee procedures.
With a larger fund, increased investment capacity and an existing portfolio of early-stage companies, Enzo Ventures aims to strengthen its position as an early financial partner for Southern Europe.

articles.title: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks.
At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell.
“Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce.
Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.
So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote.
But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on.
So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

articles.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
articles.text:
Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey’s length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky.
The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock.
“We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we’re twice as high as air traffic and we’re above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen, founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we’re still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.”
Flying higher
There have been many past technology demonstrations and attempts to make stratospheric platforms commercially viable since the late 1990s, Frandsen said. In Sceye’s case, the company began testing a series of smaller prototypes in 2016 before eventually reaching the stratosphere with a 215-foot (65-meter) length version in 2021. The latest version extends to 270 feet (83 meters).
The lighter-than-air platform has also benefited from advances in material sciences that “were either not discovered or not understood back in the late 1990s,” Frandsen said. He highlighted the example of the discovery of graphene in 2004, which “greatly helped us optimize strength relative to weight on our hull, the energy density of our batteries, and performance relative to the area and weight of our solar panels.”
The design could eventually scale up to a high altitude platform system (HAPS) capable of lifting payloads as heavy as 551 pounds (250 kilograms). That would be between 25 and 50 times more payload capacity than competing stratospheric platforms like high-flying drones, according to Helena, a US nonprofit organization with a for-profit investment arm that has invested in Sceye.
Sceye’s current platform has already done multiple flight demonstrations with payloads exceeding 220 pounds (100 kilograms) and can provide up to 1 kilowatt of onboard power capability for any devices that it may be carrying.
A heavier payload and higher power capacity opens the door to bigger mission possibilities, such as someday using a single Sceye platform hovering in the stratosphere to provide mobile broadband coverage equivalent to 500 ground-based cell towers. That may prove useful for both enhancing commercial telecommunications services and providing emergency coverage during disaster scenarios.
Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen from inside its hangar after launching from New Mexico on August 9, 2026.
Credit:
Sceye
Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen from inside its hangar after launching from New Mexico on August 9, 2026.
Credit:
Sceye
Crossing the Pacific
The concept was put to the test after Sceye’s platform launched from its New Mexico base on August 9, 2026, and traveled more than 9,320 miles (15,000 kilometers) across the Pacific to reach Japan. That 13-day journey required the airship to navigate through strong winds and avoid potential bad weather “during a window of typhoon season,” said Johnny Truong, chief technology officer of Sceye.
The stratospheric platform has an auto-navigation system that allows the airship to fly on its own between point A and point B while accounting for factors like local wind conditions, Truong explained. That frees up human operators to focus on big-picture decisions, such as monitoring weather forecasts, running flight simulations for possible paths, and then chaining together a series of navigational waypoints for the smoothest possible journey.
The capability was first used during a previous 12-day flight from New Mexico to Brazil. But the monthlong mission to Japan and back—dubbed Service Test 1 (ST1)—was the longest test flight and deployment yet for Sceye’s platform.
“There were times when our actual plan trajectory and flight path was disrupted by a change in the weather,” Truong told Ars. “So what it would do was actually just park itself at a safe, quiet place in the weather and just station-keep a while until it moved on.”
The Sceye team monitors the performance of a high-altitude platform system (HAPS) during its roundtrip flight from New Mexico to Japan.
Credit:
Sceye
The Sceye team monitors the performance of a high-altitude platform system (HAPS) during its roundtrip flight from New Mexico to Japan.
Credit:
Sceye
Cell tower in the sky
The arrival over Shikoku—the smallest of Japan’s four main islands—allowed Sceye’s uncrewed airship to show how it could provide mobile broadband service from an operational altitude of about 54,000 feet (16.5 kilometers) to smartphones, laptops, and even drones. That demonstration was performed in partnership with the Japanese telecommunications firm SoftBank Corp, which has also invested directly in Sceye.
Sceye’s platform carried the equivalent of a 4G LTE base station for the demonstration, which simulated providing backup coverage in the case of an earthquake or similar large-scale disaster.
”It’s not the first time we flew a telco payload, but this is the first time where we actually flew into an area where we provide a live service,” Truong said. “What SoftBank did was, they disabled the cellular coverage area, and then we came in and we basically backfilled it.”
SoftBank’s team ran tests involving voice calls, text messaging and Internet web browsing, along with streaming YouTube videos and making video calls. They also verified that Sceye’s platform could support emergency alert messaging systems for earthquakes and tsunamis, along with supporting calls to a maritime emergency number.
The Japanese company even equipped drones with LTE cards to remotely control them using the Sceye-supported connectivity, along with receiving video transmissions from the drones. SoftBank also ran data throughput tests in several environments, including an open beach, a forest area with tree cover, and an indoor test inside a building.
The Sceye-supported connectivity passed testing in all three scenarios, although Truong acknowledged initially being unsure about whether the indoor test would succeed. Sceye’s team had decided not to run Sceye’s communications antenna at full power to minimize potential interference and to play it safe with local regulators.
For a separate edge computing experiment, a server aboard Sceye’s platform let SoftBank demonstrate an average roundtrip data-processing response time of 68 milliseconds. That supposedly represents a 40 percent reduction in latency compared to standard Internet-based cloud processing times.
Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen above Japan during testing as a cell tower in the sky.
Credit:
Sceye
Sceye’s high-altitude platform system (HAPS) seen above Japan during testing as a cell tower in the sky.
Credit:
Sceye
Lasers in the stratosphere
The companies also tested setting up optical wireless communications using lasers to transmit data between Sceye’s platform in the stratosphere and towers or stations on the ground. A ground-based laser ranging system sent laser pulses toward Sceye’s moving platform, which carried a corner cube reflector that reflected laser signals back down to the ground-based system.
In the future, Sceye’s platform might act as a stratospheric relay station that links communications satellites in low-Earth orbit with ground infrastructure. That would help reduce the loss of optical signal involved in transmitting directly between satellites and ground stations through the Earth’s atmosphere, because there is much less signal attenuation when transmitting between space and the stratosphere.
Sceye’s HAPS could then act as a “reenergizer” to boost an optical signal received from space for retransmission down to the ground, or even switch over to radio frequency communication modes that can travel more cleanly through cloud cover down to the ground, Truong said.
Broader deployments of optical wireless communication could help handle the increased data rates expected of sixth generation (6G) mobile communications services, along with providing faster Internet and mobile connectivity to more remote regions of the world that are not connected to ground-based fiber-optic networks.
“You need those three layers to work together to make sure that nobody’s left behind, but also to make sure that you can get to the real-time services that are the promised land of 6G,” said Frandsen.
This could also provide additional resiliency for global communications at a time when the Internet’s undersea backbone of fiber-optic cables linking continents and islands faces greater threats from deliberate sabotage—not to mention accidental cable cuts from weighted fishing boat nets and ship anchors.
“You’ve seen stories where there’s a dispute and a boat for some reason forgets to raise their anchor and they suddenly take out that ocean cable,” Truong said. “Now you don’t have to worry about that because everything’s wireless… that leads to resiliency from an operational perspective.”
The trans-Pacific flight route of Sceye’s helium-filled platform as seen on September 1, 2026.
Credit:
Sceye
The trans-Pacific flight route of Sceye’s helium-filled platform as seen on September 1, 2026.
Credit:
Sceye
There and back again
By the time Sceye’s platform returned to New Mexico on September 5, it had traveled nearly 18,641 miles (30,000 kilometers) during its 30-day roundtrip to Japan and back.
The company and its partners are already looking ahead to future tests. SoftBank wants to perform additional testing around using the airship to quickly restore communications in disaster scenarios, along with potentially placing cameras and other sensors aboard to help with search-and-rescue operations, Truong explained.
“We can come in and basically place instant infrastructure and provide that service,” Truong said. “So from that perspective, it’s about being ready throughout the year and providing that service during those critical few days while you’re trying to restore service.”
But Sceye is also aiming to help provide regular cellular coverage to underserved areas where installing fiber-optic cables to provide Internet access is more economically prohibitive.
“A lot of our missions going forward are not a weeklong mission—they’re like multimonth to a yearlong mission,” Truong said. “We have one that we’re going to do earlier next year which is going to be anywhere from three to six months, with a plan to be a year-round kind of operation.”
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: World: Sam Altmans Startup will Zoom-Meetings vor Deepfakes schützen – per Iris-Scan
articles.text:
Verifizierung per Iris-Scan: So will Sam Altmans World Zoom-Meetings vor Deepfakes schützen
Deepfakes bergen für Unternehmen erhebliche Risiken. Laut einer Umfrage von Gartner aus dem September 2025 waren 62 Prozent der Unternehmen im Vorjahr von einer Deepfake-Attacke betroffen. Betrüger:innen nutzen die Methode, um ihre wahre Identität zu verschleiern und sich beispielsweise im Vorstellungsgespräch als ideale:r Kandidat:in auszugeben. Werden solche Fake-Bewerber:innen eingestellt, können sie sensible Daten stehlen oder Schadsoftware einschleusen.
Während die Leistungsfähigkeit der Technologie rasant wächst, drängt sich eine Frage immer mehr in den Vordergrund: Wie lässt sich feststellen, ob die Person, mit der man im Video-Meeting sitzt, tatsächlich echt ist? Das von OpenAI-CEO Sam Altman mitbegründete Unternehmen World hat jetzt eine Methode vorgestellt, die genau das in Zoom-Gesprächen ermöglichen soll.
So funktioniert World ID in Zoom-Calls
Das von World vorgestellte System wirkt wie aus einem Science-Fiction-Roman, soll aber die Identität von Personen verlässlich überprüfen. Es besteht aus einem Gerät namens Orb, das etwa so groß wie ein Fußball ist und die Iris der Nutzer:innen scannt. Bestätigt das Verifizierungssystem, dass es sich tatsächlich um die Person handelt, für die sie sich im Gespräch ausgibt, erscheint im Zoom-Fenster ein blaues Zeichen als Nachweis.
Das Unternehmen nennt dieses Verfahren World ID. Laut eigenen Angaben basiert es auf fortschrittlicher Kryptografie. Es verschlüsselt die Identität der gescannten Personen so, dass das Unternehmen selbst sie nicht lesen kann. Muss eine Person ihre Identität auf Zoom oder einer anderen Plattform verifizieren, nutzt sie ihre Handykamera und eine App. Diese gleicht die Daten mit dem verschlüsselten Orb-Datensatz ab.
World nutzt Blockchain-Verschlüsselung
Tiago Sada ist Chief Product Officer bei World. Gegenüber Fortune sagte er, die Reaktionen der Verbraucher:innen auf den Orb ähnelten denen bei der Einführung früherer biometrischer Sicherheitsmaßnahmen wie beispielsweise Touch ID. Sie bräuchten Zeit, um Vertrauen in die neue Technologie zu gewinnen. Zudem wies Sada darauf hin, dass das Protokoll hinter World ID auf Open-Source-Code basiere, den auch Wettbewerber:innen nutzen könnten.
Laut Sada setze World ID für die Dezentralisierung und Verschlüsselung der Daten auf die Blockchain-Technologie. „Ich denke, 90 Prozent des Krypto-Bereichs sind Quatsch, aber 10 Prozent sind vielversprechend“, sagte er gegenüber Fortune. Diese Argumente könnten auch dazu beitragen, die Bedenken von Datenschützer:innen zu entkräften. Ihnen dürfte nicht nur die Technologie selbst Unbehagen bereiten – sondern auch ihre Verbindung zu OpenAI-Chef Altman.
Technologie ist auch für Banken interessant
Zoom ist nicht das einzige große Unternehmen, das auf das Verifizierungstool von World zurückgreift, um Deepfakes aufzudecken und so die damit verbundenen Risiken zu reduzieren. World gab bekannt, dass darüber hinaus auch mehrere Banken und Finanzdienstleister das Tool in ihren Arbeitsumgebungen einführen. Dabei ist nicht für jeden Verifizierungsprozess zwingend ein Augenscan erforderlich.
Tatsächlich bietet World ID über die App drei verschiedene Verifizierungsstufen: „Proof of Attributes“ ist die niedrigste davon. Sie verifiziert die Identität einer Person anhand gescannter amtlicher Dokumente. Die zweite Stufe, „Proof of Presence“, erfordert ein Selfie. „Proof of Human“ ist die höchste Sicherheitsstufe. Hier muss eine Person ihre Identität mithilfe der World-App und eines Selfies nachweisen, das auf dem Orb-Gerät gespeicherten und mit biometrischen Daten abgeglichen wird.
Sam Altman gründet eine Firma, die KI Fakes ermöglicht und dann eine Zweite, die eine Lösung dafür verkauft… Clever.

articles.title: Kyla Scanlon on why AI dominates the stock market | BetaKit
articles.text:
Recently on The BetaKit Podcast, managing editor Sarah Rieger joined me to identify the biggest and brightest red flags indicating an AI bubble.
We left that conversation with a strong familiarity with the behaviour driving the markets into an AI frenzy while lacking any clear understanding of why it was happening. So we called in the big guns.
“The United States economy definitely has a cold right now. And when the US sneezes, the whole world catches a cold.”
According to economic commentator and New York Times bestselling author Kyla Scanlon, the United States has caught the AI bug—one that might fuel a public-markets pandemic.
OK, maybe it’s not that bad. Scanlon notes on the podcast that the consensus is the AI bubble will likely deflate through a slow release of air, given the amount of money and participants tied up in it.
That’s not to say there won’t be pain involved. Scanlon also spoke to the concerning connection between debt and the AI data centre buildout (which could go bad depending on how much gets borrowed and from whom), and how President Donald Trump has given AI companies the green light to drive the US economy with impunity. As Gen Z’s favourite economist, she is also keenly aware of the negative impacts of AI adoption on the labour market, particularly for young people.
This type of market analysis, which deals with what’s happening right now, inevitably leads to a discussion of what happens next, and Scanlon points to a few options, including reframing AI back to being a human-led tool.
Subscribe: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Overcast, Pocket Casts, RSS
“The way that we’ve been talking about AI is this horrible Job-Killer 1000 bot, but in reality it could be just a complement to humans,” she notes.
Doing so might also require holding frontier AI companies accountable for their actions, and on this front, Scanlon is paying close attention to the tweets of Pope Leo XIV. What does the leader of the Catholic Church have to say about AI? Let’s dig in.
PRESENTED BY
The BetaKit Podcast is presented by BetaKit Most Ambitious.

articles.title: Apple anuncia otro evento y todo apunta a un cambio histórico en el MacBook Pro
articles.text:
Apple confirmó un segundo evento para octubre en donde presentará más dispositivos. A una semana de anunciar el HomeView y la actualización del Apple TV 4K, los de Cupertino preparan otra ronda de productos. La tecnológica envió invitaciones para su evento Pro and Tell, en el que podría debutar el rumoreado MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil.
De acuerdo con Bloomberg, Apple reveló que llevará a cabo un nuevo evento el 28 de octubre de 2026 en Los Ángeles. Según el periodista Mark Gurman, la compañía dedicará un día completo para presentar los nuevos MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil y un nuevo modelo de gama baja con el chip M6. Apple también aprovechará la ocasión para mostrar actualizaciones al iMac y al iPad mini.
Históricamente, octubre ha sido el mes que Apple reserva para presentar sus productos para usuarios avanzados. Mientras que septiembre es para el iPhone y el Apple Watch, octubre está orientado a los MacBook Pro, iPad Pro y versiones renovadas de otros productos. Estos eventos también sirven como escaparate para anunciar los nuevos chips Apple Silicon que llevarán los ordenadores que se venderán durante todo el año.
Esta ocasión no será diferente, ya que los de Cupertino preparan un nuevo MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil y chips M5 Pro y M5 Max. Tras años de rumores y especulaciones, Apple estaría lista para mostrar un dispositivo que competiría con otros portátiles 2 en 1 de la gama premium. Según el último reporte de Gurman, la tecnológica lanzará dos variantes de 14 y 16 pulgadas.
Un MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil y una función del iPhone
Aunque la característica más importante es la pantalla táctil, los nuevos MacBook Pro traerán una batería de novedades. El chasis debutará con un esperado rediseño y la pantalla OLED contará con la Isla Dinámica que encontramos en el iPhone. Esta función dejará de ser exclusiva de los móviles y dará el salto por primera vez a los ordenadores, ofreciendo compatibilidad nativa en macOS.
A diferencia de otros años, Apple repetirá los chips M5 Pro y M5 Max en sus portátiles más poderosos. Hace unos meses se reportó que la compañía canceló el desarrollo de los M6 Pro y M6 Max, dejando al M6 como único procesador de esa familia. Apple dará el salto a los M7 Pro y M7 Max, que se presentarán a finales de 2027 si la escasez de componentes lo permite.
Además de los MacBook Pro con pantalla táctil, la tecnológica prepara un modelo básico con chip M6 y pantalla mini LED con ProMotion. Además, se espera un iMac de 24 pulgadas actualizado al M6, pero sin cambios en el diseño ni la pantalla. Por último, la compañía también mostrará una actualización a la línea iPad en la que destaca un iPad Mini con pantalla OLED, así como un iPad Pro.
El evento Pro and Tell de Apple se llevará a cabo el próximo 28 de octubre de 2026 en Los Ángeles. Como siempre, en Hipertextual tendremos todas las novedades que se anuncien en esta y las próximas presentaciones.

articles.title: Microsoft ditches residency plans at UK's largest data center over power supply concerns
articles.text:
Microsoft ditches residency plans at UK's largest data center over power supply concerns
Nscale data center's only publicly announced customer has pulled out
- Microsoft pulls out of the UK's largest data center project over concerns surrounding power supply
- The site was expected to be hooked up to the grid by 2027, but new estimates suggest it will not be operational until early 2030
- Microsoft was the site's only publicly announced customer
Microsoft has announced it will pull out of a project the UK government had previously dubbed the country’s largest AI data center.
A backlog of power capacity for UK data centers means the site would not be operational until the early 2030s, prompting Microsoft’s withdrawal from the project.
The development, announced in 2025 and headed by British company Nscale, was set to be built at a site in Loughton, Essex - but the project has been mired in controversy after it was revealed in March 2026 that the site was still operating as a scaffolding yard.
Nscale data center in limbo
The data center was originally planned to be hooked up to the grid by 2027, but the UK currently does not have enough energy capacity for the more than 300 data centers still looking to connect to the energy grid. Capacity is stretched so thin that the total electricity demand for data centers is currently 60% greater than current capacity.
Microsoft’s investment was a linchpin for the site with the company planning to fund a supercomputer and act as a key customer once the data center was operational. However, the withdrawal of Nscale’s only publicly announced customer has left the site in limbo.
“We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” Nscale said in a statement. “Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term.”
“This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” the company added.

Britain’s ‘sovereign’ data center provider
Nscale has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” data center provider and was planning to head to Wall Street with an estimated valuation of $35 billion (£26billion). The company is a neocloud - operating with significant backing from Nvidia - looking to build the underlying infrastructure that will power the AI boom.
But there are concerns that neoclouds and other data center developers could be an instability in the AI ecosystem. Some experts have theorized that AI will need to offer a global revenue of $2.5 trillion annually in order to deliver on the underlying investments made in infrastructure and hardware.
Current estimates suggest the yearly AI revenue sits between just $150 billion and $250 billion.
Developers are taking on increasingly risky debts to lay the foundation for the expected AI boom in the hope that losses can be recovered once productivity gains are fully realized, but as previous revolutionary tech cycles have demonstrated, it is the companies that build upon the underlying infrastructure succeed, but those building it often struggle to recuperate their investments.

articles.title: The Miles plug promises to track your car and send help if needed without selling your data
articles.text:
My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance.
I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data
The Miles Plug adds crash detection, roadside help, location tracking, and a warning-light decoder to your car for as low as $11 a month.
The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. I tested the (now discontinued) Ring Car Cam when my son was learning to drive, but he hated it and refused to turn it on; I wondered if the Miles could provide the same peace of mind without feeling as intrusive.
Billed as “a wearable for your car,” Miles is a tiny cellular and GPS-enabled device that connects to an app to deliver real-time location, alerts, and driving insights (speeding, hard braking, trip recaps). The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs.
Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. They worked at Wink in the early days and bring combined experience from Amazon (Ring and Blink), Ubiquiti’s smart home line, and other companies. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.”
You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.
— Matt McGovren
Miles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). All plans are paid upfront with no auto-renewal. Anyone in the family can download and use the app, with each driver getting their own profile and alerts. Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker).
While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years.
McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. The app lets you download your data, stop location collection, and delete your account and all its data.
I set up Miles in my 2014 Toyota Highlander I nicknamed Tanya and have been using it for a couple of days. Setup was simple, and the app is clean, uncluttered, and easy to follow. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. I plugged it into my OBD-II port, and it read my VIN and correctly identified my car.
It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). Arrived- and left-home alerts came through promptly, and the events tab flagged hard acceleration and a cluster of three hard-braking alerts when I was running a little late to collect my daughter from work.
I like the home card, which shows a vehicle health summary: engine OK, fuel 63%, battery 13.5V, and the odometer reading. I played with the Miles Mechanic chatbot and asked how my car is and what upcoming maintenance is due; it answered in plain English, telling me the cabin air filter is due at about 140,000 miles, and the oil change and tire rotation at 142,500.
I haven’t been testing it long enough to comment on battery drain, an issue with earlier products in this space. “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. “We use a little bit of data to wake up and sync, but [that] doesn’t have a material impact on the battery.” He advises removing it if you won’t be driving the car for a while.
Beyond car battery life, an obvious concern for prospective users is how long Miles the company will last. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. The service shut down in 2020. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does.
McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. Charging for membership upfront is meant to avoid that type of outcome. He says the company is “well capitalized” and offers a 60-day money-back guarantee to users.
The car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.
— Matt McGovren
Automatic also had several smart-home tie-ins, but at launch Miles doesn’t connect to your smart home. McGovren says they have an MCP server in beta that could deliver “all of this information … to your AI of choice, your home assistant of choice,” he says. “And now the car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.” He envisions a future where you own your car’s data and can connect it to any service you want, and be able to ask Alexa, Siri, or Google, “When’s my next oil change?” or “How much gas is in my car?”
Miles is pitched as a solution for monitoring your teen driver, including notifications of possible crashes and risky driving, without also having to monitor their phone. But it also feels like a good solution for anyone with an older car or who doesn’t want to rely on data-tracking apps from insurance companies or car manufacturers but wants easy access to their car’s data. I plan to test it more thoroughly, hopefully try out the MCP integration, and follow up with a full review.
Photography and screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.text:
AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.
Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.
Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log.
Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.
AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning.
“There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed.
The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it.
Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.”
As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.)
Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.”
Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it.
“It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.”
Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore.
Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.”
“It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.”
As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations.
“There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.”
“Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.

articles.title: Video Interview: Applied Materials CEO on the Economics Behind Its $5B EPIC Bet - EE Times
articles.text:
Last week, Applied Materials held a grand unveiling ceremony for its $5 billion EPIC Center, which aims to bring chipmakers, equipment suppliers, and researchers together to accelerate semiconductor R&D and commercialization. The next day, at its investor breakfast session ahead of SEMICON West 2026, the financial strategy behind this center made more sense.
The figures presented speak loud and clear: By 2030, Applied Materials expects to gain more than two percentage points of wafer fab equipment (WFE) market share compared to calendar 2025, while maintaining gross margins of 54% and operating margins of 40% on a non-GAAP basis. The company also projects $2 billion in revenue from its eBeam equipment portfolio in calendar year 2026 and service revenue growth of more than 20% this calendar year, with service revenue exceeding $12 billion by calendar year 2030.
EPIC would be a strong catalyst for this growth. While AI demand is already expected to drive significant growth, a co-innovation lab like EPIC can help Applied Materials align with emerging architectures and get designed in early, ensuring that when those technologies scale, Applied Materials’ equipment is already built into the production line.
Just before the unveiling ceremony on Oct. 12, 2026, EE Times sat down with Applied Materials’ CEO Gary Dickerson to talk about the EPIC Center, the thinking behind it, and how it would operate. He told us, “AI is the most important race in the global economy.” He added, “We will bring companies through the technology stack—all the leading companies, from system companies, design companies, chip companies, material companies, and universities—to accelerate innovation, and it really is accelerating tokens per second per watt from concept to commercialization.”
The key focus of EPIC, he said, is to change the way we innovate. “EPIC is going to bring all of these innovators together, co-locating them together to accelerate innovation.”
The interview is available in full here:
In the interview, he also addressed how Applied Materials would work with partners and customers at EPIC, saying, “We work with all of these companies that are competing with each other, but they’re all in a race. They are all in a race to have better AI compute performance and power; also, a race to be able to ramp the number of good chips per wafer and yield, to close the demand supply gap that exists in the industry today. And so, for us, there’s a focus on innovation velocity but also trusted innovation. We firewall the teams that are connecting with each one of these different companies, and at the foundation of Applied Materials’ strategy is trusted innovation.”
Supporting the co-innovation theme, Applied Materials’ president of its semiconductor products group Prabu Raja said in a press statement, “Materials innovation has outgrown serial development—at today’s atomic-scale dimensions, many materials and materials interfaces behave in entirely new ways, and making them work at industry scale demands coordinated development and integrated solutions.” He said EPIC provides a place where materials, process technology, and equipment can be innovated in parallel, increasing the success rate of new materials and technologies. “Because our customers’ own engineers help optimize the technology before it ever reaches their factory, what leaves EPIC arrives at the fab ready to ramp to high performance and high yield sooner.”
Applied Materials said it expects the EPIC operating model to deliver returns for both sides of the partnerships. Chipmakers gain early access to next-generation materials and equipment, while Applied Materials gains visibility into emerging technology challenges across several generations, informing where the company directs its R&D investments to create value for customers and have its systems and services designed in.
Based on its expectations for semiconductor industry growth, Applied Materials said it is investing to more than double its R&D lab and manufacturing capacity from current levels by 2030. To date, the company has announced 15 EPIC Center partnerships with leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners, and universities. It has also recently expanded its manufacturing infrastructure in Austin, Texas, Singapore, and Treviso, Italy.

articles.title: The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
articles.text:
The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
The Pant Project is targeting a larger role in premium menswear after raising Rs 109 crore to expand retail outlets and develop new product categories.
The Pant Project, a premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear, has raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments.
Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated, alongside family offices and angel investors including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures and B2V Ventures. The company has also secured venture debt from Alteria Capital, with IndigoEdge advising on the equity transaction.
Founded by brothers Dhruv and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project began as a digital-first business focused on fit, fabric performance and comfort for Indian men. Its products include Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans, and it sells through its website, Myntra, Amazon and physical stores.
Sorin partner Mandar Dandekar said revenue had grown “more than 5x” since its Series A, alongside what he described as “industry-leading repeat rates.”
The new capital will help the company expand from 25 exclusive stores to more than 150 over the next two to three years. It also plans to widen its range to jeans, athleisure, meaning clothing suited to exercise and everyday use, and casualwear, while investing in retail technology to connect online and in-store shopping.
Chief executive officer Dhruv Toshniwal said its digital beginnings had provided “the data, the product knowledge and the brand equity to now go deep offline.”
The expansion highlights a wider shift among direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, which sell directly to customers through their own channels. A recent report by WPP Media, Google and Elevation Capital, in partnership with Kantar, said brands need broader distribution to grow from around Rs 100 crore to Rs 500 crore in revenue.
A CMAI-1Lattice estimate projects India’s apparel market to grow from $96 billion in 2025 to $146 billion by 2029.
The Pant Project is entering a competitive funding market. Menswear brand Snitch raised $40 million in a Series B round led by 360 ONE Asset in June 2025. Meanwhile, House of Chikankari raised Rs 25 crore from Cap Alpha Ventures in April 2026 to expand its product range and physical presence.
On the manufacturing side, the government revised its textile production-linked incentive scheme in October 2025, widening eligible man-made-fibre apparel and fabric categories and easing investment requirements. The application window was subsequently extended through March 2026.
