articles.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data.
SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases:
- Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks.
- One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required.
- Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management.
You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration.
2026 onboarding at a glance
From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities.
Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page:
- Alibaba (Qwen): 29 models spanning reasoning (Qwen 3.8-27B), large-scale mixture-of-experts (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), agentic workflows (Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B), code generation (Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen 3 Coder 30B), speech recognition (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B), text-to-speech (Qwen3-TTS), embeddings (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B), and reranking (Qwen3-Reranker-4B).
- NVIDIA: 17 models including the Cosmos3 world foundation model family (Super, Edge, Nano), Cosmos Reason 7B, MSA-Search, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Nemotron-3-Super-120B (FP8 and BF16), Nemotron3 Ultra, Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal), and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for vision-language.
- Mistral: 7 models including the Ministral-3 family (3B, 8B, 14B in standard and BF16) and Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime for speech.
- Google: 6 Gemma 4 variants, including gemma-4-31B-it, E2B-it, E4B-it, 26B-A4B-it, assistant, and NVFP4 quantized.
- IBM: 4 models including Granite 4.0 h-micro/small/tiny and granite-speech-4.1-2b for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) across 6 languages.
- Cohere: 4 models including Command A (A100) and Rerank v3.5, v4.0 Fast, and v4.0 Pro for retrieval augmentation.
- Others: 33 models from MiniMax, Zhipu AI (GLM), DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Allen AI, Microsoft, Meta (Muse Spark), Reflection (Beam), Black Forest Labs, JetBrains, OpenBMB, BharatGenAI, Kakao, OpenFold, and more.
Model onboarding highlights
The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker.
Expanding the NVIDIA open-model portfolio
NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints.
Closing the multimodal gap
Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads.
Making creative AI accessible
Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models.
Prioritizing efficient and quantized models
Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. JetBrains Mellum2-12B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with only 2.5B active parameters for code generation. OpenBMB MiniCPM5-1B packs multimodal capabilities into 1 billion parameters. Microsoft Phi-4-mini-instruct and IBM Granite 4.0 h-tiny demonstrate that compact models serve production workloads on instance types like ml.g5.xlarge. These models can optimize latency and total cost of ownership (TCO) for targeted use cases.
Onboarding purpose-built models for targeted tasks
General-purpose LLMs are versatile, but purpose-built models are optimized for specific tasks. In 2026, we onboarded Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B for autonomous AI workflows with native tool-calling. GLM-OCR, LightOnOCR, and DeepSeek-OCR handle document text extraction. Qwen3-Reranker-4B and Cohere Rerank v4.0 improve retrieval precision in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. langcache-embed-v3-small provides lightweight embedding for semantic search. Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-TTS bring speech recognition and synthesis. OpenFold3 supports protein structure prediction for scientific computing. With these models, you can build pipelines where each stage uses the specialized tool for the job, rather than forcing a single model to do everything.
Broadening provider diversity
Reducing concentration risk in model selection is important for enterprise customers. In 2026, we expanded the catalog to include 30 providers, up from a more concentrated set in prior years. Alibaba Qwen is the single largest contributor with 29 models spanning reasoning, coding, speech, and retrieval. Zhipu AI and DeepSeek add competitive LLMs and specialized OCR. MiniMax and Moonshot AI contribute emerging architectures. Cohere brings reliable reranking. BharatGenAI and Kakao expand regional model coverage. This breadth gives customers more options for performance, cost, licensing, and language support.
SageMaker JumpStart enhancements in 2026
Beyond model onboarding, SageMaker JumpStart also shipped significant improvements in 2026 that reduce friction across the model lifecycle, from discovery to deployment.
Simplified Model Hub on the SageMaker AI console
Previously, discovering SageMaker JumpStart models required navigating into SageMaker Studio and finding the SageMaker JumpStart section in the left navigation. The new Model Hub experience surfaces the full SageMaker JumpStart catalog directly on the SageMaker AI console landing page. You can browse models by category and filter by input/output modality, publisher, model size, license, and framework. You can also view sample notebooks and open models inside Studio with a single click. This avoids the multi-step navigation that slowed initial exploration.
Pre-configured endpoint deployment options
Choosing the right instance type, serving container, and optimization settings for a model deployment typically required manual benchmarking across dozens of combinations. SageMaker JumpStart now offers named deployment configurations, with optimization options for:
- Balanced — An even tradeoff between cost, latency, and throughput for general-purpose workloads.
- Throughput optimized — Maximum tokens per second using techniques like Speculative Decoding, ideal for high-volume batch processing.
- Latency optimized — Lowest Time to First Token (TTFT), prioritizing speed for interactive applications.
- Cost optimized — Lowest infrastructure cost per request, suitable for workloads that can accept higher latency.
These configurations include Neuron-optimized setups for AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium instances, reducing deployment complexity and infrastructure costs. You can deploy a model with a single click and the right optimization profile, rather than spending weeks benchmarking configurations manually.
Hugging Face deep link integration
A new integration with Hugging Face connects model discovery directly to SageMaker Studio, for onboarded models. When browsing models on Hugging Face, you can choose Deploy on SageMaker AI or Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI. You land directly in a configured Studio environment with the model pre-loaded, permissions pre-configured, and GPU quota visibility built in. This avoids the need to set up AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, create a domain, or configure permissions before experimenting.
Getting started
There are three ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart:
- SageMaker Studio console — Open SageMaker Studio, navigate to Models → JumpStart models, and browse the catalog. Choose a model to view its details, then choose Deploy or Customize.
- SageMaker Python SDK — Deploy models programmatically using the SageMaker Python SDK. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog for SDK examples and deployment guides.
- Hugging Face deep link — Browse the HuggingFace Model Hub and choose Deploy on SageMaker AI to land directly in Studio for SageMaker JumpStart onboarded models.
Each model on SageMaker JumpStart includes deployment configurations, sample notebooks, and documentation. For a hands-on walkthrough, see our related blog post on “Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart”.
Conclusion
The first three quarters of 2026 have been a period of significant progress for Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. With over 100 new models onboarded from 30 providers, the catalog now spans a wide range of capabilities. These include frontier reasoning models, multimodal vision-language models, creative AI for image and video generation, speech recognition and synthesis, optical character recognition (OCR) and document understanding, embedding and retrieval models for RAG, agentic workflow models, and specialized scientific computing models.
These onboarding priorities reflect where we see the strongest customer demand and the greatest opportunity to accelerate AI adoption on AWS. They include expanding the portfolio, closing the multimodal gap, making creative AI accessible, prioritizing efficiency and quantization, onboarding purpose-built models, and broadening provider diversity.
Combined with the enhancements like simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and the Hugging Face deep link integration, SageMaker JumpStart continues to lower the barrier between model discovery and production deployment. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog to explore the full lineup.
Next steps
There are many ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart. Try one of these out for yourself!
- Evaluate models and choose the right one for you
- Learn how to Deploy from HuggingFace to SageMaker Studio
- Use pretrained models in case-based deployments
- Design a Physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod

articles.title: Engineer builds tiny 3D-printed single-motor drone in their bedroom — 45-degree hinged rotor and sub-0.2ms firmware control pitch and roll
articles.text:
Engineer builds tiny 3D-printed single-motor drone in their bedroom — 45-degree hinged rotor and sub-0.2ms firmware control pitch and roll
Single-motor drones could be technically simpler than helicopters or quadcopters, but they require a lot more complex programming.
A software engineer who’s also into drones and 3D printing has shared a single-motor drone that they built inside their home and tested on their bed. Joshua Bird shared a video of how they created it on YouTube, highlighting the unique technique they used to maintain controllability and stability. The design used a combination of a hinged propeller, rapid changes to the motor’s rotation speed, and a custom flight controller and motor controller firmware that allowed the motor to react to necessary changes in under 0.2 milliseconds.
Most rotary wing aircraft require a mechanism to counteract the torque generated by the motor or engine and to change its flight direction, typically with the use of a swash plate to change rotor disk attitude and a secondary propeller. While this method has been effective for decades, it has made rotary-wing aircraft heavier and more complex. This single-motor drone cut the need for a secondary mechanism by constantly adjusting the speed of the motor — speeding it up produces more reaction torque while slowing it down applies opposite reaction torque. This essentially turns into a balancing act between these two forces to reduce the torque on the drone body to a more manageable level.
The hinged rotor also relies on the same mechanism for directional control instead of relying on a swashplate. Each rotor blade sits on a 45-degree hinge that makes it pivot when the motor accelerates. As this happens, one blade pitches up to produce more lift, while the other blade pitches down, reducing lift. By accelerating and decelerating the motor as needed, Bird would be able to change the drone’s roll and pitch movement. It also combines this with the main rotor torque, motor adjustments, and the 3D-printed stabilizing fins to produce effective yaw control as well.
This was the theoretical part — the majority of the build video focused on fixing issues, including the part where Bird built a high-speed camera using a Sony camera and a flash unit controlled by a microcontroller that gets its signals from the prototype drone’s motor controller and camera shutter. This home-made high-speed camera revealed that the drone’s propellers were too soft and had to be replaced with a 3D-printed version that used sturdier filament.
The creator had to launch several test flights from their bed, many of which resulted in a crashed drone and some wall damage as they fine-tuned the drone’s programming. Bird was eventually able to make the 3D-printed drone fly, although it was limited to the bedroom because of its fixed-base IR beacon navigation method. They said that they eventually want to add a linear camera to the build so that it could take off in other environments in the future.
While other researchers and engineers have built smaller, quieter drones, with China even revealing a mosquito-sized unit, Joshua Bird’s single-motor project is still a unique take on drones. But what made the YouTube video much more interesting is the problem-solving process and the solutions that came afterward. You can check out the complete video below and even start your own similar project by looking at the Single Propeller Drone GitHub repository.

articles.title: Toyota vai produzir Corolla elétrico na China a partir de 2028
articles.text:
A Toyota prepara transformação histórica para o Corolla, seu carro mais vendido. A próxima geração do modelo terá versão 100% elétrica, cuja produção está prevista para começar em 2028 na China. O veículo também continuará disponível com motor híbrido e a combustão.
Segundo informações publicadas pelo Electrek nesta segunda-feira (19), a fabricação será realizada pela FAW Toyota Motor, joint venture da montadora japonesa com o grupo chinês FAW. A expectativa é que a nova geração seja apresentada em 2027, como modelo 2028.
Desde sua estreia, em 1966, o Corolla acumulou mais de 57 milhões de unidades vendidas no mundo. A próxima geração representa uma das mudanças mais significativas da história do veículo, que ficou conhecido pela proposta de carro acessível para o uso cotidiano.
Corolla elétrico pode ter autonomia superior a 400 km
- A expectativa é que o Corolla elétrico tenha versões com um ou dois motores e autonomia de pelo menos cerca de 400 km. Os números, porém, ainda são estimativas: a Toyota não divulgou as especificações definitivas da bateria nem os detalhes do conjunto elétrico;
- A nova geração também deverá utilizar uma plataforma capaz de acomodar diferentes tipos de motorização. A arquitetura permitirá produzir versões totalmente elétricas, híbridas, híbridas plug-in e a combustão;
- No caso da versão híbrida, a previsão é de novo motor de quatro cilindros e 1,5 litro combinado a um motor elétrico. Engenheiros da Toyota estimam que o conjunto poderá entregar cerca de 134 cavalos de potência e ser entre 10% e 20% mais eficiente que o sistema atual;
- A montadora ainda não confirmou os dados técnicos finais das diferentes versões.
Leia mais:
- Gasolina cara leva brasileiros a considerar carros elétricos
- Volvo aposta na Nvidia para criar carros que dirigem sozinhos nas cidades até 2030
- Tesla revela Roadster que “voa” e dirige de ponta-cabeça com tecnologia da SpaceX
Por que a Toyota vai produzir o Corolla elétrico na China?
A escolha da China para iniciar a produção está relacionada à estratégia da Toyota para reduzir custos e acelerar o desenvolvimento e a fabricação de veículos eletrificados.
O mercado chinês reúne fabricantes que avançaram rapidamente em tecnologias de baterias, sistemas elétricos e recursos digitais. A Toyota enfrenta concorrência crescente no país, especialmente em cenário de pressão sobre os modelos a combustão e híbridos tradicionais.
A empresa vem reorganizando suas operações locais para simplificar a produção e ampliar a oferta de tecnologias mais avançadas. A estratégia inclui suas duas joint ventures chinesas, a FAW Toyota e a GAC Toyota.
A Toyota também planeja produzir veículos elétricos de maior autonomia para a marca de luxo Lexus na China a partir de 2027.
Corolla elétrico será vendido fora da China?
Ainda não está claro se o Corolla totalmente elétrico será comercializado nos Estados Unidos. A Toyota também não confirmou todos os mercados que receberão a nova versão.
A previsão é que a nova geração mantenha parte das características do conceito apresentado pela marca no Japan Mobility Show, em 2025. O protótipo chamou a atenção pelo desenho mais esportivo, com linhas angulosas e silhueta bastante diferente da aparência tradicional do sedã.
Além da versão elétrica, a nova família Corolla deverá incluir configurações híbridas, híbridas plug-in e a combustão. Os preços ainda não foram anunciados oficialmente.
A expectativa é que a nova geração seja apresentada em 2027, com a chegada da linha 2028. Até lá, a Toyota deverá divulgar mais informações sobre autonomia, desempenho, equipamentos e disponibilidade comercial.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: How far can we push computing?
articles.text:
How far can we push computing?
Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing.
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.
On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.
In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out.
The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.
But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains.
Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.
The descent
During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The quarter-milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watchmaker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands.
The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale.
The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor.
 The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watchmaker’s lathe, under a microscope.
The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law.
Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.
Slowing down
Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling.
SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS
For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed.
Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits.
The ultimate computer
Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femtojoule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate.
These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.
The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc2, holds about 9 ×1016 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×1050 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today.
The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop.
Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10-21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch.
Memory density obeys a limit of its own, and this one reaches all the way to gravity. How many bits can a region of space hold? In 1981, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein, while working out the thermodynamics of black holes, determined the amount: The information inside any bounded region is limited by its size and the energy it contains. For a region the size of Lloyd’s ultimate laptop, that comes to about 1042 bits, some 1036 to a cubic millimeter—nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size can store today.
Approaching the limits
Over the decades, we have pushed the performance of our computers and our communications technology closer and closer to fundamental limits. The biggest change has been in the energy required for a single computation, which has dropped by 17 orders of magnitude since the 1940s, a factor of a hundred thousand trillion. But even with that big drop, we’re still a factor of several hundred thousand from the fundamental physical limit, set by information theory and the laws of thermodynamics. The largest gap exists for computational speed: Our current chips are some 35 orders of magnitude—that’s a 1 followed by 35 zeros—short of what quantum mechanics allows for a one-kilogram computer.
SOURCES: LLOYD (2000); BEKENSTEIN (1981); LANDAUER (1961); HOLEVO (1973); CAVES AND DRUMMOND (1994); BURKS (1947); BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; IEEE IRDS; NVIDIA; CISCO
The last limit is on communication—how fast information can be moved. Every wire and every fiber ultimately carries its signal on quanta, the indivisible packets (photons in the case of light) in which energy travels. In 1973, the Soviet mathematician Alexander Holevo determined the ultimate limit on how much information a stream of quanta can convey. A watt of light delivers only so many photons each second, and quantum mechanics fixes how many distinguishable ways they can arrive—how many messages a receiver could ever tell apart. A single channel carrying one watt, at the Holevo limit, could deliver on the order of 1017 bits per second. Today’s optical links, or interconnects, deliver about one-millionth that rate for the same power. But the gap is narrowing quickly inside data centers, where each generation of interconnects is asked to move more bits on less power, spending less energy on the electronics and using light to cover more of the distance.
Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun.
The room that remains
The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter.
Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation.
Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined.
But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in.
This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat.
Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication.
Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet.
Between the floor and the ceiling
It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter.
But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
 These gaps are invitations. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
For most of the last century, we proceeded down both paths together. We built more computers, and the computers themselves grew smaller and better. Now we mostly build more, and the ceiling is coming into view. A power grid can carry only so many gigawatts, and a region can spare only so much land and water. Yet every road map for what comes next is drawn from the same starting point: the machines we already have. Build more of them and you climb toward the ceiling; build better ones and you descend a little further, but only as far as the transistor’s own floor. There is a third direction. Start with a physics experiment operating at the floor and build up.
It has been done before. The transistor was a physics experiment before it was an industry; the laser was a laboratory curiosity before it carried the world’s conversations under the ocean; giant magnetoresistance went from physics discovery to the read head of every disk drive within a decade. In each case, the physics experiment came first and showed what was possible, and engineers then turned it into a machine that can be scaled up. Building the experiments that operate at these fundamental limits, and then scaling them up without losing that performance, is the work that remains. The next machines will not be reached by descent; they will be built from the bottom up. There is still plenty of room at the bottom.
Volkan Gurses is a postdoctoral researcher at MIT and a visiting researcher at Nvidia. He received his PhD in electrical engineering from Caltech. He studies the fundamental physical limits of information technologies and builds integrated circuits and systems that approach those limits.

articles.title: FritzOS 8.40 steht bereit: Was das Labor-Update auf deine Fritzbox bringt
articles.text:
FritzOS 8.40: Was die Labor-Version bringt – und welche Fritzboxen das Update jetzt erhalten
Updates für Fritzboxen können im ersten Moment etwas verwirrend sein. Denn nicht alle Geräte bekommen dieselben Aktualisierungen spendiert. Manche Fritz-Router bekommen langsamer neue Versionsnummern, während andere immer die neuesten Funktionen erhalten. Dazu kommt, dass es neben den fertigen Updates auch noch Laborversionen für Fritzboxen gibt. Dabei handelt es sich um das Betaprogramm, mit dem du vor allen anderen einen Blick auf neue Updates werfen kannst.
FritzOS 8.40 steht für diese Router bereit
Und genau ein solches Labor-Update wurde jetzt für eine Reihe von Fritzboxen bereitgestellt. FritzOS 8.40 wurde zunächst nur für einige wenige Router veröffentlicht. Jetzt hat Fritz den Test aber auf weitere Modelle ausgeweitet. Diese Fritz-Router können das Update jetzt herunterladen:
- Fritzbox 4050
- Fritzbox 4630
- Fritzbox 4690
- Fritzbox 5590 Fiber
- Fritzbox 5690 Pro
- Fritzbox 5690 XGS
- Fritzbox 6660
- Fritzbox 6670
- Fritzbox 6850 5G
- Fritzbox 6850 5G V2
- Fritzbox 6850 4G
- Fritzbox 6850 LTE
- Fritzbox 6690
- Fritzbox 6690 Pro
- Fritzbox 7510
- Fritzbox 7530 AX
- Fritzbox 7590 AX
- Fritzbox 7590
- Fritzbox 7620
- Fritzbox 7630
- Fritzbox 7690
- Fritz-Repeater 6000
- Fritz-Repeater 3000 AX
- Fritz-Repeater 1200 AX
- Fritz-Mesh-Set 1600
Um an der Beta teilzunehmen, müssen interessierte Fritz-User:innen das Update für die Router manuell von der Webseite des Herstellers herunterladen. Anschließend kannst du in die Weboberfläche des Routers wechseln und dort unter „System“ den Bereich „Update“ aufrufen. Dort lässt sich die FritzOS-Datei einfügen und auf dem Router installieren. Wie bei allen Betaprogrammen solltest du dir aber im Klaren sein, dass es noch zu etwaigen Problemen kommen kann. Muss deine Fritzbox rund um die Uhr reibungslos funktionieren, solltest du lieber auf den finalen Release von FritzOS 8.40 warten.
Was steckt in FritzOS 8.4?
Je nach Modell sind die Neuerungen von FritzOS 8.4 recht unterschiedlich. Die Fritzbox 5590 Fiber bekommt etwa neue Filterlisten für DNS-Anfragen aus dem Heim- und Gastnetz sowie mehr Auslöser für Smarthome-Routinen und eine Überlastungsschaltung für smarte Fritz-Steckdosen. Bei anderen Modellen wie der Fritzbox 7590 AX ist die Liste der Neuerungen schon deutlich länger.
Denn das Spitzenmodell von Fritz bekommt eine neue Priorisierungsfunktion, die automatisch für die beste Internetverbindung sorgen soll, einen Einrichtungsassistenten für den Wechsel von DSL auf Glasfaser sowie eine automatisierte Erkennung und Priorisierung von Videokonferenzen. Neu für viele Fritzboxen ist zudem ein SOS‑Ruf, mit dem vier Notfallnummern hinterlegt werden können, die automatisch im Ernstfall nacheinander kontaktiert werden.
Zudem gibt es einen einfachen Modus für Fritz-Fon, um die Barrierefreiheit beim Telefonieren für ältere Menschen zu verbessern. Für Menschen mit körperlicher Einschränkung lassen sich bei DECT-Telefonen mit FritzOS 8.40 zudem Softkeys als Schnellwahltasten einrichten und so mit einer Funktion oder einer Rufnummer belegen. Sämtliche Funktionen und Neuerungen für deine Fritzbox kannst du auf dieser Fritz-Webseite sehen, wenn du dein Fritzbox-Modell aus dem Dropdown-Menü auswählst.

articles.title: Anthropic signs lease for $10-billion Nova Scotia data centre
articles.text:
San Francisco-based Anthropic has been revealed as a long-term leaseholder for a large Nova Scotia data centre project—the AI giant’s first data centre in Canada.
The news: Halifax-based EverWind Fuels announced plans for a $10-billion data centre project at its existing campus in Point Tupper, NS, on Friday. The investment includes more than $8 billion to develop the campus, alongside $2 billion for its onshore wind energy portfolio.
The campus is planned to begin with a 95-megawatt (MW) phase in late 2027, followed by a 325 MW expansion slated for 2028. At full development, the campus would hold 420 MW in compute capacity.
While EverWind didn’t initially reveal the project’s inaugural long-term leaseholder, Anthropic told media that the data centre will power Claude models and serve growing demand from its Canadian and global customers.
From the source: “Canadians are using Claude in growing numbers, and we want our infrastructure to be closer to the people who rely on it,” Anthropic Canada Public Policy head Jacob Glick said in a statement, according to Global News. “Canada has set a high bar for responsible data centre development, as has the Premier of Nova Scotia, and we are committing to meeting it.”
The context: Anthropic and EverWind have both signed onto Canada’s Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, a voluntary, non-enforceable framework that guides hyperscalers and regulators on how data centre projects should consider factors like electricity and water use. So far, in line with the framework, EverWind has committed to fully funding all electricity system network upgrade costs associated with the project and to use a closed-loop cooling system.
Anthropic’s involvement in the project comes shortly after the company opened job postings for a Canadian data centre community engagement manager and compute lead, the latter of which would be responsible for bringing “gigawatts of compute online in Canada.”
Final thought: Despite public pushback, data centre projects continue to facilitate record-breaking investment for provinces. EverWind said its project represents the largest privately funded investment in Nova Scotia’s history, shortly after Bell’s $50-billion data centre buildout in Saskatchewan broke that province’s investment record as well.
Feature image courtesy Tim Houston via X.

articles.title: Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
articles.text:
For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6.
Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
The flagship earbuds now cost about as much as their predecessor.
The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review, John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments.
The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls.
The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing.

articles.title: Estaba cansado de tener varios cargadores por casa; ahora unifico todo en una única base de carga y me ha cambiado la vida
articles.text:
En mi casa cada noche, justo antes de dormir, cuando ponemos a cargar el teléfono, siempre hay un poco de desorden. Somos dos personas, los dos con teléfono, reloj inteligente y auriculares y cada dispositivo con su propio cargador. Algo tan sencillo como poner a cargarlos era un poco jaleo porque o bien tienes todos los cargadores en los enchufes conectados las 24 horas del día, con todos los cables por ahí sueltos, o bien no encuentras el que necesitas en ese momento: como la base de carga para el reloj inteligente.
Por eso, hace unas semanas decidimos poner fin a eso. Al mismo tiempo que ponemos un poco de orden en cuanto a cables, hacemos que sea mucho más sencillo cargar todos los dispositivos. En concreto, hemos comprado la base de carga UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1, para teléfono, auriculares y reloj; y la base UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1, para teléfono y auriculares.
Dos estaciones de carga simplemente perfectas
En mi caso uso un iPhone 18 Pro, un Apple Watch Series 10 y unos AirPods. En el caso de mi pareja, un iPhone 17 y unos AirPods. Los teléfonos los cargamos cada noche, mi reloj lo cargo cada dos días aproximadamente y en el caso de los auriculares, yo los cargo cada semana pero mi pareja un par de veces a la semana. Con esta actividad de carga, era necesario una estación de carga que pueda unificar en un único lugar todos los dispositivos.
A la hora de elegir la estación de carga perfecta para nosotros teníamos una serie de requisitos. La primera es la velocidad de carga. Acostumbrado a la potencia que nos da un cargador de pared, no queríamos procesos lentos de carga. En segundo lugar, queríamos una base de carga que fuese bonita. Si va a estar expuesta todo el día, tiene que ser bonita y cómoda, donde podamos dejar cada noche el dispositivo de una forma sencilla y segura.
Para reducir aún más el proceso de búsqueda, decidimos ir a una marca con prestigio, que más y mejores valoraciones positivas acumule. Y en este sentido, UGREEN es la número uno. Ya tenemos algún cable y algún cargador de ellos y cuando vimos que tenía estaciones de carga, lo tuvimos bastante claro.
UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1: el complemento perfecto para usuarios exigentes
En mi caso opté por la nueva serie MagFlow, que ha sufrido cambios considerables con respecto a la versión anterior. La estación de carga UGREEN MagFlow Pro 3 en 1 me entró por la vista desde el minuto uno, pero desde que la uso, estoy sencillamente encantado.
Uno de los aspectos más importantes y diferenciales es su sistema de refrigeración que mantiene en todo momento los dispositivos alejados de temperaturas altas. UGREEN llama a este sistema CryoPulse™ TEC Active Cooling System y lo que consigue es que el teléfono, mientras recibe potencias alta de carga, no se sobrecaliente, lo que podría afectar tanto al rendimiento como a su vida útil y salud de la propia batería.
Estamos hablando de potencias de carga de 25W usando la carga magnética, compatible con el estándar Qi2.2 . Sólo hay que acercar el teléfono por la parte del MagSafe y el teléfono empieza a cargar. En mi caso, he podido recargar la mitad de la batería de mi iPhone en menos de media hora. En el caso del Watch, recarga la batería de 0 al 80% en 30 minutos, perfecto mientras me ducho o desayuno por las mañanas. Y al mismo tiempo, también se cargan los AirPods. Es sin duda lo más cómodo que he visto en mucho tiempo: poder cargar los tres dispositivos, al mismo tiempo, y con potencias de carga muy buenas. 
Tanto el proceso de carga como la temperatura se puede controlar desde la pantalla que incorpora la base de carga. Puedes ver el estado de la carga de cada dispositivo de manera diferenciada.
Seguramente haya todavía personas que desconfían de otras marcas de cargadores diferentes al fabricante de su teléfono, pero en el caso de UGREEN no hay ningún motivo para preocuparse puesto que en todo momento, el proceso de carga es seguro, rápido y con la temperatura controlada.
UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1: carga tu reloj y auriculares
Mi pareja, al no usar reloj inteligente, no necesita una base de carga tan completa como la mía. Además no tendría sentido comprar dos iguales. Sin embargo, al ver el modelo UGREEN MagFlow 2 en 1, lo tuvimos claro: compraríamos los dos modelos.
Es una estación de carga dos en uno, para teléfono y auriculares, pero sorprende mucho su tamaño compacto, plegable y que se puede guardar y llevar a cualquier lado. De hecho cuando hemos tenido que viajar, lo hemos llevado guardado en su bolso.
Aunque sea pequeño, anda sobrado de especificaciones. Primero en potencia, donde llega a los 25W con la carga inalámbrica, también usando el estándar Qi2.2 . En segundo lugar, la potencia de su imán magnético que se adhiere al teléfono con total seguridad y firmeza gracias al uso de hasta 16 imanes.
Su diseño también hace que no sólo funcione como una base de carga, sino también como trípode. Podemos colocarlo de tal manera que podemos seguir viendo nuestra serie favorita o hacer la videollamada que teníamos pendiente, sin que la falta de batería cambie nuestros planes.
Es una estación de carga sencilla, pero muy versátil y con un precio visiblemente inferior a la anterior. Aunque la base 3 en 1 es perfecta para mí, este modelo 2 en 1 es perfecto para el 99 por ciento de la población. Para personas que buscan simplificar los cables en su casa para tener estancias mucho más limpias.
Las dos bases de carga MagFlow se pueden comprar tanto en Amazon como en la propia tienda de UGREEN. Además te recomendamos que estés pendiente porque suelen estar sujetos a bastantes ofertas, lo cual hace que sea una compra todavía más recomendable.

articles.title: Apple vient à peine de dévoiler son HomeView, mais prépare déjà une version beaucoup plus étonnante
articles.text:
Apple n’a pas encore commercialisé son premier écran connecté qu’une version plus ambitieuse se dessine déjà. Le constructeur travaillerait sur un HomeView équipé d’un bras robotisé, capable de suivre les utilisateurs dans leurs déplacements.
Apple ne manque décidément pas d’idées pour s’installer dans nos maisons. Quelques jours après avoir présenté le HomeView, son premier écran connecté destiné au salon ou à la cuisine, le constructeur préparerait déjà une déclinaison beaucoup plus sophistiquée. Et cette fois, il ne serait pas question de simplement agrandir l’affichage ou d’améliorer les haut-parleurs. Apple voudrait donner vie à son appareil, avec un bras robotisé capable d’orienter automatiquement l’écran vers la personne qui lui parle. Un concept qui rappelle certaines expérimentations du constructeur dans la robotique domestique, et qui pourrait prendre forme plus rapidement qu’on ne l’imaginait.
Un écran qui vous suit du regard dans la maison
Selon les informations de Mark Gurman, journaliste chez Bloomberg, Apple poursuivrait le développement d’une version haut de gamme de son HomeView, connue en interne sous le nom de code J595. Contrairement au modèle présenté le 13 octobre, équipé d’une dalle de 7 pouces, ce nouvel appareil profiterait d'un écran d’environ 9 pouces. Mais sa véritable particularité se trouverait sous l'affichage.
Apple envisagerait d’installer l’écran sur un bras motorisé capable de pivoter à 360 degrés. Grâce à la reconnaissance vocale, le dispositif pourrait identifier la personne qui s’adresse à Siri et orienter automatiquement son écran dans sa direction.
Imaginez un HomeView posé sur le plan de travail de la cuisine. Vous préparez le dîner, puis vous vous déplacez pour récupérer des ingrédients. Plutôt que de rester figé face à un mur, l'écran pourrait se tourner vers vous pour continuer à afficher une recette ou faciliter un appel FaceTime.
C'est du moins l’expérience qu’Apple chercherait à proposer. Pour l’instant, rien ne permet de connaître la rapidité des mouvements, la précision du suivi ou les possibilités réelles de cette articulation. La commercialisation serait envisagée en 2027 ou 2028, sans calendrier plus précis. Quant aux appellations HomeView Max, Ultra ou 360 évoquées dans la presse, elles relèvent pour le moment de la spéculation.
Apple rêve depuis longtemps d’un compagnon robotisé
L’idée n’est pas complètement nouvelle. Dès 2024, plusieurs indiscrétions évoquaient un robot domestique imaginé par Apple, avec un écran monté sur un bras articulé. En mai 2025, nous évoquions déjà une version haut de gamme de l’écran connecté d'Apple, capable d’ajuster automatiquement son orientation. Le projet était alors présenté comme un compagnon domestique doté de fonctions avancées d’intelligence artificielle.
La nouveauté, c’est qu’Apple dispose désormais d’un premier produit autour duquel construire cette gamme. Le HomeView classique, attendu le 13 novembre dans les premiers pays concernés, propose un écran tactile, des fonctions de visioconférence et l’accès aux équipements domotiques depuis une interface commune.
La version robotisée pourrait aller plus loin en rendant les interactions avec Siri AI plus naturelles. Plutôt que de placer systématiquement l’appareil face à soi, l’utilisateur pourrait lui parler depuis différents endroits de la pièce. Une approche intéressante pour un équipement destiné à être partagé entre plusieurs membres du foyer.
Reste à savoir si ce mécanisme apportera suffisamment de confort pour justifier un tarif probablement supérieur. Autre inconnue : sa disponibilité européenne. Le HomeView actuel ne sera pas commercialisé dans l’Union européenne au lancement, Apple invoquant l’absence de Siri AI sur iPhone et iPad en raison de son différend avec Bruxelles autour du DMA. Rien ne garantit que cette future déclinaison échappera aux mêmes restrictions.
Apple a donc encore du travail avant de transformer son écran connecté en compagnon robotisé. Mais à Cupertino, on semble déjà considérer qu’un écran capable de répondre à nos questions ne suffit plus. Il faudrait désormais qu’il se tourne vers nous pour le faire.

articles.title: Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups; How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
articles.text:
Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups; How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.
Dear Reader,
Rising input costs are squeezing the profitability of FMCG firms. Should you be worried about price hikes?
Not for the moment at least, as companies have absorbed a part of the inflation costs to not hurt consumer demand during the festive season. However, as firms continue to face margin pressures, decisions on price hikes could be taken post-Diwali, from December onwards, say stakeholders.
In other news, US Vice President J D Vance has admitted that his rhetoric has been “imperfect” when he referred to foreign professionals holding H-1 B visas as “indentured servants”. He clarified that his criticism was of the visa system, which gives employers too much power over foreign employees, and not targeted at H-1B visa holders.
India had condemned the terminology used to describe foreign professionals, calling it “deeply offensive” and carrying painful historical and colonial legacy connotations.
Meanwhile, the Delhi government has approved the setting up of Go-Delhi Foundation with a corpus of Rs 50 crore to empower young innovators and startups. The foundation aims to promote startups, innovation and entrepreneurship in the capital and support young people, researchers and entrepreneurs in turning their ideas into practical products and successful enterprises.
ICYMI: In their new book The Lift-Off Nation, Peak XV’s Rajan Anandan and Saurabh Srivastava make the case for India’s startup golden age. Anandan calls for greater corporate investment in R&D and startups and discusses the government’s Rs 1 lakh crore RDI scheme.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Peak XV’s big bets on Indian startups
- How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Here’s your trivia for today: Which company’s famous plaid pattern is called ‘novacheck’?
Venture capital
Peak XV is taking bigger bets on Indian startups
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.
During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Bhatnagar said the success of companies such as Zomato and the growing acceptance of startups in India’s public markets have fundamentally changed what founders and investors believe is possible.
Key takeaways
- Bhatnagar was gung-ho about the ambition and aspiration of Indian founders which has grown multifold over the years. “The startup ecosystem is in a much better place today than it was 20 years back. The biggest difference is in ambition,” he said.
- He believes AI can be a big advantage for a country like India, and startups should be rooted in India but build for the global market.
- “I really hope we now see a 10x unleashing of entrepreneurial energy because it's become so much easier to launch a product, to try it in the marketplace, than ever before. You don’t need as much capital.”
ICYMI
How Tally stayed relevant for 40 years
Tally Solutions’ journey began much before the SaaS, UPI, GST, and startup boom. Founded in 1986, the accounting software company has outlasted several technology cycles and built a customer network of close to three million.
At TechSparks 2026, Tally’s Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka explained how Tally, a homegrown product company, has stayed relevant over four decades.
Key takeaways
- Nupur Goenka attributed Tally's success to its focus on ownership. Tally handcrafted its stack from the start, she said, with its own database, its own memory manager, and a programming language invented in-house.
- Tejas Goenka stressed on the company’s founding principle. “The cost post-purchase should be near zero,” he said, recalling the days when releases were shipped with a support team of one.
- Going forward, Tally is betting on new geographies, particularly the Middle East and Africa. “We have an incredible two, three decades in front of us... It would be a shame if we let that opportunity slip to create an impactful technology company out of this country,” said Tejas.
News & updates
- AI advancements: Rapidly improving AI capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said, with one of the company's internal models  forecasting that, under certain conditions, it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
- Export curbs: China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
What you should watch out for
Jio Platforms’ IPO will open for subscription from October 21 to October 23. This is expected to be the largest public issue in Indian stock market history.
Which company’s famous plaid pattern is called ‘novacheck’?
Answer: Burberry

articles.title: One Compromised Login Exposed Millions of California Students’ Records
articles.text:
Personal information on current and former California public school students was copied from a file transfer system belonging to Educational Testing Service (ETS), according to the California Department of Education (CDE).
ETS is a nonprofit that handles state and federally mandated testing under a contract with the state. The organization supports California’s CAASPP and ELPAC assessment programs and relied on a secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) site to share testing data with CDE.
The organization spotted unauthorized activity on the site on September 25, but the earliest access dates back to late May.
“The investigation determined that an unauthorized party used a compromised login credential at various times during the period from May 22, 2026 to September 18, 2026 to access the SFTP site to copy files containing California student information,” according to the CDE’s breach notice.
No victim count has been provided, but the notice says, “Information about California students, including but not limited to all students enrolled in the three previous school years, was accessed and copied.”
CDE’s own enrollment figures put that in perspective: more than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California public schools in 2025-2026. The department’s incident FAQ notes that the impacted population also extends to students who left a California school as far back as 2006 and whose transfer to another school was not confirmed with CDE.
Compromised records can include information such as student name, birth date, home address, school, district and grade, state and local ID numbers, gender, race or ethnicity, primary language, country of origin and English learner status.
Some entries go further, revealing disability and Section 504 status, the primary disability type, testing accommodations, English proficiency data, and test registration and results. They may also indicate whether a student qualifies for Title I, McKinney-Vento or military-connected student designations.
The notice says the files did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or financial account or payment card details. Information on parents and guardians was not involved either.
ETS shut down the account the intruder used and pulled the SFTP site offline. Its response also includes building a replacement site with stronger safeguards.
The official disclosures do not explain how the login credential was compromised, and they do not identify the attacker.
“After working with law enforcement as well as with cybersecurity experts, ETS has taken steps to reduce the potential risk of the data being made publicly accessible,” the notice states. ETS did not elaborate, but said its web monitoring has so far found no evidence that the data has been published.
CDE informed county and district superintendents and charter school administrators of the incident in a letter dated October 2, two weeks before family notifications started. According to that letter, ETS stopped its regular processing of enrollment data and suspended some testing work while its systems’ security was evaluated.
Student notifications started going out on October 16, and CDE expects them to continue into early November. Affected current and former students can sign up for two years of free identity protection services.
Related: Deal Reached With Hackers to Delete Data Stolen From the Canvas Educational Platform
Related: Mount Royal University Confirms Data Stolen in Ransomware Attack

articles.title: Inside the Underground Market for Know Your Client Services
articles.text:
In February 2026, the operator of OnlyFake pleaded guilty in the United States for his role in a service that generated more than 10,000 fraudulent digital identity documents. Customers could create passports, driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, and documents from dozens of countries, then choose whether each appeared as a scan or a photograph of a physical ID.
According to the U.S. Department of Justice, the documents allowed cybercriminals to conceal their identities, circumvent identity checks at banks and cryptocurrency exchanges, and launder money.
The activity extends beyond fabricated documents. In underground communities monitored by Flare's platform, actors advertise manipulated photographs and videos, assistance with live identity verification, and accounts they claim have already passed identity checks.
Each year, Flare collects hundreds of thousands of search results related to Know Your Client (KYC) services and the trade in verified accounts. Activity observed between March and September 2026 shows how these offerings are packaged and promoted across underground markets.
What is KYC?
It is the process that financial institutions use to establish a customer’s identity and assess the risk of providing services to them.
Depending on the level of risk, they may validate the document, compare its photograph with a live image, confirm control of contact details, request information about the source of funds, and screen the customer against sanctions and politically exposed person lists.
KYC continues after the account opening through transaction monitoring and additional verification when information changes or activity appears unusual. The Financial Action Task Force describes customer due diligence as identifying the customer, understanding the purpose of the relationship, and monitoring it over time.
Is a Fake Identity Already Getting Past Your Checks?
Underground sellers package forged documents, deepfakes, and live verification help to pass identity checks.
Flare monitors criminal forums for exposed identities, stolen credentials, and active sessions, so you can invalidate access before it becomes account takeover or fraud.
Free 2-Week Trial
How KYC identity fraud works
The steps and image below illustrate how actors assemble the elements used in KYC identity fraud:
- Identity data establishes the applicant’s claimed personal details.
- Documents are presented to substantiate those details.
- Photographs or videos associate the claimed identity with a face.
- Device and browser preparation makes the application session appear consistent with a legitimate customer’s.
- Live verification is attempted by a human operator or with synthetic media.
Building the identity package
In March 2026, Flare observed a forum seller offering generated or edited identity and financial documents tailored to individual verification requests, including bank statements and other records that platforms may use to confirm an applicant’s address, income, or account ownership.
The offer of complete KYC packages shows how sellers adapt several documents to the requirements of a particular platform or customer. Names, photographs, addresses, and other details must remain consistent across the application because a mismatch can trigger rejection or further review.
This preparation creates the identity package later used during the facial or live verification stage.
Bypassing live identity checks
Many KYC systems compare the photograph on an identity document with a live image of the applicant. Some use passive liveness checks, which analyze a short camera recording for signs of a real person. Others use active checks that ask the applicant to turn their head, speak, blink, or read numbers shown on screen.
To bypass these checks, actors advertise altered photographs and AI-generated videos based on the face shown in the identity document. Some tools claim to change the operator’s appearance during a live session, allowing the false face to follow instructions in real time by replacing the image coming from the physical camera with altered footage.
Flare also observed advertisements for “human KYC,” in which a person completes facial or video verification using identity material prepared for the application.
In one recruitment post, an actor sought someone who could use deepfake tools to alter the camera image during a live check and appear as the person named in the identity documents.
In another example, Flare researchers observed a threat actor advertising guidance for a live number-reading check. The applicant must respond to content presented during the session, thus the offered bypass requires coordination and adaptation rather than the submission of a prepared object.
Support after the account is delivered
Flare researchers observed sellers offering continued verification and account-recovery assistance after delivering a completed account, and the recruitment post above included help when a platform requested another identity check following handoff.
When a later check requires the identity material or participant used during enrollment, the buyer may remain dependent on the seller, extending the original KYC service beyond the sale and helping preserve the appearance that the verified customer still controls the account.
Detecting KYC abuse
FinCEN has warned financial institutions that criminals are using deepfakes and fraudulent identity documents to bypass customer verification controls.
Its alert recommends examining the complete application because differences between the applicant’s identity information, supporting records, facial images, and account activity may reveal that several elements were prepared by different people or tools.
NIST recommends collecting identity documents and facial images directly during the verification session, checking whether they have been altered, and detecting software that replaces the footage from a physical camera.
Unpredictable instructions, such as asking an applicant to make a particular movement or read changing numbers, can make prepared recordings harder to use, while information about the device can help determine whether the session comes from ordinary customer equipment.
Applying these checks together gives organizations a better chance of detecting the combined use of false documents, deepfakes, and human operators described in underground KYC advertisements.
Flare gives organizations additional visibility by monitoring criminal forums for exposed identities, stolen credentials, active login sessions, and threats connected to their organization. Security teams can use these alerts to identify affected accounts, invalidate exposed access, and investigate identity-related activity before it develops into account takeover or further fraud.

articles.title: On a déjà testé le Xiaomi 18 Pro : nos premières conclusions avant sa sortie en France — Frandroid
articles.text:
Présenté en Chine le 23 septembre, le Xiaomi 18 Pro suscite un fort engouement. Sa sortie en Europe est confirmée d’ici la fin de l’année. Ce serait le premier modèle Pro de la marque vendu en France depuis le Xiaomi 13 Pro, sorti en 2023. Pour nous faire une idée sans attendre, nous avons acheté un exemplaire chinois et l’avons passé au crible au fil de plusieurs articles.
Précision importante : il s’agit d’un modèle chinois. Nous avons pu passer l’interface en français et installer les services Google, mais certains éléments restent en chinois. La batterie de la version française sera sans doute moins grosse que les 7 000 mAh de notre exemplaire chinois, et le logiciel pourra encore évoluer d’ici la sortie. Ce qui suit ne préfigure donc pas exactement l’expérience que vous aurez en France. Il en donne toutefois un aperçu détaillé.
Photo : il bat l’iPhone 18 Pro… sauf en ultra grand-angle
Nous avons réalisé un comparatif photo opposant le Xiaomi 18 Pro à l’iPhone 18 Pro. Globalement, le Xiaomi 18 Pro remporte la majorité des duels. En plein jour, il débouche mieux les ombres et restitue plus de détails.
De nuit, sa colorimétrie est plus juste et il ne souffre pas des images fantômes (lumières parasites) que nous avons repérées sur l’iPhone.
Son zoom numérique grimpe jusqu’à x120. Ce niveau de grossissement ne servira presque jamais : le zoom optique de son téléobjectif de 200 mégapixels s’arrête à x3,2.
L’ultra grand-angle est son point faible. Son capteur de 50 mégapixels est petit et placé à part, sous l’écran arrière. De nuit, il produit des bords flous, là où l’iPhone garde un bon niveau de détails. En portrait, les deux font des choix différents : flou plus intense et teinte plus chaude chez Apple, bokeh plus naturel mais carnation plus pâle chez Xiaomi.
Performances : attention à la chauffe
Nous avons testé les performances du Xiaomi 18 Pro. Pour rappel, il embarque le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, à ne pas confondre avec la version Extreme réservée au Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.
Le bilan ? Le Xiaomi 18 Pro ne manque pas de ressources, mais ce premier test ne révèle pas le saut de performances qu’on était en droit d’espérer d’une nouvelle génération de puce. Précisons une fois de plus qu’il ne s’agit pas, sur le papier, de la puce la plus puissante de Qualcomm pour la nouvelle génération.
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro se hisse donc au niveau des meilleurs smartphones Android actuels, sans pour autant creuser l’écart. Selon le prix auquel il sera proposé en France, ce n’est pas nécessairement un problème.
La chauffe est son vrai point noir, avec environ 50 °C sur les deux faces dès AnTuTu 10. Sur notre test de CPU Throttling, le smartphone bride sa puce en dents de scie, avec des chutes brutales vers 25 % de ses performances. Cela pourrait se traduire par des baisses de fluidité lors de longues sessions de jeu. Une mise à jour logicielle pourrait corriger ce comportement sur la version française, attendue d’ici la fin de l’année.
Écran arrière : les fonctions qui nous ont plu
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro se distingue surtout par son écran de 2,7 pouces au dos, hérité du Xiaomi 17 Pro. Il sert d’abord de retour caméra pour prendre des selfies avec le meilleur capteur, ou pour montrer le cadrage à la personne photographiée.
Il permet aussi de répondre à un appel sans retourner le téléphone, d’afficher la météo ou le compteur de pas en fond d’écran, de piloter la musique ou ses appareils Xiaomi Home, ou encore de suivre un minuteur.
On regrette des paramètres encore fouillis et mal traduits. La version chinoise propose aussi des cartes pour DiDi (VTC) et AMap (navigation), deux services chinois qu’on aimerait voir remplacés par des équivalents disponibles en France.
Pour aller plus loin, nous vous avons listé nos 5 fonctions favorites sur l’écran arrière du Xiaomi 18 Pro.
Une application générée par IA sur l’écran arrière
Depuis les paramètres « Affichage arrière », le Xiaomi 18 Pro permet de créer une application pour l’écran arrière à partir d’un simple prompt. Nous avons demandé, à l’oral, un simulateur de dé à 20 faces pour Donjons et Dragons. L’IA a réécrit et enrichi notre consigne, puis a livré une application fonctionnelle en environ cinq minutes.
L’application générée par IA affiche donc un icosaèdre animé, un historique des lancers et, après une seconde demande, un bouton de remise à zéro.
La fonction est encore en bêta et limitée à 20 prompts sur le modèle chinois du Xiaomi 18 Pro.
Écran anti-espion : moins efficace que Samsung, mais une alerte bien vue
Comme le Galaxy S26 Ultra, le Xiaomi 18 Pro propose un affichage de confidentialité matériel.
Dans notre comparaison, Samsung masque mieux l’écran, y compris vu du haut ou du bas, ce que Xiaomi ne fait pas.
En revanche, Xiaomi a une bonne idée avec son « Avis de confidentialité ». Grâce à la reconnaissance faciale, le téléphone vous alerte via l’HyperIsland si quelqu’un regarde votre écran par-dessus votre épaule. La détection a fonctionné lors de nos essais.
Ce qu’il faut retenir
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro se montre très convaincant en photo, original avec son écran arrière et plein d’idées côté logiciel. Ses performances le placent au niveau des meilleurs Android du moment, sans les dépasser. Sa gestion de la chauffe est en revanche son principal défaut. Beaucoup dépendra désormais de la version française : son logiciel, sa traduction, ses fonctions IA et, bien sûr, son prix. Nous ne manquerons pas de le retester à sa sortie.
