articles.title: Las consolas de ahora se encarecen por la RAM, pero Sonic iba como un tiro hace 35 años en una Mega Drive con 64 KB
articles.text:
Cuando empecé a jugar a las consolas solo podías ser de dos bandos: o de Mario o de Sonic. O lo que es lo mismo: tenías que decidirte entre Nintendo y su Super Nintendo o Sega y su Mega Drive. Las dos empresas marcaban el rumbo de los videojuegos a comienzos de los 90, al menos en el ámbito doméstico. Y cada una necesitaba distinguirse con algún rasgo único. En Sega optaron por la velocidad.
Sonic iba rápido, la Mega Drive no. El hardware de la máquina no estaba mal para la época, pero tenía ciertas limitaciones. El obstáculo estaba, principalmente, en el procesador: el Motorola 68000 que montaba, a 7,67 MHz, era un chip bastante apto, pero carecía de un componente especializado en cálculos matemáticos complejos. Sus 64 KB de memoria RAM tampoco ayudaban (con otros 64 KB dedicados a vídeo).
Dado que Mega Drive necesitaba un Sonic a la altura para vender la máquina, en Sega le encargaron el proyecto a Yuji Naka, cocreador de la saga. Según explicaba en este vídeo con motivo del vigésimo aniversario de Sonic, Yuji tenía claro que los programadores no podían renunciar a la velocidad.
Naka lo explicaba así al recordar el origen del proyecto:
"Me gustan las cosas rápidas y pensé que sería interesante crear un juego en el que, cuanto más hábil te volvieras, menos tiempo necesitaras para completar un nivel".
"Los videojuegos de aquella época no tenían sistemas para guardar las partidas, así que cada vez que jugabas tenías que empezar desde el principio. Hoy en día puedes retomar un juego desde donde lo dejaste, pero entonces era necesario comenzar de cero".
"Como consecuencia, los jugadores repetían el primer nivel una y otra vez, hasta que terminaban dominándolo. Por eso pensamos que estaría bien aprovechar esa habilidad para que pudieran completar los niveles cada vez más rápido. Esa es la idea que dio origen a la velocidad de Sonic. También creímos que esta característica ayudaría a diferenciar a Sonic de Mario".
Un rival para Mario. Sega buscaba plantarle cara al dominio de Nintendo y su NES. El equipo que acabaría convirtiéndose en el Sonic Team quería crear un juego de acción frenético basado en la inercia y la velocidad. Ahora puede parecer algo corriente, pero a comienzos de los 90 no había nada parecido.
Recorrer el Green Hill Zone, sobre todo los míticos loopings, exigía simular continuamente las trayectorias mediante fórmulas trigonométricas. Calcular senos y cosenos en tiempo real habría saturado el procesador de la Mega Drive, con sus correspondientes tirones. Así que el equipo de Naka diseñó un motor a medida para superar esas limitaciones.
La solución. Esta consistía en guardar en el cartucho una especie de catálogo con los resultados listos de antemano. En vez de repetir operaciones complejas a cada momento, el motor de Sonic consultaba una tabla para encontrar el valor de cada ángulo y determinar cómo debía afectar al movimiento. Eran las llamadas tablas de consulta o "lookup tables".
Además de las tablas, los programadores del Sonic Team diseñaron otras soluciones ingeniosas para superar las limitaciones de la máquina:
- Dos sensores bajo los pies: detectaban la distancia al suelo y calculaban la inclinación de las pendientes para adaptar el movimiento de Sonic.
- Velocidad e impulso: la física permitía a Sonic aprovechar su velocidad para recorrer pendientes y superar los famosos loopings.
- Movimiento y animación independientes: la posición se actualizaba 60 veces por segundo (en NTSC, en Europa jugábamos con los 50 Hz de la versión PAL). Y los sprites cambiaban según la velocidad del personaje.
- Código optimizado: Naka utilizó la técnica loop unrolling para eliminar comprobaciones repetitivas y ahorrar ciclos del procesador Motorola 68000.
- Recursos concentrados en pantalla: los enemigos y objetos fuera de cámara dejaban de procesarse para reducir la carga del sistema.
- El mito del Blast Processing: Sega convirtió esa fluidez en un reclamo publicitario, aunque la rapidez de Sonic se debía principalmente a la optimización del código, no a un componente secreto.
Sega y Sonic Team lograron un juego que, a día de hoy, sigue maravillando por lo veloz que va, incluso en la Mega Drive, una máquina de hace 36 años. Aún recuerdo aquella primera vez que metí el cartucho en la consola, cargué el nivel Green Hill y me maravillé porque Sonic iba mucho más rápido que mi propia vista. No he vuelto a tener esa sensación de velocidad con ningún otro juego.
La optimización es historia. Yuji Naka y Sega demostraron que el ingenio y la optimización terminan rompiendo las barreras de la máquina. Es una lección que no parece haber cuajado lo suficiente, porque los desarrolladores de hoy en día tienden a crear auténticos monstruos con sus juegos. Gigas de recursos, requerimientos altísimos de hardware... Y luego tenemos consolas que son cada vez más caras solo para dar cobertura a todas esas necesidades.
La ironía de la vida parece que ha dejado a Nintendo como auténtica heredera de toda aquella optimización: los juegos de la Switch son un monumento a la optimización. Porque Sonic no necesitó una consola más potente para correr más rápido: requirió programadores que supieran aprovechar hasta el último ciclo del procesador. Treinta y cinco años después, no sería mala idea recuperar aquella filosofía.

articles.title: La psicología dice que las personas que dejan el móvil boca abajo no es para ocultar nada; en realidad, es una táctica para evitar distracciones
articles.text:
Una comida, dos personas. Antes de que llegue la primera ración, uno de los comensales gira su teléfono y lo deja sobre el mantel con la pantalla hacia abajo. Hay quien lo interpreta como desconfianza, pero la explicación es otra: quiere librarse de las notificaciones y las llamadas entrantes y de la presión constante de estar disponible en todo momento. Al fin y al cabo, es solo una interpretación, y no se apoya en ningún experimento científico que estudie sus motivaciones.
Lo que sí han estudiado los experimentos es el efecto de tener el móvil a la vista.
En la Universidad de Essex, Andrew Przybylski y Netta Weinstein realizaron un experimento con parejas de desconocidos que hablaban entre ellos durante diez minutos con un teléfono o un cuaderno sobre una mesa cercana.
En su trabajo, publicado en el Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, el teléfono se asoció con una menor cercanía y una conversación de menor calidad y, en un segundo experimento, con una menor confianza y empatía, aunque solo cuando hablaban de algo personal: con un tema trivial no hubo diferencias. Después, otro grupo de científicos, ya fuera del Reino Unido, llevó la comparación a conversaciones reales.
Shalini Misra, de Virginia Tech, observó 100 conversaciones reales entre dos personas en entornos informales. Aquellas que tuvieron lugar sin ningún dispositivo a la vista salieron mejor valoradas. “En presencia de un dispositivo móvil hay menos contacto visual”, resumía la investigadora.
Matt Johnson, profesor en la Hult International Business School, recopiló varios de estos trabajos en su artículo ‘The Psychology of the Face-Down Phone’ (la psicología del móvil boca abajo). Según los experimentos que recoge, no hace falta usar el aparato para que afecte a la atención, y cuanto más difícil es la tarea, más pronunciado es el efecto.
También repasa los experimentos de Elizabeth Dunn (Universidad de Columbia Británica): en grupos de tres a cinco personas sentadas en una cafetería, quienes tenían el teléfono sobre la mesa (¡cualquiera podría hacer esto!) se sintieron más distraídos y disfrutaron mucho menos del encuentro.
¿Y qué ocurre con la práctica de poner el móvil boca abajo?
El experimento más conocido sobre el tema es el de “pérdida cognitiva” (“brain drain”) de Adrian Ward y sus colegas de la Universidad de Texas en Austin, en el que 520 estudiantes realizaron una serie de pruebas de memoria y razonamiento. El móvil se situaba o en otra habitación, o en el bolsillo o el bolso de los participantes, o sobre la mesa, donde se les indicaba que lo pusieran boca abajo en un sitio marcado del escritorio.
Fueron las personas que lo dejaron sobre la mesa las que obtuvieron los peores resultados en las pruebas. Según el trabajo, publicado en 2017, la mera presencia del propio smartphone reduce la capacidad cognitiva disponible, aunque no se use ni se piense en él.
Quienes lo dejaron en otra habitación obtuvieron los mejores resultados, mientras que los del bolsillo o del bolso obtuvieron resultados intermedios. Girar el móvil lo quita de la vista, pero el cacharro sigue ahí. En un segundo experimento del mismo trabajo, el efecto se mantuvo con el teléfono apagado del todo, algo que se repasaba en mayo de 2026.
¿Son suficientes las pruebas?
No del todo. Una réplica directa del experimento hecha en la Universidad de Western Ontario, publicada en Acta Psychologica en octubre de 2022, encontró que el efecto no se repetía: no hubo diferencias entre tener el móvil sobre la mesa, en el bolsillo o fuera.
Sin embargo, un equipo de la Universidad de Augsburgo juntó 22 estudios en un metaanálisis publicado en Behavioral Sciences en septiembre de 2023 y sí encontró el efecto, sobre todo en pruebas de memoria y atención, más débil en tareas sencillas y más fuerte en los estudios hechos en Asia que en los de Europa y Norteamérica.
Además, se aconseja precaución al sacar conclusiones sobre quien deja el móvil boca abajo, porque puede hacerlo por razones muy variadas: educación, costumbre o pura comodidad.
Cómo hacer que el gesto sirva para algo más
La forma más sencilla de que girar el teléfono tenga sentido es que lo silencie. Esta opción está disponible en los teléfonos Pixel de Google, en la función Silenciar al girar, que llegó a los Pixel 2 en noviembre de 2019 con una actualización de Bienestar digital y activaba el modo No molestar al poner el teléfono boca abajo.
Los propietarios de iPhone no tienen esta función incorporada, pero los modos de Concentración se pueden activar a mano o programar para que se enciendan solos a una hora concreta. Esto último es útil si la comida o la reunión tiene una hora fija.
Por último, no existe ningún ajuste, ni en iPhone ni en Android, que elimine la distracción de tener el móvil cerca durante una comida o una reunión. En el experimento de la Universidad de Texas en Austin, lo que mejor funcionó fue dejar el teléfono en otra habitación; la réplica de Western Ontario no encontró esa diferencia, y el metaanálisis de Augsburgo sí encontró el efecto, sobre todo en memoria y atención.

articles.title: Deux palettes de cartes graphiques Nvidia ont disparu : la cargaison valait 440 000 euros
articles.text:
Où sont passées deux palettes remplies de cartes graphiques haut de gamme, des RTX 5090 de Nvidia ? Voici la question que se pose le distributeur brésilien Oderço, dont la cargaison semble avoir été perdue après son arrivée dans un aéroport. Une affaire pas banale : la marchandise est évaluée à 2,5 millions de réais brésilien, soit près de 440 000 euros de prix de revient. C’est d’autant plus troublant que les cartes graphiques comme celle-ci sont très recherchées : elles permettent de faire fonctionner des IA, ou bien de miner des cryptomonnaies.
Une soixantaine de RTX 5090 disparaissent dans un aéroport au Brésil
Ce 16 octobre, le distributeur brésilien d’informatique Oderço a publié une vidéo sur ses réseaux sociaux. Il y révèle l’affaire de la disparition de ces cartes graphiques. Au total, une soixantaine de cartes graphiques auraient disparu, si l’on en croit les estimations de Toms’s Hardware. Réparties sur deux palettes, ces GeForce RTX 5090 sont fabriquées par Zodiac, avec plusieurs versions commercialisées.
Selon Oderço, les deux palettes sont bien arrivées au terminal de fret de Guarulhos, l’un des principaux aéroports d’Amérique latine, situé près de São Paulo. Mais ensuite, plus rien : lors des étapes suivantes de la chaîne logistiques, plus aucune nouvelle de ces palettes. Le distributeur n’a pas indiqué quand est-ce que cette perte a été constatée. Une surprise de taille pour Oderço : son président Oderço Matos l’affirme, jamais une marchandise n’a disparu en 38 ans d’activité.
Dans sa vidéo, Oderço Matos demande des explications à GRU Airport, à l’administration fiscale brésilienne ainsi qu’à la police fédérale : « J’aimerais savoir où elles sont. Deux palettes ne disparaissent pas toutes seules dans un aéroport international. » De son côté, GRU Airport reconnaît l’incident et indique avoir engagé les démarches nécessaires depuis. L’entreprise qui exploite cet aéroport de Guarulhos précise avoir prévenu les autorités et qu’une procédure d’indemnisation a été enclenchée. Mais pour le moment, on ignore ce qui a pu arriver à cette marchandise de cartes graphiques : erreur de manutention, problème douanier, vol. Toutes les hypothèses restent possibles.
Pourquoi la disparition de ces cartes graphiques est sensible
Lancée en janvier 2025, la RTX 5090 est la carte graphique grand public la plus puissante de Nvidia. Avec ses 32 Go de mémoire en GDDR7, elle est très recherchée chez les joueurs PC, puisqu’elle permet de faire fonctionner n’importe quel jeu avec les meilleurs paramètres graphiques. Problème, elle est parfois difficile à trouver et surtout, elle est chère. En France, sa Founders Edition avait été lancée il y a près de deux ans à 2 349 euros. Comptez plutôt… 6 500 euros en ce moment, comme l’a fait remarquer Cowcotland.
Une envolée des prix qui n’est peut-être pas terminée. Nvidia l’a reconnu après des rumeurs de l’arrêt de la production, l’entreprise a des problèmes d’approvisionnement. Des problèmes qui sont liées au fait que les fabricants se concentrent sur des puces faites pour faire fonctionner des IA. Elle privilégient ces modèles à plusieurs dizaines de milliers d’euros qui ne sont pas destinés au grand public, dont Nvidia. Si ces deux palettes ont été volées, les voleurs pourront revendre ces cartes graphiques, qui pourront être utilisées pour faire fonctionner quelques modèles d’IA, ou bien miner des cryptomonnaies.

articles.title: Elon Musk promises to give every child in America a free SpaceX share next year
articles.text:
What just happened? Elon Musk makes a lot of big promises, not all of which come to pass, but it's hard to see how he'll renege on this one. The world's richest person says he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America next year, adding that "this will be the first of many."
Musk explained the plan on his X platform. He didn't elaborate, so we don't know details such as what ages will qualify for a free share, how he intends to distribute them, and exactly when the giveaway will take place in 2027.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 19, 2026
It's estimated that Musk would be required to give a share to around 72 million people under the age of 18. SpaceX's share price is currently $146, so that would represent stock worth about $10.5 billion.
Musk certainly has plenty of SpaceX shares to hand out. The company's SEC filing in August showed he owned 6.42 billion shares as of June 30, including shares held in trusts for which he acts as trustee, restricted stock, and shares that could be issued upon exercising options.
Musk's announcement comes soon after Anthropic, xAI's rival, said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good." The company later said that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion. Anthropic's IPO could value the firm at more than $1 trillion
Musk responded to the Anthropic announcement by writing "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."
The moves also echo the thinking behind Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for children that give eligible US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 a $1,000 government-funded head start. Families, employers, and other donors can add money, which is invested in funds tracking US stocks to help children build wealth as they grow up.
There's already a SpaceX connection to the program. The company's chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, has pledged more than $320 million of her own SpaceX stock to help fund Trump Accounts for over two million children.

articles.title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON.
Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains.
With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing.
With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary.
In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting.
What’s new in Pegasus 1.5
Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions:
- Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated.
- Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen.
- On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response.
- Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2.
Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including:
- Video-to-text generation: Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content.
- Granular visual comprehension: Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames.
- Temporal grounding: Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos.
- Multimodal understanding: Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis.
- Multilingual support: Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese.
How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock
Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated.
| Setting | Value | 
| Model ID | twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0 | 
| AWS Region | US West (Oregon), us-west-2 | 
| Inference | On-demand | 
| APIs | InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream | 
Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field:
| Analysis mode | analysisMode | You send | You get back | 
| General | general (default) | A text prompt in inputPrompt | A text answer in message, or JSON when you supply a schema | 
| Time-based metadata | time_based_metadata | Segment definitions in responseFormat | A segments list with start and end times and the fields you asked for | 
You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location (s3Location) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string (base64String) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips.
To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID.
Getting started with Pegasus 1.5
The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure you have:
- An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.
- Python 3.10 or later, with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) installed.
- AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
- Model access enabled for TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in the Amazon Bedrock console.
- Videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, or short clips you can send inline.
The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5.
Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission.
Send your first request
Install Boto3:
The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL.
The response carries the answer in message, the token counts in input_tokens and output_tokens, and the reason generation ended in stopReason. A stopReason of length means the answer reached maxOutputTokens before it finished, so check it before you rely on the output:
Request fields for general mode:
| Field | Required | Description | 
| inputPrompt | Yes | The question or instruction about the video | 
| mediaSource.s3Location.uri | One video source is required | S3 URI of the video | 
| mediaSource.s3Location.bucketOwner | With uri | AWS account ID that owns the bucket | 
| mediaSource.base64String | One video source is required | Base64-encoded video, up to 25 MB | 
| temperature | No | Randomness of the output, from 0 to 1. Default 0.2 | 
| maxOutputTokens | No | Maximum tokens to generate, from 512 to 98,304 | 
| responseFormat | No | A JSON Schema the answer must follow | 
| analysisMode | No | general (default) or time_based_metadata | 
For a short clip, you can send the video inline instead of from S3:
Note that the preceding example uses the optional includeMetering attribute. includeMetering: True makes Pegasus 1.5 add two billing-usage fields to the non-streaming response: outputTokenCount and inputVideoSecond (the analyzed video’s duration in seconds).
Stream the response
For interactive applications, InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer in chunks as it’s generated. Each chunk carries the next piece of text in message:
Return structured JSON
In general mode, you can constrain the answer to a JSON Schema so downstream code can parse it directly. Set responseFormat.type to json_schema and put the schema under jsonSchema. The answer arrives in message as a JSON string:
Video segmentation: Turning video into structured data
Time-based metadata generation is where Pegasus 1.5 differs most from earlier versions. Instead of a prompt, you send one or more segment definitions, and the model returns every segment of the video that matches each one.
Set analysisMode to time_based_metadata and responseFormat.type to segment_definitions. The definitions take the place of inputPrompt, so leave that field out. Each definition has:
- id: a name for the definition, returned on every segment it matches.
- description: what a matching segment looks like.
- fields: the values to extract for each segment, each with a name, a type (string, boolean, number, integer, array, or timestamp), and a description.
The following example identifies each editorial section in a news broadcast and returns a title, summary, and key topics for each one:
The previous sample code when tested against a sports clip may produce an output like the following sample.
Each segment carries start_sec, end_sec, and the fields you defined. segmentTimeFormat controls how the times are written: seconds returns numbers you can do arithmetic on, while hh:mm:ss and hh:mm:ss.fff return readable timestamps as strings. The response also includes a definition_errors list, which is empty when every definition was processed.
A single request can include multiple segment definitions, for example one for editorial sections and another for on-screen brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns the matches for all of them in one segments list, and tags each segment with _definition_id so you can tell them apart. The following example adds a second definition to the previous request and groups the results:
Because the schema is defined once, the same definitions can be applied across an entire video library, producing consistent metadata for every asset.
Multimodal prompting: Adding visual context to your queries
Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe.
For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search.
Reference images attach differently depending on the mode. In general mode, put them in promptV2.mediaSources, alongside the question in promptV2.inputText. In segmentation mode (analysisMode: time_based_metadata), attach them to the mediaSources of each segment definition inside responseFormat.segmentDefinitions. A definition can then match a visual reference as well as a text description. Each image needs a name, a media_type of image, and exactly one source: either an inline base64String or an s3Location with uri and bucketOwner. A single request can carry up to 30 reference images.
A general-mode request asks the model about an object shown in a reference image. The following sample payload and response provide an example in general mode.
In segmentation mode, the reference image lives inside the definition, so Pegasus returns only the segments where that product appears. The following sample payload and response provide an example in segmentation mode.
Monitoring usage
Pegasus 1.5 publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace under its model ID, including Invocations, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, and InvocationClientErrors. Use them to track volume and latency. Pair them with application inference profiles when you need usage broken down by application.
Use cases
Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video:
- News and broadcast archives: Teams can define editorial segments, topics, and speaker changes once, then catalog years of footage that was previously searchable only by transcript keywords.
- Sports broadcasters and leagues: Detect plays, scoring events, and other key moments across full-length game footage, speeding up highlight production.
- Streaming applications: Scene-level metadata supports moment-based recommendations, contextual ad placement, and segment-level brand safety review.
In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model.
Input requirements
Pegasus 1.5 supports the following video specifications:
- Duration: Up to 2 hours.
- File size: Up to 2 GB from Amazon S3, or up to 25 MB as a base64 string.
- Resolution: 360×360 to 5184×2160.
- Aspect ratio: Between 1:1 and 2.4:1, or their inverses.
- Formats: FFmpeg-supported formats.
Now available
TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is available today on Amazon Bedrock in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Check the full Region list for future updates, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for pricing information. Pegasus 1.5 is billed through AWS Marketplace, so its charges appear on your AWS bill and in AWS Cost Explorer under TwelveLabs rather than Amazon Bedrock.
To get started:

We’re excited to see what you build with TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: Avec sa future Koala, Fiat veut sa part de la 2 CV électrique à 15 000 €
articles.text:
Pendant le Mondial de l’Auto de Paris 2026, Citroën a attiré tous les regards avec le concept de sa future 2 CV électrique. Le genre de succès que d’autres marques aimeraient également avoir, y compris au sein du groupe Stellantis. C’est ainsi que Fiat préparerait sa jumelle de la « deuche ». Arnaud Belloni, directeur général de Fiat depuis le 1er septembre 2026, l’a confirmé pendant le salon dans des propos rapportés par le magazine britannique Autocar ce 19 octobre : « Nous préparons une petite voiture qui sera basée sur la 2 CV ».
Les deux modèles partageront la nouvelle plateforme de Stellantis, conçue pour la catégorie européenne E-Car qui doit encore voir le jour. Le nom du modèle n’est pas arrêté, mais Fiat a déposé la marque Koala. « Nous avons un Koala, un Panda et un Grizzly », a résumé Arnaud Belloni, dans la lignée des noms d’animaux (citadine Grande Panda et SUV Grizzly).
La petite Fiat est déjà aussi avancée que la 2 CV
La future Fiat doit devenir l’alternative électrique à la Panda thermique, rebaptisée Pandina. Disponible en Europe depuis près de quinze ans, elle reste la voiture la plus vendue en Italie. Fiat promet d’ailleurs de garder une petite voiture essence abordable au catalogue. Gaetano Thorel, patron de Fiat en Europe, disait plus tôt cette année chercher une solution multi-énergie.
François Leboine, directeur du design de Fiat, assure que le modèle est « aussi prêt que la 2 CV », mais que ce n’était « pas le bon moment » pour le montrer. Selon lui, Fiat ne voulait pas voler la vedette à Citroën sur son salon national.
Le style pourrait reprendre des idées d’un concours organisé cette année auprès d’étudiants italiens. Le public a voté pour l’Ippo, une citadine très carrée qui rappelle les Panda d’antan et d’aujourd’hui. En revanche, la voiture ne jouera pas la carte du pur néorétro comme la 2 CV. Arnaud Belloni parle d’une « approche très différente ». Grosso modo, évoquer le passé sans le ressusciter trait pour trait.
Une voiture taillée pour une règle pas encore votée
Fiat et Citroën misent sur la future réglementation E-Car, une catégorie réservée aux petites électriques de moins de 4,2 mètres. Stellantis et Renault la réclamaient depuis l’été 2025, et la Commission européenne l’a proposée le 16 décembre 2025 dans son paquet automobile, sous le nom de « petites voitures abordables ». Les constructeurs espèrent obtenir des règles allégées pour ces modèles, notamment sur les aides à la conduite imposées par le règlement GSR2, afin de faire baisser les prix.
La catégorie s’inspire des « kei cars » japonaises. Là-bas, ces mini-voitures limitées à 3,4 mètres et moins taxées représentent près de 40 % des ventes de voitures neuves. La version européenne serait bien plus permissive. Avec une limite de 4,2 mètres, même une Renault 5 de 3,9 mètres entrerait dans les clous.
Sauf que le texte n’est pas encore adopté par le Parlement européen et les États membres. Le calendrier laisse de la marge, puisque la 2 CV de série n’est attendue qu’à la fin de 2028.
Fiat n’a donné ni prix, ni autonomie, ni date. Le seul repère vient de Citroën, qui vise environ 15 000 euros pour sa 2 CV de 3,76 mètres, soit environ 5 000 euros de moins que l’ë-C3, affichée à partir de 19 990 euros hors aides. Pour mémoire, Fiat promettait déjà en 2023 de rejoindre le club des électriques à moins de 25 000 euros.

articles.title: Bristol’s Siloton wins €9.98 million Innovate UK contract to develop its handheld eye imaging system | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Siloton, a Bristol-based MedTech startup specialising in miniaturised optical technology for medical imaging, has been awarded a €9.98 million (£8.4 million) contract to accelerate development of its handheld eye imaging system, which makes detecting and monitoring retinal diseases more accessible to patients.
Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), awarded the contract through its Contracts for Innovation: Quantum Missions Primer initiative. The programme helps public sector organisations solve some of their most complex challenges by running competitive funding opportunities to develop new technologies.
Alasdair Price, CEO of Siloton, said, “Winning this Innovate UK contract allows us to accelerate the development of our systems, explore manufacturing and assembly in the UK, and help a groundbreaking new technology be adopted by the NHS more quickly.
“Many early-stage companies struggle to get beyond the well-known ‘valley of death’ in developing new products – particularly in healthcare – but this will support us through that crucial phase, bringing the Siloton system closer to being in patients’ hands and building a technology that can be used worldwide.”
Siloton was founded in April 2020 in Bristol, UK and is an alumnus of the Quantum Technologies Enterprise Centre (QTEC) incubator programme. The company is on a mission to ensure people with eye disease can receive sight-saving eye scans wherever and whenever they need them.
The company says it specialises in miniaturised optical technology for medical imaging, using photonic chips and OCT to detect and monitor major diseases. Its products are built around Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), a technique widely used to detect and monitor some of the world’s most prevalent diseases, including age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma. It can also detect conditions such as multiple sclerosis, diabetes, and certain types of cancer.
OCT uses light to create detailed images of the inside of the eye, helping clinicians identify a range of health conditions and monitor their progress over time, Siloton explains.
However, according to the company, OCT systems are confined to specialist environments because the underlying optical hardware is large and fragile, limiting access.
Siloton claims that its photonic chip technology compresses a tabletop’s worth of heavy, expensive, and fragile components, such as mirrors, lenses, and fibre-optics, onto a single piece of material smaller than a coin. The UK startup notes that, like the chips that power phones, these are mass-manufacturable and can be used anywhere on or off planet Earth.
The company also notes that its GiraffeOCT is designed as an easy-to-use, binocular-style system that makes diagnosing and monitoring a range of treatable retinal diseases more affordable and accessible.
The company’s photonic chips are instrumental in delivering OCT at scale and power its new generation of portable eye scanners. Its core focus is on developing a complete ophthalmic OCT system for use in the clinic, community, and home.
The UK startup also highlighted that since 2025, it has started to make its chip technology available for use in other market segments through its OCT-Chip Development Kits.
The contract, delivered over two years, will help Siloton accelerate the design of the in-clinic and at-home versions of its GiraffeOCT optical coherence tomography (OCT) device, as well as complete trials on both systems. The startup expects the funding could cut the development process by up to two years.
Siloton will work with Sunderland Specialist Eye Hospital on clinical trials over the course of the contract for its in-clinic device, giving patients across the North East and North Cumbria access to the technology during its development. York Health Economics Consortium will also use this data to refine its cost-saving estimates for the NHS.
The startup expects the project to create several high-skilled jobs over the next two years, with the Siloton team expected to grow to 16 by August 2028. The roles will support the miniaturisation of the systems’ electronics, product development, and manufacturing plans across specialisms including photonics, electronics, and software development.
It plans to raise further investment following the contract win, strengthening its cash position for the next few years and supporting the development of its second-generation CheetahOCT device, designed to measure different retinal layers and expand the number of conditions it can detect.
“Developing the in‑clinic and at‑home versions of the system will help the government meet its ambitions of moving care into the community and bringing quantum technologies into the NHS. The contract will also allow us to expand our technology to cover a wider range of diseases, integrate our second‑generation BlueJay chip – the same architecture used in our system for astronauts – and build out the cloud platform that underpins the service,” added Price.
In August 2024, the company secured €1.02 million (£860k) in funding, and in 2022 announced the first closing of its investment round, totalling €558.4k (£470k). It is supported by key players in the ophthalmology space, including Moorfields Eye Hospital and the Macular Society. Its customers include the European Space Agency, which needs a long-term solution to monitor eye problems that astronauts frequently develop while in space.

articles.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
The only way to solve this problem is for a federal and state laws to make it illegal to ever pay a ransom. No exceptions.
Nah, just let Elon and the rest of the Tech Geniuses to solve the problem.
Can’t tell if you’re being serious or not.
Either way, threat intelligence organizations already exist.

articles.title: Tenstorrent secures $1.5 billion USD at $6.2-billion valuation to challenge GPU dominance
articles.text:
Canadian-founded, United States (US)-based AI infrastructure company Tenstorrent announced today that it has closed $1.5 billion USD ($2.1 billion CAD) in Series E funding to fuel its global expansion plans.
The equity round, which was led by new US investors Trace Capital and Innovation X, gives Tenstorrent a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion USD (almost $8.8 billion CAD), more than twice the $2.6 billion USD mark that Tenstorrent was valued at when the company closed its nearly $700-million USD Series D in late 2024. Since then, Tenstorrent has begun shipping its Galaxy servers commercially.
“The future of compute is open, scalable, and owned by the people building on it.”
Jim Keller, Tenstorrent
Tenstorrent plans to use this capital to fund volume manufacturing of those Galaxy servers, the development of next-generation hardware and intellectual property (IP), and hiring, as it looks to compete with Nvidia and other established AI chipmakers and challenge traditional graphics processing unit (GPU) dominance in AI with an open-source approach it claims is cheaper, more scalable, and easier to customize.
“We built one architecture and sell it at every size,” Tenstorrent CEO Jim Keller said in a statement. “The future of compute is open, scalable, and owned by the people building on it.”
A Tenstorrent spokesperson told BetaKit over email that Canadian investors also participated in the round, but declined to share specific names. Tenstorrent’s existing Canadian backers include Export Development Canada, Toronto’s Georgian, and the Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan. Montréal-based early Tenstorrent investor Real Ventures sold its stake last year, returning the entirety of its $88-million third fund.
The Tenstorrent spokesperson also declined to share any more details regarding the structure of its Series E, including whether it involved any secondary capital, or disclose Tenstorrent’s total funding to date.
RELATED: US chip giant AMD to acquire Taalas
Founded in 2016 in Toronto by former AMD employees Ljubisa Bajic (who went on to build Taalas, which AMD recently agreed to acquire), Ivan Hamer, and Milos Trajkovic, Tenstorrent is developing what the company describes as “a general-purpose AI platform” for running large language models, video models, and image models.
The firm builds and sells AI compute “at every level,” from single cards and workstations to racks and superclusters, providing the hardware necessary for AI training and inference. Tenstorrent’s customers include chip designers, sovereign infrastructure providers, and inference platforms. The company also licenses its AI and RISC-V IP to clients who want to own and customize their silicon, including LG and Samsung.
Tenstorrent is betting that the future of AI inference is open-source, and views its software as a differentiator compared to competitors. “We built a scalable, open-source software stack because we believe customers want flexibility and control,” the Tenstorrent spokesperson said, adding that, “AI models keep changing, so hardware has to run whatever comes next.”
Tenstorrent’s clients and partners include FinTech firm Virtu Financial, data centre provider Equinix, and AI companies like ai& and Smallest.ai.
Keller, a renowned chip designer who also previously worked at AMD as well as Apple, Intel, and Tesla, took over for Bajic as Tenstorrent CEO in 2021. Tenstorrent quietly relocated from Canada to the US in 2023, moving its headquarters from Toronto to Santa Clara, California, to raise more money from American investors and prepare for an eventual initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq or New York Stock Exchange.
RELATED: AI chipmaker Tenstorrent closes nearly $700-million USD Series D at $2.6-billion valuation
Despite this, Tenstorrent has retained a strong presence in Canada; Toronto remains its largest office, housing 200 of its 1,000 employees. The company also still makes a number of its parts at Vexos Canada’s Markham site.
This summer, The Information and Bloomberg reported that Tenstorrent has drawn takeover interest from larger US chipmakers Intel (Keller’s previous employer) and Qualcomm. While Keller told EE Times that he has met with the CEOs of both firms to pitch them on Tenstorrent’s hardware IP, he said an IPO remained the company’s target at that time.
The Tenstorrent spokesperson declined to comment on those reports, the status of those discussions, or the company’s IPO ambitions.
Last year, Tenstorrent made an acquisition of its own, snapping up Blue Cheetah Analog Design to bolster its in-house chip design capabilities, reportedly explored another fundraise, and shed 7.5 percent of its workforce amid a shift from enterprise to developer sales.
UPDATE (10/19/26): This story has been updated to note that Real Ventures sold its stake in Tenstorrent last year.
Feature image courtesy Tenstorrent.

articles.title: "Hochspekulative Anlagen": Sparkassen starten Kryptohandel – und warnen Kunden davor
articles.text:
Die Sparkassen steigen in das Geschäft mit Kryptoanlagen wie Bitcoin und Ethereum ein. Ab sofort können die ersten Kunden Kryptowährungen über die bestehende Sparkassen-App handeln, wie der Deutsche Sparkassen- und Giroverband (DSGV) der Nachrichtenagentur dpa mitteilte. Das Angebot stehe zum Start bei den ersten teilnehmenden Sparkassen zur Verfügung, pro Monat sollen 30 bis 40 weitere Häuser dazukommen.
Bitcoin-Handel bei der Sparkasse
Vorgesehen sind zunächst Kryptowährungen wie Bitcoin, Ethereum, Ripple, Solana und Polygon, so der DSGV. „Das Angebot richtet sich an Kundinnen und Kunden, die eigenständig Kryptowährungen kaufen, verkaufen und verwahren möchten. Eine Beratung oder aktive Bewerbung durch die Sparkassen in der Breite ist nicht vorgesehen.“ Einen einheitlichen bundesweiten Starttermin für das Angebot, das vom Sparkassen-Wertpapieranbieter Dekabank bereitgestellt wird, gebe es nicht.
„Wann eine Sparkasse startet, entscheidet sie selbst“, sagte Joachim Schmalzl, Geschäftsführendes Vorstandsmitglied des DSGV, der dpa. „Das Interesse in der Gruppe ist groß, und Woche für Woche werden weitere Institute hinzukommen. Im ersten Halbjahr 2027 wollen wir bereits einen großen Teil der interessierten Sparkassen angebunden haben.“
Kryptowährungen beliebt, aber riskant
    „Wir haben sehr genau abgewogen, ob und wie ein Krypto-Angebot zu uns passt.“
Kryptowährungen sind gerade bei jungen Menschen beliebt. Den Handel mit Bitcoin und Co. bieten Smartphone-Banken wie N26, Trade Republic und Revolut seit geraumer Zeit an, zuletzt stiegen auch Volksbanken in das Geschäft ein. Bei den Sparkassen gab es lange Bedenken, da Kryptowährungen stark schwanken und als riskant gelten. Auch wenn manche Kryptowährungen langfristig stark zugelegt haben: Kritiker warnen immer wieder vor Spekulationsblasen.
„Wir haben sehr genau abgewogen, ob und wie ein Krypto-Angebot zu uns passt“, sagte Schmalzl. Entscheidend sei die Nachfrage der Kunden gewesen und dass es einen verlässlichen europäischen Rechtsrahmen gebe. Ziel des Angebots ist laut DSGV, Kundinnen und Kunden, die sich bewusst für Krypto entscheiden, einen Zugang im regulierten Umfeld zu ermöglichen. Verwahrt werden die Kryptowerte durch die Dekabank in Kooperation mit der Börse Stuttgart.
„Kryptowährungen bleiben aus Sicht der Sparkassen hochspekulative Anlagen“, betont der DSGV. Kunden würden ausdrücklich „auf starke Kursschwankungen und das Risiko eines Totalverlusts“ hingewiesen. Für die breite langfristige Vermögensbildung stünden weiterhin Wertpapieranlagen, Sparpläne und Beratung im Vordergrund.

articles.title: Apple teases MacBook Pro event next week
articles.text:
Apple has sent invites to a second product launch this month, and it’s scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles.
Apple teases MacBook Pro event next week
Following Apple’s smart home-focused launch earlier in the month, Apple is hosting another product event soon.
At the event, Apple is set to announce new Macs and a refreshed iPad Mini, according to Bloomberg. The big announcement is expected to be a new MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen that’s also lighter and has an iPhone-like Dynamic Island. But Apple is also planning on revealing a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a new iMac with the M6 chip, which was recently introduced with the Mac Mini. Apple’s updated iPad Mini will apparently finally get an OLED screen as well and put the selfie cam on the landscape edge.
“Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” Apple’s SVP Marketing Greg Joswiak says in a teaser on X.
This second October launch follows Apple’s smart home-focused “Welcome home” event on October 13th, which included the new HomeView smart home hub, an updated Apple TV 4K and Siri Remote, and a second-generation HomePod Mini.

articles.title: 7 plazas, 775 CV, 100% eléctrico y que carga casi igual de rápido que un gasolina: así es el BYD Atto 8
articles.text:
BYD sigue sumando modelos a su catálogo europeo, y esta vez lo hace con el BYD Atto 8, un SUV 100% eléctrico que presume de un tamaño increíble y una velocidad de carga espectacular, a la espera, eso sí, de que la red de cargadores permita esa potencia de carga.
Sobre el papel, es un SUV todocaminos como otros que hemos visto, pero bajo el capó esconde dos motorizaciones eléctricas en versiones de 462 y 775 CV, batería de 115 kWh y hasta 653 kilómetros de autonomía, unas cifras impresionantes si tenemos en cuenta su tamaño y su peso.
Quizás la más impresionante de estas dos versiones es la BYD Atto 8 Excellence AWD, que monta dos motores eléctricos y ofrece un sistema de tracción total. Es la versión que mencionaba anteriormente de más de 700 CV, lo que permite a este Atto 8 acelerar de 0 a 100 km/h en tan solo 4,6 segundos, aunque pierde autonomía respecto a la versión más comedida de 462 CV. En este sentido, mientras que esta última ofrece hasta 653 km de autonomía por carga, la versión Excellence se queda en los 602, que tampoco está nada mal.
BYD Atto 8: carga al 97% en menos de 10 minutos
Pero en este caso poco importan unos kilómetros más de autonomía, puesto que el mayor atractivo de este BYD Atto 8 es su potencia de carga. Utilizando el sistema de Flash Charging de la compañía, junto a su tecnología de baterías, permite cargar al 97% en tan solo 9 minutos. Algo sencillamente impresionante. Y si lo quiere más rápido, el BYD carga del 10% al 70% en tan solo 5 minutos.
Lógicamente, esta potencia de carga no se consigue con los cargadores normales, puesto que requiere su propia infraestructura. Y en específico, al sistema de carga Flash Charging de BYD. La compañía busca llenar el continente de este sistema de carga, y tiene planeado poner más de 3000 de estas estaciones por toda Europa, incluyendo 300 de ellas solo en España, aunque lógicamente esto llevará un tiempo.
Sobre su disponibilidad y precios, se espera que el BYD Atto 8 llegue a España en algún momento del primer trimestre del 2027. Aunque no se ha confirmado la fecha exacta, así como tampoco el precio de las dos versiones disponibles, que se conocerán conforme se vaya acercando su fecha de comercialización.

articles.title: Voici les grandes étapes du Starship que le calendrier de la NASA fixe à SpaceX
articles.text:
À quoi faut-il s’attendre pour le programme spatial lunaire de la NASA et, plus particulièrement, pour tout ce qui est prévu du côté de SpaceX dans le cadre des missions Artémis ? L’agence spatiale américaine a fait un point à l’occasion du Congrès international d’astronautique (IAC), qui se tenait à Antalya, en Turquie, du 5 au 9 octobre 2026.
Un point d’autant plus nécessaire que les contours du programme Artémis ont évolué au cours des derniers mois. Steve Creech, qui dirige à la NASA le programme des atterrisseurs lunaires habités (HLS, pour Human Landing System), a présenté un calendrier actualisé pour le Starship, avec des jalons attendus trimestre par trimestre.
L’actuel planning découle du remaniement annoncé le 27 février 2026 par Jared Isaacman, administrateur de la NASA. Artémis III devait être le premier alunissage habité depuis Apollo 17, en 1972. Elle est devenue une mission d’essais en orbite autour de la Terre, avec quatre astronautes à bord, dont un Européen.
D’après la présentation, Artémis III doit décoller en 2027 (cela correspond aux plans présentés ce printemps) pour tester l’amarrage du vaisseau Orion avec les deux atterrisseurs en concurrence, celui de SpaceX et le Blue Moon de Blue Origin. Le premier alunissage passe à Artémis IV, début 2028, et le deuxième à Artémis V, fin 2028.
Les deux engins sont très différents. Le Starship lunaire est l’étage supérieur de la fusée lui-même : 52 mètres de haut, six moteurs Raptor au méthane, une cabine tout en haut et un ascenseur pour descendre les astronautes jusqu’au sol. Le Blue Moon, lui, mesure 16 mètres et ses passagers descendent par une échelle.
Ce calendrier laisse à Starship un peu plus d’un an pour réussir deux choses qu’il n’a jamais faites : faire le plein en orbite, puis se poser sur la Lune sans équipage, avant la fin de 2027. Le créneau est très serré, mais SpaceX a récemment progressé avec le Starship, notamment en matière de vol orbital.
Le plein en orbite début 2027, la Lune fin 2027
Voici les grandes étapes que le calendrier de la NASA fixe à SpaceX :
- fin 2026 : premier Starship rattrapé par la tour de lancement, premier vol depuis la Floride, première réutilisation d’un propulseur Super Heavy V3, et fin de la construction de « Cabin One », une cabine d’équipage grandeur nature testée au sol à Starbase, au Texas ;
- début 2027 : démonstration de transfert de carburant et deuxième pas de tir en Floride ;
- printemps 2027 : test des pieds d’atterrissage, essais du sas sur Cabin One et transport du vaisseau de test vers la Floride par barge ;
- été 2027 : mission Artémis III ;
- fin 2027 : premier vol d’un ravitailleur, lancement de l’atterrisseur de démonstration et alunissage sans équipage.
Pour la NASA, le transfert de carburant est l’un des plus gros défis techniques du programme.
Starship arrive en orbite les réservoirs quasi vides, car il a brûlé l’essentiel de son méthane et de son oxygène liquides pour quitter la Terre. Pour filer vers la Lune, il doit donc être rempli par d’autres Starship, qui servent de ravitailleurs. Ces liquides sont stockés sous les -160 °C, et personne n’a encore fait ce transfert d’un vaisseau à l’autre à cette échelle.
SpaceX n’a pas encore remporté la mise (le premier alunissage n’est pas attribué)
L’affaire n’est pas encore gagnée pour SpaceX. La NASA écrit noir sur blanc que l’atterrisseur d’Artémis IV n’est pas choisi à ce jour. Certes, SpaceX avait été retenu seul en 2021 pour ce premier alunissage. Depuis, il faut compter avec Blue Origin, qui prévoit son propre atterrissage sans équipage au cours du premier trimestre 2028. La concurrence est là.
SpaceX a d’ailleurs déjà pris du retard. Dans un rapport publié le 10 mars 2026, l’inspection générale de la NASA estime que le Starship lunaire a pris au moins deux ans de retard depuis la signature du contrat, en juillet 2021, et que d’autres décalages sont à prévoir. Les échéances posées par Elon Musk peinent ainsi à être respectées.
Au-delà de ce premier alunissage, la présentation esquisse la suite pour SpaceX, après 2028. Une version cargo de Starship, capable de déposer environ 15 tonnes sur la Lune, devrait y livrer un rover pressurisé développé par l’agence spatiale japonaise (JAXA). La NASA compte confier cette mission à SpaceX, mais pas avant son exercice budgétaire 2032, qui démarre en octobre 2031.
Jared Isaacman doit faire le point sur Artémis III et Artémis IV ce vendredi 23 octobre, à 20 heures (heure de Paris), lors d’une conférence de presse au centre spatial Kennedy, en Floride.

articles.title: Exploited Fortinet Bug Linked to Stealthy FortiGate Implant in Telecom Hack
articles.text:
A suspected state-sponsored threat actor exploited multiple Fortinet vulnerabilities in an attack against a telecommunications organization, Palo Alto Networks reports.
The intrusion, attributed to UNC5820 (tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-0954), occurred in September 2024 and resulted in long-term access to the victim’s environment.
Initial access was obtained through the exploitation of a critical remote code execution (RCE) bug in FortiManager, tracked as CVE-2024-47575 and patched in October 2024 as a zero-day.
Shortly after the patches were rolled out, Mandiant warned that UNC5820 had been exploiting the flaw, named FortiJump, since at least June 2024.
A fresh report from Palo Alto Networks shows that UNC5820 also exploited CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal vulnerability affecting multiple Fortinet products, as part of the same intrusion.
Impacting FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager and patched in April 2026, the security defect could allow authenticated attackers to write or delete arbitrary files. Fortinet flagged its exploitation as a zero-day at the time of disclosure.
On Friday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2025-61624 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, urging federal agencies to patch it immediately.
UNC5820 appears to have exploited the path traversal as a zero-day to deploy a previously unknown FortiGate implant dubbed PeerStitch.
The ARM64 malware resides in memory, avoids opening listening ports or initiating outbound network connections, and communicates through the traffic generated by legitimate processes on the appliance.
As part of the observed attack, UNC5820 exploited FortiJump to access a central FortiManager instance, registered a rogue Virtual FortiGate appliance, and exfiltrated a configuration archive containing details on FortiManager, more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls, and the victim’s network.
UNC5820 exploited CVE-2025-61624 to gain root access to the underlying firewall operating system, dropping a script to initiate the PeerStitch deployment.
Written in C, the implant acts as a ‘one-shot process memory patching injector’ targeting the central system and traffic logging, and the IKE/IPsec VPN service daemons in FortiOS to create a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between them and bypass default FortiOS security validations.
As part of the attack, the threat actor was also seen impersonating FortiManager in FortiGate-to-FortiManager (FGFM) communications to issue commands from external infrastructure and “took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts”.
According to Palo Alto Networks, UNC5820 asserted the management identity either by terminating the authentic FortiManager’s session by exploiting CVE-2024-26008, or by reusing exfiltrated secrets and authenticating as the legitimate FortiManager.
“The discovery of the PeerStitch implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring,” Palo Alto Networks notes.

articles.title: Anthropic wants AI models blocked only if they threaten over $1 billion in damage or more than 50 deaths or serious injuries
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Anthropic is pitching a draft AI safety bill to lawmakers. That might sound like a good thing, but there are some eyebrow-raising sections. One of them is that the government should be able to block the release of a new AI model, but only if it has the potential to cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or seriously injure more than 50 people. It seems causing $999 million worth of damage and killing 49 people isn't really a problem.
Politico obtained the confidential draft of the proposal, which a company spokesperson said included "sensible policies we believe Congress should act on."
The headline provision would allow the government to block only models that could cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or injure 50 or more people.
Moreover, the risk posed by the model must stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack. Politico notes that the language mirrors California's AI laws, including SB 5, which was signed last year.
The bill proposes that independent evaluators, registered with the Commerce Department, periodically evaluate the lab and its frontier models. It's also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if their independence remains unaffected.
If an evaluator discovers these alarming-sounding potential risks in an AI model, they are required to report their findings to Commerce within 72 hours of completing their assessment.
The Commerce Department would then have to present the evidence before a federal judge in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the model's release should be stopped. The proposal also states that no other US department, agency, or office could suspend the model's development, deployment or internal use.
"This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic's Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June," the Anthropic spokesperson added.
There have been plenty of concerns over the runaway pace of AI development recently. Following the numerous incidents of AI agents going rogue and hacking other companies, an Anthropic researcher resigned with a warning that AI could end the human race. The company even highlighted these risks in its preliminary IPO prospectus.
Lawmakers have been proposing AI safety rules in the wake of these incidents. Bernie Sanders wants to ban superintelligence and sentence developers who ignore the rules to 20 years in prison. There was also President Trump's Joint Commitment On Frontier Responsibilities, though that "morally binding" agreement relies largely on tech companies policing themselves.
