articles.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI.
For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription.
The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability.
In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription.
Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch
Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile. We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile. The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected.
We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile. Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target.
From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution.
We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size.
Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD
Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills.
In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels.
| Layer | What we found and changed | Gain | 
| FFN | The reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute. | 2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 | 
| Depthwise conv1d | The experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput. | 1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 | 
| Conv2d | The model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32. | Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32 | 
Data-parallel runtime in Rust
Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica.
Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API (libnrt). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size.
We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline.
Cost saving impact
We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running.
Conclusion
In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads.
To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation, which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from. The Neuron developer tools documentation covers the profiling and agentic tooling we used here, including Neuron Explorer and Neuron Agentic Development. For instance sizes and pricing, see Amazon EC2 Trn2 Instances. For help scoping a similar port, contact the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering.

articles.title: Switzerland's Nouscom bags €120 million to bring innovative cancer immunotherapy closer to clinical trials | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Basel-based Nouscom, a clinical-stage, cancer interception focused BioTech developing next-generation immunotherapies, today announced the closing of an oversubscribed €120 million ($135 million) Series D financing to fund the advancement of an investigational off-the-shelf neoantigen-based cancer immunotherapy.
The round was co-led by M Ventures and Revelation Partners alongside new investors Angelini Ventures, the EIB, and Neva SGR (Intesa Sanpaolo Group). Existing investors, 5AM Ventures, Andera Partners, Bpifrance, CDP Venture Capital, EQT Life Sciences, Indaco Venture Partners, Panakes Partners, Versant Ventures and XGEN Ventures, all participated in the round.
“Over two million LS carriers live with up to an 80% lifetime cancer risk and nothing to offer them but surveillance and surgery“, says Marina Udier, Ph.D., Chief Executive Officer of Nouscom. “We built Nouscom to change that equation. This financing, alongside the data we are presenting at ESMO, puts us closer to a world where cancer is stopped before it starts. I am grateful to our new and existing investors for backing that conviction, and to the team behind NOUS-209.”
Nouscom’s Series D comes alongside a series of European oncology financings reported in 2026.
In France, ErVimmune raised €17 million to advance its off-the-shelf cancer vaccine, while Brenus Pharma secured €11 million for immunotherapy development. Germany’s Kupando added €10 million, while UK-based STORM Therapeutics, also backed by M Ventures, raised €47.5 million and Engitix secured €21 million. In Switzerland, Moonlight AI raised €2.8 million for adjacent cancer-diagnostics technology.
These six rounds total approximately €109.3 million, rising to €229.3 million including Nouscom’s financing.
EU-Startups previously featured Nouscom in 2019 and reported M Ventures’ participation in Basel-based FoRx Therapeutics’ €42 million financing in 2025.
“This significant financing reflects the confidence of our investors in Nouscom’s vision, team and the transformative potential of cancer interception,” said Göran Ando, M.D., Independent Chair of the Board of Nouscom. “With this backing, we are well positioned to accelerate NOUS-209’s clinical development and our commitment to those living with Lynch Syndrome. I am delighted to welcome our new investors, whose support further strengthens Nouscom as we enter this next chapter.”
Founded in 2015, Nouscom is a clinical-stage BioTech company innovating next-generation neoantigen-targeted immunotherapies to treat cancer at all stages, from early cancer interception to late-stage metastatic disease.
Its proprietary viral vector platform enables broad and durable immune activation by delivering optimised neoantigens that train the immune system to recognise and fight cancer.
Nouscom’s lead programme, NOUS-209, is an off-the- shelf immunotherapy in advanced clinical development for cancer interception in LS and the treatment of MSI mCRC. The company’s clinical stage 10 portfolio also includes NOUS-PEV, a personalized neoantigen immunotherapy, with published data from a successfully completed Phase 1b trial.
Dr. Hakan Goker, Managing Director and Head of Biotechnology Investments at M Ventures, says: “What sets Nouscom apart is its unique cancer interception approach and the platform that enables it. Maturing clinical evidence and a regulatory-aligned path into a registration-enabling trial in such an unchartered space is a rare combination for a private biotech company and the commitment of the investor syndicate underpins this deep conviction.”
Proceeds from the Series D round will fund the advancement of NOUS-209, an investigational off-the-shelf neoantigen-based cancer immunotherapy, through a single, global, registration-enabling clinical trial for cancer interception in Lynch Syndrome (LS) carriers, for which FDA has granted Fast Track designation.

articles.title: Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit
articles.text:
Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit
Russia didn’t burn that fuel by accident: it’s likely spying on the satellite and testing the West.
A Russian military satellite, Cosmos 2612, has closed to roughly 3 miles, from a previous distance of more than 200 miles, of the U.S.-owned radar satellite that operates in a fleet that supports Ukraine, Axios reports. The unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit, which astronomer Jonathan McDowell says may be the first of its kind, raises alarm in the West. The position change, which was likely not an accident as fuel is scarce, is probably a provocation and an attempt to spy on the satellite.
LeoLabs said in a statement Friday that the movement “appears to be a deliberate approach” toward ICEYE-X36, with uncertain intent and behavior that “warrants continued monitoring.” Roughly 3 miles is too close for comfort in satellite terms: there is no strict legal limit on how close satellites can get, but countries generally keep at least 6 miles (9.7 km) apart, University of Mississippi space law professor Aaron Brynildson told Axios. The approach was made without the owner’s consent, and Russia hasn’t said what the military satellite carries.
Some clues may come from the target’s operational purpose. ICEYE-X36 is a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite which can image through cloud cover and at night. It was launched in March 2024 on a SpaceX Falcon 9. It’s registered to ICEYE US, the U.S. arm of the Finland-founded company. The satellite, which is in a roughly 545 km (339 mi) sun-synchronous orbit, is part of a fleet that has supplied Ukraine with information since 2022. This includes a deal earlier this year with a customer in Ukraine’s defense ministry, but a Ukrainian official told Axios it’s unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports the country; ICEYE and the Defense Department declined to comment.
In May, the majority of the six military satellites Russia launched in April via a Soyuz-2.1b, Cosmos 2609–2614, shifted their orbits about 0.8 degrees to match X36’s orbital plane. Cosmos 2609 passed within 2.5 km (1.6 mi) on May 26. Cosmos 2612, on the other hand, drifted off X36’s plane by about 0.24 degrees by Sept. 30, up to about 28 km side to side, according to Greg Gillinger, a space analyst with Integrity ISR.
Then, Cosmos 2612 made separate burns from Sept. 30 through Oct. 16 to match altitude, eccentricity, and orbital period, Dutch satellite tracker Marco Langbroek wrote. By Saturday night, he estimated from public orbital data, it was within “a few hundred meters or possibly (much) closer.”
These movements appear deliberate and cost a lot of fuel, which the Center for Strategic and International Studies calls “a limited resource on a satellite.” Close-proximity work can be benign, it says, but policymakers should assume the Russian satellite “could take an action that threatens the commercial satellite,” and the U.S. and Europe should decide how to respond to any hostile act in space and make a statement on the decision. Back in July 2020, Russia’s Cosmos 2543 released an object at up to 186 m/s (416 mph) relative to itself, an action which was condemned by the U.S. and U.K.
Intent was less clear earlier this year, when McDowell told Meduza the orbital data showed no sign of the stable, close distance that tracking ICEYE-X36 would require. Now, he says it is an unapproved meeting and is not alone. Gillinger says the setup “removes any remaining doubt for me that Cosmos 2612 is interested in ICEYE X36.” Langbroek adds that “I was skeptical” at first but now calls it “completely non-consensual,” though he cautions it would be difficult to pin any X36 failures on 2612’s actions.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In a Reuters report less than two weeks ago, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company moved its satellite after May, only to draw more Russian maneuvers, which Germany’s Space Command head, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, described as “chasing.” Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at U.S. space intelligence firm Slingshot Aerospace, added that the moves may have been meant for surveillance, to prepare for future interference, or to signal capability. Western officials reportedly describe such trailing as a way to gather intelligence and test the West’s tolerance.
No statement from Russia is on record. Gillinger also told readers to “watch Cosmos 2611 and 2613, whose planes are converging on ICEYE X37’s,” with crossings expected around Nov. 6 and Nov. 15.

articles.title: Musk pledges to give 'every kid in America' one of his SpaceX shares | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth.
It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate.
President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors.
Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO.
On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead.
“This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock.
There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more.
Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. However, a recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. Nearly 60% has gone to another charity, called The Foundation, run by his money manager, Jared Birchall.

articles.title: Thanks, AI: The PlayStation 6 could be priced over $1,000 as leaker claims its memory and storage alone cost Sony $680 thanks to the AI-drive component crisis
articles.text:
The PlayStation 6 could cost over $1,000 as leaker claims its memory and storage alone will cost Sony $680
The most expensive games console ever?
- A leaker has claimed the PlayStation 6’s storage and memory alone could cost $680
- That lines up with past predictions that the console will cost $1,000 or more
- Sony has remained silent on the potential cost of its next-generation device
It’s no secret that the ongoing AI-driven RAM crisis has pushed component prices to extraordinarily unpleasant highs, and that’s made everything from graphics cards to new smartphones more expensive. Now, it looks like the misery could be spreading to the upcoming PlayStation 6, with some predictions indicating that an eye-watering price tag of $1,000 or more could be on the horizon.
That idea comes from renowned leaker KeplerL2 on the NeoGAF forums, who recently argued that the procurement cost to Sony of the PlayStation 6’s memory and storage alone comes to $680. That’s before we even consider other components like the GPU, CPU, and motherboard, and it makes for grim reading for anyone hoping for a reasonably priced console from Sony.
The context here is that KeplerL2’s comment was made in response to another forum member. That person had expressed doubts over KeplerL2’s previous prediction that the total bill of materials for the PlayStation 6 would come to $960. That prediction was made in July 2026, and with prices only increasing since then, the final bill to Sony could easily push past the $1,000 mark — especially if the RAM and storage come to $680 before anything else is factored in.
While some games consoles have historically been sold at a loss in order to drive software sales, Sony has said in recent months that “As a principle, we do not intend to sell hardware at significant losses.” That suggests that if the PlayStation 6’s bill of materials really does come to $960 — or more — then that’s likely to be close to the price that consumers will be asked to pay.
More bad news for PlayStation fans
KeplerL2 is a well-known leaker in the world of consoles and computing hardware, and in recent weeks they have made claims surrounding console release dates, the performance of the next Xbox, and AMD’s own version of DLSS 5. Their past track record gives them a degree of credibility, but as with every so-called leak and rumor, it’s sensible to treat it with a dose of skepticism until it is confirmed.
Still, given the way hardware prices are going, it wouldn’t be too surprising to see the PlayStation 6 debut at $1,000 or more. Costs of the priciest PlayStation components — including the memory, storage, and GPU — are way up compared to when the PlayStation 5 launched and are showing no signs of slowing down. In fact, they could get worse over the next year or two.
Sony has not made any comments on which way prices for the PlayStation 6 might go, so we’ll have to wait and see for now. But combined with the news that Sony is planning to ditch physical discs altogether in the near future, the future could be tough for PlayStation gamers.

articles.title: Vírus que afetou Carlos Alberto de Nóbrega pode atingir o coração; entenda
articles.text:
O vírus Coxsackie, conhecido por causar a síndrome mão-pé-boca, geralmente provoca infecções leves, mas, em casos raros, pode atingir o coração e provocar alterações no ritmo cardíaco. Foi o que aconteceu com o apresentador Carlos Alberto de Nóbrega, de 90 anos, que precisou de um marcapasso após uma infecção agravar uma insuficiência cardíaca preexistente.
Internado no Hospital Sírio-Libanês, em São Paulo (SP), desde a semana passada, o apresentador contraiu o Coxsackie tipo 2. A infecção agravou seu quadro cardíaco, provocando bradicardia, condição em que o coração bate mais devagar do que o normal, e outras arritmias.
A cirurgia para implantação do aparelho, inicialmente prevista para segunda-feira (19), foi adiada para terça-feira (20). Segundo a assessoria, Carlos Alberto está estável e sem complicações. Sua esposa, Renata de Nóbrega, que é médica, também apresentou sintomas da infecção, mas não precisou ser internada.
O que é o vírus Coxsackie?
- Os coxsackievírus pertencem ao grupo dos enterovírus, que também inclui o vírus da poliomielite. Eles são divididos em dois ramos: A e B, associados a diferentes manifestações da infecção;
- O ramo A reúne 23 tipos e está relacionado à síndrome mão-pé-boca, doença contagiosa que afeta principalmente crianças pequenas. Já o ramo B tem seis tipos e é mais associado a complicações em órgãos internos, como coração, pâncreas, fígado e sistema nervoso;
- O tipo 2 existe nos dois ramos. A informação divulgada sobre o caso de Carlos Alberto de Nóbrega, porém, não esclarece a qual deles pertence o vírus identificado no apresentador;
- A infecção é bastante comum e, na maioria das vezes, passa despercebida. Um levantamento realizado na Itália encontrou sinais de contato anterior com o vírus em cerca de sete em cada dez pessoas analisadas;
- Os sintomas geralmente se assemelham aos de um resfriado, uma diarreia ou uma febre de curta duração. Por isso, muitas pessoas se recuperam sem saber qual vírus causou o quadro;
- A transmissão ocorre principalmente pelo contato com fezes contaminadas. O vírus pode continuar sendo eliminado dessa forma por semanas após o desaparecimento dos sintomas. Também pode circular pela saliva e por gotículas respiratórias, além de permanecer em superfícies e objetos, facilitando a disseminação em casas, creches e escolas.
Como o vírus pode atingir o coração?
O Coxsackie entra no organismo pela boca, multiplica-se no intestino e pode alcançar a circulação sanguínea. Pelo sangue, chega a diferentes tecidos e consegue invadir células que apresentam estruturas às quais o vírus se liga.
No coração, essas estruturas estão presentes nas junções entre as células do músculo cardíaco, regiões importantes para a passagem dos sinais elétricos que coordenam os batimentos.
Segundo Ricardo Kazunori, cirurgião cardiovascular da BP — A Beneficência Portuguesa de São Paulo, o vírus pode danificar diretamente as células, enquanto a resposta do sistema imunológico provoca inflamação adicional.
Esse processo pode causar miocardite, inflamação do músculo cardíaco. Quando a inflamação alcança o sistema elétrico do coração, os sinais responsáveis por coordenar as batidas podem ficar mais lentos ou ser interrompidos parcialmente. O resultado pode ser uma alteração do ritmo cardíaco, incluindo a bradicardia observada no caso do apresentador.
Na maioria dos casos de miocardite viral, as falhas de condução são passageiras. Entretanto, há relatos raros de bloqueios elétricos irreversíveis que exigiram a implantação definitiva de um marcapasso, inclusive após infecção pelo Coxsackie B2.
O aparelho emite impulsos elétricos para ajudar a manter o ritmo cardíaco quando o coração não consegue gerar ou conduzir os sinais adequadamente. Ele trata a alteração dos batimentos, mas não elimina o vírus responsável pela infecção.
Leia mais:
- Brasil testa novo tratamento injetável de ação longa para HIV
- Sangue tipo B tem mais risco de diabetes, mas hábitos pesam mais
- Por que têm aumentado os casos de câncer entre adultos mais jovens?
Quem corre maior risco de complicações?
Embora a maioria das infecções seja leve, alguns grupos estão mais sujeitos a quadros graves. Entre eles estão recém-nascidos, pessoas com o sistema imunológico enfraquecido e pacientes com doenças preexistentes no coração ou no cérebro.
No caso de quem já tem insuficiência cardíaca, uma inflamação adicional pode agravar o funcionamento de um órgão que já apresenta dificuldade para bombear sangue com eficiência.
Alguns sintomas exigem avaliação médica urgente, especialmente quando há suspeita de comprometimento cardíaco ou neurológico:
- Dor no peito;
- Falta de ar;
- Palpitações;
- Febre persistente;
- Dor de cabeça intensa acompanhada de rigidez no pescoço;
- Confusão mental ou convulsões.
Em bebês, febre acompanhada de dificuldade para mamar, sonolência excessiva ou irritabilidade também exige atendimento imediato.
O Coxsackie pode atingir ainda o pâncreas. Pesquisas investigam possível relação entre infecções persistentes e o desenvolvimento do diabetes tipo 1, mas essa hipótese continua em estudo.
Nos quadros leves, o diagnóstico costuma ser feito com base nos sintomas, sem necessidade de exames específicos. Em situações graves ou atípicas, especialmente envolvendo recém-nascidos e pessoas com imunidade baixa, os médicos podem recorrer a testes que detectam o material genético do vírus em amostras de sangue, líquor ou tecido cardíaco.
Existe tratamento para o Coxsackie?
Não há medicamento específico capaz de eliminar o coxsackievírus, nem vacina disponível contra ele. O tratamento depende dos sintomas e dos órgãos afetados.
Nos casos leves, os cuidados incluem hidratação e medicamentos para aliviar febre e dor. Quando há miocardite, pode ser necessário monitorar o funcionamento do coração e utilizar medicamentos para tratar a insuficiência cardíaca.
Nas formas mais graves, o paciente pode precisar de suporte mecânico para manter a circulação sanguínea. Se a infecção provocar alterações importantes no ritmo cardíaco, um marcapasso pode ser necessário para corrigir o problema elétrico.
A prevenção depende principalmente de medidas de higiene. Lavar as mãos com água e sabão, especialmente após usar o banheiro ou trocar fraldas e antes de preparar ou consumir alimentos, é uma das principais formas de reduzir a transmissão.
Também é importante limpar superfícies e objetos tocados com frequência e evitar compartilhar talheres e itens pessoais durante a infecção. A higiene merece atenção especial durante a gravidez, já que a mãe pode transmitir o vírus ao bebê.
No caso de Carlos Alberto de Nóbrega, a infecção agravou uma condição cardíaca que já existia. A implantação do marcapasso busca corrigir a alteração no ritmo dos batimentos provocada por essa combinação.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
articles.text:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.
Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
The proposed nuclear plant would provide 960 megawatts to power the grid — and Amazon’s data centers.
No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.
Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.
This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.
Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

articles.title: Rozvelt built a high-tech mask for hunters. Defence buyers see something bigger. | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Montréal startup behind a breath-filtering mask for recreational hunters is now expanding into the defence sector, a move that has brought international partnerships and fresh funding.
Rozvelt, which makes odour-masking headgear, announced on Monday that it has secured $3.1 million CAD in seed funding from a number of angel investors, led by Benoit Robert, a partner at wealth management firm Evovest. The company plans to use the funding to expand its breathable headgear product line to cater to the military, law enforcement, and first responders, following a burst of interest from those markets.
“Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation.”
Nicholas Monette, Rozvelt
Rozvelt’s consumer headgear, called Vektr, was designed to filter out odour particles exhaled by the wearer, but not particles that are inhaled. It connects magnetically to an adjustable band that wraps around the head, with a removal clasp near each ear. The company claims recreational hunters, as well as wildlife photographers and nature observers, can use it to conceal their scent.
According to Rozvelt co-founder and CEO Nicholas Monette, the pivot began when Rozvelt presented at the SHOT Show in Las Vegas, run by the US Firearm Industry Trade Association. The company was approached by hunters and defence companies who told them there was a bigger problem its masks could tackle.
Shooting a gun can expose people to lead particles from ammunition, which is associated with health issues like cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and kidney failure. They suggested that Rozvelt make its headgear dynamic, so it could switch between filtering exhales (to stop the wearer’s scent) and filtering inhales (protecting the wearer from dangerous particles). Beyond just lead exposure, the masks could serve as a kind of personal protective equipment, fit for combat and other hazardous environments. That’s now what it plans to focus on with its fresh funding, in addition to starting production of the consumer Vektr product in Canada this fall.
“When we saw all this traction in defence, that’s when we took the product and went into all the biggest defence shows,” Monette said in an interview. That included the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland, a NATO conference in Luxembourg, and SEECAT in Japan—which is where BetaKit reached him by phone.
RELATED: Rozvelt bets on hardware for hunters amid tariff-spurred funding crunch
The company launched last year at the height of the Canada-US trade war, at possibly the “worst time” to raise money for a hardware company due to investor concerns about tariff impacts. Trade tensions between Canada and the US are now impacting Rozvelt, but not in the same way. Monette said that his company’s position as a Canadian startup with dual-use applications (both civilian and military) has made it an attractive partner for international investors in Europe and Asia. One example is Rozvelt’s partnership and planned distribution agreement with Japan’s Seaprex, an industrial marine manufacturer with defence applications.
Having the Canadian brand behind them was a tailwind. “Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation,” Monette said.
This comes amid tens of billions of defence dollars committed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government and an explosion in support programs for companies making dual-use technologies. But Monette said Canada’s defence gold rush wasn’t what prompted the switch—international interest came first. He added that Rozvelt is looking to sell to the Canadian Armed Forces as soon as possible.
At the same time, he said, Rozvelt is open to pursuing deals with the US military. “If they want to work with us, we’ll work with them,” Monette said.
Feature image courtesy Rozvelt.

articles.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).
One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector, which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA, the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based: After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.
This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.
In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.
We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.
Push-based KV transfer
This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.
Architecture overview
Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:
- It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
- It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.
The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.
The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.
Implementation details
The protocol has three logical steps.
1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.
2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.
3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.
Threading model
The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.
The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.
Timing comparison of pull and push
The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.
The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.
Performance data
For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.
The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.
This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.
How to run benchmark
To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use NixlPushConnector instead of NixlConnector.
Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment.
As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this.
Related resources
Acknowledgments
We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

articles.title: « Ça fait mal au cœur » : vitrines brisées et 30 000 euros de préjudice, une boutique de vélos électriques Voltaire dévastée en pleine nuit
articles.text:
La boutique du Sentier de Voltaire, marque française de vélos électriques urbains créée en 2019, a été saccagée et pillée dans la nuit de dimanche à ce lundi 19 octobre. Elle se trouve au 9 bis boulevard Poissonnière, dans le 2e arrondissement de Paris. Des individus cagoulés ont cassé les vitrines et forcé l’entrée, avant de repartir avec des vélos électriques et du matériel informatique.
« Plus qu’une simple boutique, ce lieu abrite également nos bureaux »
Grégoire Lieurade, cofondateur de Voltaire, nous a raconté ce lundi le déroulé des événements : « Les faits ont eu lieu cette nuit, vraisemblablement aux alentours d’une heure du matin, selon le voisinage qui nous a informés du cambriolage. »
Il poursuit : « Le préjudice aujourd’hui, c’est une douzaine de vélos et des ordinateurs. On m’a dit que c’était une trentaine de milliers d’euros. Voilà, ça fait mal au cœur, comme tu peux l’imaginer. »
Sur Instagram, la marque rappelle que le lieu ne sert pas qu’à vendre des vélos : « Plus qu’une simple boutique, ce lieu abrite également nos bureaux. C’est donc aussi beaucoup de travail, d’énergie et d’investissement de toute une équipe qui sont touchés aujourd’hui. »
Une trentaine de commerces pillés à Paris la même nuit
Voltaire est loin d’être la seule enseigne touchée. Selon France Info, une trentaine de commerces ont été pillés à Paris dans la soirée du dimanche 18 octobre, au lendemain des manifestations du 17 octobre.
« Évidemment, c’est dur à encaisser. Malheureusement, c’est la vie de milliers de commerçants ce matin, et c’est une nouvelle fois dur à encaisser. Mais il faut faire avec », poursuit Grégoire Lieurade.
Assurance, police, barricades : Voltaire avance à tâtons
Pour la suite, rien n’est encore réglé, admet Grégoire Lieurade. « Pour les prochaines étapes, évidemment, c’est essayer de voir avec l’assurance ce qu’elle peut faire, mais aujourd’hui, on n’a aucune garantie. Et d’un point de vue juridique, évidemment, on s’est rapprochés des policiers. Mais là aussi, en toute honnêteté, tout est encore trop neuf. »
En attendant, la marque a décidé de fermer ses portes et de se protéger. « Ce qui est sûr, c’est qu’on ferme la boutique de Sentier jusqu’à nouvel ordre, évidemment. Et concernant la boutique Marais, on est en train d’installer des barricades pour essayer de se protéger. »
Le pillage tombe d’autant plus mal pour Voltaire. Placée en liquidation judiciaire en janvier 2026, la marque a été rachetée le 25 mars par Ultima Mobility, un fabricant lyonnais de vélos électriques qui détient aussi Bohême et Larrun.
Pour les clients, la marque a donné quelques consignes sur Instagram : « Nos boutiques du Sentier et du Marais seront fermées jusqu’à nouvel ordre. Nos équipes prendront directement contact avec les clients dont les vélos sont actuellement en SAV afin de les tenir informés de la situation. » Si votre Voltaire est au service après-vente (SAV), ne vous déplacez pas et attendez que l’équipe vous appelle.
Frandroid apporte tout son soutien à la marque Voltaire.

articles.title: Los despidos sin indemnizar ni justificar se disparan tras la reforma laboral y ya suman casi 3,2 millones
articles.text:
Los contratos indefinidos también pueden durar semanas; durante el periodo de prueba la empresa puede, con carácter general, acabar con la relación laboral sin tener que indemnizar y sin acreditar una causa. Su uso ha ido en aumento desde la reforma laboral de 2022; las bajas que se acumulan están en torno a los 3,2 millones, según Colpisa.
La información puede recogerse en la tabla de la Seguridad Social: en el periodo comprendido entre enero de 2022 y agosto de 2026 se registran 3.188.254 bajas por no superar la prueba con contratos indefinidos; los datos de 2026 son provisionales.
Hay que tener en cuenta lo antecedente: en 2025 se registraron 723.763, frente a los 75.004 de 2021, lo que son casi diez veces más. Si lo comparamos con 2019 (justo antes de la pandemia), las cifras fueron de 132.534, y el último año completo multiplica esa cifra por 5,46.
Nosotros ya hablamos del repunte de estos ceses. La dificultad que esto plantea se encuentra en que un contrato indefinido no tiene fecha de finalización; sin embargo, es algo que no impide que pueda terminar durante la prueba. Para quien ha cambiado de trabajo, tal posibilidad puede afectar a la estabilidad prevista por el contrato y a la protección por desempleo.
Una empresa puede prescindir de un trabajador porque no se ha adaptado al puesto, pero también (y aquí entra la picaresca) puede utilizar la prueba para una necesidad temporal. Las estadísticas que conocemos no permiten calcular cuántas de estas bajas son fraudulentas, ni adjudicarlas todas ellas a una causa única.
El Real Decreto 723/2026, publicado en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) y en vigor desde el 5 de octubre, refuerza la obligación de las empresas de facilitar información escrita sobre el periodo de prueba. Su régimen general sobre relaciones laborales de más de cuatro semanas exige comunicar por escrito la duración concreta de la prueba y las obligaciones para realizarla, aunque mantiene la posibilidad de terminar el contrato durante ella sin una indemnización automática.
También debe indicarse la función que se desempeña, diferenciando entre salario base y complementos, y exponer con claridad el cálculo de las cantidades variables de la remuneración, así como la jornada, los turnos de trabajo y las vacaciones. Si se utilizan algoritmos para tomar decisiones sobre las condiciones laborales, se informará de su existencia y sus reglas de funcionamiento. En el caso de contratos anteriores al 5 de octubre, la información pendiente puede solicitarse y deberá remitirse en treinta días hábiles.
Para nuevas contrataciones, la comunicación de estas condiciones se realizará antes del inicio del trabajo; puede incorporarse al contrato o a un documento adicional en papel o formato electrónico. La información ya facilitada al trabajador, si está completa y la tiene en su poder, no tiene que repetirse.
La prueba tiene sus límites
Es necesario saber que existe una precisión a la hora de aceptar seis meses de prueba. El artículo 14 del Estatuto remite en primer lugar a las disposiciones del convenio colectivo; si este no establece otra duración, se impone, para los técnicos titulados, un plazo máximo de seis meses y, para el resto de los trabajadores, de dos meses. En las empresas con menos de 25 trabajadores, el máximo es de tres meses para quienes no son técnicos titulados.
El Estatuto también establece que, cuando se han desempeñado las mismas funciones anteriormente en la misma empresa, el pacto de prueba es nulo, cualquiera que haya sido la modalidad de contratación anterior.
Asimismo, el Estatuto garantiza el derecho a la protección frente a la extinción por embarazo o maternidad, salvo que concurran motivos no relacionados con el embarazo o la maternidad. Y cuando el trabajador esté en prueba, tendrá los derechos y obligaciones correspondientes al puesto de trabajo, salvo los relativos a la resolución del contrato; la ausencia de obligación de indemnizar no exime a la empresa de la obligación de abonar el salario por el trabajo realizado.
La concreción de la duración de esta prueba no es una obligación descubierta en octubre de 2026, y la sentencia 551/2025 del Tribunal Supremo, de 5 de junio de 2025, publicada en el BOE, recuerda su doctrina. La remisión a un convenio colectivo que no fija una duración concreta, sino únicamente un límite superior, no basta. Si el convenio estipula una duración exacta, la remisión puede ser válida.
Esa sentencia recuerda además que el objetivo de la prueba es comprobar la idoneidad del trabajador para el puesto de trabajo, dejando claro que la libertad para decidir no ampara decisiones discriminatorias ni vulneraciones de derechos fundamentales.
Si el periodo de prueba resulta inválido o el cese es discriminatorio, el trabajador podrá impugnar la extinción. El artículo 103 de la Ley reguladora de la jurisdicción social establece un plazo de veinte días hábiles para presentar la demanda por despido; las normas de este capítulo se aplican también a la impugnación de otras decisiones empresariales de extinción, con las especialidades necesarias. Se trata, por tanto, de un plazo de caducidad; merece la pena revisar el contrato y la notificación de la baja para evitar que se pierdan los días.
El riesgo al cambiar de trabajo
La prestación por desempleo merece una aclaración independiente. El Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal incluye entre las situaciones legales de desempleo el cese por no superar la prueba a iniciativa del empresario y establece condiciones sobre cómo terminó el empleo anterior. Que la empresa acabe con la relación laboral con un trabajador en periodo de prueba no significa que este se vea privado automáticamente de todos los derechos a la prestación por desempleo.
Debe reunir los requisitos correspondientes a la prestación que solicite. Existe, no obstante, una excepción notable en el caso de aquellos que abandonan un trabajo para incorporarse a otro. El SEPE explica en la pregunta frecuente sobre la baja voluntaria que, si la segunda empresa acaba con la relación laboral por no superar la prueba antes de que haya transcurrido un plazo de tres meses desde esa salida voluntaria del empleo anterior, no se podrá optar por la prestación por desempleo. La causa y la fecha en que se produjo el cese del primer trabajo pueden ser decisivas.
La tendencia continúa, desgraciadamente. Las bajas de trabajadores con contratos indefinidos por no superar la prueba, registradas entre enero y agosto de 2026, ascendieron a 505.065, frente a las 478.268 de los mismos meses de 2025: un aumento del 5,6 %. Eso sí, se trata de datos provisionales y anteriores a la fecha de entrada en vigor del decreto.

articles.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
articles.text:
The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.
Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.
NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.
An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.
Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:
Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.
OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.
Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library.
Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.
The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.
Learn more about NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme.

articles.title: Zyklus-Apps im Check: 4 von 17 wollen ohne Grund den Standort tracken
articles.text:
Zyklus-Apps im Check: 4 von 17 wollen den Standort tracken
Während es in vielen Ratgebern im Internet darum geht, ob Zyklus-Apps mit Vorhersagen des Eisprungs als valide Verhütungsmethode taugen, wird ein Aspekt dabei oft außer Acht gelassen: Wie steht es eigentlich um den Datenschutz? articles.title: ResolvMD expands medical billing tech into Ontario | BetaKit
articles.text:
ResolvMD, an Alberta startup streamlining medical billing for doctors, has expanded its services into Ontario.
ResolvMD uses AI-integrated software to automate, manage, and optimize billing claims for Canadian doctors. Founded in 2019 by Calgary-based physicians Dr. Marshall Ross and Dr. Ryan Allen, as well as former investment banker Patrick Onyekweli, the startup uses a proprietary “physician insight portal” to check medical claims for errors or missing billing codes, and then submit those claims to provincial health authorities. Combining both AI-driven tools and human billing specialists, the “full service” platform also assists with claim preparation, rejections, and collects and provides data to medical practices on their billing trends.
“Over the course of an entire career … missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected.”
Lauren Hauswirth, ResolvMD
Under Canada’s universal healthcare system, doctors and medical clinics bill provincial and territorial health authorities for the services they provide using a complex system of billing codes that are used to represent everything from a routine assessment to the time of day a patient was seen.
Lauren Hauswirth, the head of growth for ResolvMD, said codes and billing systems differ across jurisdictions, but that a single patient visit can often include several different billing codes.
“A single visit can have five or more codes, and each represents a monetary value,” Hauswirth said, adding that the breadth and complexity of coding guidelines and processing systems can often result in physicians leaving money they’re entitled to on the table.
“Over the course of an entire career, those missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected,” Hauswirth added.
Moving east
Since its founding, ResolvMD has grown its client base to around 1,700 of Alberta’s roughly 14,000 registered physicians, leveraging financing from firms like PaceZero Capital Partners for product development across the province. Now, the startup has moved into Ontario, Canada’s largest medical billing market.
ResolvMD soft-launched in Ontario this past August, with an official launch taking place in early October at Ontario’s Digital Health Conference. Since then, Hauswirth said the company has added around 150 more clients onto the ResolvMD platform, which takes 1.95 percent of all of the paid claims it processes under individual user plans.
“It’s been growing quickly,” Hauswirth said. “We’re getting in front of a lot of physicians through our national partners.”
Ontario is home to more than 31,000 practicing physicians, according to the Ontario Medical Association.
New markets, new systems
Setting up shop in Ontario meant transitioning ResolvMD’s tech from AHS’s billing system to OHIP’s. To do that, the startup built a new operating system, which it says passed Ontario’s conformance testing—a mandatory technical review process required by provincial health authorities—earlier this year. It also hired a team of Ontario-based billing experts, which help review and address claims processed through the platform.
While ResolvMD is focusing on building its brand recognition in Ontario, where it faces competition from a handful of already established billing companies, the company told BetaKit in an interview that its experience building for Ontario could lend itself to expansions elsewhere, too.
“British Columbia is definitely the next place there could be an opportunity,” Hauswirth said. “That’s what we’re evaluating right now.”
Hauswirth added that ResolvMD is also considering international expansion opportunities alongside the potential for further Canadian expansion.
If there were to be a second Canadian expansion into British Columbia, Hauswirth said it would likely occur in 2027.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
articles.text:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer.
Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.
This article has been updated to clarify Laplace’s relationship with Nvidia.

articles.title: Mercedes-AMG GT SUV contre Porsche Cayenne : le duel des monstres électriques à plus de 1 000 ch
articles.text:
Le Mondial de l’Auto vivait son dernier week-end Porte de Versailles quand la division sportive de Mercedes a présenté son nouveau SUV électrique baptisé « GT », le samedi 17 octobre 2026. La présentation a eu lieu au Mercedes-Benz Museum de Stuttgart, pendant une fête organisée pour les 140 ans de la marque. D’après le communiqué de Mercedes-AMG, c’est le premier grand SUV entièrement développé par AMG en 59 ans d’histoire. Il annonce une puissance allant jusqu’à 1 169 ch et une recharge capable d’encaisser 710 kW.
En face, le concurrent tout désigné est le nouveau Porsche Cayenne Electric, qui dans sa version la plus poussée Turbo revendique 1 156 ch. Lequel des deux SUV électriques de Stuttgart prend l’avantage sur le papier ? Nous avons comparé leurs fiches techniques, de la puissance au prix.
Puissance : AMG dépasse de 13 ch, Porsche garde le chrono
Le nouvel AMG GT SUV reprend la technique de la berline AMG GT Coupé 4 Portes électrique, dévoilée en mai avec son faux bruit de V8. On retrouve la même plateforme AMG.EA et, sur les GT 55 et GT 63, les mêmes moteurs à flux axial. Il simule lui aussi le son d’un V8 ou d’un six-cylindres (selon la version), avec de faux passages de rapports.
En haut de gamme, l’AMG GT 63 SUV annonce 1 169 ch et 2 000 Nm de couple. Le Cayenne Turbo Electric atteint 1 156 ch et 1 500 Nm. Les 13 ch d’écart ne pèsent pas lourd. Le Mercedes revendique en revanche 500 Nm de couple de plus.
Attention à la lecture de la fiche technique, car Mercedes affiche un 0 à 100 km/h en 2,5 secondes mesuré avec un « 1-foot rollout ». En mesurant ainsi, le chronomètre ne démarre qu’après les 30,48 premiers centimètres (un pied), qui sont les plus lents du départ arrêté. Sans cette astuce, le GT 63 passe à 2,7 secondes, alors que Porsche annonce 2,5 secondes pour le Cayenne Turbo.
Un cran plus bas, le GT 53 SUV et le Cayenne S Electric affichent tous les deux 544 ch. Cependant, le SUV Porsche monte à 666 ch avec le Launch Control et passe de 0 à 100 km/h en 3,8 secondes, contre 4,2 secondes pour le Mercedes. Point pour Porsche.
Ces chronos concernent des SUV de plus de 2,5 tonnes. Mercedes annonce 2 525 kg pour le GT 53 et jusqu’à 2 715 kg pour le GT 55 doté de la grande batterie, pour 5,08 mètres de long.
Recharge : l’avance d’AMG dépend de la borne
Côté batterie, Mercedes propose 106 ou 128 kWh utiles, avec une architecture 800 volts. Ses cellules cylindriques baignent directement dans une huile qui ne conduit pas l’électricité, pour que la puissance reste stable même quand on la sollicite longtemps. Porsche annonce quant à lui 113 kWh pour son Cayenne électrique, mais en capacité brute : environ 108 kWh sont réellement utilisables, soit entre les deux batteries de Mercedes.
Sur le papier, la recharge tourne à l’avantage d’AMG : jusqu’à 600 kW en pic avec la petite batterie, 710 kW avec la grande, et un 10 à 80 % en 11 ou 12 minutes. Le Cayenne plafonne à 400 kW dans des conditions très particulières (390 kW dans les conditions optimales retenues par Porsche) et passe de 10 à 80 % en moins de 16 minutes. Avantage Mercedes ?
Les chiffres d’AMG supposent une borne capable de suivre. Mercedes le précise lui-même : sur une borne de 400 kW, le 10 à 80 % prend 14 minutes avec la batterie de 106 kWh et 16 minutes avec celle de 128 kWh. C’est donc à peu près le temps du Cayenne.
Autonomie : Mercedes grappille des km
Côté autonomie, le Mercedes-AMG GT 53 SUV annonce 597 à 668 km WLTP, tandis que les GT 55 et GT 63 promettent entre 620 et 700 km. En face, le Cayenne S Electric atteint 653 km, le Cayenne Turbo Electric 622 km, et le Cayenne S Coupé Electric, plus aérodynamique, 669 km. Sur le papier, Mercedes annonce le rayon d’action le plus généreux, mais seulement avec la batterie de 128 kWh. Avec celle de 106 kWh, les GT 55 et GT 63 tombent à 525-585 km, sous le Cayenne Turbo Electric.
Prix : encore un peu d’attente
Mercedes décline son SUV en trois versions. Le GT 53 SUV (544 ch, deux moteurs classiques) sera commandable ce mardi 20 octobre, à partir de 113 050 euros (prix allemand). Les GT 55 SUV (816 ch) et GT 63 SUV (1 169 ch), qui ont trois moteurs, n’arriveront qu’au printemps 2027, et leur prix n’est pas encore connu.
Porsche a donc onze mois d’avance. Le constructeur a ouvert les commandes du Cayenne Electric en novembre 2025. En France, la gamme SUV compte trois versions : le Cayenne Electric (408 ch, 107 600 euros), le Cayenne S Electric (544 ch, 129 200 euros) et le Cayenne Turbo Electric (1 156 ch, 167 200 euros).
Mercedes-AMG GT SUV vs Porsche Cayenne Electric
| Caractéristique | Mercedes-AMG GT 53 SUV | Mercedes-AMG GT 55 SUV | Mercedes-AMG GT 63 SUV | Porsche Cayenne Electric | Porsche Cayenne S Electric | Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric | 
| Puissance | 544 ch | 816 ch | 1 169 ch | 442 ch | 666 ch | 1 156 ch | 
| 0 à 100 km/h | 4,2 s | 3,1 s | 2,7 s | 4,8 s | 3,8 s | 2,5 s | 
| Batterie (kWh) | 106 | 106 / 128 | 106 / 128 | 113 | 113 | 113 | 
| Autonomie WLTP (km) | 597-668 | 525-585 / 620-700 | 525-585 / 620-700 | 568-641 | 588-653 | 557-622 | 
| Recharge max (kW) | 600 | 600 / 710 | 600 / 710 | 390 | 390 | 390 | 
| 10-80 % (min) | 11 | 11 / 12 | 11 / 12 | 16 | 16 | 16 | 
| Prix | 113 050 €(Allemagne) | N.C. | N.C. | 107 600 € | 129 200 € | 167 200 € | 
Vainqueur : impossible de départager
Si le Mercedes-AMG GT SUV prend l’avantage sur la recharge, à condition de trouver une borne de plus de 400 kW, et sur l’autonomie maximale, à condition de choisir la batterie de 128 kWh, le Porsche Cayenne Electric reste le plus rapide à puissance comparable.
Les différences entre les deux monstres allemands se jouent véritablement dans un mouchoir de poche. Finalement, ce sera surtout la question du design qui permettra de faire votre choix.
