articles.title: Disney veut récupérer les équipes et la technologie de Character.ai
articles.text:
Character.AI a déposé le bilan le 12 octobre, et Disney propose 20 millions de dollars pour une licence sur sa technologie, en plus d'embaucher la majorité de ses salariés. Le dossier déposé au tribunal montre surtout ce que le contrat laisse de côté : l'application, les modèles et les données des utilisateurs.
Les documents remis au tribunal des faillites du Delaware, repris par Bloomberg et TechCrunch, donne une idée de ce que Disney emporterait. À ce stade, la vente doit encore être validée par un juge et reste ouverte à d'autres offres.
Des salariés et une licence, mais ni l'application ni les données
Nous rapportions récemment que Character.AI avait ouvert une procédure de Chapter 11, c'est-à-dire une restructuration, et que le service restait accessible. Disney y a le statut de "stalking horse". Concrètement, l'entreprise a fait son offre de 20 millions de dollars, dont 7,5 millions déjà versés. Disney fixe alors une base que d'autres acheteurs peuvent battre aux enchères. Pour passer devant lui, un concurrent doit couvrir cette offre, ajouter 700 000 dollars de frais de rupture dus à Disney et proposer au moins 1 million de plus.
L’opération se fait en deux temps. Le 18 septembre, avant la faillite, Character.AI a signé un premier accord avec Disney. Cette dernière s’est engagé à faire une offre d’emploi à au moins 60 salariés, dont le directeur général Karandeep Anand, devenu directeur technique de Disney. La “vaste majorité” des équipes aurait accepté. TechCrunch estime leur rémunération à 60 millions de dollars par an, Bloomberg à 180 millions sur trois ans, avec 30 millions de primes de rétention en plus. Un contrat de transition, signé le même jour, les laisse aider Character.AI à faire tourner la plateforme jusqu’à cinq mois. Si un autre acheteur l’emporte, il pourra proposer un poste à 80% d’entre eux.
Disney obtient une licence perpétuelle, mondiale et non exclusive lui autorisant à utiliser, copier et modifier certaines technologies et certains brevets de Character.AI, sans en devenir propriétaire. Le contrat exclut la marque, le nom de domaine, les applications grand public, les données d'entraînement et les modèles conversationnels finalisés. Il écarte également les données des utilisateurs regroupant informations personnelles, messages saisis et réponses générées. Si aucune offre ne porte sur la plateforme, ou si la vente à Disney n'est pas validée, l'entreprise mettra la clé sous la porte.
Disney ne reprend aucune dette de Character.AI. Selon l'avocat Patrick Collins, cité par Bloomberg, cette protection ne couvre que les responsabilités antérieures à la clôture de la vente. Des procureurs généraux d'États demandent à tout acquéreur de la plateforme une vérification d'âge et des garde-fous pour les mineurs. En janvier, nous apprenions que Google et Character.AI avaient conclu un accord amiable avec plusieurs familles, dont celle de Sewell Setzer III, 14 ans. Les enquêtes des autorités restent ouvertes. Les offres concurrentes sont attendues le 20 novembre. Si elles arrivent, l'enchère aura lieu le 23, et le juge examinera la vente le 24.
Source : Techcrunch, Bloomberg

articles.title: Stockholm’s Vessla exits stealth with €2.94 million to bring AI agents to property management | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Vessla, a Stockholm-based AI startup building an agentic operating system for real estate, has emerged from stealth with €2.94 million ($3.3 million) pre-Seed funding.
The funding round was more than 2× oversubscribed and was led by Seedcamp. Other investors joining the round include Inception Fund, Tiny VC, operators from Lovable and OpenAI, founders Lukas Saari of Tandem Health and Fredrik Hjelm of Voi and Pit, alongside a number of angel investors.
“Property operations combine recurring work with complex processes and exceptions that require judgment. Vessla is building for both. The Vessla team has expertise in developing bleeding edge AI applications, and their experience from deploying those in high-stakes enterprise settings play a big role in why they are seeing such interest from leading players in the industry in such a short time,” said Felix Martinez, Partner at Seedcamp.
Founded earlier this year, Vessla is trying to solve a familiar but persistent problem facing property management: information is scattered across multiple systems, and connecting them falls on people. It says a single maintenance request can require checking property records, contacting a supplier, updating a work order, and following up on an invoice, each step carried out in a different system,
To solve this dependence on discrete systems, Vessla layers its AI agents across those existing systems, equipping them with the relevant context and operating rules to carry out tasks reliably. However, it also ensures that decisions that require human judgement are handled by people responsible for making them.
In addition to AI agents, the startup is building an operating system that spans entire property portfolios, connecting leasing, building operations, and investment planning. Vessla says property teams set priorities and retain decision-making authority, while agents identify opportunities to grow rental income, reduce operating costs, and help coordinate and execute work across the portfolio.
“We believe AI will fundamentally change how property companies operate, from maintenance and costs to leasing and rental income. The hard part is making it work at scale across the systems and processes those companies already rely on. That is what we are building. As AI takes on more of the execution, people’s judgment, relationships and responsibility become even more important,” said Orman Gazvini, CEO of Vessla.
The founding team of the startup has a deep and varied expertise in building and deploying autonomous AI systems in demanding enterprise environments. Gazvini previously advised major software companies at McKinsey and worked on strategy and M&A at Pophouse.
Kasper Janehag, CTO of Vessla, began his career in the space industry and contributed to NASA’s Mars 2020 mission, before leading enterprise-scale AI transformations at QuantumBlack, McKinsey’s AI division. Chief scientist Arash Dabiri brings hands-on experience building and evaluating agentic AI applications from Andon Labs and QuantumBlack. The broader team also brings experience from Legora, Stanford, and Netlight.
“AI can look impressive in a demo. The real test is whether it can handle the messy, consequential work of a complex business. That requires deep integrations with vast amounts of context, rigorous evaluation and clear limits on what agents can do. We are building Vessla to meet that standard across entire property portfolios,” said Janehag.
The company is already working with some of the largest commercial and residential property owners and operators in the Nordics. While it didn’t specify how it plans to use the funding, since it is coming out of stealth, the funding will likely be used to scale its solution.

articles.title: Anthropic Acquires Confidential AI Startup Opaque Systems
articles.text:
Anthropic has acquired Opaque Systems, a company that developed technology for using sensitive data in AI systems while keeping it protected by the underlying hardware.
Opaque announced the deal last week, saying its team is joining Anthropic. Financial terms were not disclosed.
Opaque started as a research project at UC Berkeley’s RISELab a decade ago. Its founders include Ion Stoica, co-founder of Databricks and Anyscale, and Raluca Ada Popa, an encryption and systems security researcher who now works at Google DeepMind. Aaron Fulkerson joined as CEO in October 2023.
The company turned its confidential computing research into technology used in production AI deployments. Over time, it broadened that work beyond protecting data and models.
“As AI evolved, so did the problem we set out to solve. Protecting data and models was no longer enough. Organizations also needed a way to independently verify how AI systems and agents behaved,” Opaque said.
“That led us to expand our work from confidential AI to verifiable AI: replacing trust assumptions with cryptographic evidence of what ran, where it ran, and under what policies,” the company added.
Opaque also worked with the wider community on open projects that address trust and security for AI agents and models. These include the Agent Governance Toolkit, TRACE, Confidential MCP and Weight Custody Manifest.
Opaque this year raised a $24 million Series B round at a $300 million valuation. The company listed Anthropic among its customers, alongside ServiceNow and Accenture.
Opaque’s website now states that its team “is joining Anthropic to carry our work forward, and Opaque Systems is winding down its operations.”
The company has not said what the wind-down means for its existing customers.

articles.title: Ces box Orange et SFR peuvent se faire pirater à distance grâce à une faille Wi-Fi
articles.text:
La faille a été découverte par Quentin Kaiser, un chercheur belge spécialisé dans la cybersécurité. Présentée à la conférence Hexacon de Paris, la vulnérabilité se trouve dans une vieille version du WPS de Broadcom, un fabricant dont les puces sont présentes dans de nombreuses box. Il s’agit de la fonction qui permet de connecter un appareil au Wi-Fi sans taper le mot de passe.
 just confirmed the presence of Broadcom’s vulnerable wps_monitor in ZTE F680 v4 deployed by MasMovil, ThailandToT, Telkom, Linkstar, Mnc, Viettel, VNPT, EgyptTEData, Ais, MTN, FranceReunicable, RTC, Indosat, MAXCom, EKT, OSP, and Moldtelecom https://t.co/Q5o5dwqQja
— Quentin Kaiser (@qkaiser) October 17, 2026
Le chercheur explique avoir découvert un problème au niveau de la gestion des données échangées lors de la procédure de connexion sans mot de passe. En exploitant la brèche, un pirate peut prendre le contrôle de la box sans en connaître le mot de passe, et même sans être connecté au réseau. Il doit simplement se trouver à la portée du réseau Wi-Fi.
« On peut obtenir un accès complet à un routeur depuis l’autre côté de la rue, sur une proportion importante des box en Belgique, et probablement ailleurs », explique Quentin Kaiser.
Lors de ses démonstrations, le chercheur a récupéré le mot de passe Wi-Fi d’une box belge, puis en a pris le contrôle total en s’appuyant sur la vulnérabilité. Il explique s’être servi de « modèles d’IA de pointe » pour dénicher la faille en moins d’une semaine.
« J’aurais pu mener cette recherche seul, mais cela m’aurait pris des mois », ajoute le chercheur.
À lire aussi : Google corrige 37 nouvelles failles Chrome, l’IA accélère encore la cadence des mises à jour
Un bug vieux de seize ans
La défaillance n’est pas nouvelle. D’après le chercheur, elle se trouve dans le logiciel de Broadcom depuis 2010. L’entreprise a corrigé le tir avec une mise à jour en 2018, mais de nombreux fabricants de box ne l’ont jamais installée. De facto, seize ans après son apparition, la faille est toujours exploitable sur des appareils qui sont toujours en service.
Comme le souligne l’expert, Broadcom a toujours refusé d’attribuer un numéro CVE à la vulnérabilité, c’est-à-dire l’identifiant officiel qui sert à alerter l’ensemble des fabricants d’un problème dans un logiciel. C’est en partie pourquoi les équipements sont restés privés de correctifs pendant plus d’une décennie.
À lire aussi : Des failles de sécurité dans plus de 16.000 Orange Livebox
Quelles box sont concernées en France ?
Pour déterminer le nombre d’appareils encore vulnérables, le chercheur a sillonné Paris et scanné tous les réseaux Wi-Fi environnants. Il s’est ainsi rendu compte que la Livebox 5 d’Orange et les box SFR « Box Plus » étaient toujours vulnérables. Celles-ci n’ont jamais eu droit à un correctif pour la faille de Broadcom. Attention, seules la version Sagemcom Fast5656 de la Livebox 5 et la version NB6VAC de la box de SFR sont vulnérables. A contrario, la Livebox 6 d’Orange et la Bbox Wi-Fi 7 de Bouygues Telecom ont eu droit à une mise à jour. Aucune Freebox n’est visiblement touchée.
Mauvaise nouvelle, ça ne sert à rien de changer son mot de passe Wi-Fi. Le défaut se corrige uniquement par une mise à jour de la box déployée par l’opérateur. On vous conseille donc de laisser votre box installer ses mises à jour automatiquement. Le chercheur y voit surtout un avertissement d’une accumulation de « notre dette technique », qui « finira par nous être réclamée ». Pour l’heure, rien n’indique que la faille a été exploitée par des cybercriminels.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes classic Outlook bug that hid Copilot buttons
articles.text:
Microsoft has fixed a known issue that removed the Copilot Chat and Copilot buttons in the classic Outlook desktop mail client for some Windows users.
As explained in an updated support document, affected users with the Copilot Chat (Basic) license or a Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium) account no longer saw Copilot buttons in the side navigation and above the ribbon.
Those impacted by this experienced one or more of the following issues:
- The Copilot button missing from the top-right area above the ribbon.
- The Copilot icon missing from the left app bar or More Apps area in classic Outlook.
- In Add Apps, Copilot may appear as an available app, but selecting Open does nothing.
- Adding Copilot through ribbon customization may show the command as unavailable or grayed out.
- Copilot remains available from other entry points, such as Outlook on the web or the Microsoft Copilot standalone app or web experience.
Microsoft first announced in June that it had fixed the bug with a service change, but last month it said it had started investigating again after recent updates caused it to resurface.
Now, Microsoft says it has finally resolved this classic Outlook issue, blaming it on a bug that prevented Outlook from retrieving some account information from the user's Outlook profile.
"We fixed an issue in classic Outlook that could cause the Copilot entry point to be missing from the navigation pane when required account information could not be retrieved from the user’s Outlook profile. The Copilot button might be missing for several different reasons, including licensing, Microsoft 365 app configuration, update channel, privacy settings, or other environmental factors," an update to the original support document reads.
"Because the missing button is a symptom that can have multiple underlying causes, we recommend following the guidance in Copilot troubleshooters and How to find and enable missing Copilot button in Microsoft 365 apps to identify and resolve the issue."
Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for those still affected by this known issue, which requires enabling the "Show Apps in Outlook" option in classic Outlook settings by selecting the File tab, then going to Options > Advanced and checking the "Show Apps in Outlook" box under "Outlook panes."
Affected users can also use the new Outlook email client or Outlook Web Access (OWA), which are not affected by this bug, or create a new Outlook profile.
Since the start of the year, Microsoft has also resolved known issues that prevented some classic Outlook users from sending emails via Outlook.com and rendered the classic Outlook client unusable when enabling the Microsoft Teams Meeting Add-in.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

articles.title: Alienware AW3226Q Tandem WOLED 32-Inch Review
articles.text:
The Dell Alienware AW3226Q is the cheapest 4K OLED gaming monitor yet to offer an RGB stripe subpixel layout. This display uses the latest generation of Tandem WOLED technology, including the much sought-after RGB stripe configuration, but costs just $700. That makes it one of the cheapest 4K OLEDs overall, and by far the most affordable way to get this type of WOLED panel.
The AW3226Q uses a variant of the 32-inch 4K panel we recently reviewed in the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM. That Asus model features the flagship version of this 2026 panel, with a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1080p 480Hz dual mode. The Alienware variant reduces the refresh rate to 165Hz at 4K and omits dual mode entirely, but otherwise retains the same core panel technology, including the glossy screen coating.
Now, while the Asus model is being sold at a whopping $1,400, Dell's model costs just half as much at $700. Yes, the refresh rate is reduced, but the overall package is substantially cheaper. In fact, despite offering newer panel technology, the AW3226Q launches at the same price as discounted, previous-generation 165Hz QD-OLED and WOLED monitors, making for an interesting comparison.
Other specs of interest include a DisplayHDR True Black 400 certification, Dolby Vision support, and the usual adaptive sync and variable refresh rate capabilities, in this case branded as both FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync Compatible.
RGB Stripe: Subpixel Layout and Text Clarity
Before getting into the results, here's a quick recap of what this panel offers and why the RGB stripe layout matters.
In 2026, LG Display offers two main variants of Tandem WOLED technology. One retains the white subpixel, which has been the standard configuration for LG panels for years, resulting in an RGWB subpixel layout. The other uses a pure RGB stripe, a new configuration for 2026 that matches the traditional subpixel arrangement used by LCD panels, delivering similarly excellent text clarity.
Despite omitting the white subpixel in the RGB version, both are still WOLED panels, as the W in WOLED refers to the underlying white-light emission technology, not the presence of a white subpixel.
The main benefits of RGB stripe include full compatibility with subpixel font rendering, resulting in the best text clarity you can currently get from an OLED display, and much higher color brightness than RGWB panels. There's also significantly reduced gray banding, leading to better overall screen uniformity.
However, as with most things, there are trade-offs. Removing the white subpixel leads to lower peak white brightness than RGWB panels in both SDR and HDR content, as we'll explore later in this review. It also results in worse efficiency in certain situations. Which option is better ultimately depends on your priorities, and that's why LG Display offers both variants.
One of the biggest selling points of RGB stripe is text quality, and text certainly looks excellent on the AW3226Q. That's thanks to a combination of the RGB stripe layout and glossy screen coating. The latter eliminates the slight haze associated with matte surfaces, improving the perceived sharpness of fine details like text. Compared to a typical IPS LCD, most of which use matte coatings, the AW3226Q actually looks better when displaying text.
However, we're talking about a relatively high pixel density here at 140 PPI. While RGB stripe is the best subpixel layout for text clarity, it doesn't have a huge advantage over other OLED layouts, such as triangular RGB on QD-OLEDs or RGWB on conventional WOLEDs.
The high pixel density tends to mask the artifacts associated with these other layouts, so unless you're particularly sensitive to issues like color fringing, there's a good chance you won't notice much difference between an RGB stripe WOLED and a QD-OLED.
Screen Coating: It's Glossy
The AW3226Q uses the same type of glossy screen coating we've seen on other glossy WOLED monitors. Dell doesn't have a specific brand name for this coating, unlike Asus with its "TrueBlack Glossy" branding, but the results are essentially the same.
The screen maintains excellent black levels across a variety of environments, including brighter rooms, without the purple tint or raised blacks associated with QD-OLED panels. This is a key advantage of glossy WOLED over glossy QD-OLED: WOLED panels like this maintain meaningfully deeper blacks under moderate ambient lighting.
The trade-off is reflectivity. Glossy WOLED has a more pronounced mirror-like finish and is more likely to reflect your surroundings than QD-OLED. Which option works best depends heavily on your setup. If lights or sunlight from a window hit the display directly, those reflections will be more noticeable on WOLED, so avoiding direct light sources is particularly important.
HDR Performance and Configurations
As with other RGB stripe WOLEDs we've tested, HDR performance is one of the more interesting aspects of this display. All the fundamentals are here: perfect black levels, per-pixel lighting control, and effectively infinite contrast. OLED can display bright pixels directly alongside dark ones without blooming or zone bleed, making it an excellent technology for HDR.
However, unlike previous WOLEDs with a white subpixel, the new RGB stripe models perform quite similarly to QD-OLEDs in HDR, for better and sometimes for worse. This extends to the HDR configurations, with the AW3226Q offering three main modes similar to those found on QD-OLED monitors. Dell provides several additional options, but we'll focus on the best configurations.
The first is DisplayHDR True Black, which offers broadly accurate EOTF tracking in both bright and dark content. In other words, the screen generally delivers the brightness levels requested by HDR content. However, peak brightness is limited to just 400 nits, a significant trade-off. We also observed some panel dimming in bright scenes, though it wasn't huge.
The second option is HDR Peak 1000, which behaves similarly to the peak brightness modes found on QD-OLED monitors. It unlocks the panel's full brightness potential, reaching up to 1,000 nits for small highlights while maintaining good accuracy in dark scenes.
The downside is panel dimming in bright scenes. When the display encounters content with a high average brightness level, it can reduce the brightness of every pixel by roughly half. This makes bright scenes look noticeably dimmer than intended, reducing the impact HDR should deliver in these situations.
The third option is HDR Peak 1000 Bright, which attempts to correct this behavior by boosting brightness in brighter scenes for more accurate EOTF tracking. Unfortunately, it also raises the brightness of dark content, making those scenes considerably brighter and less accurate than they should be. Like the regular Peak 1000 mode, it retains access to 1,000 nits of peak brightness.
There are positives and negatives to Dell's approach. Having all three configurations gives users plenty of choice over how HDR content looks, but there's no single mode that delivers accurate performance in both bright and dark scenes. Bright content generally looks best in True Black or Peak 1000 Bright, while darker scenes are better served by the regular Peak 1000 mode. This isn't entirely Dell's fault. Panel limitations force manufacturers to make these compromises, and we've seen similar behavior across many QD-OLED and RGB stripe WOLED monitors.
There are a few other details worth mentioning. By default, Dell uses display-side tone mapping to provide a gradual brightness roll-off when HDR content exceeds the panel's capabilities. The roll-off varies depending on the peak brightness metadata sent to the display and generally does a decent job of preventing highlight clipping. However, it can also limit brightness in certain situations.
Compared to other HDR monitors, both Peak 1000 and True Black deliver decent accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs better than the PG32UCWM, which only offers a boosted brightness configuration, and ends up similar to QD-OLEDs like the MSI 321UPX.
In bright scenes, True Black is somewhat underwhelming compared to the equivalent HDR mode on the Gigabyte MO32U24. Meanwhile, Peak 1000 suffers from significant inaccuracies caused by panel dimming, though its behavior is comparable to other OLED monitors with similar limitations.
Color accuracy is decent without being exceptional. Performance is comparable to the AW3926QW, while color space coverage reaches a respectable 78% of Rec. 2020. That's slightly higher than the PG32UCWM and in the same ballpark as 32-inch 4K QD-OLED monitors. Color volume is also higher than on the Asus model and comes very close to QD-OLED, though it still trails slightly. This is one area where RGB stripe WOLED has a significant advantage over previous-generation WOLED panels.
HDR Brightness
Starting with synthetic HDR brightness tests, the AW3226Q reaches 260 nits at full screen, matching first-generation QD-OLED panels and previous-generation WOLEDs.
That's 13% brighter than the PG32UCWM, although it falls short of the AW3926QW, which currently delivers the highest full-screen brightness we've measured from an RGB stripe WOLED. There's also a gap to the latest 2026 QD-OLED panels, such as the Gigabyte MO32U24 and Asus PG32UCDM3, which reach 300 nits or more, around 15% brighter than the Alienware.
Brightness at a 10% window was disappointing on our unit, reaching just 430 nits. That's 16% below the PG32UCWM when comparing peak modes, and also behind previous-generation QD-OLEDs.
Performance recovers with a 2% window, where the AW3226Q manages to exceed 1,000 nits, similar to current QD-OLED offerings. However, WOLEDs with a white subpixel, such as the XG32UCWMG, can achieve higher brightness in this test. Dell's 39-inch AW3926QW ultrawide also gets brighter despite using largely similar technology.
Moving to real-scene brightness, the AW3226Q struggles in its True Black configuration. We recorded an average of just 291 nits, which is 23% behind the 2024-generation QD-OLED panel used in the MSI 322URX in its True Black mode. It's also more than 30% behind the newer 2026 panel found in the MO32U24 using its HDR mode. It's difficult to recommend True Black on the Alienware because it simply isn't very bright, rarely reaching 400 nits in our tests.
Peak 1000 is better, but still somewhat underwhelming. Compared directly with the RGB stripe WOLED panel in the PG32UCWM, the Asus was 8% brighter on average. However, the Asus uses a boosted brightness configuration that avoids panel dimming at the expense of accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs much better in that regard.
A typical 32-inch 4K QD-OLED from 2024, such as the MSI 321UPX, is also 13% brighter on average when comparing peak modes. Both panels exhibit similar brightness behavior across individual tests, but the QD-OLED generally comes out ahead.
The reality is that this RGB stripe WOLED panel isn't especially bright in HDR and suffers from many of the same weaknesses as QD-OLED. It's certainly not unusable, reaching over 850 nits in real-world scenes and up to 1,000 nits in smaller highlights, but peak brightness is clearly not one of its strengths.
Dolby Vision
The AW3226Q also supports Dolby Vision, which is enabled by default but can be disabled through the OSD. There are no additional configuration options, and brightness is limited to around 450 nits, similar to the True Black HDR mode. When connected to a Windows PC, the monitor generally operates in Dolby Vision mode, switching to HDR10 when compatible content is detected. This involves a brief black screen as the display changes modes.
For the most part, this works reasonably well. The monitor correctly switches to HDR10 in many games, allowing users to take advantage of brighter configurations such as Peak 1000. However, HDR10 detection isn't always reliable, and the display sometimes remains in Dolby Vision mode. We encountered this behavior when watching HDR YouTube videos in Chrome, for example.
For Windows users, we'd generally recommend leaving Dolby Vision disabled. Very few PC games support it, and none have been released recently. Some streaming services may use Dolby Vision, but for gaming, sticking with HDR10 avoids unnecessary mode switching.
Dolby Vision becomes more useful when connecting other devices. Many media players support Dolby Vision playback through streaming apps, while the Xbox Series X also supports Dolby Vision gaming. Even then, the limited brightness of Dell's Dolby Vision implementation means HDR10 may sometimes be the better option.
Motion Performance
Motion performance is one of the key differences between this 165Hz OLED and most competing models, which offer 240Hz refresh rates. An important consideration when buying an OLED, especially one with a lower refresh rate, is that motion clarity is directly tied to refresh rate.
At the same refresh rate, two OLED monitors will look virtually identical in motion clarity, so the refresh rate you'll actually use matters more than the monitor's maximum capability. For example, a 240Hz OLED and a 165Hz OLED running a game at 120 FPS with a 120Hz refresh rate will deliver essentially the same experience.
Higher refresh rate OLEDs become beneficial when you can take advantage of their additional headroom. Running at 240Hz produces a clearer image than at 165Hz, with better smoothness and responsiveness. However, if you play most games below 165 FPS, the benefits of a 240Hz model will be relatively small.
This raises the question of how much you're sacrificing by choosing a cheaper 165Hz model. In our opinion, higher refresh rate variants are best suited to multiplayer gaming. If you play a lot of fast-paced competitive titles where motion clarity and low input latency are priorities, 240Hz is the better choice. For story-driven games, 165Hz is often more than sufficient for an excellent experience.
However, 165Hz monitors have less headroom for future GPU upgrades and frame generation. With frame generation enabled, you generally want to stay within the monitor's refresh rate ceiling to avoid tearing. On a 165Hz display using 2x frame generation, the maximum base rendering rate before exceeding that ceiling is approximately 82 FPS. In other words, even with frame generation, you're limited to the input latency characteristics of a game running at around 80 FPS, plus any additional frame generation overhead.
On a 240Hz display, that base rendering rate increases to 120 FPS, which provides a more responsive experience. This is a potential limitation of 165Hz displays, even for single-player gaming.
Input lag is as expected, with a processing delay below 1ms. Our latency measurements combine processing delay and refresh lag to provide a useful indication of overall responsiveness.
The fastest 240Hz OLEDs lead the charts, while 144Hz and 165Hz models generally sit further down due to their lower refresh rates. That's ultimately the main difference between the AW3226Q and faster OLED alternatives: the lower refresh rate results in somewhat higher latency.
SDR Performance
The AW3226Q performs quite well out of the box in SDR grayscale testing. An average Delta E of around 5 is better than usual, with very good color temperature and reasonable gamma tracking. However, like many wide-gamut monitors, it doesn't enable sRGB emulation by default, so colors appear oversaturated out of the box.
Default Color Performance
There are two ways to achieve more accurate SDR colors: the dedicated sRGB mode in the OSD or Windows Auto Color Management (ACM). The latter produces reasonably accurate results, but Dell's built-in sRGB mode is even better, although it locks several settings and offers limited customization.
Default ACM Color Performance
Despite those restrictions, the sRGB mode is outstanding. Grayscale calibration is nearly perfect across the board, while saturation performance is excellent, with fantastic adherence to the Rec. 709 color space.
sRGB Mode Color Performance
A ColorChecker Delta E ITP average of just 1.53 is the sort of performance we typically see after a full manual calibration, making additional calibration unnecessary for most users.
Compared to other monitors we've tested, the AW3226Q ranks among the very best for sRGB accuracy. A handful of models deliver similarly impressive results, but that ColorChecker score is particularly exceptional. Across 202 sRGB modes we've tested over the years, the AW3226Q ranks third overall, with Dell monitors occupying all three top spots.
SDR brightness is largely as expected given the full-screen HDR results. The AW3226Q reaches 254 nits with a full-screen white image, putting it on par with 2024-generation QD-OLED panels. Most OLEDs fall within this range, with only the latest models, such as 2026 QD-OLEDs, pushing into the 300-nit territory. We still consider 250 nits sufficient for most users. Minimum brightness is also very good, and Dell uses a uniform brightness configuration in SDR mode.
Uniformity
Uniformity is an interesting aspect of the AW3226Q. Thanks to the new RGB stripe Tandem WOLED design, gray uniformity has improved significantly compared to previous WOLED panels, something further helped by the lower 165Hz refresh rate.
There's minimal dirty screen effect when viewing dark grays and virtually no dark gray banding. This makes the AW3226Q a better option for productivity work, particularly in applications with gray backgrounds, than previous WOLED displays.
However, the panel isn't without uniformity issues. In its settled state, the edges are dimmer than the center, creating a mild vignette effect that we don't typically see on QD-OLEDs or even other WOLED panels. This is reflected in the higher Delta E measurements around the edges. The PG32UCWM exhibited similar behavior to some degree, although it's more noticeable on our Alienware unit. By comparison, QD-OLED panels typically deliver better edge-to-edge uniformity.
This issue is further exacerbated by dynamic edge dimming through a system called CPC, or Convex Power Control. CPC dims the edges of the screen during dynamic content, including gaming, making the vignette effect more pronounced than our static uniformity measurements suggest. The effect can be difficult to spot while gaming, as the constantly changing imagery tends to hide uniformity problems. We also didn't notice any saturation issues around the edges of this display.
CPC is an OLED care feature designed to reduce the risk of burn-in, but unfortunately, Dell provides no option to disable it. In fact, the AW3226Q offers no user control over its OLED care settings. On several competing monitors from brands like Asus and MSI, users can adjust these features, including disabling edge dimming to restore better panel uniformity. With the Alienware, you're stuck with Dell's default configuration.
Finally, full-screen white power consumption came in at 94 watts, similar to QD-OLED alternatives and 6 watts lower than the PG32UCWM. However, removing the white subpixel makes the AW3226Q less efficient than the previous-generation RGWB WOLED panel used in the XG32UCWG. Gaming power consumption is considerably lower, averaging a very manageable 42 watts in our test.
Ports, Features and Design
The AW3226Q comes with a standard selection of ports, including one DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, two HDMI 2.1 ports supporting the full 48 Gbps bandwidth with DSC, and a three-port USB 5 Gbps hub.
The USB hub is quite convenient, with one Type-A port on the back, another Type-A on the bottom edge, and a USB-C port alongside it. The USB-C connection supports data and 15W power delivery, but not DisplayPort Alt Mode.
All display inputs support the full 4K 165Hz at 10-bit through DSC. One of the HDMI ports also supports eARC, which could be useful in certain setups. There's a 3.5mm audio jack, but no built-in speakers.
Dell has included several features in the OSD, controlled through a directional toggle on the rear of the display. These include multiple picture presets and color controls, a dark stabilizer, picture-in-picture mode, and RGB lighting controls. Most gaming-specific features are grouped under AlienVision, which allows you to display crosshairs and apply color filters to selected areas of the screen.
Unfortunately, Dell offers virtually no control over its OLED care features. Dell has implemented the usual protections, including pixel shifting and automatic dimming in certain situations, but these features are always enabled and cannot be adjusted or disabled. On the positive side, Dell continues to offer a three-year warranty covering burn-in.
As for the design, the AW3226Q follows Alienware's recent aesthetic, although this model has a darker, almost black finish rather than the dark blue used on earlier versions. It's a relatively minimalist design that isn't overly "gamery," and I think it looks great. Build quality and surface finishes are also good, despite most of the exterior being plastic.
The Alienware logo on the rear features some RGB lighting, although it's fairly subtle on this model. Ergonomics are good, with height, tilt, and swivel adjustments, along with a compact, squarish base that doesn't occupy much desk space and still allows you to place items on top of it.
The front looks excellent, with uniform bezels and that attractive glossy finish. I also love that Dell has abandoned the curve here. The AW3226Q uses a standard flat panel, unlike the original 32-inch QD-OLED AW3225QF, which featured a curved display.
A Great OLED Faces Tough Competition
Overall, the Dell Alienware AW3226Q is a bit of a mixed bag. There are certainly aspects of this monitor that I really like, but whether we'd recommend buying it depends on a few factors. The 32-inch 4K OLED market is extremely competitive, especially on pricing, making it difficult for the AW3226Q to stand out even at its $700 MSRP.
Let's start with the good stuff. This monitor gives you a brand-new RGB stripe WOLED panel with an excellent glossy finish for half the price of the Asus PG32UCWM we recently reviewed. The main sacrifice is refresh rate, dropping from 240Hz to 165Hz, along with the removal of dual mode support. Otherwise, performance is very similar, making Dell's offering a much more affordable way to access this panel technology.
And there are good reasons to go for an RGB stripe WOLED. Performance is quite similar to QD-OLED, including excellent color brightness and good gray uniformity, but it also addresses some of QD-OLED's weaknesses.
While color fringing isn't a major issue on 32-inch 4K QD-OLEDs, the RGB stripe layout eliminates it thanks to a subpixel arrangement better suited to text rendering. The glossy coating is another significant advantage, delivering deeper blacks across more lighting conditions without the reddish-purple tint associated with QD-OLED.
Dell has also done an excellent job in a few areas. The sRGB mode is outstanding, with near-perfect SDR calibration. We also appreciate having all three main HDR configurations available. Dolby Vision and HDMI eARC are welcome additions that aren't available on every competitor.
As for downsides, HDR brightness in particular is somewhat disappointing. Panel dimming in bright HDR scenes used to be something you could avoid by choosing WOLED over QD-OLED, but the new RGB stripe WOLED panels exhibit similar behavior.
Between panel dimming and the limitations of this new RGB stripe design, the AW3226Q is actually less bright in HDR scenes than first-generation 32-inch 4K QD-OLED panels released more than two years ago.
So, should you buy the AW3226Q?
The first comparison worth making is against similarly priced 165Hz QD-OLED monitors using the original 2024 panel design. Models like the Asus XG32UCDS can typically be found for around $700, exactly the same price as the Alienware. So at price parity, the Alienware AW3226Q is the better buy. Panel performance is similar except for slightly lower HDR brightness. However, the Tandem WOLED panel has superior screen coating, which avoids the raised black issue, and its RGB stripe layout, which is better suited to text rendering.
What holds us back from giving the AW3226Q a broader recommendation is that 4K 240Hz OLED monitors aren't much more expensive, and sometimes cost exactly the same. In recent weeks, 32-inch 4K 240Hz QD-OLEDs have regularly been available for around $750, with recent sales bringing models like the MSI 321UPX down to $700.
That puts the AW3226Q in a more difficult position. For the same $700, or perhaps a $50 premium, you can get a 240Hz QD-OLED with broadly similar panel performance. Instead of comparing two OLED technologies at the same price and refresh rate, you're now weighing the advantages of RGB stripe WOLED against a substantially higher refresh rate. Do you prioritize the better motion clarity, responsiveness, and headroom of a 240Hz monitor, or the superior screen coating and text clarity of the AW3226Q?
It's a tough choice. If you really dislike the raised blacks and reddish-purple tint of QD-OLED, this Tandem WOLED is a better fit. But for most gamers, we would pick the 240Hz option.
Of course, pricing varies by region and it's also worth noting that we're comparing discounted prices for QD-OLED monitors that have been on the market for months against the launch MSRP of a brand-new product. Dell could easily make the AW3226Q a more compelling option with a price adjustment. At $700, it's a good monitor facing some very strong competition. At a lower price, it could become a much easier recommendation.

articles.title: Aujourd'hui, la France décolle pour Mars : le rover Idefix va rouler sur une lune où vous pèseriez 40 grammes
articles.text:
Aujourd'hui, la France décolle pour Mars : le rover Idefix va rouler sur une lune où vous pèseriez 40 grammes
Va-t-on enfin savoir comment Mars a obtenu ses minuscules lunes ? Idéfix, le rover français décollera le 19 octobre à bord de MMX, la mission japonaise. Le petit véhicule va devoir apprivoiser une gravité totalement folle pour aider à collecter des échantillons et les ramener sur Terre.
C'est l'un des décollages les plus attendus de l'année pour une mission extrêmement ambitieuse. Et la France y prend part très activement. Le 19 octobre prochain, la mission internationale MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) doit s'envoler avec comme objectif de percer enfin les mystères des deux lunes de Mars, Phobos et Deimos.
Portée par la JAXA (Japon) aux côtés du CNES, du DLR, de la NASA et de l'ESA, la mission embarque une armada d'instruments de précision et un petit rover éclaireur prénommé Idefix. Décryptage d'un défi d'ingénierie hors norme.
D'où viennent les deux petites lunes martiennes ?
En ligne de mire scientifique : trancher un débat vieux de plusieurs décennies. Phobos et Deimos sont-elles de simples astéroïdes capturés par la gravité martienne ou sont-elles nées des débris projetés lors d'un choc titanesque subi par Mars dans sa jeunesse ?
La mission MMX décollera à bord du nouveau lanceur lourd japonais H3, récemment certifié après des débuts chaotiques et quelques explosions. Les récents tirs ont été des succès rassurants (voir en fin d'article).
Le piège orbital : impossible de tourner autour de Phobos
Naviguer autour de Phobos relève du casse-tête de mécanique spatiale.
Il est techniquement impossible de placer une sonde en orbite classique autour d'une si petite lune (24 km pour Phobos et 12 pour Déimos). Sa masse minime génère un champ de pesanteur balayé par la gravité de Mars, distante de seulement 6 000 km. La zone d'attraction de Phobos ne dépasse pas quelques centaines de mètres.
Pour stationner à ses côtés pendant trois ans, les pilotes vont exploiter des orbites quasi-satellitaires (QSO). La sonde MMX tournera physiquement autour de Mars, mais calera au millimètre près sa vitesse pour “escorter” Phobos pas à pas.
Idefix : 25 kg sur Terre, 15 grammes sur Phobos
Avant que le vaisseau principal ne touche le sol, MMX va larguer Idefix, un rover de 25 kg développé par le CNES et le DLR. Pourquoi lui avoir donné le nom du petit chien téméraire d'Obélix ? La raison la plus évidente tient à une filiation avec Astérix, le premier satellite tricolore, lancé en 1965, faisant de la France la troisième nation spatiale de l'histoire.
Sur Phobos, la gravité est environ 2 000 fois plus faible que sur Terre. Les calculs sont saisissants :
- Un adulte de 75 kg sur Terre n'y pèserait que 40 grammes.
- Le rover Idefix de 25 kg sera quant à lui attiré vers le sol de Phobos comme s'il ne pesait que 15 grammes.
La moindre impulsion risquant de l'expulser dans l'espace, Idefix avancera à une vitesse d'escargot : entre 1 et 3 cm par seconde. S'il se retourne au largage ? Ses quatre jambes motorisées lui permettent de se redresser en autonomie.
Le souvenir de Rosetta et Philae
Ce scénario rappelle la mission Rosetta en 2014, où l'atterrisseur Philae avait rebondi à la surface de la comète 67P à cause d'une microgravité mal anticipée.
Idefix sert de crash-testeur pour évaluer la consistance du sol avant l'atterrissage du module principal. Mais MMX va plus loin : au lieu d'analyser les échantillons sur place, la sonde rapportera au moins 10 grammes de poussière sur Terre à l'horizon 2031. Une première.
Les instruments embarqués
Pour accomplir sa mission, le duo sonde-rover intègre le haut du panier de la technologie spatiale avec 12 instruments parmi lesquels :
Sur la sonde mère :
- MIRS : spectromètre infrarouge (CNES/Observatoire de Paris) pour analyser la composition minérale et traquer l'eau.
- MEGANE : spectromètre gamma et neutrons (NASA).
- TENGOO & OROCHI : caméras téléobjectif et grand-angle haute résolution.
- LIDAR & SAMPLER : altimètre laser et système de prélèvement de sol.
Sur le rover Idefix :
- RAX : spectromètre Raman pour l'étude cristalline des roches.
- miniRAD : radiomètre thermique.
- NavCAM & WheelCAM : caméras de navigation et optiques braquées sur les roues pour observer l'interaction mécanique avec le régolithe.
Souhaitons toute la réussite possible à cette très belle mission, qui, en cas de succès, nous réservera très certainement de superbes découvertes scientifiques.

articles.title: Salários em tecnologia se aproximam dos R$ 40 mil; veja principais cargos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Salários em tecnologia se aproximam dos R$ 40 mil; veja principais cargos
Guia Salarial 2027 da Michael Page mostra que IA é diferencial no mercado de tecnologia, mas não significa maior salário.
O Guia Salarial 2027 da Michael Page aponta um forte crescimento da inteligência artificial no mercado de tecnologia, com 33% das empresas destacando o domínio de ferramentas do tipo como um diferencial no próximo ano. Mas em termos salariais, a área não tem profissionais de IA no topo: enquanto especialistas na ferramenta têm ganhos de R$ 14 a 20 mil, gerentes recebem até R$ 37 mil em grandes empresas.
As maiores remunerações seguem com profissionais em engenharia de dados, que podem chegar a R$ 42 mil mensais. Outras áreas mais tradicionais, como ciência de dados, engenharia de software e segurança da informação, já batem os R$ 40 mil. Isso mostra que, apesar do maior espaço para IA na indústria, as áreas mais valorizadas do setor seguem sendo aquelas mais especializadas.
Além disso, a pesquisa também aponta a flexibilidade como predominante no setor, com 51% apostando no trabalho híbrido. O Tecnoblog teve acesso exclusivo ao recorte de tecnologia do levantamento, que foi realizado em 1.955 empresas, considerando 15 setores diferentes e mais de 400 cargos. Ao todo, 5.762 profissionais foram entrevistados.
O principal destaque do Guia Salarial da Michael Page é o avanço da IA no mercado de tecnologia. Aparecendo entre áreas tradicionais como ciência de dados e engenharia de software, por exemplo, especialistas e gerentes de IA ganham relevância em 2027.
De acordo com a pesquisa, 36% das empresas de tecnologia destacam a importância de conhecimentos em inteligência artificial nos próximos 12 meses como diferencial na hora de contratar. Por aqui, 40% do mercado também oferece acesso amplo a modelos de IA, enquanto quase metade (49%) afirma ter a tecnologia como uma das prioridades.
Veja a seguir a relação de cargos levados em conta no levantamento da Michael Page para o mercado de tecnologia em 2027:
| Cargo | Menor salário | Maior salário | 
|---|---|---|
| Gerente de engenharia de dados | R$ 28 mil | R$ 42 mil | 
| Gerente de ciência de dados | R$ 28 mil | R$ 42 mil | 
| Gerente de segurança da informação | R$ 28 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de TI/Business Partner de TI | R$ 30 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de engenharia de software | R$ 25 mil | R$ 40 mil | 
| Gerente de infraestrutura | R$ 23 mil | R$ 38 mil | 
| Gerente de IA | R$ 22 mil | R$ 37 mil | 
| Especialista de TI/Business Partner de TI | R$ 20 mil | R$ 35 mil | 
| Especialista de cloud | R$ 22 mil | R$ 30 mil | 
| Especialista em ciência de dados | R$ 18 mil | R$ 28 mil | 
| Especialista em IA | R$ 14 mil | R$ 20 mil | 
A pesquisa é categórica: apesar do aumento do espaço no setor, profissionais de IA não têm necessariamente os maiores salários. Segundo Lucas Oggiam, diretor executivo da Michael Page Brasil, “ter uma habilidade muito procurada e consequentemente mais valorizada ajuda”, mas o cenário muda ao “ampliar seu escopo” e “responder pelo resultado daquela área”.
Frente a profissionais de engenharia de dados e de software, por exemplo, profissionais de IA seguem atrás em termos de salário, mesmo para cargos de liderança: gerentes das respectivas áreas ganham até R$ 42 e R$ 40 mil, enquanto o teto para quem trabalha diretamente com inteligência artificial é de R$ 37 mil.
Outro dado que reforça a relevância de áreas tradicionais frente ao crescimento da IA é a valorização salarial. A Michael Page enviou ao Tecnoblog um comparativo dos levantamentos feitos em 2025 e 2026 com os números projetados para 2027, destacando o aumento nos ganhos do setor por cargo.
Veja as áreas que mais tiveram valorização salarial no mercado de tecnologia nos últimos dois anos:
| Cargo | 2025 | 2026 | 2027 | Variação | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gerente de qualidade de software | R$ 20 a 25 mil | R$ 22 a 34 mil | R$ 23 a 36 mil | +31% | 
| Gerente de engenharia de software | R$ 24 a 30 mil | R$ 24 a 38 mil | R$ 25 a 40 mil | +21% | 
| Gerente de infraestrutura | R$ 23 a 28 mil | R$ 22 a 36 mil | R$ 23 a 38 mil | +19% | 
| Gerente de ciência de dados | R$ 27 a 38 mil | R$ 27 a 40 mil | R$ 28 a 42 mil | +8% | 
Gerentes de qualidade de software passaram a ganhar 31% a mais em relação a 2025, a maior valorização do mercado de tecnologia, enquanto lideranças de engenharia de software vêm logo atrás, com 21% de valorização. Completam o quadro os gestores de infraestrutura e ciência de dados, com 19% e 8%, respectivamente.
A flexibilização do presencial também foi levada em conta. No mercado de tecnologia, somente 17% das empresas apostam na presença física de seus funcionários, enquanto 28% têm um formato totalmente home office. Ir ao escritório algumas vezes na semana é o mais comum: 51% do mercado opera de forma híbrida. Para os profissionais da área, também pesam fatores como desafio técnico e autonomia.
Se o acesso às novas tecnologias é um diferencial, o tipo de gestão também importa: 63% dos funcionários entrevistados vêem uma liderança “desmotivadora” como motivo para abandonar projetos. Para o diretor executivo Lucas Oggian, a “retenção continua sendo muito humana”. Ainda assim, chama atenção que apenas 3% das empresas do setor veem impacto da liderança na manutenção dos seus funcionários.

articles.title: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
articles.text:
Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. However, at $649 it’s a much more tempting price.
Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
At $649, it’s a much better deal. However, the new, faster M6 version is only $130 more.
The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Given that this sale price makes it just $50 more than the original price instead of $200, it’s a good time to buy if you want to spend as little as possible on a modern Mac desktop.
Aside from some impressive generational leaps in processing power, you aren’t missing out on a ton by skipping the M6 model and opting for the M4. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost.
Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini
More Verge-approved deals
- Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The price hasn’t gone below $1,299.99 before, so it’s a good time to consider an upgrade. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99.
- For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. This seems like a fantastic option for anyone on a budget. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model.
- It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

articles.title: Amazon casse le prix du MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro, une machine surpuissante avec 48 Go de RAM et 1 To de SSD — Frandroid
articles.text:
Si l’iPhone Duo occupe l’actualité d’Apple, un ordinateur portable de la marque retient aussi l’attention aujourd’hui. Le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro est le format XXL du modèle 14 pouces que nous avons testé et noté 10/10. La configuration proposée ici associe 48 Go de mémoire vive à 1 To de stockage. En pleine crise de la RAM, qui fait grimper le prix des machines riches en mémoire, voir ce modèle perdre 560 euros sur Amazon est une bonne nouvelle pour les créatifs et les développeurs.
Pourquoi choisir le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro ?
- Un grand écran Mini-LED de 16 pouces avec ProMotion
- 48 Go de mémoire vive et 1 To de SSD NVMe
- La puce M5 Pro, épaulée par la puce réseau N1
Sur Amazon, le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro en 48 Go et 1 To voit son prix chuter à 3 499 euros en noir sidéral, contre 4 059 euros chez Apple.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Apple MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro (2026). Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un écran Mini-LED qui profite des 16 pouces
Le MacBook Pro 16 M5 Pro de 2026 reprend la recette des anciens modèles. On retrouve le châssis unibody qui a fait ses preuves, toujours aussi classieux, solide et sans fioritures. Ceux qui espéraient un renouvellement esthétique devront encore patienter.
Une fois allumée, la machine dévoile l’un de ses points forts, son écran Mini-LED. Lors de notre test du modèle 14 pouces, son contraste quasi infini, son pic de luminosité (1 600 nits en HDR) et sa précision colorimétrique nous avaient convaincus. Couplé au 120 Hz, c’est l’un des meilleurs écrans du marché, tout simplement.
Sur 16 pouces, la surface de travail gagne en confort pour la retouche ou le montage. Seul bémol, cette encoche disgracieuse qu’Apple ne semble pas vouloir abandonner. Quant au format, il n’a rien d’un ultraportable. Le 14 pouces affiche déjà 1,60 kg sur la balance, et cette version plus grande sera plus encombrante dans un sac avec ses 2,14 kg.
Un M5 Pro taillé pour les gros projets
À l’intérieur de ce MacBook Pro 16 se trouve la fameuse puce M5 Pro, qui embarque 18 cœurs CPU et 20 cœurs GPU. Elle est ici associée à 48 Go de RAM et à un SSD de 1 To.
Cette configuration a de la marge pour les projets lourds en montage vidéo ou en développement. La machine s’adresse avant tout aux professionnels du montage vidéo, de la 3D et de l’IA. Pour un usage bureautique, son prix est difficile à justifier.
Lors de notre test du modèle 14 pouces, sa batterie de 72,4 Wh nous avait déjà impressionnés par son endurance. Sur cette version 16 pouces, Apple fait grimper l’accumulateur à 100 Wh. Malgré le grand écran, Apple annonce jusqu’à 24 heures de streaming vidéo et 17 heures de navigation web, contre 22 et 14 heures pour le 14 pouces M5 Pro. Apple mesure ces chiffres avec une luminosité réduite, donc en usage professionnel, comptez plutôt sur une grosse journée loin d’une prise. Enfin, côté connectique, le MacBook propose trois ports USB-C Thunderbolt 5 (jusqu’à 120 Gbit/s), un port MagSafe 3 pour la charge, mais aussi un port HDMI, un lecteur de carte SDXC et une prise casque 3,5 mm.
Pour en savoir plus, n’hésitez pas à lire notre test du MacBook Pro 14 M5 Pro.
Si vous hésitez encore, découvrez notre guide des meilleurs PC portables du moment afin de comparer ce MacBook Pro à d’autres machines haut de gamme.
